Hence I have no doubt that you, to whom sacred things and persons are matters of daily care, will not disdain these laboured efforts of mine on this subject, such as they are, especially those worked out under your episcopal jurisdiction, under your patronage.

units.la: QVantis animæ humanæ sit in deliciis oculos in anteaſta retorquere, reſque olim geſtas, tanquam præsentes perluſtrare, expendere, contemplari, nemo nescit qui secum habitat, suámque naturam non ignorat. Hoc autem è summis animæ rationalis oblectamentis ne penitus destituti languesceremus, inventa est Divina scribendi ars, quâ quicquid in animo vel sub oculis habemus, certis quibusdam characteribus, variisque linearum figuris aliorum conceptibus repræsentemus. Hujus enim artis ope, cœlitus haud dubie primo dimissæ, patres majoresque nostri pleraque memoratu digna quæ suis temporibus gesta fuerunt, posteritati, nobisque benevoli tradiderunt: usque adeo ut nos etiam, qui extremas mundi colimus ætates, quamplurima eorum quæ multis abhinc annorum centuriis, imò quidem ab ipsa rerum origine peracſta sunt, non minus quàm illi quibus ante oculos obversabantur, pro certis & perspectis habeamus. Verumenimvero nihil propemodum utilitatis, jucunditatis nihil ex antiquis istis commentariis hauriatur, nisi tempus quo gesta fuit, aque ac ipsa res gesta nobis constiterit. Hinc est quod alia atque scribendi ars necesse fuit institueretur, quâ nimirum quæcunque olim Acta describuntur, suis temporibus assignemus. Hæc, hæc igitur est Ars illa perinsignis, perutilis, perneccessaria, quam hoc opusculo paucis explicare molitus sum. Quum enim in Scaligerum, Petavium, aliósque, qui rei Chronologicæ operam dederunt, oculos conjecissem, inclytam hanc Artem ab iis tot intricatis obvolutam.
units.tr: How much delight the human soul takes in turning its eyes back upon past times, and in surveying, weighing and contemplating deeds done long ago as if they were present, no one who lives with himself and knows his own nature is unaware. So that we might not, entirely deprived of this among the highest pleasures of the rational soul, grow utterly languid, the divine art of writing was invented, by which we represent to others, by certain characters and various figures of lines, whatever we have in mind or before our eyes. For by the help of this art, undoubtedly first sent down from heaven, our fathers and forefathers handed down to posterity, and to us, most of the memorable things done in their times, and did so out of goodwill. So much so that we too, who live in the last ages of the world, hold as certain and well known very many things that were done many centuries ago, indeed from the very beginning of things, no less than those who had them before their eyes. But truly almost no usefulness or pleasure can be drawn from these ancient records unless the time in which a deed was done is as clear to us as the deed itself. Hence it was necessary that another art of writing be established, by which, namely, we may assign to their proper times whatever deeds are described in the old records. This, this then, is that most distinguished, most useful and most necessary art, which I have undertaken to explain briefly in this little work. For when I had cast my eyes upon Scaliger, Petavius and others who have devoted their labour to chronology, I saw this famous art wrapped up by them in so many intricacies

units.la: lutam quaestionibus, tot spinosis laceratam controversiis, tot incertis refertam commentis, tam denique nulla, vel obscura saltem methodo traditam animadverti, ut quispiam non sine summa difficultate, maximoq; temporis dispendio, unicam hanc Artem, eamque e facillimis, edisceat. Quapropter me nec actum nugas nec acturum confisus sum, si sacram hanc Artem perplexis omnibus controversiis, tricisque contortis exutam nude proponerem, atque instituerem. Ex hisce itaque principiis coortae sunt Institutiones hae Chronologicae manibus & censurae tuae subjectae. In quibus quidem concinnandis hoc unicum mihi propositum fuit, ut quaecunque temporibus distinguendis necessario requirantur, eaque sola traderem. Et quidem inani spe diu flagravi, si quippiam quod in quovis hucusque edito tractatu Arti Chronologicae prorsus requisitum extat, in hoc tractatulo desideretur: In quo nihilominus multa, eademque scitu dignissima reperies, quae alibi frustra quaeres. Ipse enim in computis plerisque Chronologicis perficiendis alias atque alii methodos instituì, faciliores nimirum & per Arithmetices solius praecepta procedentes. Mecum enim recolens, quot & quantis erratis, iisque non ᾿τπλησιαστικοῖς tantum, sed & ἀνλοξαςικοῖς (ut itä loquar) obnoxiae sunt tabulae Chronologicae, (quod si libitum vel necessarium fuerit, quamplurimis ex iis etiam qui optime de republica Chronologica meruerunt productis exemplis demonstrare poteram) neglectis tabulis, universa postulata Chronologica per Arithmeticae solius regulas soluta dedi. In quibus itaque perlegendis Ciceronem expectes nolim, non enim oratorem ago, sed chronologum: Chronologum (inquam) quem vel non barbarè loqui, est eloquentem esse. Nec quidem in nodis Chronologicis dissolvendis liceat nobis esse tam disertis. Res enim ipsa nonnunquam ab intellectu, tyronum praecipuè, non facilè perspiciatur, quae tamen si dictis phaleratis, bullatis verbis, & selectis oratorum vestiretur elegantiis, magis adhuc tecta, magis involuta redderetur. Quocirca, si modo verba rei, quam sub ma
units.tr: entangled in questions, torn by so many thorny controversies, filled with so many uncertain inventions, and finally handed down by a method that is absent or at least obscure, so that anyone who wishes to learn this single art, which is among the easiest, can do so only with the greatest difficulty and a great loss of time. For this reason I trusted that I would neither be wasting effort on trifles nor be doing so in the future, if I set out and taught this sacred art stripped of all the perplexing controversies and twisted tangles. From these principles the present Chronological Institutes have arisen, and I place them in your hands and under your judgment. In putting them together, my one aim was to deliver whatever is necessarily required for distinguishing times, and only that. I have long nursed the vain hope that if anything absolutely required for the chronological art, found in any treatise published so far, were missing from this little work, it would be missing here. Yet in it you will find many things, and things most worth knowing, which you would seek in vain elsewhere. In carrying out most of the chronological computations myself, I adopted methods different from those of others, namely easier ones that proceed by the precepts of arithmetic alone. For when I reflect on how many and how great errors, not only "ecclesiastical" but also "astronomical" (if I may so put it), chronological tables are liable to, errors which I could demonstrate by very many examples drawn from those who have deserved best of chronological scholarship, I set the tables aside and solved every chronological problem by the rules of arithmetic alone. So in reading these pages you should not expect Cicero, for I am not pleading as an orator but working as a chronologer; a chronologer who does not speak barbarously is, I would say, already eloquent. Nor, in untying chronological knots, may we be so eloquent. For the matter itself is sometimes not easily grasped by the understanding, especially of beginners, and if it were dressed in ornate sayings, bombastic words and the chosen elegances of orators, it would be rendered even more hidden and more obscure. Wherefore, if only the words of the matter, which under my hand

Hujusmodi autem est Chronologia, utpote quæ characteres quosdam efficit quibus tempora præterita à se invicem distinguat, résque olim gestas ac descriptas suis temporibus assignet, ut non ipse tantùm res, sed & ipsa quoque tempora quibus evenerunt, certis indiciis nobis constent.
units.tr: (the knowledge of which is by nature from first principles), that is knowledge [ἡ γνῶσις αὐτῆς φύσει ἀρχαί, ἐπιστήμη]: For when someone believes that a thing is in some way so, and its principles are known to him, then he is said to know, as the same author argues, ibid. Chronology, however, supplies principles of this kind, by which we may attain such knowledge and be made more certain about the times in which events are recorded. For this reason it is not itself a science, but rather a means by which something is known. The definition of art fits Chronology exactly: Art is a certain habit, effective together with true reason [ἡ μὲν γὰρ τέχνη ἕξις μετὰ λόγου ἀληθοῦς ποιητικὴ ἐστιν], Aristotle, ibid. chapter 4. That is, it is a habit by which we produce some effect from certain principles. Chronology is of this kind, since it produces certain marks by which past times are distinguished from one another and assigns the events of former days, once recorded, to their own times, so that not only the events themselves but also the times in which they happened are established for us by certain indications.

units.la: 2. Differentia Chronologiæ sumitur ex objecto & officio.
units.tr: 2. The difference of Chronology is taken from its object and its function.

units.la: Objectum Chronologiæ est Tempora, non Tempus. Chronologus enim unum & singulare tempus non considerat, sed diversa confert, ut hoc ab isto distinguat. Num si ex. gr. Christi natalem examinet, annum & diem quo natus est, ut in se consideratum non inquirit, sed quatenus relationem habet ad tempus præsens, vel ad aliam certam epocham tanquam terminum, ad quem anni diésque à Christi nativitate elapsi numerandi sunt. Adeò ut duo saltem tempora Chronologus perpetuò respicit, ut unius ab altero distantiam exploratam habeat. Unde etiam officium Chronologiæ patet, nimirum diversa hujusmodi tempora à se invicem secernere, ut quantum ab uno ad alium effluxerit, computaret. Ex. gr. Historici tradunt urbem Romam anno tertio Olympiadis sextæ conditam fuisse. Jam Chronologiæ est hunc annum ab aliis quibuscunque tam præteritis quàm suturis distinguere, ut quot annis præteriit æram Christianam, quot Diocletianeam, quot Hegiram, quot præsentem annum, & quibus indiciis distincta hujusmodi temporis intervalla constant. Et sic in aliis.
units.tr: The object of Chronology is times, not time. For the chronologer does not consider one single time, but compares different times in order to distinguish this one from that. For example, if he examines the birth of Christ, he does not inquire into the year and day on which he was born as considered in itself, but insofar as it bears a relation to the present time, or to some other fixed epoch as a terminus, from which the years and days elapsed since Christ's birth are to be counted. Thus the chronologer always has in view at least two times, so that he may know the distance of one from the other. Hence the function of Chronology also becomes clear: namely, to separate such different times from one another, so that he may compute how much time has flowed from one to another. For example, historians report that the city of Rome was founded in the third year of the sixth Olympiad. It is now the task of Chronology to distinguish this year from all other years, whether past or future, so that it may tell how many years have passed since the Christian era, how many since the Diocletian era, how many since the Hegira, and how many since the present year, and by what indications such intervals of time are established. And so on for other cases.

units.la: 3. E prædictis liquet inter Chronologiam aliásque universas tam artes quàm scientias multùm interesse, inter eas etiam quibus incumbit temporis tractatio. Nam nulla est ars, nulla scientia, quæ sub eadem notione tempus contemplatur atque Chronologia. Physica tempus perlustrat, sed ut naturam ejus definiat, non ut partes distinguat. Astronomia tempus dispicit, sed quatenus ad motus cœlestes, non quatenus ad res terrestres respectum habet. Musica etiam tempus pertractat, sed ut longitudine ac brevitate partium incisum, & dispari sonorum interstitio temperatum, non ut historiæ subserviens. Quin & ipsa etiam Historia tempus consideret necesse est, sed istud tantùm describat quo res gestæ sunt, non ut ab aliis temporibus secernat: Adeò ut Historia quodammodo materiem suppeditet Chronologiæ, Chronologia formam det Historiæ; illa res gestas describit, hæc easdem suis temporibus affigit. Sine Historia nulla est Chronologia, sine Chronologia nulla certa Historia. E quibus consequens est, Chronologiam distinctè ab aliis arti fundandæ & constituendæ satis esse idoneam, quippe quæ tempora aliter atque aliæ quævis artes vel scientiæ pertractant. Nam tempora ab historicis tantùm adnotata certis quibusdam indiciis ac characteribus ita distinguit, ut quæcunque ab eis tantùm describuntur, propriis suis temporibus applicentur, II. Partes Chronologiæ duæ sunt μιεικὴ & χαρακτηριsμικὴ. III. Pars μιεικὴ est quæ temporis naturam ac partes explicat. IV. Pars χαρακτηριsμικὴ, quæ de ipsis characteribus agit, sive notis, quibus tempora distinguantur.
units.tr: 3. From what has been said it is clear that Chronology differs greatly from all other arts and sciences, including those that concern the treatment of time. For there is no art or science that contemplates time under the same aspect as Chronology. Physics surveys time, but in order to define its nature, not to distinguish its parts. Astronomy examines time, but insofar as it relates to the heavenly motions, not insofar as it relates to earthly things. Music also treats time, but as divided by the length and shortness of its parts and measured by the unequal intervals of sounds, not as serving history. Indeed History itself must consider time, but it only describes the time in which events took place and does not separate it from other times. Thus History in a way supplies the matter for Chronology, and Chronology gives form to History: the one describes events, the other assigns those same events to their own times. Without History there is no Chronology, and without Chronology no certain History. From this it follows that Chronology is distinct from other arts and is sufficiently fitted to be founded and established as an art, since it treats times differently from any other arts or sciences. For it distinguishes the times noted only by historians by certain fixed indications and characters, so that whatever is described by them is applied to its own proper times.

That is, it is a habit by which we produce some effect from certain principles. Chronology is of this kind, since it produces certain marks by which past times are distinguished from one another and assigns the events of former days, once recorded, to their own times, so that not only the events themselves but also the times in which they happened are established for us by certain indications.

units.la: 2. Differentia Chronologiæ sumitur ex objecto & officio. Objectum Chronologiæ est Tempora, non Tempus. Chronologus enim unum & singulare tempus non consider at, sed diversa confert, ut hoc ab isto distinguat. Num si ex. gr. Christi natalem examinet, annum & diem quo natus est, ut in se consideratum non inquirit, sed quatenus relationem habet ad tempus præsens, vel ad aliam certam epocham tanquam terminum, ad quem anni diésque à Christi nativitate elapsi numerandi sunt. Adeò ut duo saltem tempora Chronologus perpetuò respicit, ut unius ab altero distantiam exploratam habeat. Unde etiam officium Chronologiæ patet, nimirum diversa hujusmodi tempora à se invicem secernere, ut quantum ab uno ad alium effluxerit, computaret. Ex. gr. Historici tradunt urbem Romam anno tertio Olympiadis sextæ conditam fuisse. Jam Chronologiæ est hunc annum ab aliis quibuscunque tam præteritis quam suturis distinguere, ut quot annis præterfit æram Christianam, quot Dioclesianeam, quot Hegiram, quot præsentem annum, & quibus indiciis distincta hujusmodi temporis intervalla constant. Et sic in aliis.
units.tr: 2. The difference of Chronology is taken from its object and function. The object of Chronology is times, not time. For the chronologer does not consider one single time, but compares different times in order to distinguish this one from that. For example, if he examines the birth of Christ, he does not inquire into the year and day on which he was born as considered in itself, but insofar as it bears a relation to the present time, or to some other fixed epoch as a terminus, from which the years and days elapsed since Christ's birth are to be counted. Thus the chronologer always has in view at least two times, so that he may know the distance of one from the other. Hence the function of Chronology also becomes clear: namely, to separate such different times from one another, so that he may compute how much time has flowed from one to another. For example, historians report that the city of Rome was founded in the third year of the sixth Olympiad. It is now the task of Chronology to distinguish this year from all other years, whether past or future, so that it may tell how many years have passed since the Christian era, how many since the Diocletian era, how many since the Hegira, and how many since the present year, and by what indications such intervals of time are established. And so on for other cases.

units.la: 3. E prædictis liquet inter Chronologiam aliásque universas tam artes quàm scientias multùm interesse, inter eas etiam quibus incumbit temporis tractatio. Nam nulla est ars, nulla scientia, quæ sub eadem notione tempus contemplatur atque Chronologia. Physica tempus perlustrat, sed ut naturam ejus definiat, non ut partes distinguat. Astronomia tempus dispicit, sed quatenus ad motus cœlestes, non quatenus ad res terrestres respectum habet. Musica etiam tempus pertractat, sed ut longitudine ac brevitate partium incisum, & dispari sonorum interstitio temperatum, non ut historiæ subserviens. Quin & ipsa etiam Historia tempus consideret necesse est, sed illud tantum describat quo res gestæ sunt, non ut ab aliis temporibus secernat: Adeò ut Historia quodammodo materiem suppeditet Chronologiæ, Chronologia formam det Historiæ; illa res gestas describit, hæc easdem suis temporibus affigit. Sine Historia nulla est Chronologia, sine Chronologia nulla certa Historia. E quibus consequens est, Chronologiam distinctè ab aliis arti fundandæ & constituendæ satis esse idoneam, quippe quæ tempora aliter atque aliæ quævis artes vel scientiæ pertractat. Nam tempora ab historicis tantùm adnotata certis quibusdam indiciis ac characteribus ita distinguit, ut quæcunque ab eis tantùm describuntur, propriis suis temporibus applicentur,
units.tr: 3. From what has been said it is clear that Chronology differs greatly from all other arts and sciences, including those that concern the treatment of time. For there is no art or science that contemplates time under the same aspect as Chronology. Physics surveys time, but in order to define its nature, not to distinguish its parts. Astronomy examines time, but insofar as it relates to the heavenly motions, not insofar as it relates to earthly things. Music also treats time, but as divided by the length and shortness of its parts and measured by the unequal intervals of sounds, not as serving history. Indeed History itself must consider time, but it only describes the time in which events took place and does not separate it from other times. Thus History in a way supplies the matter for Chronology, and Chronology gives form to History: the one describes events, the other assigns those same events to their own times. Without History there is no Chronology, and without Chronology no certain History. From this it follows that Chronology is distinct from other arts and is sufficiently fitted to be founded and established as an art, since it treats times differently from any other arts or sciences. For it distinguishes the times noted only by historians by certain fixed indications and characters, so that whatever is described by them is applied to its own proper times.

units.la: II. Partes Chronologiæ duæ sunt θεωρητικὴ & χαρακτηριστικὴ. III. Pars θεωρητικὴ est quæ temporis naturam ac partes explicat. IV. Pars χαρακτηριστικὴ, quæ de ipsis characteribus agit, sive notis, quibus tempora distinguantur.
units.tr: II. The parts of chronology are two: the theoretical [θεωρητικὴ] and the characteristic [χαρακτηριστικὴ]. III. The theoretical part is that which explains the nature and parts of time. IV. The characteristic part deals with the characters themselves, or marks, by which times are distinguished.

units.la: 1. Ex iis quæ modò commentati sumus, hujus divisionis ratio satis elucescit. Quandoquidem enim tempora sunt objectum sive etiam subjectum Chronologiæ, & officium ejus temporum distinctio, utrumque horum tam subjectum vid. quàm officium distinctè explicandum est; ut Institutiones hasce Chronologicas perfectas redderemus. Et subjectum quidem primum sibi locum vendicat. Nemo enim temporum distinguendorum rationem imbibat, nisi qui varias temporum partes ac annorum formas priùs intelligit. Ut nulla est enim ratio tam fera, nulla tam inculta, quæ aliquam temporum rationem non inivit; sic omnes propemodum, antiquitùs præsertim, in iis ad usum civilem applicandis discrepârunt. Hi enim ad Solis, illi ad Lunæ motus menses annósque suos exigebant, nec desunt qui ad utriusque. Quinetiam nec inter omnes convenit de ipsis diei nec ipsius horæ partibus, adeò ut frustra temporum distinctionem aggredietur, qui eorundem ut à variis usitatorum gentibus cognitionem non præmisit.
units.tr: 1. From what we have just discussed, the reason for this division becomes quite clear. For since times are the object, or also the subject, of chronology, and its task is the distinguishing of times, both of these must be explained distinctly, the subject as much as the task, if we are to render these Chronological Institutes complete. And the subject certainly deserves to come first. For no one can grasp the method of distinguishing times unless he first understands the various parts of time and the forms of the years. Just as there is no nation so savage and so uncultivated that it has not devised some method of reckoning time, so almost all have differed in applying these to civil use, especially in antiquity. For some regulated their months and years by the motions of the Sun, others by those of the Moon, and there are those who used both. Indeed, not even all agree on the parts of the day itself or of the hour. So he will attempt the distinction of times in vain who has not first learned about these things from the various peoples in common use.

units.la: 2. Hinc igitur est quod nos in duas hasce partes, ut omnimodo distinctas, Institutiones nostras Chronologicas dispescimus: Quarum primam vocamus χρονικὴν, q.d. Temporariam propterea quòd tempori ejúsque partibus explicandis insumitur. Alteram χαρακτηριστικὴν Characteristicam, eò quòd characteres sive notas chronologicas, quibus tempora distinguantur, suísque temporibus res olim gestæ designentur, à capite ad calcem tractat.
units.tr: 2. Hence it is that we divide our Chronological Institutes into these two parts, as entirely distinct. The first of these we call the [χρονικὴ], that is, the Temporal, because it is devoted to explaining time and its parts. The second we call the [χαρακτηριστικὴ], the Characteristic, because it treats, from beginning to end, of the chronological characters or marks by which times are distinguished and by which events of the past are assigned to their proper times.

units.la: CAP. II. De Tempore.
units.tr: CAP. II. On Time.

units.la: Χρόνος ἐστὶν ἀριθμὸς κινήσεως κατὰ τὸ πρότερον καὶ ὕστερον.
units.tr: Time is the number of motion according to the before and the after [Χρόνος ἐστὶν ἀριθμὸς κινήσεως κατὰ τὸ πρότερον καὶ ὕστερον].

units.la: Tempus est numerus motus secundùm prius & posterius.
units.tr: Time is the number of motion according to prior and posterior.

units.la: I. HÆc optima temporis definitio ab Aristotele tradita l. 4. φυσικῆς ἀκροάσεως, ut intelligatur, tenendum est primò numerum duplicem esse numerantem & numeratum: ὁ γὰρ χρόνος ἐστὶ τὸ ἀριθμούμενον, ἢ ἐχ ᾧ ἀριθμῶμεν, Tempus est illud quod numeratur, non quo numeramus; ut ibidem docet Philosophus: i. e. non est numerus binarius, ternarius, &c. sed ipse motus numeratus. Deinde, tenendum est etiam Solem & Lunam (quorum præcipuè conversionibus tempus mensuratur) orbem continuò circumrotari, idque duplici quidem motu; uno εἰς τὰ προηγούμενα, in antecedentia signorum, viz. ab Ariete ad Piscem, à Pisce ad Aquarium, ab Aquario ad Capricornum, &c. alio εἰς τὰ ἑπόμενα, in consequentia signorum, ab Ariete ad Taurum, à Tauro ad Geminos, & sic deinceps motu priori, ut ab ortu ad occasum, dies numerantur; posteriori, ut ab occasu ad ortum anni. Quocirca dies, anni, tempúsque adeò universum nihil aliud est, quàm luminarium motûs collecti & numerati. Et quidem secundùm prius & posterius. Nam cùm luminaria in continuo versentur fluxu, aliæ motuum istiusmodi partes priores sint, posteriores aliæ necesse est. Tempus autem ab utroque motu, tam priori videlicet sive præterito, quàm posteriori sive futuro, numeratur; ipsúmque ideò vel præteritum est vel futurum: non tamen absolutè, sed relativè; nihil enim est præteritum, nihil futurum, nisi comparativè ad præsens.
units.tr: I. This excellent definition of time is given by Aristotle in book 4 of the Physics [φυσικῆς ἀκροάσεως]. To understand it, we must hold, first, that number is twofold, numbering and numbered. For time is that which is numbered, not that by which we number [ὁ γὰρ χρόνος ἐστὶ τὸ ἀριθμούμενον, ἢ ἐχ ᾧ ἀριθμῶμεν], as the Philosopher teaches in the same place. That is, time is not the number two, three, and so on, but the motion itself, as numbered. Next, we must hold that the Sun and Moon, by whose revolutions time is chiefly measured, continually circle the heavens, and this with a twofold motion: one towards the things that precede [εἰς τὰ προηγούμενα], that is, towards the preceding signs, namely from Aries to Pisces, from Pisces to Aquarius, from Aquarius to Capricorn, and so on; the other towards the things that follow [εἰς τὰ ἑπόμενα], that is, towards the following signs, from Aries to Taurus, from Taurus to Gemini, and so on. By the former motion, from east to west, days are counted; by the latter, from west to east, years. Hence days, years, and time as a whole are nothing other than the collected and counted motions of the luminaries. And indeed time is measured according to prior and posterior. For since the luminaries are in continual flux, some parts of such motion must be earlier and others later. Time is numbered by both motions, the earlier, that is, the past, and the later, that is, the future; and so it is either past or future. Yet this is not absolute but relative, for nothing is past or future except in comparison with the present.

units.la: II. Tempus aliud est Prolepticum, aliud Historicum.
units.tr: II. Time is of two kinds: the proleptic and the historical.

units.la: III. Tempus Prolepticum est quod Mosaica motuum cœlesti- um ratiocinia præcessisse fingitur.
units.tr: III. The prolepticus time is that which is pretended to have preceded the Mosaic calculations of the heavenly motions.

units.la: I. Quicquid certi de motuum cœlestium atque adeò temporis ipsius initio habemus, libris Mosaicis acceptum referimus. Verùm enimvero nonnullæ sunt epochæ, ut periodus Juliana, & triplex Græcorum computus, ut & antiquæ quædam historiæ, Manethonis præsertim Hierophantæ Ægyptiaci, quæ temporis primordium ut à Mose constitutum antecessisse finguntur. Quo fit ut Chronologi, ne quid ad perfectam rerum tam ficte quàm verè traditarum scientiam desideraretur, tempus quoddam προλαμβάνει postulare cogantur, ita dictum quod προλαμβάνει, i. e. anticipat & antevertit verum & Mosaicum temporis exordium.
units.tr: I. Whatever we have as certain concerning the motions of the heavenly bodies, and indeed concerning the very beginning of time, we credit to the books of Moses. Yet there are some epochs, such as the Julian period and the threefold reckoning of the Greeks, as well as certain ancient histories, especially those of Manetho the Egyptian priest, which are feigned to have preceded the beginning of time as established by Moses. As a result, the chronologers, lest anything be lacking to a complete knowledge of matters handed down as much falsely as truly, are compelled to postulate a certain time <hi>προλαμβάνει</hi> [prolambanei], so named because it <hi>προλαμβάνει</hi> [prolambanei], that is, anticipates and comes before the true and Mosaic beginning of time.

units.la: IV. Tempus Historicum est quod à Mosaicâ rerum epochâ computatur.
units.tr: IV. The historical time is that which is reckoned from the Mosaic epoch of the world.

units.la: I. Varro, teste Censorino, tria discrimina temporum esse tradit. Primum ab hominum principio ad cataclysmum priorem, quod propter ignorantiam vocatur ἄδηλον. Secundum à cataclysmo priore ad Olympiadē primam, quod quia in eo multa fabulosa referuntur, μυθικὸν nominatur. Tertium à primâ Olympiade ad nos, quòd dicitur ἱστορικὸν, quia res in eo gestæ veris historiis continentur. Censorin. c. 21. Nimirum Varro, ut libris Mosaicis destitutus, non potuit non ignorare, quid à primo homine ad diluvium accideret, & propterea tempus illud ἄδηλον sibi, aliisque Ethnicis non immeritò nuncupavit, ut & illud quod à diluvio ad primam fluxit Olympiadem μυθικὸν, quoniam Οὐδὲν Ἕλλην πρὸ Ὀλυμπιάδων ἀκριβῶς ἱστόρηται, nihil ante Olympiades accuratè scriptum fuit, ut rectè ait Justinus Martyr ad Græc. cohort. & Africanus μέχρι μὲν Ὀλυμπιάδων ἰδίᾳ ἀκριβῶς ἱστόρηται τοῖς Ἕλλησι, πάντων Συρίας ἀνδρῶν, ἡ κοινὴ μὲν αὐτοῖς πρὸ τῶν συμμαχιῶν, Ante quidem
units.tr: I. Varro, according to Censorinus, hands down three divisions of time. The first runs from the beginning of humankind to the first cataclysm, and on account of ignorance it is called obscure [ἄδηλον]. The second runs from the first cataclysm to the first Olympiad, and because many fabulous things are related in it, it is called mythical [μυθικὸν]. The third runs from the first Olympiad to our own time, and it is called historical [ἱστορικὸν], because the deeds done in it are contained in true histories. Censorin. c. 21. Clearly Varro, being without the Mosaic books, could not help being ignorant of what happened from the first man to the flood, and so not unreasonably named that period obscure for himself and other Gentiles. Likewise he named the period from the flood to the first Olympiad mythical, since "Nothing before the Olympiads has been accurately recorded by a Greek" [Οὐδὲν Ἕλλην πρὸ Ὀλυμπιάδων ἀκριβῶς ἱστόρηται], as Justin Martyr rightly says in his Cohortatio ad Graecos, and Africanus says: "Up to the Olympiads the Greeks have an accurate history of their own, but of all the men of Syria, their common history [ἡ κοινὴ μὲν αὐτοῖς] before the alliances [πρὸ τῶν συμμαχιῶν]. Before

units.la: Olympiades nihil certi à Græcis in historia traditur, omnibus confusis nec ullâ ex parte sibi consentientibus, Afr. apud Euseb. de Præp. Evang. l 10. c. 10. Ethnicis igitur nullum tempus proprie historicum audiat, nisi quod primam Olympiadem sequitur. Nos autem, qui Mosaicis gaudemus ratiociniis, ab ipso primo homine mundóque condito historias nostras exordiamur. Et ideirco totum temporis quod ab ipsis motuum cœlestium carceribus ad hanc usque metam sive tempus præsens effluxerit, Historicum jure nominemus.
units.tr: the Olympiads, nothing certain is handed down by the Greeks in history, everything being confused and in no part consistent with itself, Africanus, quoted in Eusebius, De Praeparatione Evangelica bk. 10, c. 10. Therefore the Gentiles have no time that is properly historical except what follows the first Olympiad. But we, who rejoice in Mosaic reasoning, begin our histories from the first man himself and the world when it was created. And so we may rightly call Historical the whole of the time that has run from the very starting-gates of the heavenly motions down to this goal, that is, the present time.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAP. III.

units.la: De Scrupulo.
units.tr: On the Scruple.

units.la: Temporum partes sunt Scrupulum, Hora, Dies, Hebdomas, Mensis, & Annus.
units.tr: The parts of time are the scruple, the hour, the day, the week, the month, and the year.

units.la: I. Tempus, ut civilem ad usum melius accommodetur, in varias hasce partes distribuitur, è quibus majores è minoribus collectis oriuntur. E Scrupulis enim colliguntur Horæ, ex Horis Dies, è Diebus Hebdomades, ex Hebdomadibus Menses, è Mensibus Anni. Quapropter ut omnes hasce partes distinctius explicatas demus, à minoribus ad majores progrediendum est. II. Scrupulum est minima pars temporis. III. Estque vel Horarium, vel Diurnum. IV. Scrupulum Horarium est commune, vel Chaldaicum. V. Scrupulum commune est vel primum, vel à primo ortum. VI. Scrupulum commune primum est sexagesima pars Horæ.
units.tr: I. Time is divided into these various parts so that it may be better adapted to civil use, and the larger parts arise from the smaller ones collected together. For scruples are gathered into hours, hours into days, days into weeks, weeks into months, and months into years. Therefore, to set out all these parts more distinctly, we must proceed from the smaller to the larger. II. A scruple is the smallest part of time. III. It is either horary or diurnal. IV. The horary scruple is either common or Chaldaic. V. The common scruple is either the first, or derived from the first. VI. The first common scruple is the sixtieth part of an hour.

units.la: I. Horam quamlibet in sexaginta partes æquales partiti sunt Antiqui, propterea quòd numerus sexagenarius multiplices admittit divisiones. Nam resolvi potest in bis triginta, ter viginti, quater quindecim, quinquies duodecim, & sexies decem. Et idcirco commodissima videtur hæc Horæ distributio. Vocatur autem hoc Scrupulum etiam Momentum, necnon Minutum.
units.tr: I. The ancients divided any hour into sixty equal parts, because the number sixty admits of many divisions. For it can be resolved into twice thirty, three times twenty, four times fifteen, five times twelve, and six times ten. And so this division of the hour seems most convenient. This scruple is also called Momentum, and likewise Minutum.

units.la: VII. Scrupulum & primo ortum est sexagesima pars Scrupu- li primi.
units.tr: VII. The second scruple, derived from the first, is the sixtieth part of the first scruple.

units.la: I. Ut quælibet Hora in 60 partes æquales dispescitur; sic & quælibet ex istis partibus in totidem particulas subdividitur, quæ Scrupula secunda nuncupantur. Qui autem exactiores adhuc Astronomicos, vel etiam Chronologicos, suos efficerent epilogismos, quodvis è Secundis hisce Scrupulis in 60 Tertia, quodlibet Tertium in totidem Quarta, quodlibet Quartum in totidem Quinta, & sic usque ad Decima diducunt.
units.tr: I. Just as any hour is divided into 60 equal parts, so each of these parts is again subdivided into the same number of smaller particles, which are called second scruples. Those who wish to make their astronomical or even chronological calculations more exact divide any of these seconds into 60 thirds, any third into the same number of fourths, any fourth into the same number of fifths, and so on as far as tenths.

units.la: VIII. Scrupulum Chaldaicum est millesima octogesima pars Horæ.
units.tr: VIII. The Chaldaic scruple is the one thousand and eightieth part of an hour.

units.la: I. Scrupulum hoc Chaldaicum idcirco nominatur quòd à Chaldæis institutum fuit, ab aliis autem orientalibus (ut Judæis, Arabibus, &c.) usurpatur. Et hæc quidem Chaldaica Horæ distributio ob eandem rationem instituta fuit, atque communis; eò videlicet quòd in tot æquales partes diduci queat. Nam in 1080 continentur bis 540, ter 360, quater 270, quinquies 216, sexies 180, octies 135, novies 120, decies 108, quindecies 72, & vicies 54. Ab ipsis orientalibus vocantur hæc Scrupula הלקים Helachim Particulæ. Porrò, ut Scrupulum quodlibet commune in 60, sic Chaldaicum quodlibet in 76 particellas nonnunquam subdividitur, quæ רגעים Momenta nuncupantur.
units.tr: I. This scruple is called Chaldaic because it was instituted by the Chaldeans, but it is used by other Orientals (such as the Jews, the Arabs, etc.). This Chaldaic division of the hour was instituted, and is in common use, for the same reason: namely, that it can be divided into so many equal parts. For 1080 contains twice 540, three times 360, four times 270, five times 216, six times 180, eight times 135, nine times 120, ten times 108, fifteen times 72, and twenty times 54. Among the Orientals these scruples are called הלקים [Helakim], "particles". Moreover, just as the common scruple is sometimes divided into 60, so the Chaldaic scruple is sometimes divided into 76 small particles, which are called רגעים [Momenta].

units.la: IX. Scrupula
units.tr: IX. The scruples

units.la: XI. Scrupula hæc vel Chaldaica in communia, vel Communia in Caldaica reducenda sunt.
units.tr: XI. These scruples, whether Chaldaic or common, are to be reduced into common or Chaldaic scruples.

units.la: X. Ut scrupula Chaldaica sive Helakim in communia convertas, propositá Partiaris per 18. Quotus dit scrupula communia prima, deinde residuum multiplices in 60, & productum itidem per 18 distribuas quotus enim ostendet Scrupula etiam secunda quæsita.
units.tr: X. To convert Chaldaic scruples, or helakim, into common ones, divide the number proposed by 18. The quotient gives the first common scruples; then multiply the remainder by 60 and divide the product again by 18; the quotient will show the second scruples sought.

units.la: 1. In quolibet scrupulo Chaldaico 18 communia continentur, quocircà quæcunq; proponantur Helakim Chaldaica, ti per 18 dividantur, quotus exhibebit scrupula communia prima in ipsis comprehensa. Et residuum per regulam proportionis in 60 ductum, & per eundem numerum 18 divisum, quot etiam scrupula secunda primis sint annectenda monstrabit.
units.tr: 1. In each Chaldaic scruple there are 18 common ones; therefore, whatever Chaldaic helakim are proposed, if you divide them by 18, the quotient will give the first common scruples contained in them. And the remainder, multiplied by 60 according to the rule of proportion and divided by the same number 18, will show how many second scruples are to be added to the first.

units.la: 2. Ex. gr. Mensis Judaicus definitur diebus 29, horis 12. & helakim 793. Si scire vellem quot scrupula communia in hisce 793 helakim continentur, 793 per 18 divido, quotus est 44. & residuum. 1. quod in 60 ductum & per 18 divisum in quoto dat 3. in residuo 6. Ergo helakim 793 sunt scrupula communia 44′. 3″. Si scrupula etiam tertia assequerer, ultimæ Divisionis residuum 6 in 60 duco & productum 360 per 18 divisum in quoto dat 20. Ergo mensis Judaicus est dier.29.h.12.793. sive dier. 29.hor.12. 44′. 3″. 20‴.
units.tr: 2. For example, the Jewish month is defined as 29 days, 12 hours, and 793 helakim. If I wished to know how many common scruples are contained in these 793 helakim, I divide 793 by 18; the quotient is 44, and the remainder is 1. Multiplying this by 60 and dividing by 18, the quotient is 3, and the remainder is 6. Therefore the 793 helakim are 44′ 3″ common scruples. If I were to find the third scruples as well, I multiply the remainder 6 of the last division by 60, and divide the product 360 by 18; the quotient is 20. Therefore the Jewish month is 29 days, 12 hours, 793 helakim, or 29 days, 12 hours, 44′ 3″ 20‴.

units.la: 3. Aliud exemplum. Annus Judaicus simplex est dierum 354. hor. 8. 876. Si hæc helakim 876 in scrupula communia reduceres, distribuas 876 per 18, quotus dat scrupula prima 48. residuum est 12 quod in 60 ductum, & per 18 divisum in quoto dat scrupula secunda 40. in residuo 0. Ergo helakim sive scrupula Chaldaica 876 sunt communia 48′. 40″. 0‴.
units.tr: 3. Another example. The simple Jewish year is 354 days, 8 hours, 876 helakim. If you were to reduce these 876 helakim to common scruples, divide 876 by 18; the quotient gives the first scruples, 48. The remainder is 12, which multiplied by 60 and divided by 18 gives in the quotient the second scruples, 40, with remainder 0. Therefore the 876 helakim, or Chaldaic scruples, are 48′ 40″ 0‴ common.

units.la: XI. Ut scrupula communia in Chaldaica reducas scrupula data primà multiplices in 18. & producto reservato, si quæ sunt scrupula secunda: Ea etiam in 18 ducas & Productum dividas per 60, cujus divisionis quotum annectes numero reservato sive producto prioris multiplicationis, aggregatum est numerus helakim quæsitus.
units.tr: XI. To reduce common scruples into Chaldaic ones, multiply the given first scruples by 18, and keep the product aside. If there are second scruples too, multiply them also by 18 and divide the product by 60; add the quotient of this division to the number kept aside, that is, to the product of the first multiplication. The sum is the number of helakim sought.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Si scrupula communia 48′ 40″ reducerem in Chaldaica, primò multiplico 48 in 18, & producto 864 reservato, multiplico & 40 in 18 & productum 720 divido per 60, cujus divisionis quotum 12 numero reservato 864 adjicio, summa est 876. Ergò scrupulis communibus 48′. 40″. respondent helakim Chaldaica 876.
units.tr: 1. For example, if I were to reduce the common scruples 48′ 40″ into Chaldaic ones, I first multiply 48 by 18, and keeping the product 864 aside, I also multiply 40 by 18 and divide the product 720 by 60. I add the quotient 12 to the number 864 kept aside; the sum is 876. Therefore the common scruples 48′ 40″ correspond to the Chaldaic helakim 876.

units.la: 2. Si scrupula quoque tertia revocanda proponantur, etiam ea in 18 multiplicanda & per 60 dividenda sunt, & quotus ad secundæ divisionis productum aggregandus. Ex. gr. Si proponantur 44′. 3″. 20‴ in helakim reducenda, primò multiplico 44 in 18. numerus producti reservandus est 792. Deinde 3 multiplico in 18, & producto 54 reservato, tertia 20‴ in 18, duco & productum 360 divido per 60, & quotum 6 adjicio ad productum præcedentis multiplicationis, viz. 54. Summam 60 divido per 60 & quotum 1. ad productum primæ multiplicationis 792 adjicio, Summa est 793. Ergò scrupula communia 44′. 3″. 20‴. sunt helakim Chaldaica 793.
units.tr: 2. If third scruples are also proposed to be brought back, these too must be multiplied by 18 and divided by 60, and the quotient added to the product of the second division. For example, if 44′ 3″ 20‴ are proposed to be reduced to helakim, first I multiply 44 by 18; the product 792 is to be kept. Then I multiply 3 by 18, and keeping the product 54 aside, I multiply the third scruples 20‴ by 18 and divide the product 360 by 60; I add the quotient 6 to the product of the preceding multiplication, namely 54. I divide the sum 60 by 60, and the quotient 1 I add to the product of the first multiplication, 792. The sum is 793. Therefore the common scruples 44′ 3″ 20‴ are the Chaldaic helakim 793.

units.la: XII. Scrupulum Diurnum est sexagesima pars diei.
units.tr: XII. A daily scruple is the sixtieth part of a day.

units.la: 1. Ptolemæus aliiq; post eum Astronomi totum nonnunquam diem in 60 partes æquales dispescunt, quæ scrupula sive sexagena diei vocantur; quorum etiam singula in totidem secunda distribuuntur, & secunda itidem in tertia, tertia in quarta, & sic deinceps pariter atq; in scrupulis horariis diducuntur.
units.tr: 1. Ptolemy and, after him, other astronomers sometimes divide the whole day into 60 equal parts, which are called scruples or sexagesimal parts of the day. Each of these scruples is further divided into sixty seconds, the seconds into thirds, the thirds into fourths, and so on in the same way as hourly scruples are subdivided.

units.la: XIII. Si scrupula haec diurna in horas & horarum scrupula convertenda, propositae multiplices in 1440, & productum dividas per 60. nam hujus divisionis quotus per 60 etiam distributus, in quoto dabit horas, in residuo scrupula quaesita.
units.tr: XIII. If these daily scruples are to be converted into hours and hourly scruples, multiply the proposed quantities by 1440 and divide the product by 60. For the quotient of this division, divided again by 60, gives the hours in the quotient, and the sought-for scruples in the remainder.

units.la: 1. Quaelibet, ut neminem latet, dies horis constat 24, hora quaelibet scrupulis 60, quapropter si 24 ducas in 60, producetur numerus scrupulorum totius diei, viz. 1440, per haec igitur scrupula horaria, si multiplices diurna proposita, in horaria convertentur.
units.tr: 1. Every day, as no one is unaware, consists of 24 hours, and each hour consists of 60 scruples. Therefore, if you multiply 24 by 60, you get the number of scruples in the whole day, namely 1440. So if you multiply the proposed daily scruples by these hourly scruples, they are converted into hourly ones.

units.la: 2. Ex. gr. Proponantur scrupula diurna 43 in horas & horarum scrupula reducenda. 43 in 1440 ductis, productum est 61920 quod per 60 divisum in quoto dat 1032. Ergo scrupula diurna 43 sunt horaria 1032. quae si per 60 distribuantur, in quoto dabunt horas 17, in residuo scrupula 12'. ut scrupula diurna 43 sint horae 17, 12'.
units.tr: 2. For example, let the daily scruples 43 be proposed to be reduced to hours and hourly scruples. Multiplying 43 by 1440 gives 61920, which divided by 60 gives 1032 in the quotient. Therefore the daily scruples 43 are 1032 hourly scruples. If these are divided by 60, the quotient gives 17 hours and the remainder gives 12 scruples, so that the daily scruples 43 are 17 hours, 12 scruples.

units.la: 3. Eodem modo procedendum est si scrupula dierum secunda primis annectantur; hoc tantum observato quod in scrupulis dierum secundis computandis ultimae divisionis, quotus pro horis dat scrupula prima, & residuum pro primis secunda. Ut si propositia fuissent scrupula diurna 43'. 43''. ista 43 secunda in 1440 etiam ducenda sunt, sed ultimae divisionis quotus 17 non dabit horas & scrupula prima, sed scrupula prima 17', & secunda 12''. quae prima 17 primis 12 prius inventis annectenda sunt, & sic scrupula diurna 43'. 43'' efficiunt horas 17. 29'. 12''.
units.tr: 3. The same procedure applies if daily seconds are added to daily scruples, with this one point observed: in computing the daily seconds, the quotient of the last division gives the scruples for the hours, and the remainder gives the seconds for the scruples. Thus, if the daily scruples 43' 43'' had been proposed, these 43 seconds must also be multiplied by 1440; but the quotient 17 of the last division will give not hours and scruples, but scruples 17' and seconds 12''. These 17 scruples must be added to the 12 scruples found earlier, and so the daily scruples 43' 43'' make 17 hours, 29' 12''.

units.la: 4. Aliud exemplum. Proponantur scrupula diurna 35'. 22''. in horas & horarum scrupula convertenda. Primo 35 in 1440 multiplicata producunt 50400. quae per 60 divisa dant horas praecise 14. & eodem modo scrupula proposita secunda 22 in 1440 ducta producunt 31680. quae per 60 divisa, in quoto dant 528 scrupula secunda; quae etiam per 60 distributa fiunt 8', 48''. Ergo scrupula diurna 35'. 22''. sunt horae 14. 8'. 48''.
units.tr: 4. Another example. Let the daily scruples 35' 22'' be proposed to be converted into hours and hourly scruples. First, 35 multiplied by 1440 gives 50400, which divided by 60 gives exactly 14 hours. Likewise, the proposed 22 seconds multiplied by 1440 give 31680, which divided by 60 gives 528 second-scruples in the quotient; these, divided again by 60, become 8' 48''. Therefore the daily scruples 35' 22'' are 14 hours, 8' 48''.

units.la: XIV. Ut è contrà horas & scrupula horaria in diurna convertas, horas & scrupula proposita in secunda redu- cas, & summam per 1440 partiaris, quotus enim dabit scrupula dici prima, & residuum in 60 ductum & per 1440 divisum secunda exhibebit.
units.tr: XIV. How, conversely, to turn hours and hour-minutes into day-minutes: reduce the hours and the given minutes to seconds, and divide the sum by 1440. The quotient will give the first day-minutes, and the remainder, multiplied by 60 and divided by 1440, will give the seconds.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Sint horæ 12. 32′ in sexagena diurna revocanda; primò multiplico 12 in 60, producto 720 adjicio scrupula appensa 32′. Et sic colliguntur scrupula prima 752, quæ per 60 iterum multiplicata, reducuntur in scrupula secunda 45120. Hæc autem per 1440 divisa in quoto dant scrupula diurna prima 31, & residuum faciunt 480, quod per 60 multiplicatum producit 28800. Hoc productum per 1440 divisum in quoto dat scrupula diurna secunda 20″. Ergo horæ 12, 32′ sunt sexagena dierum 31′, 20″.
units.tr: 1. For example, let there be 12 hours 32′ to be converted into day-sexagesimals. First I multiply 12 by 60, and to the product 720 I add the 32′ given. So the first minutes come to 752, which multiplied again by 60 are reduced to 45120 seconds. Divided by 1440, these give in the quotient 31 day-minutes, and they leave a remainder of 480, which multiplied by 60 gives 28800. Divided by 1440, this product gives in the quotient 20″ of day-seconds. Therefore 12 hours 32′ are 31′ 20″ of day-sexagesimals.

units.la: 2. Verùm hanc per præcedentem regulam examinemus. Nam una ex altera probetur. Juxta primus igitur regulæ præcedentis exemplum, convertamus horas 17, 29′, 12″, in scrupula diurna. Horæ 17 in 60 ductæ producunt 1020, quæ cùm scrupulis primis appensis 29 efficiunt 1049. Hæc in 60 ducta producunt scrupula secunda 62940, quibus adjicienda sunt scrupula secunda appensa 12; ut summa scrupulorum secundorum sit 62952, quæ per 1440 divisa in quoto dant 43′, & residuum faciunt 1032, quod in 60 ductum & per 1440 divisum dat etiam 43″. Igitur horæ 17, 29′, 12″, sunt sexagena diurna 43′, 43″. Ergo rectissimè procedit calculus. Et eâdem quoq; methodo horæ 14, 8′, 48″, scrupula sive sexagena diurna efficiunt 35′, 22″, juxta posterius regulæ præcedentis exemplum.
units.tr: 2. But let us test this by the preceding rule, so that each proves the other. Following the first example of the preceding rule, let us convert 17 hours 29′ 12″ into day-minutes. 17 hours multiplied by 60 give 1020, which together with the 29 given first minutes make 1049. Multiplied by 60, these give 62940 seconds, to which the 12 given seconds must be added. So the sum of seconds is 62952, which divided by 1440 gives 43′ in the quotient, and leaves 1032. This, multiplied by 60 and divided by 1440, also gives 43″. Therefore 17 hours 29′ 12″ are 43′ 43″ of day-sexagesimals. The calculation thus proceeds quite correctly. And by the same method, 14 hours 8′ 48″ make 35′ 22″ of day-sexagesimals, according to the second example of the preceding rule.

units.la: CAP. IV. De Hora.
units.tr: CHAP. IV. On the Hour.

units.la: I. Hora est pars diei. II. Estque vel æqualis, vel inæqualis: III. Hora æqualis est vel simplex, vel composita. IV. Hora æqualis simplex est vicessima quarta pars ῥ ῥυχσπμίςῳ sive diei civilis.
units.tr: I. The hour is a part of the day. II. It is either equal or unequal. III. An equal hour is either simple or composite. IV. A simple equal hour is the twenty-fourth part of the nychthemeron [νυχθημέρου], that is, of the civil day.

units.la: I. HÆ horæ æquales vocantur & ἰσημερινὰ Æquinoctiales, propterea quòd totum æquatoris circulum in 24 æquales partes distribuunt; quo evenit ut horis hisce singulis gradus æquatoris 15 competunt, nam 15 in 24 ducti gradus æquatoris universos 360 producunt. Sol igitur quâlibet horâ æquinoctiali gradus 15 motu suo medio peragrat: Et hinc est quod singulis 15 longitudinis alicujus loci gradibus una hora æquinoctialis ab Astronomis numeratur, & unicuiq; gradui scrupula horaria communia quatuor. Æquales idcirco nominantur, quia semper sibi constant, nunquam variatæ; ut quæ non majores sunt tempore diurno nec nocturno minores, sed per totum annum sibi similes fluunt, ab uno diei civilis puncto ad idem, ut à media nocte ad mediam noctem, vel à meridie ad meridiem numeratæ. Et hæc est vulgaris diei partitio tam Chronologicis quàm Astronomicis aptissima ratiocinis.
units.tr: I. These equal hours are also called Equinoctial [ἰσημερινά], because they divide the whole circle of the equator into 24 equal parts. So each of these hours corresponds to 15 degrees of the equator, since 15 multiplied by 24 gives the full 360 degrees. The sun therefore traverses 15 degrees in each equinoctial hour by its mean motion. Hence astronomers count one equinoctial hour for every 15 degrees of longitude of any place, and four common minutes of time for each degree. They are called equal because they always keep to themselves and never vary: they are neither longer in the day nor shorter at night, but flow alike through the whole year, counted from one point of the civil day back to the same point, as from midnight to midnight or from noon to noon. This is the common division of the day, and the most suitable one for chronological as well as astronomical reckoning.

units.la: V. Hora æqualis composita est, quæ à duabus horis sim- plicibus conflata, totam diem civilem in 12 æquales partes dissecat.
units.tr: V. The composite equal hour is the one formed from two simple hours, which cuts the whole civil day into 12 equal parts.

units.la: 1. Hanc diei civilis in 12 æquales partes divisionem Græcos à Babyloniis olim didicisse, testis est Herodotus, l. 2. UfurUsurpatur & ab ipso Epiphanio, ut qui annum definit Julianum πεντηκοντα ... ἡμερῶν ὡ ὥρων πρ.ῶν; diebus 365 & horis 3. Epiph. her. 24. horis tribus, nimirum compositis, quae sex simplices efficiunt. Nam annus Julianus, ut cuiq; notum est, ultra dies 365 horas 6 simplices colligit.
units.tr: 1. That the Greeks long ago learned from the Babylonians this division of the civil day into 12 equal parts is attested by Herodotus, book 2. Epiphanius himself also uses it, when he defines the Julian year as 365 days and 3 hours (Epiph. Haer. 24), meaning composite hours, which make six simple ones. For the Julian year, as everyone knows, exceeds 365 days by 6 simple hours.

units.la: 2. Coeterum horae istae compositae, Astronomis Chataiae & Igurae praecipuè in usu sunt, qui quamlibet duodecimam hujusmodi diei civilis partem Chag vocant, & unicuiq; Chag suum imponunt nomen ab animale aliquo desumptum. vid. 1. Zeh mus. 2. Chiu bos 3. Tem pardus. 4. Mau lepus. 5. Chin crocodilus. 6. Siz serpens. 7. Von Equus. 8. Vi Ovis. 9. Shin Simia. 10. Tou Gallina. 11. Sou Canis. 12. Cai Porcus. Porrò, quaelibet Chag sive duodecima pars συγκρίσεως in octo particulas subdividitur, quarum singulas Geh appellant, adeò ut quaelibet Geh quartae horae aequinoctialis partì respondeat.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, these composite hours are especially in use among the astronomers of Cathay and the Uighurs, who call each such twelfth part of the civil day a Chag, and give each Chag its own name taken from some animal: (1) Zeh, mouse; (2) Chiu, ox; (3) Tem, leopard; (4) Mau, hare; (5) Chin, crocodile; (6) Siz, serpent; (7) Von, horse; (8) Vi, sheep; (9) Shin, monkey; (10) Tou, hen; (11) Sou, dog; (12) Cai, pig. Furthermore, each Chag, or twelfth part of the composite day [συγκρίσεως], is subdivided into eight particles, which they call Geh, so that each Geh corresponds to a fourth part of an equinoctial hour.

units.la: VI. Hora inaequalis est duodecima pars diei seorsim à nocte, veletiam noctis seorsim à die.
units.tr: VI. An unequal hour is the twelfth part of the day taken separately from the night, or of the night taken separately from the day.

units.la: 1. Horae inaequales vocantur eò quòd unà cum diebus naturalibus quotidie crescunt vel decrescunt; atq; ideò semper sibimet sunt inaequales, nam horae diurnae majores sunt in aestate, in hyeme minores: nocturnae è contrà in hyeme majores, & minores in aestate. Nec unquam aequales sunt praeterquàm in punctis aequinoctialibus, quando & horis aequalibus sunt aequales. Vocantur &horae καιρικαί propterea quòd καιροῖς, i.e. per tempestates variantur. Per hasce igitur horas inaequales sive καιρικὰς dividitur dies quaelibet naturalis, ut & nox, in 12 aequales partes. Dies autem ab ortu solis ad occasum, nox ab occasu ad ortum computatur.
units.tr: 1. The unequal hours are so called because they grow or shrink each day along with the natural days. Thus they are always unequal to one another: daytime hours are longer in summer and shorter in winter, and night hours are the reverse, longer in winter and shorter in summer. They are equal only at the equinoctial points, when they are also equal to the equal hours. They are also called seasonal hours [καιρικαί], because they vary according to the seasons [καιροῖς], that is, by weather. Every natural day, and likewise the night, is divided into 12 equal parts by these unequal or seasonal hours. The day is reckoned from sunrise to sunset, and the night from sunset to sunrise.

units.la: 2. Horas hasce καιρικὰς indigitat sospitator noster Joh. 11. 9. usitat, sunt et à Judaeis, Romanis, & Graecis antiquis; ab ipso etiam Ptolemaeo Astronomorum principe, in Almagesto, sive libro praeclaro μαθηματικῆς συντάξεως.
units.tr: 2. Our Saviour indicates these seasonal hours in John 11:9, and they were in use among the Jews, the Romans and the ancient Greeks. Ptolemy too, the prince of astronomers, uses them in the Almagest, that is, in his famous book of the mathematical syntaxis [μαθηματικῆς συντάξεως].

units.la: VII. Ut longitudinem horæ cujuslibet inæqualis computes, Arcum diurnum vel nocturnum in scrupula horaria prima reducas, hæc enim per 12 divisa scrupula prima dabunt, quæ hora quælibet ϗαιρικὴ sibi vendicat.
units.tr: VII. To compute the length of any unequal hour, reduce the daytime or nighttime arc into first minutes of time; for divided by 12 these give the minutes which each seasonal hour claims for itself.

units.la: 1. Arcus diurnus est longitudo diei ab ortu solis ad occasum, nocturnus noctis ab occasu solis ad ortum longitudo. Ut arcum autem diurnum vel nocturnum in quolibet loco mensuratum habeas, elevatio poli & locus solis in Zodiaco necesse est præcognoscantur. Ex hisce enim præmissis ortus & occasus solis quotidie deprehenditur, & consequenter horæ ϗαιρικαὶ longitudo.
units.tr: 1. The day arc is the length of the day from sunrise to sunset, and the night arc the length of the night from sunset to sunrise. To have the day or night arc measured in any place, one must know beforehand the elevation of the pole and the position of the sun in the zodiac. From these premises the rising and setting of the sun is found each day, and consequently the length of the seasonal hour.

units.la: 2. Ex. gr. Proponatur dies Junii undecimus hoc anno Christi 1667, ut longitudinem inæqualium ejus horarum computemus Londini. Elevatio poli, sive latitudo Londini est 51, 32', Junii undecimo Sol primum cancri punctum ingreditur. Ortus igitur est Sol horâ 3, 45', occidit horâ 8, 15'. Arcus diurnus est horarum 16, 30', quæ in scrupula redacta sunt 990, hæc per 12 divisa in quota singulis horis ϗαιρικαῖς scrupula horaria 82 largiuntur: adeo ut quælibet hora ϗαιρικὴ sit scrupulorum 82, sive horæ unius ὡρομετρίας & scrupulorum 22.
units.tr: 2. For example, let us take the 11th day of June in this year of Christ 1667, and compute the length of its unequal hours at London. The elevation of the pole, or latitude of London, is 51° 32'. On June 11 the sun enters the first point of Cancer. The sun therefore rises at 3h 45' and sets at 8h 15'. The day arc is 16h 30', which reduced to minutes gives 990. Divided by 12, this gives 82 minutes of time for each seasonal hour. So each seasonal hour is 82 minutes, that is, 1 hour and 22 minutes of hour-measure [ὡρομετρίας].

units.la: 3. Porro si horæ cujuslibet ϗαιρικῆς initium quæras, die propositio horas completas in 82 multiplices, & productum per 60 partiaris, nam quotiens dabit horas æquales, & residuum scrupula ad minutum quo Sol ortus est adjicienda, ut initium, horæ ϗαιρικῆς quæsitæ deprehendas. Ut si scirem horæ quintæ ϗαιρικῆς initium die propositio, quatuor horæ jam completæ sunt. Ergo multiplico 82 in 4, & productum 328 divido per 60, quotiens est 5, residuum 28. Ergo horæ 4, ϗαιρικαὶ ὡρομετρίας 5, 28', adæquant. Addas 5. 28', ad momentum quo Sol ortus est, sive ad hor. 3, 45', post mediam noctem ⁊. Summa est hora 9, 13. Quinta ergo hora καιρικὴ coepit horâ 9, 13′, ante meridiem. Demas horas 16, 30′, sive arcum diurnum, ex horis 24, 0′, & relinquetur arcus nocturnus eundem excipiens diem 7, 3′′, quæ in scrupula redacta fiunt 45 c, quæ per 12 divisa singulis horis καιρικαῖς nocturnis scrupula horaria 37′ attribuunt. Occidit Sol horâ 8, 15′. Ergò quinta hora καιρικὴ nocturna coepit horâ 10, 43′, post meridiem.
units.tr: 3. Further, if you want the beginning of any seasonal hour, take the completed hours of the given day, multiply them by 82, and divide the product by 60. The quotient gives equal hours and the remainder gives minutes, which are to be added to the time at which the sun rose, to find the beginning of the seasonal hour sought. For example, if I wish to know the beginning of the fifth seasonal hour of the given day, four hours are already complete. So I multiply 82 by 4, and divide the product 328 by 60. The quotient is 5 and the remainder 28, so 4 seasonal hours amount to 5h 28' of hour-measure. Add 5h 28' to the moment of sunrise, that is, to 3h 45' after midnight. The sum is 9h 13'. So the fifth seasonal hour began at 9h 13', before noon. Subtract the day arc of 16h 30' from 24h 0', and the remaining night arc, covering the same day, is 7h 30'. Reduced to minutes this gives 450, which divided by 12 gives 37' for each nocturnal seasonal hour. The sun sets at 8h 15'. Therefore the fifth nocturnal seasonal hour began at 10h 43', after noon.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: De Die.
units.tr: On the Day.

units.la: I. Dies est vel naturalis vel civilis. II. Dies naturalis est spatium temporis orientem, & occidentem solem interfluens.
units.tr: I. The day is either natural or civil. II. The natural day is the space of time lying between the sun's rising and its setting.

units.la: I. Ohannes de sacro Bosco, aliiq; sententiam ejus amplectentes; Diem distinguunt in naturalem & Artificialem. Naturalem vocant quam nos civilem. Artificialem autem quam nos naturalem. Verùm nostra distinctio, ut antiquior; preferenda videtur, quam & ipse Censorinus tradit; apud quem hæc legere est, Superest pauca de die dicere, quæ ut mensis & annus partim naturalis, partim civilis est. Naturalis dies est, tempus ab oriente sole ad solis occasum, cujus contrarium tempus est nox ab occasu solis usq; ad exortum. Civiliter autem dies vocatur tempus quod fit uno cœli circumactu; quo dies verus & nox continetur. Censor. de die nat. c. 23. Quin etiam hæc non antiquissima tantùm sed & aptissima videtur diei distinctio. Enimvero ipsâ quoq; naturâ dies à nocte distinguitur; atque ideò istud temporis spatium quo Sol horizontem nostrum illuminat,dies naturalis merito nuncupatur, ut contrarium nox naturalis: 2. Dies hæc naturalis perpetuo variatur: nam à solstitio Hyberno ad æstivum quotidie crescit, decrescit autem ab æstivo ad Hybernum; adeò ut cùm Sol Cancrum ingreditur, dies naturalis fit longissima & nox brevissima, brevissima vero dies & nox longissima cùm Capricornum: Nec unquam dies naturales noctibus exæquantur præterquam in punctis æquinoctialibus, cùm Sol nimirùm primum vel Arietis vel Libræ punctum invadit,
units.tr: I. John of Holywood (Sacrobosco) and others who embrace his opinion divide the day into the natural and the artificial. They call the natural what we call the civil, and the artificial what we call the natural. But our distinction, being the older, seems preferable, and Censorinus himself hands it down; in him one may read: "It remains to say a little about the day, which, like the month and the year, is partly natural and partly civil. The natural day is the time from the sun's rising to the sun's setting, whose opposite is the night, from the sun's setting until its rising. The day in the civil sense, however, is the time that is completed by one turn of the heavens, which contains both the true day and the night." (Censorinus, On the Natal Day, ch. 23.) Indeed this division seems not only the most ancient but also the most fitting. For nature itself distinguishes day from night; and so that span of time in which the sun lights up our horizon is rightly called the natural day, as its opposite is the natural night. 2. This natural day varies continually: for from the winter solstice to the summer it grows longer each day, and from the summer back to the winter it shortens; so that when the sun enters Cancer the natural day becomes longest and the night shortest, and when it enters Capricorn the shortest day and longest night occur. Nor are the natural days ever equal to the nights except at the equinoctial points, when the sun, of course, enters the first point either of Aries or of Libra.

units.la: III. Dies Civilis est temporis spatium quo Sol ab uno puncto ad idem, ut à media nocte ad mediam noctem circumvol- vitur, atque ideo noctem etiam naturalem comprehendit.
units.tr: III. The civil day is the space of time in which the sun revolves from one point back to the same point, as from midnight to midnight, and so it also embraces the natural night.

units.la: 1. Cœli, vel (uti loqui solent antiqui) supremus Orbis ab ortu ad occasum indies circumrotatur; sole interim ab occasu ad ortum paulatim regrediente. Dies itaque Civilis unà constat æquatoris ab ortu ab occasum circumvolutione; & tanto præterea temporis intervallo, quanto Sol indies ab occasu ad ortum retrò provehitur. Quod tamen perpetuo non est ejusdem quantitatis, idque propter Zodiaci obliquitatem & solis anomaliam. Et hinc est quòd Astronomi medium & æqualem solis motum investigare coacti sint, juxta quem Dies civilis sive æquatio est istud temporis spatium quo Sol æquatoris scrupula 59'. 8". 19'. 43'". 47"''. percurrit.
units.tr: 1. The heavens, or (as the ancients were wont to speak) the highest sphere, turn daily from east to west, while the sun in the meantime gradually moves back from west to east. The civil day therefore consists of one revolution of the equator from east to west, together with that additional interval of time by which the sun is carried back from west to east each day. This, however, is not of the same amount at all times, on account of the obliquity of the zodiac and the sun's anomaly. And hence it is that astronomers have been obliged to investigate the mean and equal motion of the sun, according to which the civil day, or equation, is that span of time in which the sun traverses 59' 8" 19''' 43'''' 47''''' of the equator.

units.la: IV. Diei Civilis quatuor constituuntur epochæ, vel enim ab occasu solis ad occasum, vel ab ortu ad ortum, vel à meridie ad meridiem, vel à media nocte ad mediam noctem computatur.
units.tr: IV. Four epochs of the civil day are established, for it is reckoned either from sunset to sunset, or from sunrise to sunrise, or from noon to noon, or from midnight to midnight.

units.la: V. 1. Ab occasu solis diem auspicati sunt Judæi, Athenienses, Arabes, Bohemi, Silesii.
units.tr: V. 1. The Jews, the Athenians, the Arabs, the Bohemians and the Silesians began the day at sunset.

units.la: 1. Hoc primum & antiquissimum fuit diei Civilis exordium, ipsis mundi primordiis institutum; quibus vespera mane, nox diem praecessit: atque ideo prima nominatur, Gen. 1. Hinc est quod Judaei idem diei principium etiamnum observant; ut & alii propemodum Universi; qui ad Lunae motus menses annosque suos dirigebant; pariter ac Judaei, ut Athenienses, Arabésque. Nimirum primum mensis anni ve diem exordiri non potuerunt prius quam Luna post Synodum apparuerit. Nova vero Luna non die sed nocte se primo videndam praebet, & hinc fortassis evenit, ut nox ante diem naturalem, vel dies Civilis ab initio noctis naturalis iis praecipue computetur.
units.tr: 1. This was the first and most ancient beginning of the civil day, instituted at the very dawn of the world; for in it evening preceded morning, and night preceded day, and so it is called the first day in Genesis 1. Hence the Jews still observe this beginning of the day, as do almost all the nations who regulated their months and years by the motions of the moon, just as the Jews did, such as the Athenians and Arabs. Indeed they could not begin the first day of the month or year before the moon had appeared after conjunction. A new moon, however, shows itself to be seen first not by day but by night, and hence perhaps it came about that for them especially the night is counted before the natural day, or the civil day begins with the beginning of the natural night.

units.la: 2. Et Athenienses quidem diem suum Civilem ab hac Epocha deduxisse testantur, Varro, Plinius, Censorinus, Theodorus Gaza, alii: Arabas autem, Georgius Cryfococces, & Ulul Beig. Idem etiam diei Civilis initium Bohemos, Silesios, Italos, Austricoíque observasse scribit Gassendus. Quibus annumerari possunt nomades Lybiae, veteres Germani, Galli, aliique qui tempora sua non per dies ut nos, sed per noctes ut Arabes numerabant, ut noctem dies praeferentes. Quam etiam ob rem veteres Graeci non ἡμέρνύκτιον ut S. Basilius in Hexaem, sed νυχθήμερον appellitabant, noctem ante diem collocantes.
units.tr: 2. The Athenians indeed are attested to have reckoned their civil day from this epoch, by Varro, Pliny, Censorinus, Theodorus Gaza and others; the Arabs by George Cryfococces and Ulugh Beg. Gassendi writes that the Bohemians, Silesians, Italians and Austrians likewise observed this beginning of the civil day. To these may be added the nomads of Libya, the ancient Germans, the Gauls and others who counted their times not by days as we do, but by nights as the Arabs do, placing the day after the night. For this reason also the ancient Greeks called the day-and-night not hēmērnyktion as St. Basil does in the Hexaemeron, but nychthēmeron, placing the night before the day. [ἡμέρνύκτιον; νυχθήμερον]

units.la: VI. 2. Ab exortu solis Babylonii praesertim & Graeci recentiores.
units.tr: VI. 2. From sunrise: the Babylonians especially, and the more recent Greeks.

units.la: 1. Hoc de Babyloniis affirmat Censorinus, dicens, Babylonii quidem a solis exortu ad exortum ejusdem astri diem statuerunt. Censor. c. 23. Et Plinius, Babylonii inter duos solis exortus. Plin. l. 2. c. 77. Quod confirmatur etiam a Varrone apud Macrobium & Aulum Gellium. Idem de Graecis recentioribus ut & Romanis asserit Theodorus Gaza, & de Norimbergensibus Gassendus.
units.tr: 1. Censorinus affirms this of the Babylonians, saying: "The Babylonians indeed reckoned the day from the sunrise to the sunrise of the same star." (Censorinus, ch. 23.) And Pliny: "The Babylonians [reckon the day] between two sunrises." (Pliny, bk. 2, ch. 77.) This is confirmed also by Varro, cited by Macrobius and Aulus Gellius. Theodorus Gaza asserts the same of the more recent Greeks and of the Romans, and Gassendi of the people of Nuremberg.

units.la: VII. 3. A meridie ad meridiem Umbri & Astronomi.
units.tr: VII. 3. From noon to noon: the Umbrians and the Astronomers.

units.la: 1. De Umbris à meridie ad meridiem diem suum Civilem computantibus locupletes habemus testes antea citatos, Varronem, Plinium & Censorinum.
units.tr: 1. For the Umbrians, who reckon their civil day from noon to noon, we have rich witnesses, already cited: Varro, Pliny and Censorinus.

units.la: 2. De Astronomis satis constat. E quibus tamen Alphonsus in tabulis Alphonsinis, diem suum ab ista meridie quæ diem propositum antecedit auspicatur: ut diem secundum Januarii à meridie primi. At Tycho Brahæ, Longomontanus in Danicis, Keplerus in Rudolphinis; Eichstadius, & plerique recentiores ab ipsa diei labentis meridie, ut secundum Januarii ab ipsa meridie istius diei: Quod in Astronomicis Epilogismis est inprimis observandum.
units.tr: 2. The practice of the Astronomers is well established. Among them, Alphonsus in the Alphonsine Tables begins his day from the noon that precedes the day in question, so that the second of January runs from the noon of the first. But Tycho Brahe, Longomontanus in the Danish tables, Kepler in the Rudolphine tables, Eichstadt, and most recent writers begin from the noon of the day that is currently running, so that the second of January runs from the noon of that same day. This must be carefully noted in the Astronomical Epilogisms.

units.la: VIII. 4. A media nocte ad mediam noctem, Ægyptii antiqui, Romani, nos.
units.tr: VIII. 4. From midnight to midnight: the ancient Egyptians, the Romans, and we.

units.la: 1. Romanos antiquos ab hac epocha diem incepisse fidem facit Censorinus, hisce verbis, Caeterum Romani à media nocte ad mediam noctem diem esse existimaverunt. Judicia sunt sacra publica, & auspicia etiam Magistratuum, quorum si quid ante medium noctis est actum, diei qui praeterit adscribitur, si quid autem post mediam noctem & ante lucem factum est, eo die gestum dicitur qui eam sequitur noctem. Cens. c. 23. Idem de Ægyptiis & Hipparcho tradit Plinius, l. 2. c. 77. Verum Astronomicae Hipparchi observationes ut à Ptolemaeo traditae, unà cum Ptolemaicis ab exortu solis progrediuntur. Quam quoque π̄ ιυχσnμίμ Epocham Chataiae & Igurae Astronomi: Item Copernicus, Reynoldus in Prutenicis, & Petavius in Parisinis observant, hi enim omnes à media nocte diem auspicantur. Nicolaus Mulerus tabulas suas Frisicas & meridiei & mediae nocti accommodavit. Haec apprime sunt necessaria quae à Chronologo perdiscantur, ne unum cum alia diem confundat.
units.tr: 1. That the ancient Romans began the day at this epoch is attested by Censorinus, in these words: Moreover, the Romans have held that the day runs from midnight to midnight. Public judgments are sacred, and so are the auspices of magistrates; if anything was done before midnight, it is assigned to the day that is passing, but if anything was done after midnight and before dawn, it is said to have been done on the day that follows that night. Censorinus, chapter 23. Pliny, book 2, chapter 77, hands down the same for the Egyptians and for Hipparchus. Yet the astronomical observations of Hipparchus, as transmitted by Ptolemy, together with the Ptolemaic ones, proceed from sunrise. The astronomers of Cathay and of Igura likewise observe this epoch; so too Copernicus, Reinhold in the Prutenic tables, and Petavius in the Parisian tables, for all of these begin the day from midnight. Nicolaus Mulerus adapted his Frisian tables to both noon and midnight. These matters are especially necessary for the chronologer to learn thoroughly, lest he confuse one day with another.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: De Hebdomade.
units.tr: On the Hebdomad.

units.la: Hebdomas est septem dierum Systema.
units.tr: A hebdomad is a system of seven days.

units.la: 1. HOC septem dierum Systema ab ipso mundi conditore institutum fuit, qui tam exemplo quàm præcepto homines sex diebus laboribus operam dare, septimo animum levare docuit. Et hinc est quod ab ipsis rerum incunabulis septima quoque dies à Patriarchis & Judæis celebrata fuit. A quibus etiam Gentiles institutum hoc acceptum observabant; unde Hesiodus initio ἡμαρ.
units.tr: 1. This system of seven days was instituted by the Creator of the world himself, who taught humankind, by example as well as by precept, to labour on six days and to rest their minds on the seventh. Hence it is that from the very beginnings of things the seventh day was also kept by the Patriarchs and the Jews. The Gentiles too observed this institution received from them; whence Hesiod, at the beginning of [ἡμαρ]:

units.la: Πρῶτον ἔνη, πευτάς τε ἡ ἰβδόμη ἱερὸν ἦμαρ,Primum novilunium, quartaque & septima sacra dies.
units.tr: First the new moon, and the fourth and the seventh, a holy day. [Πρῶτον ἔνη, πευτάς τε ἡ ἰβδόμη ἱερὸν ἦμαρ]

units.la: Alia septimæ cujusque diei celebrate vestigia; apud Homerum, Callimachum, Suetonium, Lucianum, aliósque Ethnicos Scriptores extant: unde Theophilus Antiochenus, Περὶ τῆς ἱβδόμης ἡμέρας ἣν πάντες ἑορτάζουσιν, De septima die quam omnes celebrant. Ad Autol. l. 2.
units.tr: Other traces of the celebration of every seventh day survive in Homer, Callimachus, Suetonius, Lucian, and other pagan writers. Hence Theophilus of Antioch, On the seventh day, which all keep [Περὶ τῆς ἑβδόμης ἡμέρας ἣν πάντες ἑορτάζουσιν], De septima die quam omnes celebrant, To Autolycus, book 2.

units.la: 2. Veteres autem Romani non Hebdomades sed Ogdoades peregisse videntur: idque propter nundinas quæ nono quolibet die celebratæ sunt, eâ tamen ratione, ut ipsi nundinarum dies unà putabantur; adeò ut septem tantùm dies solidi nundinas interfluerent, ut è Dyonysio Halicarnassensi & Varrone liquet. Et hinc factum est, quod in Augusti Kalendario, Romæ non ita pridem effossa, non septem, ut in nostris, sed octo notantur dies, octo istis literis, A. B. C. D. E. F. G. H. quæ rursum de novo incipientes totum percurrant Annum, non secus ac in nostris Kalendariis septem ex istis literis, viz. usq; ad G. inclusivè numeratis, ab initio ad anni finem ordine funguntur.
units.tr: 2. The ancient Romans, however, seem not to have reckoned by hebdomads but by ogdoads. This was on account of the market days (nundinae), which were held every ninth day; yet they were counted in such a way that the market day itself was reckoned as one of the days, so that only seven full days lay between markets, as is clear from Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Varro. Hence it is that in the Augustan calendar, dug up at Rome not long ago, not seven but eight days are marked, with these eight letters, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, which, beginning again anew, run through the whole year; just as in our calendars seven of these letters, namely up to and including G, are assigned in order from the beginning to the end of the year.

units.la: II. Nomen Hebdomadis dierum vel commune vel proprium est.
units.tr: II. The name of the days of the hebdomad is either common or proper.

units.la: III. Nomen omnibus Hebdomadæ diebus commune est Feria.
units.tr: III. The name common to all the days of the hebdomad is feria.

units.la: I. Quælibet Hebdomadis dies Feria nuncupatur, à Chronologis præsertim & Ecclesiasticis: Non quod in dies singulos Feriari necesse sit, sed propterea quòd paschalis olim prima fuit anni septimana, cujus singuli dies Feriati erant, & ab opere faciendo immunes, & idcirco singuli reliquarum etiam septimanarum eam consequentium dies Feriæ nominantur.
units.tr: I. Any day of the hebdomad is called feria, chiefly by chronologers and churchmen. This is not because it is necessary to keep a holiday on every single day, but because the first week of the year in the paschal reckoning once had all its days as holidays, free from work; and for this reason each of the following days of the other weeks too is called a feria.

units.la: IV. Nomina propria sunt vel Ethnica vel Christiana.
units.tr: IV. The proper names are either pagan or Christian.

units.la: V. Ethnica dierum nomina à planetis desumuntur, ut prima vocetur Solis, altera Lunæ, tertia Martis, quarta Mercurii, quinta Jovis, sexta Veneris, & septima Saturni.
units.tr: V. The pagan names of the days are taken from the planets: the first is called Sun's, the second Moon's, the third Mars's, the fourth Mercury's, the fifth Jupiter's, the sixth Venus's, and the seventh Saturn's.

units.la: I. Hæc Planetarum nomina ab Ægyptiis primò diebus indita fuisse testatur, Dio Cassius, l. 37.
