Qui duas etiam profert rationes quare idem Planetarum ordo in diebus ac in Cælis non observatur. Quarum una Harmonica est, altera Astrologica. Ratio Harmonica est ut Planetarum nomina diebus ἀπὸ προσώπων imponerentur. Diatesseron enim primas in musicis consonantiis obtinet, cujus ratio est sesquitertia, vel ut 4 ad 3, ut sit quartus sonus à primo inclusivè. Cæterum ordo Planetarum Cœlestis est Saturnus, Jupiter, Mars, Sol, Venus, Mercurius, Luna. Sol igitur quartus est à Saturno inclusivè, Luna à Sole, Mars à Luna; & sic deinceps. Et hinc est quod Planetæ in diebus denominandis ordine hoc harmonico progrediuntur, Saturnus, Sol, Luna, Mars, Mercurius, Jupiter, Venus,
units.tr: I. Dio Cassius, book 37, testifies that these names of the planets were first given to the days by the Egyptians. He also gives two reasons why the same order of the planets is not kept in the days as in the heavens. One is harmonic, the other astrological. The harmonic reason is that the names of the planets were imposed on the days from the persons [ἀπὸ προσώπων]. For the diatessaron holds the first place among musical consonances, and its ratio is sesquitertian, or 4 to 3, so that the fourth note is counted from the first inclusive. Now the celestial order of the planets is Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon. The Sun is therefore fourth from Saturn inclusive, the Moon from the Sun, Mars from the Moon, and so on. And hence the planets, in naming the days, proceed in this harmonic order: Saturn, Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus.

units.la: 2. Altera ratio est Astrologica, ut à quotidiano Planetarum dominio sumpta. Veteres enim Astrologi singulis singulorum dierum horis unum è Planetis præficiebant, ut primæ horæ primi diei septimanæ Saturnus præesset, secundæ Jupiter, tertiæ Mars,& sic usque ad octavam horam cui Saturnus iterum dominatur. Hoc autem ordine cùm Planetæ suis fungantur officiis, primam proximi diei horam Sol sibi subjectam vendicabit, primam tertii diei Luna, quarti Mars, quinti Mercurius,sexti Jupiter,septimi Venus, & deinde Saturnus in præsidium suum in primam proximi sive octavi diei horam iterum recurret. Et quoniam dies quælibet ab isto Planeta nomen sortita est quæ primæ ejus horæ præsidet, Saturnum Sol, Solem Luna, Lunam Mars, & sic deinceps excipiat necesse est.
units.tr: 2. The other reason is astrological, taken from the daily rule of the planets. For the ancient astrologers assigned one of the planets to each hour of each day: Saturn presided over the first hour of the first day of the week, Jupiter over the second, Mars over the third, and so on up to the eighth hour, over which Saturn again rules. In this order, since the planets perform their offices in turn, the Sun claims for itself the first hour of the next day, the Moon the first of the third day, Mars the fourth, Mercury the fifth, Jupiter the sixth, Venus the seventh, and then Saturn returns to its post at the first hour of the next or eighth day. And since each day has taken its name from the planet that presides over its first hour, it must follow that Saturn is succeeded by the Sun, the Sun by the Moon, the Moon by Mars, and so on.

units.la: VI. Nomina Christiana singulis Hebdomadæ diebus juxta ordinem cujusque suum imponuntur, ut una vocetur pri- ma, proxima secunda, & sic deinceps.
units.tr: VI. Christian names are imposed on the days of the hebdomad according to their order, so that one is called the first, the next the second, and so on.

units.la: 1. Omnes propemodum Orientales, ut Syri, Arabes, Æthiopes, & Persæ Christiani, non diem tantum Saturni sed & totam Hebdomadem Sabbat, sive Sanbat, appellant, & reliquas Hebdomadis ferias juxta ordinem suum à Sabbat denominant, ut diem solis primam Sabbat, Lunæ secundam, &c. Et aliquoties simpliciter primam, secundam, tertiam, quartam, &c. omissâ videlicet die.
units.tr: 1. Almost all Eastern Christians, such as the Syrians, Arabs, Ethiopians and Persians, call not only the day of Saturn but the whole hebdomad Sabbat or Sanbat, and they name the remaining days of the hebdomad by their order from the Sabbath, so that the day of the sun is the first after the Sabbath, the day of the moon the second, and so on. And sometimes they simply say first, second, third, fourth, and so on, the day in question being understood.

units.la: 2. Romani, Græcíque, præsertim Christiani æquè ac Gentiles Planetaria dierum nomina nonnunquam usurpant. Veteres quidem pariter ac recentiores. Nam Dies Solis apud Justinum Martyrem occurrit Apol. 2. Et dies Saturni æquè ac Solis apud Tertullianum Apol. c. 16. Verùm diem Solis sive primam septimanæ Feriam Κυριακὴν Dominicam sæpiùs appellant, nomine ab ipsis scripturis sacris deducto, ubi dicitur, Ἐγενόμην ἐν πνεύματι ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ, Apoc. 1. 10. 3. Persæ Gentiles Hebdomades non observant, sed singulis Mensis cujuslibet diebus propria imponunt nomina, quæ sic se habent. 1. Ourmuzd. 2. Behman. 3. Ardabahesht. 4. Sharivar. 5. Esphandarmod. 6. Chordad. 7. Mordad. 8. Dibadur. 9. Azur. 10. Aban. 11. Chaur. 12. Mah. 13. Tir. 14. Jius. 15. Dibameler. 16. Meher. 17. Surush. 18. Resh. 19. Fervardin. 20. Beheram. 21. Ram. 22. Bad. 23 Dibadin. 24 Din. 25. Erd. 26. Ashtad. 27. Osman. 28. Ramiyad. 29. Marasfend. 30. Anizan. Quinque autem [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters], sive Musterapa hoc modo denominant:
units.tr: 2. Romans and Greeks, especially Christians as well as Gentiles, sometimes use the planetary names of the days, both the ancients and the more recent writers. For the day of the Sun occurs in Justin Martyr, Apology 2, and the day of Saturn as well as of the Sun in Tertullian, Apology chapter 16. Yet they more often call the day of the Sun, that is the first feria of the week, Lord's [Κυριακήν], a name derived from the sacred Scriptures themselves, where it is said: I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day [Ἐγενόμην ἐν πνεύματι ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ], Revelation 1:10. 3. The Persian Gentiles do not observe hebdomads, but give proper names to the individual days of each month, which are as follows: 1. Ourmuzd. 2. Behman. 3. Ardabahesht. 4. Sharivar. 5. Esphandarmod. 6. Chordad. 7. Mordad. 8. Dibadur. 9. Azur. 10. Aban. 11. Chaur. 12. Mah. 13. Tir. 14. Jius. 15. Dibameler. 16. Meher. 17. Surush. 18. Resh. 19. Fervardin. 20. Beheram. 21. Ram. 22. Bad. 23. Dibadin. 24. Din. 25. Erd. 26. Ashtad. 27. Osman. 28. Ramiyad. 29. Marasfend. 30. Anizan. The five [illegible] days, or Musterapa, they name in this way:

units.la: 1. Ahnud. 2. Ashnud. 3. Esphendermed. 4. Vahesht. 5. Heshunesh. E quibus diebus iste qui idem quod ipse Mensis sortitur nomen Festus habetur.
units.tr: 1. Ahnud. 2. Ashnud. 3. Esphendermed. 4. Vahesht. 5. Heshunesh. Of these days, the one that receives the same name as the month itself is regarded as the festival.

units.la: CAP. VII. De Mense.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. On the Month.

units.la: I. Mensis est Systema 30 plus minus dierum.
units.tr: I. A month is a system of about 30 days.

units.la: II. Estque vel Naturalis vel Civilis.
units.tr: II. It is either natural or civil.

units.la: III. Naturalis est vel Lunaris vel Solaris.
units.tr: III. A natural month is either lunar or solar.

units.la: I. HAS mensium distinctiones Censorinus olim observavit. Dicit enim, Mensium genera duo, nam alii sunt Naturales, alii Civiles. Naturalium species duæ, quod partim Solis, partim Lunæ esse dicuntur. Cens. c. 22. Nos autem Lunarem Solari præponimus mensi, eò quòd ut annus ad solis, sic mensis ad Lunæ motus præcipuè dirigitur.
units.tr: I. Censorinus long ago noted these distinctions of months. For he says: There are two kinds of months, for some are natural and others civil. There are two species of natural months, since they are said to belong partly to the sun and partly to the moon. Censorinus, ch. 22. But we put the lunar month before the solar, because just as the year is chiefly governed by the motions of the sun, so the month is chiefly governed by the motions of the moon.

units.la: IV. Mensis Lunaris est vel Periodicus, vel Synodicus.
units.tr: IV. A lunar month is either periodic or synodic.

units.la: 1. Nonnulli tertium Mensem Lunarem addunt, illuminationis dictam, quod temporis est intervallum à prima Lunæ post coitum φάσιν usque ad ultimam ante subsequens novilunium fluens: vel quod idem est, totum illud temporis spatium quo Luna non ob vicinitatem ejus ad solis centrum occultata, faciem suam nobis videndam præbet, quod est dierum præterpropter 26. nonnunquam aliquid amplius, aliàs minus aliquid deprehenditur. Tempus autem quo Lunæ facies nobis penitus absconditur Interlunium vocatur.
units.tr: 1. Some add a third lunar month, called the illuminated month, which is the interval of time running from the moon's first appearance [φάσιν] after conjunction to its last appearance before the following new moon. Or, what comes to the same thing, it is the whole span of time during which the moon, not hidden from us by its nearness to the centre of the sun, shows us its face. This is roughly 26 days, sometimes a little more and sometimes a little less. The time during which the face of the moon is entirely hidden from us is called the interlunium.

units.la: V. Mensis periodicus est temporis Spatium quo Luna ab uno Zodiaci puncto digressa, ad idem redit, eique dierum circiter, 27. h. 7.
units.tr: V. The periodic month is the span of time in which the moon, having departed from one point of the zodiac, returns to the same point; it is about 27 days and 7 hours.

units.la: VI. Mensis Synodicus est spatium temporis quo Luna solem post Synodum relinquens, eundem assequitur, eique rursum conjungitur, eique dierum 29. hor. 12. 44'. 3''.
units.tr: VI. The synodic month is the span of time in which the moon, leaving the sun after conjunction, overtakes it again and is rejoined to it; it is 29 days, 12 hours, 44' 3''.

units.la: I. Ponamus enim Lunam hodie cum sole congredi sive conjunctam esse primo Libræ puncto, ut Sol & Luna in isto puncto simul versentur. Post dies 27, & horas circiter 7, Luna ad idem punctum iterum redibit, absolutâ nimirum suâ periodo, unde illud temporis Spatium Mensis periodicus nominatur. Luna vero ad hoc punctum regressa, solem ibi non inveniet, ubi reliquit, quippe qui motu suo is тi inima istis 27 diebus ad vigesimum septimum ejusdem signi gradum promovetur. Luna igitur cum sole priùs rursum conjungi nequit, quàm istos 27 libræ gradus etiam percurrit: quibus peragrandis duos dies & horas circiter 5 requirit, medio viz. suo motu 5 adeò ut totum temporis spatium quod Luna duas inter Synodos movetur, fit dier. 29. h. 12. 44'. 3''. quod igitur Mensis Synodicus appellatur.
units.tr: I. Let us suppose that the moon today meets or is conjoined with the sun at the first point of Libra, so that the sun and moon are together at that point. After 27 days and about 7 hours, the moon will return to the same point, having completed its period; this span of time is therefore called the periodic month. But the moon, having returned to this point, will not find the sun where it left it, since the sun, by its own motion, has during those 27 days advanced to the twenty-seventh degree of the same sign. So the moon cannot be joined to the sun again until it has also traversed those 27 degrees of Libra. To traverse them takes about two days and 5 hours at its average motion. So the whole span of time the moon takes between two conjunctions is 29 days, 12 hours, 44' 3'', and this is called the synodic month.

units.la: 2. In Mensibus hisce percurrendis Luna varias subit mutationes. Nam uno circiter ante & post Synodum die nobis tota velatur, secundo circiter post conjunctionem die,
units.tr: 2. In running through these months the moon undergoes various changes. For about one day before and one day after the conjunction it is wholly veiled from us; about the second day after conjunction

units.la: • manosdiis μηνες ἁπλῶς Falcata, octavo Δι�ότομο Dimidiata, duodecimo ἀμφίωσις Gibbosa, decimo quinto πανσέληνο Plena, & rursum duodevigesimo ἀμφίωσις, vigesimo tertio Διχότομο, duodetrigesimo μηνες ἁπλῶς apparet. Quas Lunæ configurationes Græci σχηματισμοὺς vocant.
units.tr: • it is a bare crescent [μηνοειδής], on the eighth day halved [διχότομος], on the twelfth gibbous [ἀμφίκυρτος], on the fifteenth full [πανσέληνος]; and again, on the twenty-second gibbous [ἀμφίκυρτος], on the twenty-third halved [διχότομος], and on the twenty-eighth it appears as a bare crescent [μηνοειδής] again. The Greeks call these appearances of the moon figures [σχηματισμοὺς].

units.la: VII. Mensis Solaris est temporis spatium quo Sol quovis Zodiaci percurrit signum.
units.tr: VII. The solar month is the span of time in which the sun traverses any one sign of the zodiac.

units.la: 1. In Zodiaco duodecim numerantur Signa, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpius, Sagittarius, Capricornus, Aquarius, Pisces. Tempus igitur quod Sol singulis hisce signis motu suo ἐν τῷ ἑπιμένα peragrandis absumit, Mensis solaris nominatur. At quoniam longius in aliquibus ex hisce signis quàm in aliis moretur, hinc Menses hi solares evadunt inæquales. Verùm si medii defectum inter & excessum assumantur, quilibet eorum erit dierum 30. hor. 10. 29'. 5''.
units.tr: 1. Twelve signs are counted in the zodiac: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces. The time the sun takes in its own course to pass through each of these signs is called a solar month. But since the sun lingers longer in some of these signs than in others, these solar months turn out unequal. If, however, we take the mean between the deficiency and the excess, each of them is 30 days, 10 hours, 29' 5''.

units.la: VIII. Mensis Civilis est numerus dierum quem unaquæque Civitas pro instituto observat.
units.tr: VIII. The civil month is the number of days that each state observes by its own institution.

units.la: 1. Menses tam solares quàm Lunares præter dies completos, horas insuper atque Scrupula colligunt, unde usui civili aptè non accommodentur. Hinc unaquæque civitas vel natio certum quendam dierum numerum instituit, qui tamen quàm proximè Luminarium ad motus accederent, eúmque Mensem appellant.
units.tr: 1. Both solar and lunar months gather, besides whole days, also hours and scruples, so they are not suitable for civil use. Hence each state or nation establishes a certain fixed number of days, chosen to come as close as possible to the motions of the luminaries, and calls this a month.

units.la: 2. Qui Annis Lunaribus utuntur, Menses suos alternis 29, & 30 dierum constituunt; propterèa quòd Mensis Lunaris sit dierum 29, & hor. 12. circiter, quæ bis collectæ solidum efficiunt diem. Quibus anni solares magis arridént, isti Menses suos diversimodè definiunt. Nam in anno Juliano nonnulli Menses sunt 31, alii 30, unus nunc 28, nunc 29 dierum. In anno Ægyptiaco omnes Menses sunt ϛɩɑκοντα Ϛɩωρʹ, sive triccnarii quorum ad calcem quinque ἐπαγόμεναι adjiciuntur. Sed de hisce posthæc agendum erit.
units.tr: 2. Those who use lunar years make their months alternately 29 and 30 days long, because a lunar month is about 29 days and 12 hours, and these twelve-hour halves, collected in pairs, make a full day. Those who prefer solar years define their months in different ways. In the Julian year some months have 31 days, others 30, and one has 28 or 29. In the Egyptian year all the months are thirty-day months [τριάκοντα ἡμερῶν], called triacenarii, and at the end five epagomenal days [ἐπαγόμεναι] are added. But these matters must be discussed later.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: De Anno.
units.tr: On the Year.

units.la: Annus est Systema Mensium. II. Estque vel Cœlestis vel Civilis. III. Cœlestis est vel Solaris vel Lunaris.
units.tr: A year is a system of months. II. It is either celestial or civil. III. The celestial year is either solar or lunar.

units.la: I. NUllus est è septem Planetis, à cujus revolutione per Zodiacum annus non constituatur. Sed usus obtinuit, ut ex eorum tantum Planetárum, qui nobis majores videntur, solis videlicet & Lunæ, motibus, Annus mensuretur. Annuas igitur aliorum Planetarum conversiones prætereo, ut & totius Firmamenti per Zodiacum, cujus circumvolutio Magnus nonnullis Annus vocatur.
units.tr: I. There is none of the seven planets by whose revolution through the Zodiac a year is not measured. But custom has prevailed that the year is measured only by the motions of those planets which appear larger to us, namely the Sun and the Moon. I therefore pass over the annual revolutions of the other planets, as also that of the whole firmament through the Zodiac, whose circuit some call the Great Year.

units.la: IV. Annus Solaris est vel Tropicus vel Sydereus. V. Annus Tropicus est temporis spatium quo Sol ab uno aliquo è punctis Cardinalibus digressus ad idem revertitur; estque dier. 365. hor. 5. 49′.
units.tr: IV. The solar year is either tropical or sidereal. V. The tropical year is the span of time in which the Sun, departing from one of the cardinal points, returns to the same point; it is 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes.

units.la: I. Puncta Cardinalia duo æquinoctia totidemque solstitia dicuntur, quæ quoniam τροπαί Græcis vocantur, hinc annus hic Tropicus, sive vertens nominatur: ut & Æquinoctialis si ab æquinoctio, solstitialis si à solstitio utrovis numeretur.
units.tr: I. The cardinal points are the two equinoxes and the two solstices. Because the Greeks call these tropai [τροπαί], this year is called Tropical, or "turning," and likewise Equinoctial if it is counted from an equinox, or Solstitial if it is counted from a solstice.

units.la: 2. Quanta vero sit exacta anni Tropici mensura, nondum inter ipsos convenit Astronomos. Hi enim plus, illi minùs quàm scrupula 49′ ultra dies 365 & horas 5, ei largiuntur. Nos scrupulis secundis quæ prima 49′ vel excedunt, vel ad ea complenda desiderentur; neglectis, annum Tropicum diebus 365, horis 5, 49′ præcisè definimus; & pronunciamus solem Luminarium principem omnia Zodiaci signa motu suo ᾿εἰς τὰ ἰπώμεια, sive ab occasu ad ortum isto temporis intervallo perlustrare.
units.tr: 2. As to how exact the measure of the tropical year is, the astronomers have not yet agreed among themselves. For some grant it more, others less, than 49 minutes beyond 365 days and 5 hours. We, neglecting the seconds, which either exceed the first 49 minutes or are wanting to complete them, define the tropical year precisely as 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes; and we declare that the Sun, the prince of the luminaries, traverses all the signs of the Zodiac with its motion, going from west to east [εἰς τὰ ἑῷα], in this interval of time.

units.la: 3. Non quòd Sol eodem temporis tractu singula Zodiaci signa percurrat. Nam in Arcu signiferi ab Ariete ad Libram porrecto diuùs moratur, quàm in altero qui à Libra ad Arietem extenditur; idque propter solis, terræ respectu, eccentricitatem quæ efficit, ut Sol aliquando à terrâ altior subvehatur, ut in ἀπογείῳ, aliàs ei propinquior & in περιγείῳ existat. Et quo ἀπογείῳ propinquior est, eò tardior, quo remotior, eò celerior nobis motus videtur. Quo fit ut ex Tychonis sententiâ, Sol ab Ariete ad Libram, sive ab æquinoctio Verno ad Autumnale, non minori temporis spatio quam dieb. 186. hor. 18. 30′ moveatur, à Libra autem ad Arietem non majori quàm dieb. 178. hor. 11. 19′. Verùm à quocunque puncto cardinali Sol digrediatur, post dies 365 horas 5, 49′ ad idem regredietur; adeò ut si, verbi gratiâ, Sol hoc anno primum Arietis punctum invadat, & sic æquinoctium Vernum conficeret Martii 10 meridie post evolutos dies 365 h. 5 49′ ad idem ejusdem signi punctum iterum revertetur, & idem restituet æquinoctium. Hoc igitur est istud temporis intervallum, quem Annum Tropicum appellamus.
units.tr: 3. Not that the Sun runs through the individual signs of the Zodiac in the same span of time. For it lingers longer on the arc of the zodiac stretching from Aries to Libra than on the other, which extends from Libra to Aries. This is because of the eccentricity of the Sun relative to the earth, which makes the Sun at times carried higher from the earth, as at apogee [ἀπογείῳ], and at other times nearer to it, and at perigee [περιγείῳ]. And the nearer it is to apogee, the slower, and the farther, the faster its motion appears to us. Hence, according to Tycho's opinion, the Sun moves from Aries to Libra, that is, from the vernal to the autumnal equinox, in a span of time not less than 186 days, 18 hours, 30 minutes, and from Libra to Aries in no more than 178 days, 11 hours, 19 minutes. Yet from whatever cardinal point the Sun sets out, after 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes it returns to the same point. So if, for example, the Sun this year takes up the first point of Aries and thus completes the vernal equinox on March 10 at noon, then after 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes have passed it will again return to the same point of that sign and restore the same equinox. This, then, is the interval of time which we call the tropical year.

units.la: VI. Annus Sidereus est temporis spatium quo Sol ab unâ ad eandem stellam fixam circumvolvitur, estque dier. 365. hor. 6. 9′. 11″. 22‴.
units.tr: VI. The sidereal year is the span of time in which the Sun revolves from one and the same fixed star back to it; it is 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, 11 seconds, 22 thirds.

units.la: 1. Nimirum stellæ quoque fixæ pariter ac Planetæ tardo quodam, & sero tandem intellecto motu, orientem versus revolvuntur, idque in singulos quidem annos gr. o. o′. 49″. 49″. 54″. Sol igitur ab aliquâ stellâ fixâ digressus cùm an-num suum Tropicum absolverit, eandem stellam fixam non assequitur, usque dùm scrupula 49′. 45″. ulteriùs peragravit; quæ non nisi hor. 0. 20′. 11″. 22‴. permetiri queat. Addas igitur horas 0. 2c′. 11″. 22‴. ad dies 365 hor. 5. 49′. & exurget anni siderei quantitas dier. 365. hor. 6. 9′. 11″. 22‴.
units.tr: 1. Indeed the fixed stars too, like the planets, revolve eastward by a certain slow motion, understood only late, namely by 0 degrees, 0 minutes, 49 seconds, 49 thirds, 54 fourths in each year. Therefore the Sun, having set out from some fixed star and completed its tropical year, does not reach that same fixed star until it has traversed a further 49 minutes, 45 seconds; and this can be measured only in 0 hours, 20 minutes, 11 seconds, 22 thirds. Add, then, 0 hours, 20 minutes, 11 seconds, 22 thirds to 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes, and the quantity of the sidereal year arises: 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, 11 seconds, 22 thirds.

units.la: VII. Annus Lunaris est Systema mensium duodecim Lu-narium, estque dierum 354. hor. 8. 48′.
units.tr: VII. The lunar year is a system of twelve lunar months; it is 354 days, 8 hours, 48 minutes.

units.la: 1. Mensis Lunaris, ut modo insinuavimus, est dierum 29. hor. 12. 44′. quæ duodecies multiplicata producunt anni Lunaris quantitatem dier. 354. hor. 8. 48′. Aufer dies 354. hor. 8. 48′. è diebus 365 hor. 5. 49′. & reliqua fit differentia anni Tropici & Lunaris, d. 10. hor. 21. 1′. Et quoniam hi undecim propemodum dies ad annum Lu-narem quotannis adjiciuntur ut Tropicum exæquet, hinc Epactales, sive Epacta nuncupatur.
units.tr: 1. A lunar month, as we have just hinted, is 29 days, 12 hours, 44 minutes. Multiplied twelve times, these produce the quantity of the lunar year: 354 days, 8 hours, 48 minutes. Subtract 354 days, 8 hours, 48 minutes from 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes, and the remaining difference between the tropical and lunar year is 10 days, 21 hours, 1 minute. And since nearly these eleven days are added to the lunar year each year so that it may equal the tropical, it is therefore called the epactal year, or Epact.

units.la: VIII. Anni Civiles sunt quibus civitates vel gentes pro arbitrio utuntur.
units.tr: VIII. Civil years are those which cities or peoples use at their discretion.

units.la: IX. Sunt que vel Solares vel Lunares.
units.tr: IX. These are either solar or lunar.

units.la: X. Solares sunt qui ad solis motus exiguntur.
units.tr: X. Solar years are those which are fitted to the motions of the sun.

units.la: XI. Sunt vel vagi vel fixi.
units.tr: XI. They are either wandering or fixed.

units.la: XII. Solares fixi sunt quorum initia in eădem tempestate fixa manent, quales sunt Julianus, Gregorianus, Attiacus, Gelaleus, &c.
units.tr: XII. Fixed solar years are those whose beginnings remain fixed at the same season, such as the Julian, Gregorian, Attic, Jalali, etc.

units.la: XIII. Solares vagi sunt quorum initia per omnes anni Tro-pici tempestates vagantur, cujusmodi sunt Nabonasareus, & Tezdegerdicus.
units.tr: XIII. Wandering solar years are those whose beginnings wander through all the seasons of the tropical year, such as the Nabonassarean and the Yazdegerdian.

units.la: XIV. Anni Lunares sunt qui ad Lunæ motus accommodantur.
units.tr: XIV. Lunar years are those which are adapted to the motions of the moon.

units.la: XV. Hi sunt etiam vel Fixi vel Vagi.
units.tr: XV. These too are either fixed or wandering.

units.la: XVI. Lunares Fixi sunt qui embolismo in eădem propemodum anni tempestate perpetuò cohibentur, cujusmodi sunt Atticus, & Judaicus.
units.tr: XVI. Fixed lunar years are those which are held constantly, by the intercalary month, at nearly the same season of the year, such as the Attic and the Jewish.

units.la: XVII. Anni Lunares vagi sunt qui singulas anni tempestates effrænatè percurrunt, qualis est solus annus Alukamuiedicus.
units.tr: XVII. Wandering lunar years are those which run unrestrainedly through every season of the year, such as the Alukamuiedic year alone.

units.la: I. Hìc nudas annorum Civilium definitiones exhibemus, propterea quòd omnes isti Civiles anni sigillatim sunt exponendi: non tamen Methodo quâ hìc proponuntur, idcirco quod nonnullæ sunt nationes & civitates quæ diversas annorum formas admiserunt: Atque ideo Methodum nostram in Civilibus hisce annis explicandis à populis usitantibus potiùs quàm ab annis usitatis contexere multùm præstat.
units.tr: I. Here we set out the bare definitions of the civil years, because all these civil years are to be explained one by one. Yet they are not set out here in the method in which they are proposed, because there are some nations and states which have admitted various forms of years. Therefore it is far better, in explaining these civil years, to frame our method from the peoples who use them rather than from the years themselves.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: De anno Juliano, & Gregoriano.
units.tr: On the Julian and Gregorian year.

units.la: Anni Civiles Chronologo præcipuè perdiscendi sunt Romanus, Ægyptiacus, Persicus, Syriacus, Græcus, Judaicus, Muhammedanus.
units.tr: The civil years a chronologer must especially learn are the Roman, Egyptian, Persian, Syrian, Greek, Jewish, and Muhammadan.

units.la: II. Annus Romanus duplex est Julianus & Gregorianus.
units.tr: II. The Roman year is of two kinds, the Julian and the Gregorian.

units.la: I. ANtiquum Romanorum annum ante Julium Cæsarem iis usitatum hîc praetereo, utpote de quo vix quippiam certi traditum habemus. Annum à Romulo urbis conditore institutum, aliquo saltem modo Lunarem fuisse, plusquam verisimile est, ut & eundem, decem con-stitisse mensibus, juxta ista Nasonis Carmina Fast. l. I.
units.tr: I. I pass over here the ancient Roman year used before Julius Caesar, since we have little certain tradition about it. That the year instituted by Romulus, the founder of the city, was at least in some sense lunar is more than probable, and that it consisted of ten months, according to these verses of Ovid, Fasti book 1:

units.la: Tempora digereret cum conditor Urbis, in anno Constitut Menses quinque bis esse suo.
units.tr: When the founder of the City arranged the seasons, he made the year consist of five months, twice over.

units.la: 2. Hanc, qualiscunque fuit, anni rationem à Romulo constitutam. Numa Pompilius successor ejus immutavit, aliósque duos adjecit Menses, Januarium, puta & Februarium, totúmque definivit annum communem diebus 355: quem ut intra cardines Solares cohiberet, post annos duos 22, post duos alios 23 dies inter terminalia & regifugium, hoc est inter 23, & 24 Februarii intercalandos docuit: Quos dies Mensem μηρύσιον vocavit, teste Plutarcho. Intercalandi verò potestas tota penes pontifices fuit, qui tamen eâ usque adeò sunt abusi, ut ante Julii Cæsaris ætatem Menses Hiberni in Autumnum, autumnales in æstatem, & sic deinceps retroversi sunt.
units.tr: 2. Romulus set up this year, whatever its form was. His successor Numa Pompilius changed it, adding two more months, January and February, and fixed the whole common year at 355 days. To keep it within the limits of the solar year, he taught that after two years an intercalary period of 22 days, and after two more years one of 23 days, was to be inserted between the Terminalia and the Regifugium, that is, between 23 and 24 February. Plutarch reports that he called these days the μηρύσιον [μηρύσιον]. The power of intercalation lay wholly with the pontiffs, but they so abused it that before the time of Julius Caesar the winter months had slipped back into autumn, the autumn months into summer, and so on in turn.

units.la: III. Annus Julianus est Solaris fixus, diebus constans 365, horis 6.
units.tr: III. The Julian year is a fixed solar year, consisting of 365 days and 6 hours.

units.la: 1. Hic Annus Julianus dicitur à Julio Cæsare Dictatore qui primus eum instituit. Hic enim annum Romanorum civilem pontificum licentiâ depravatum animadvertens, Lunarem anni formam penitus abrogavit, ejúsque loco Solarem instituit. Et ut Menses in pristinas sedes revocaret, non tantum dies 23 inter terminalia & regifugium anno quo huic castigationi operam locavit, auctoritate suâ pontificiali intercalavit, sed & alios dies 67 inter Novembrem & Decembrem inseruit unde quantitas istius anni evasit dier. 445. Et cùm ab Ægyptiis didicisset annum Solarem esse dierum 365 hor. 6, hinc eam anni quantitatem à Romanis observari decrevit. Annus quo hæc gesta sunt erat per Jul. 4668, ante Christum 46. Qui & annus Confusionis vocatur, ut dier. 445. IV. Annus Julianus est vel communis vel Bisextilis. V. Annus Communis est dierum 365. Bisextilis dier.366.
units.tr: 1. This year is called the Julian after Julius Caesar, the Dictator, who was the first to institute it. Noticing that the civil year of the Romans had been corrupted by the licence of the pontiffs, he entirely abolished the lunar form of the year and put a solar one in its place. In order to restore the months to their former places, in the year in which he undertook this correction he not only intercalated by his own pontifical authority the 23 days between the Terminalia and the Regifugium, but also inserted another 67 days between November and December, so that the length of that year came to 445 days. And since he had learned from the Egyptians that the solar year is 365 days and 6 hours, he decreed that the Romans should observe this length of year. The year in which these things were done was Julian year 4668, 46 years before Christ. It is also called the year of Confusion, since it had 445 days. IV. The Julian year is either common or bissextile. V. A common year has 365 days; a bissextile year has 366 days.

units.la: 1. Julius Cæsar, ut dixi, anni Romani quantitatem fore dierum 365. hor. 6. decrevit. At sex istæ appensæ horæ quater collectæ horas 24, id est solidum constituunt diem. Quapropter annos tres dierum fore tantùm 365, & quarto diem istum è 6 horis quater collectis productum, intercalatum fore pronunciavit; ut dierum esset 366.
units.tr: 1. As I said, Julius Caesar decreed that the length of the Roman year should be 365 days and 6 hours. But those six hours, gathered up four times, make 24 hours, that is, one full day. Therefore he pronounced that three years would have only 365 days, and that in the fourth year that day, produced from the six hours gathered four times, would be intercalated, so that the year had 366 days.

units.la: 2. Dies iste intercalaris eodem in loco inserendus fuit, quo Mensis in anno Pompiliano, viz. post terminalia, sive Feb. 23. Cæterum Februarii 23 est septimus Kalendas Martii, & Feb. 24 Sextus Kal. Martii, hinc est quod anno intercalari sextus Kal. Martii bis numeretur, unde non dies tantùm ipse, sed & totus annus Bisextilis nominatur.
units.tr: 2. This intercalary day was to be inserted in the same place where the month was placed in the Pompilian year, namely after the Terminalia, that is on 23 February. Now 23 February is the seventh day before the Kalends of March, and 24 February the sixth before the Kalends of March. Hence in an intercalary year the sixth before the Kalends of March is counted twice, and so not only that day but the whole year is called bissextile.

units.la: VI. Menses in anno Juliano unà cum ipsorum quantitate, in hoc latercùlo exhibentur.
units.tr: VI. The months of the Julian year, together with their lengths, are shown in this little table.

units.la: Menses Juliani | Dies Men-fis. | Dies Coll. Januaris. | 31 | 31 Februarius. | 28 | 59 Martius. | 31 | 90 Aprilis. | 30 | 120 Maius. | 31 | 151 Junius. | 30 | 181 Julius. | 31 | 212 Augustus. | 31 | 243 September. | 30 | 273 October. | 31 | 304 November. | 30 | 334 December. | 31 | 365
units.tr: Months of the Julian year | Days of the month | Cumulative days. January | 31 | 31. February | 28 | 59. March | 31 | 90. April | 30 | 120. May | 31 | 151. June | 30 | 181. July | 31 | 212. August | 31 | 243. September | 30 | 273. October | 31 | 304. November | 30 | 334. December | 31 | 365

units.la: 1. In hoc pinacidio non tantùm expansorum sive singulorum, sed & collectorum, quantitatem Mensium videre est. Menses autem hic descripti sunt anni communis, nam in Bisextili Februarius dies 29 habet. Januarius perpetuò chorum ducit in anno Juliano, ut Martius in anno Pompiliano. Julius & Augustus Quintilis & sextilis olim vocati sunt eò quòd iste quintus, hic sextus erat à Martio inclusivè.
units.tr: 1. In this table one can see the length of the months both singly and cumulatively. The months are described here for a common year, since in a bissextile year February has 29 days. January always leads the way in the Julian year, as March does in the Pompilian. July and August were formerly called Quintilis and Sextilis, because the one was the fifth and the other the sixth month counting inclusively from March.

units.la: 2. Quilibet ex hisce Mensibus in tres partes distribuitur, Kalendas, Nonas, & Idus vocatas. Kalendæ dicitur primus Mensis cujusque dies. Martius, Maius, Julius & October sex habent Nonas, reliqui Menses quatuor. Juxta istos versiculos,
units.tr: 2. Each of these months is divided into three parts, called the Kalends, Nones, and Ides. The first day of each month is called the Kalends. March, May, July and October have six Nones; the remaining months have four. According to these lines:

units.la: Sex Majus nonas, October, Julius, & Mars, Quatuor at reliqui, dabit idus quilibet Octo.
units.tr: May, October, July and March have Nones on the sixth; the others have them on the fourth; every month has Ides on the eighth.

units.la: Hæ Mensium Julianorum partes ordine retrogrado numerantur. Januarius quatuor habet nonas: Idcirco post Kalendas sequitur quartus nonas, deinde tertius, tum pridie nonas. Quintus ergo dies est primus Nonarum, sive ipsæ nonæ. Nonas excipiunt Idus perpetuo octo, retrò quoque numeratæ; ut sextus Januarii dies vocetur 8 Idus, Septimus 7, Octavus 6 Iduum vel Idus, & sic usque ad 13 qui Idus dicitur. Dies cujuslibet Mensis qui Idus sequuntur à Kalendis proximi Mensis, retro putatis numerantur; ut dies 14 Jan. est undevigesimus à Kalendis Februarii inclusive, dicitur itaque 19 Kal. Feb. & dies 15 Januarii, est 18 Kal. Feb. & sic usque ad ultimum Januarii qui scribitur Pridie Kal. Feb. & sic in reliquis Mensibus, ut è Kalendario Juliano ad calcem harum institutionum descripto, clarius elucescet.
units.tr: These parts of the Julian months are counted backwards. January has four Nones, so after the Kalends comes the fourth of the Nones, then the third, then the day before the Nones. The fifth day is therefore the first of the Nones, that is, the Nones themselves. The Nones are followed by the Ides, always eight, likewise counted backwards, so that the sixth day of January is called the eighth before the Ides, the seventh the seventh, the eighth the sixth before the Ides, and so on up to the 13th, which is called the Ides. Any day of a month that falls after the Ides is counted backwards from the Kalends of the next month; thus 14 January is the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, inclusive, and so it is called the 19th before the Kalends of February; 15 January is the 18th before the Kalends of February; and so on until the last day of January, which is written as the day before the Kalends of February. The same holds for the other months, as will be clearer from the Julian calendar printed at the end of these institutes.

units.la: 3. Et hæc quidem Mensium Julianorum partitio, ab ipso Romulo primò instituta fuit, quam non tantum Numa Pompilius, sed & Julius Cæsar retinuit, ut stata sacra ab ipso Romulo instituta religiosè custodiret. Quo factum est ut Romani scriptores quoto die Mensis quippiam gestum fuerit, nostrûm ad instar, nunquam exprimunt; sed quoto die Kalendarum, Nonarum vel Iduum; ut si Septembris quartum indigitarent, non dicerent Sept. 4. Sed Pridie Nonas Septembris. Si Sept. 24. exprimerent, 8 Kal. Oct. dicunt, & sic in reliquis,
units.tr: 3. This division of the Julian months was first instituted by Romulus himself, and was retained not only by Numa Pompilius but also by Julius Caesar, so that the fixed sacred days instituted by Romulus would be religiously observed. As a result, Roman writers never expressed the day of the month on which something happened in our manner, but always by the day before the Kalends, Nones or Ides. So if they wished to indicate 4 September, they would not say 4 September, but the day before the Nones of September. If they wished to express 24 September, they say the eighth day before the Kalends of October, and so on for the rest.

units.la: VII. Annus Gregorianus est Julianus castigatus.
units.tr: VII. The Gregorian year is the Julian year corrected.

units.la: VIII. Inter annum Julianum & Gregorianum hoc tantùm interest, quòd post annum Christi 1600, è singulis quatuor annis centesimis, qui omnes in formâ Juliana sunt Bissextiles, in Gregoriana tres primi sunt communes, & quartus solus Bissextilis.
units.tr: VIII. Between the Julian and the Gregorian year the only difference is this: after the year of Christ 1600, of each set of four centennial years, which are all bissextile in the Julian form, in the Gregorian form the first three are common and only the fourth is bissextile.

units.la: I. Synodus Oecumenica Niceæ habita anno Christi 325 paschalem celebritatem die Dominicâ, quæ plenilunium istud excipit quod æquinoctium vernum proximè secutum est, peragendam sancivit. Æquinoctium porro vernum istis temporibus die 20 vel 21 Martii commissum est, duo namque dies æquinoctiis perpetuo sunt assignandi propter annos communes & Bissextiles. Ad plenilunia verò quotannis invenienda, patres illi cyclum Lunarem, aureum numerum dictum instituebant, qui plenilunia sive quartus decimas ut iis persuasum fuit, in singulos annos indigitarent. Verùm enim verò cyclum istum Lunarem plenilunia non rectè post aliquas annorum centurias judicare, & ipsa etiam æquinoctia versus mensium initia in anno Juliano retroversa esse tandem aliquando deprehensum fuit; adeo ut anno Christi 1582 æquinoctia diebus decem, quatriduo plenilunia retroacta sint; & æquinoctium istud quod temporibus Nicenis Martii 20, anno Christi 1582 Martii 10, & plenilunium quod tunc temporis Aprilis 5, jam Kalendis Aprilibus commissum sit.
units.tr: I. The Ecumenical Council held at Nicaea in the year of Christ 325 decreed that the paschal celebration should be kept on the Sunday following the full moon that comes next after the vernal equinox. In those times the vernal equinox fell on 20 or 21 March, since two days must always be assigned to the equinox because of common and bissextile years. To find the full moons each year, the Fathers instituted a lunar cycle, called the golden number, which they believed would indicate the full moons, or fourteenth days, for each year. But it was later discovered that this lunar cycle did not correctly show the full moons after some centuries, and that the equinoxes themselves had slipped back in the Julian year relative to the beginnings of the months; so that in the year of Christ 1582 the equinoxes were ten days early and the full moons four days early. The equinox which in Nicene times fell on 20 March fell in 1582 on 10 March, and the full moon which then fell on 5 April now fell on the Kalends of April.

units.la: II. Hinc est quod anno Christi prædicto 1582 Gregorius 13 pontifex Romanus cyclo Lunari abrogato, ejus loco cyclum quendam epactarum substituit, & ut æquinoctium vernum ad sedes Nicenas revocaret, ex anno prædicto 1582 Mense Octobri decem dies subtraxit, ut diem Octobris quartum non quintus, sed decimus quintus proximus exciperet; ut ita dies decimus quo æquinoctium consectum sectum fuit, vigesimus diceretur; & undecimus, vigesimus primus. Quos dies æquinoctia ne postea deserrent versus Mensis principium adhuc retroversa, novam hanc anni formam ab ipso Gregorianam dictam instituit: quâ annis, quibuslibet 400 tres dies intercalares omittuntur. Idque hâc quidem ratione, omnes centesimos à Christo annos in formâ Juliana Bissextiles esse neminem fugiat. Gregorius autem edicto suo sancivit, ut post annum Christi 1600, è quatuor annis centesimis, unus isque ultimus tantum Bissextilis esset, reliqui tres communes, dierum solummodo 365. Ex. gr. ut anni in Æra Christiana 1700, 1800, 1900 qui formâ Juliana sunt Bisextiles jam fiant communes, sed annus 2000 pristino more Bissextum suum retineat; & sic postea anni 2100, 2200, 2300 sint communes, at 2400 Bissextilis: ut quemadmodum annus quisque quartus in Æra Christi Bisextilis est, reliqui communes, sic in Gregoriana anni formâ post annum 1600, quadringentesimus quisque erit Bissextilis, reliqui vero omnes Communes.
units.tr: II. Hence it is that in the year of Christ 1582 Pope Gregory XIII, having abolished the lunar cycle, substituted in its place a certain cycle of epacts; and, so that the vernal equinox might be brought back to the seat it had at Nicaea, he subtracted ten days from the month of October in the aforesaid year 1582, so that the fifth day of October was not followed by the sixth but by the fifteenth; thus the tenth day, on which the equinox had been fixed, came to be called the twentieth, and the eleventh was called the twenty-first. And so that the equinoxes should not again slip back toward the beginning of the month, he instituted this new form of the year, called Gregorian after himself: in it three intercalary days are omitted in every 400 years. And this is done for the following reason: let no one forget that in the Julian form all the centennial years from Christ are bissextile. Gregory, however, decreed by his edict that after the year of Christ 1600, of the four centennial years only the last one should be bissextile, and the other three common, of 365 days only. For example, the years 1700, 1800 and 1900 in the Christian Era, which in the Julian form are bissextile, now become common, but the year 2000 retains its bissextile status according to the old custom; and so afterwards the years 2100, 2200 and 2300 are common, but 2400 is bissextile. Thus, just as every fourth year in the Christian Era is bissextile and the rest common, so in the Gregorian form of the year, after the year 1600, every four-hundredth year will be bissextile and all the rest common.

units.la: 3. Porro quoniam annis 400 plus minus æquinoctia in anno Juliano tribus diebus retroaguntur, propter dierum Bissextilium, citius quam par fuit, intercalationem, hinc isto annorum numero Bissextis omissis tribus, iisdem propemodum diebus, viz. Martii 20 & 21 perpetuò fixa videntur. Novam hanc anni formam invenit Aloysius Lilius, unde & Liliana pariter ac Gregoriana nonnunquam audit; & propterea quòd paucis tantum abhinc annis instituta fuit, hinc Stylus novus vocatur, ut vetus Julianus.
units.tr: 3. Moreover, since in about 400 years the equinoxes in the Julian year fall back by about three days, on account of the intercalation of bissextile days being done more quickly than it should have been, so with three of these years' bissextiles omitted, the equinox seems to be fixed more or less on the same days, namely March 20 and 21. This new form of the year was devised by Aloysius Lilius, whence it is also sometimes called Liliana as well as Gregoriana; and because it was instituted only a few years ago, it is called the New Style, as the Julian is the Old Style.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: De anno Ægyptiaco & Æthiopico.
units.tr: On the Egyptian and Ethiopian year.

units.la: Annus Ægyptiacus est solaris.
units.tr: The Egyptian year is solar.

units.la: II. Estque vel vagus vel fixus.
units.tr: II. It is either wandering or fixed.

units.la: III. Annus Ægyptiorum vagus, qui & Nabonasareus, diebus constat præcisè 365.
units.tr: III. The wandering Egyptian year, which is also called Nabonassarean, consists of exactly 365 days.

units.la: I. HIC Ægyptiorum annus Nabonasareus idcirco vocatur, quòd in Epochâ à Nabonasari Chaldæorum regis primordio computatâ, usurpatur: Vagus autem est. Námque per omnes anni Juliani tempestates, initium ejus divagatur. Enimverò annus Julianus, ut modò diximus, est dier. 365. hor. 6. E quibus horis quater collectis quarto cuivis anno solidus dies productus intercalatur, ut quartus quisque annus sit dierum 366. At at annus hic Nabonasareus horas istas negligit, dies colligens præcisè 365. Quo fit ut annus quisque Julianus quartus Nabonasarĕum uno die superet, adeò ut quadriennio quolibet vertente caput anni Nabonasarei in anno Juliano retrovertatur, & solidum diem anticipet.
units.tr: I. This Egyptian year is called Nabonassarean because it is used in the era reckoned from the beginning of the reign of Nabonassar, king of the Chaldeans. It is wandering, however, for through all the seasons of the Julian year its beginning drifts. The Julian year, as we have just said, is 365 days and 6 hours. Every four years these hours are gathered together and one full day is intercalated in the fourth year, so that every fourth year has 366 days. But this Nabonassarean year ignores those hours and counts exactly 365 days. So each fourth Julian year overtakes the Nabonassarean year by one day, and in any four-year period the beginning of the Nabonassarean year moves back within the Julian year and anticipates it by a whole day.

units.la: 2. Ex. gr. Incipiat annus Nabonasareus Juliano quolibet propósito Jan. 31. post annos quatuor incipiet Jan. 30. post octo ad Jan. 29 retrovertetur. Et sic anni Nabonasarei 1461, totum annum Julianum retrò perambulabit; adeo ut anni Nabonasarei 1461, Julianos tantùm 1460 constituant. Nam si multiplices 365 in 4 numerus productus erit 1460, quæ periodus Sothiaca vocatur. Post annos itaque Julianos 1460 sive Nabonasareos 1461 neomenia (ita vocatur prima mensis cujusque dies) Thoth qui primus est Ægyptiorum mensis, ad eundem, unde digressa est, anni Juliani diem regredietur: quo fit, ut uno anno Juliano currente duo Nabonasarei nonnunquam incipiant. Nam si anno Juliano Biffextili annus Nabonasareus ineat Kal. Januariis, alter etiam Nabonasareus ultimo Decembris inibit.
units.tr: 2. For example, let the Nabonassarean year begin on January 31 of some Julian year. After four years it begins on January 30, and after eight on January 29. Thus 1461 Nabonassarean years traverse the whole Julian year backwards, so that 1461 Nabonassarean years make only 1460 Julian years. For if you multiply 365 by 4, the product is 1460; this is called the Sothic period. After 1460 Julian years, or 1461 Nabonassarean years, the neomenia of Thoth (the first day of each month is so called), which is the first month of the Egyptians, returns to the same Julian day from which it departed. Hence in a single Julian year two Nabonassarean years sometimes begin. For if in a bissextile Julian year a Nabonassarean year begins on January 1, another Nabonassarean year will also begin on the last day of December.

units.la: 3. Primus annus Nabonasareus coepit anno per. Jul. 3967 Feb. 26. Ab hac igitur Epocha reliqui anni Nabonasarei sunt computandi. Et hoc quidem est vagum istud & desultorium anni genus quod Ægyptii usque ad Antonii & Cleopatræ cladem in usum civilem asciverunt, quódque Mathematicis ac Astronomis usque ad Ptolemæi ævum in usu fuit. Cujus itaque rationem Chronologus necesse est perspectam habeat.
units.tr: 3. The first Nabonassarean year began on February 26 of the Julian period year 3967. From this era, therefore, the remaining Nabonassarean years are to be counted. This wandering and roving kind of year is the one the Egyptians adopted for civil use until the defeat of Antony and Cleopatra, and it was in use among mathematicians and astronomers until the age of Ptolemy. The chronologer must therefore have a clear grasp of its principle.

units.la: IV. Annus hic Nabonasareus duodecim constat mensibus, πγιαχοσημέροις & quinque ἐπαγομέναις.
units.tr: IV. This Nabonassarean year consists of twelve months of thirty days each and five epagomenal days.

Mecheir. | 30 | 180 Φαμενωθ. Phamenoth. | 30 | 210 Φαρμουθι. Pharmuthi. | 30 | 240 Παχων. Pachon. | 30 | 270 Παυνι. Pauni. | 30 | 300 Επιφι. Epiphi. | 30 | 330 Μεσορι. units.tr: Egyptian month (days; cumulative days): Thoth (30; 30); Paophi (30; 60); Athyr (30; 90); Choiak (30; 120); Tybi (30; 150); Mecheir (30; 180); Phamenoth (30; 210); Pharmuthi (30; 240); Pachon (30; 270); Pauni (30; 300); Epiphi (30; 330); Mesori (30; 360); Epagomenai (5; 365).

units.la: 1. Hoc pinacidium non nomina tantùm ac ordinem mensium Ægyptiacorum exhibet, sed & mensium etiam tam Collectorum quàm expansorum dies, quorum usus statim patebit; omnes, ut vides, menses sunt τεταρτ Σημεια, sive tricenarii: E quibus Thoth primum locum sibi vendicat, cujus prima dies, sive neomenia, est & anni prima. Quinque ἐπαγόμεναι ἡμέραι, i. e. Dies adjectitii ad finem anni sive post Mesori perpetuò collocantur.
units.tr: 1. This little table shows not only the names and order of the Egyptian months but also the days of the months, both as separate amounts and as running totals. Its use will be clear at once. As you see, all the months are of thirty days, that is, tricenary. Of these, Thoth claims the first place, and its first day, or neomenia, is also the first day of the year. The five epagomenal days, that is, the "added days," are always placed at the end of the year, after Mesori.

units.la: V. Si propositio quolibet anno Nabonasareo, initium ejus in Juliano quaeras, annum datum per 4 dividas, quotum e 57 subtrahas (si minor sit quàm 57, sin major ex 422,) & numerus residuus erit dies Julianus à Kal. Jan, in quem neomenia Thoth incidit.
units.tr: V. If you wish to find the Julian date of the beginning of a given Nabonassarean year, divide that year by 4 and subtract the quotient from 57 (if it is less than 57; if it is greater, subtract it from 422). The remaining number is the Julian day counted from January 1 on which the neomenia of Thoth falls.

units.la: 1. Annus propositus per 4 idcirco dividendus est quòd annis Nabonasareis 4 vertentibus solidus dies Julianus anticipatur. Si datos igitur annos per 4 partiaris, quot exhibebit dies Julianos anticipatos, sive quòd idem est, Bissextiles omissos, qui si ex 57 subtrahantur, relinquetur dies quo annus propositus init, eò quòd primus annus Nabonasareus coepit Feb. 26, qui est 57 à Kalendis Januariis.
units.tr: 1. The given year must be divided by 4 because, as four Nabonassarean years pass, one whole Julian day is anticipated. So if you divide the given years by 4, the quotient shows the number of Julian days anticipated, or, what amounts to the same thing, the bissextile days omitted. If these are subtracted from 57, what remains is the day on which the given year begins, because the first Nabonassarean year began on February 26, which is 57 days after January 1.

units.la: 2. Ex. g. Ptolemaeus, l. 5. p. 125, ed. gr. ait lunam defecisse τῷ ϛ ἔτει Ναβονασσαρου, ὃ ἐστι ᾳʹζ ἀπὸ Ναβοναςσαρου, ἐπ' Αἰγυπτίων Ἀθύρ ἐκ τῆς τὴν ἐν ὥρᾳ ιαʹ ἐν νυκτὶ. Anno Nabopollosari quinto, qui est 127 à Nabonasaro, secundum Ægyptios Athyr 27 sequente 28 horâ undecimâ definiente. Si initium anni hujus Nabonasarei 127 in anno Juliano deprehenderem, primò 127 divido per 4, quotiens est 31. Igitur 31 subduco è 57 & relinquitur 26, qui est dies à Kal. Jan, cui neomenia Thoth anno hoc propositio coincidit. Coepit ergo hic annus propositus 127 Jan. 26. Porro si deprehensâ neomeniâ Thoth diem Athyr 27 hic descriptum invenirem, consulo supra scriptum mensium Ægyptiacorum laterculum, ubi in diebus collectis invenio à neomeniâ Thoth ad neomeniam Athyr effluxisse dies 60, quibus adjicio 27, summa est 87. Ergo dies Athyr 27 est 87 à neomeniâ Thoth inclusâ. clusa. Neomenia Thoth incidit in diem 26 à Kal. Jan. adeò ut dies 25 elapsi sunt priusquam annus hic Nabonasareus incepit. Quocirca ad 25 addo prædictos 87, summa est 112. Incidit igitur Athyr 27 in diem à Kalendis Januariis 112, is est Aprilis 21, quòd è Kalendario ad finem harum institutionum descripto patet. Est enim annus per. Jul. 4093 qui & Bissextilis, & quidem nocte diem Aprilis 21, & 22 sive ut Ptolemæus ait Athyr 27, & 28 interfluente Lunam defecisse tabulæ Astronomicæ fidem faciunt.
units.tr: 2. For example, Ptolemy (book 5, p. 125, Greek edition) says that the moon was eclipsed in the sixth year of Nabonassar, which is the 127th from Nabonassar, according to the Egyptians on Athyr 27, with the following 28th, at the eleventh hour of the night [τῷ ϛ ἔτει Ναβονασσαρου, ὃ ἐστι ᾳʹζ ἀπὸ Ναβοναςσαρου, ἐπ' Αἰγυπτίων Ἀθύρ ἐκ τῆς τὴν ἐν ὥρᾳ ιαʹ ἐν νυκτὶ]. "In the fifth year of Nabopolassar, which is 127 from Nabonassar, according to the Egyptians Athyr 27, the following 28th, the hour ending at the eleventh hour." If I wanted to find the Julian date of the beginning of this Nabonassarean year 127, I would first divide 127 by 4, giving a quotient of 31. I subtract 31 from 57, leaving 26, which is the day counted from January 1 on which the neomenia of Thoth coincides with this year. So this year 127 began on January 26. Next, having found the neomenia of Thoth, if I find the day Athyr 27 described here, I consult the table of Egyptian months above. There, among the running totals, I find that 60 days have elapsed from the neomenia of Thoth to the neomenia of Athyr. Adding 27 gives 87, so Athyr 27 is the 87th day counting from the neomenia of Thoth inclusive. The neomenia of Thoth falls on the 26th day from January 1, so 25 days had passed before this Nabonassarean year began. Therefore I add the 25 to the aforesaid 87, and the sum is 112. Athyr 27 thus falls on the 112th day from January 1, that is April 21, as is clear from the calendar described at the end of these institutions. For the year of the Julian period is 4093, which is also bissextile, and indeed on the night of April 21 and 22, or as Ptolemy says Athyr 27 and 28, the astronomical tables confirm that the moon was eclipsed.

units.la: 3. Si quotus excedat 57 adjiciendi sunt unius anni Juliani dies, sive 365 & ¼ summâ 422 quotus est subtrahendus. Ex. gr. Idem Ptolemæus ait Lunam defecisse anno 31 Darii Hystaspis, Nabonasari 257 κατ' Αυγυστως τυβι ; ἐις τὴν ⁊ secundum Ægyptios Tybi 3 sequente 4, Ptol. l. 4. p. 102. Si anni hujusce Nabonasarei 257 initium compertum haberes, 257 partiaris per 4, quotus 64 major est quàm qui ex 57 subduci queat, addas igitur 365 ad 57, è summâ 422 subduc quotum tuum 64, & residuum erit 358. Ergo anno Nabonasari 257 neomenia Thoth incidit in diem 358 Kal. Jan. i. e. in Decembris 24. A neomeniâ Thoth ad neomeniam Tybi dies effluxerunt 120. Erat igitur tertia Tybi 123 à neomeniâ Thoth. Ad dies igitur anni Juliani qui completi sunt priusquam cœpit hic annus Nabonasareus, viz ad 357 addé 123 è summa 480 ut dies anni Juliani excedente, subtrahas dies unius anni Juliani sive 365, & relinquetur 115. Tertius ergo dies Athyr incidit in diem 115 à Kal. Jan. sive in April. 25.
units.tr: 3. If the quotient exceeds 57, the days of one Julian year must be added, that is 365 and a quarter, making 422, and the quotient must be subtracted from that sum. For example, the same Ptolemy says that the moon was eclipsed in the 31st year of Darius Hystaspes, Nabonassar 257, according to the Egyptians on Tybi 3, with the following 4th [κατ' Αυγυστως τυβι ; ἐις τὴν ⁊]; Ptolemy, book 4, p. 102. If you knew the beginning of this Nabonassarean year 257, divide 257 by 4. The quotient, 64, is greater than can be subtracted from 57, so you add 365 to 57, and from the sum 422 you subtract your quotient 64. The remainder is 358. Therefore in Nabonassar year 257 the neomenia of Thoth falls on the 358th day from January 1, that is, on December 24. From the neomenia of Thoth to the neomenia of Tybi, 120 days have elapsed, so the third day of Tybi was the 123rd day from the neomenia of Thoth. To the 357 days of the Julian year that were completed before this Nabonassarean year began, add these 123, giving 480. Since this exceeds the days of a Julian year, subtract 365, and 115 remains. So the third day of Tybi falls on the 115th day from January 1, that is, on April 25.

units.la: 4. Si annus propositus sequatur Nabonasareum 1472, sive per. Jul. 5437 & nihil post divisionem supererit, adjiciendum est unitatem è quoto, priusquam subductio fiat. Ex. gr. Hoc anno Christi 1667, per. Jul. 6380 annus Nabonasareus 2416 init, ut è methodo secundo Libro tradita liquet. Si 2416 per 4 distribuas, quotus erit 604. o. sed quoniam nihil post divisionem restat, & hic annus sequitur annum Nabonasareum 1472 sive per. Jul. 5437, hinc è quoto subducenda est unitas, ut fiat 603, hic autem major est, quàm ut è numero etiam 422 subtrahatur, ergo ad 422 alios adde 365, è summâ 787 aufer quotum tuum unitate mutilatum, sive 603 & relinquitur dies 184 à Kal. Januariis. Hoc igitur anno Christi 1667 annus Nabonasareus 2416 iniit Julii 3. Dies quo hæc commentatus sum, erat Septembris duodecimus, qui etiam est duodecimus Athyr, nam Athyr unà cum Septembri init.
units.tr: 4. If the given year follows Nabonassarean year 1472, that is Julian period 5437, and nothing remains after the division, one must add a unit to the quotient before the subtraction is made. For example, in this year of Christ 1667, Julian period 6380, the Nabonassarean year 2416 begins, as is clear from the method given in the second book. If you divide 2416 by 4, the quotient is 604, with nothing left over. But since this year follows the Nabonassarean year 1472, that is Julian period 5437, one unit must be subtracted from the quotient, making 603. This is greater than can be subtracted from 422, so add 365 to 422 and from the sum 787 take away your quotient reduced by a unit, that is 603. There remains 184 days from January 1. So in this year of Christ 1667, the Nabonassarean year 2416 began on July 3. The day on which I wrote these notes was September 12, which is also Athyr 12, since Athyr begins together with September.

units.la: V. Annus Ægyptiacus fixus qui & Actiacus, est ejusdem quantitatis atque Julianus.
units.tr: V. The fixed Egyptian year, which is also called the Actiac, has the same length as the Julian.

units.la: 1. Hic annus vocatur Actiacus, propterea quòd paucis post Actiacam victoriam annis Alexandrini, reliquíque Ægyptii unà cum jugo Romanorum hanc anni formam admittebant; quo tempore popularis Ægyptiorum annus vagari desiit Embolismo restrictus, vago & Nabonasareo Mathematicis solis relicto.
units.tr: 1. This year is called the Actiac because, a few years after the Actian victory, the Alexandrians and the rest of the Egyptians, under the yoke of the Romans, adopted this form of year. At that time the popular Egyptian year, restrained by the embolism, ceased to wander, and the wandering Nabonassarean year was left only to the mathematicians.

units.la: 2. Hæc igitur anni ratio quam in Æra Actiacâ & Diocletianeâ veteres usurpant, ejusdem est quantitatis, cujus Julianus. Diebus enim constat 365 horis 6, è quibus horis quater collectis exurgit dies quarto cuivis anno interserendus, vel potius adjiciendus.
units.tr: 2. This system of year, then, which the ancients use in the Actiac and Diocletianic eras, has the same length as the Julian. For it consists of 365 days and 6 hours, and from the four hours collected every fourth year there arises a day to be inserted, or rather added, in that year.

units.la: VI. Differt hic annus Actiacus à Juliano. VII. Primò, mensium nominibus & quantitate, quæ eadem in hoc anno sunt quæ in Nabonasareo.
units.tr: VI. This Actiac year differs from the Julian. VII. First, in the names and lengths of the months, which in this year are the same as in the Nabonassarean.

units.la: 1. Hic enim annus Actiacus 12 istis mensibus constat & quinque Epagomenis, de quibus modo dictum est in anno Nabonasareo, viz. Thoth, Paophi, &c. adeò ut quamvis anni non tamen mensium Julianorum quantitatem admiserunt.
units.tr: 1. For this Actiac year consists of those same twelve months and the five Epagomenae, which were just mentioned in the Nabonassarean year, namely Thoth, Paophi, and so on. So although they admitted the length of the Julian years, they did not admit the length of the Julian months.

units.la: VIII. Secundò, principio. Nam annus Julianus à Kal. Jan. Actiacus ab Aug. 29 init.
units.tr: VIII. Secondly, in the beginning. For the Julian year begins on the Kalends of January, while the Actiac begins on August 29.

units.la: 1. Annus Ægyptiorum vagus 724 primus erat à quo fixi numerantur; verum 724 per 4 divisi in quoto dant 181, quotus hic ex 422 subtractus relinquit 241. Hic igitur annus Nabonasareus 724 coepit die 241 à Kal. Jan. is est Aug. 29. Et hinc est quod omnes anni Ægyptiorum fixi ab isto die proceeduut, eo tantùm excepto qui annum intercalarem proximè sequitur, utpote qui Aug. 30 incipit, ob diem ad finem anni praecedentis adjectam.
units.tr: 1. The wandering Egyptian year, 724 years from its first year, was the starting point from which the fixed years are counted. But 724 divided by 4 gives 181 as the quotient, and subtracting this from 422 leaves 241. So this year 724 of the Nabonassarean era began on day 241 from January 1, which is August 29. Hence all the fixed Egyptian years proceed from that day, except only the one that immediately follows the intercalary year, which begins on August 30, because of the day added at the end of the preceding year.

units.la: IX. Tertio. Intercalandi loco. Nam in anno Juliano dies intercalaris inter 23, & 24 Feb. in Actiaco inter Aug. 28, & 29 inseritur.
units.tr: IX. Thirdly, the place of intercalation. For in the Julian year the intercalary day is inserted between February 23 and 24; in the Actiac between August 28 and 29.

units.la: 1. Nimirum Ægyptii ne pristinam mensium tricenariorum quantitatem immutarent, diem hunc intercalarem post ἐπαγόμενας ad anni videlicet finem adjiciebant, quo fit ut in anno embolimeo Epagomenæ sint sex, quæ in communi quinque tantùm numerantur.
units.tr: 1. Clearly the Egyptians, so as not to change the old length of the thirty-day months, added this intercalary day after the Epagomenae, that is, at the very end of the year. As a result, in the embolismic year there are six Epagomenae, whereas in an ordinary year only five are counted.

units.la: X. Quartò, anno intercalari; qui in Actiacâ formâ non idem est atque in Juliana, sed proximè praecedens.
units.tr: X. Fourthly, the intercalary year, which in the Actiac form is not the same as in the Julian, but is the one immediately preceding.

units.la: 1. In anno igitur quadriennii Juliani sive post Bissextilem tertio, neomenia Thoth in Aug. 30 incidit; ut annus Christi huic praesenti proximus, putà 1668 est Bissextilis, praesens ergo sive 1667 est tertius post Bissextilem, atque idcirco in anno Actiaco qui hoc currente definit, dies intercalaris inter Aug. 28, & 29 inseritur, quo fit ut annus Actiacus hoc currente Juliano iniens, & in Bissextilem incurrens, ab Aug. 30 oriatur.
units.tr: 1. In the year that is third after the bissextile in the Julian four-year cycle, the new moon of Thoth falls on August 30. Since the Christian year next after the present one, namely 1668, is bissextile, the present year, 1667, is therefore the third after the bissextile. Consequently, in the Actiac year which ends in this current year, the intercalary day is inserted between August 28 and 29. As a result, the Actiac year that begins in this current Julian year, and runs into the bissextile, starts on August 30.

units.la: 2. Ex. gr. D. Ambrosius ait, Sicut septuagesimo sexto anno die imperii Diocletiani factum est. Nam tunc vigesimo octavo die Pharmutii mensis qui est nono Kalendas Maii, dominicam Paschæ celebravimus sine ullâ dubitatione majorum. Ambr. Epist. l. 10. ep. 83. ad episcopos Æmiliæ. Scire vellem in quem diem anni Juliani conveniat 28 Pharmutii hic memoratus.* Annus Diocletiani 76 iniit anno Christi 359. Nam si ad 76 addas 283 summa est 359, porro annus Christi 360 est Bissextilis. Annus igitur Diocletianeus 76 ut proximus post intercalarem Actiacum coepit Aug. 30. Is est dies à Kal. Jan. 241. A neomeniâ Thoth inclusive ad Phamenoth exeuntem sive Pharmutium ineuntem dies colliguntur 210. Pascha hoc anno celebratum est Pharmutii 28, addas igitur 28 ad 210, summa est 238. Ergò Pharmutii 28 est 238 à neomeniâ Thoth, inclusivè sive quod idem est, à die 241 à Kal. Jan. exclusivè, Anno Christi 359. Cœterùm 241, & 238 collecti producunt 479. E quibus subducto 366 (eò quòd annus hic Actiacus in Bissextilem Julianum incurrat) & relinquitur dies à Kal. Jan. 113, is est Aprilis 23, sive 9 Kal. Maii. Ergo anno Diocletiano 76 Pharmutii 28 in nonum Kalendas Maij anno Christi 360 convenit, ut rectè tradit Eruditissimus pater.
units.tr: 2. For example, St Ambrose says: "As happened in the seventy-sixth year of the reign of Diocletian. For then, on the twenty-eighth day of Pharmuthi, which is the ninth day before the Kalends of May, we celebrated Easter Sunday without any doubt among the elders." (Ambrose, Epist. book 10, ep. 83, to the bishops of Aemilia.) I should like to know on which day of the Julian year the 28th of Pharmuthi mentioned here falls. The seventy-sixth year of Diocletian began in the year of Christ 359, for if you add 283 to 76 the sum is 359; the year of Christ 360 is bissextile. The seventy-sixth year of Diocletian, as the year next after the intercalary Actiac, began on August 30. This is day 241 from January 1. From the new moon of Thoth inclusive to the end of Phamenoth, which is the beginning of Pharmuthi, 210 days are counted. Easter was celebrated this year on Pharmuthi 28, so add 28 to 210; the sum is 238. Therefore Pharmuthi 28 is 238 days from the new moon of Thoth inclusive, or, what is the same, from day 241 from January 1 exclusive, in the year of Christ 359. Moreover, 241 and 238 together make 479. From these subtract 366 (because this Actiac year runs into the Julian bissextile), and there remains day 113 from January 1, which is April 23, or the ninth day before the Kalends of May. So in the seventy-sixth year of Diocletian, Pharmuthi 28 falls on the ninth day before the Kalends of May in the year of Christ 360, as the most learned father rightly teaches.

units.la: 3. Hoc igitur obiter notandum est, quod quandocunque in annis Ægyptiacis tam fixis quàm vagis computandis transitus fit ab anno Juliano communi ad Bissextilem post Feb. 24, de summâ collectâ dies 366 detrahendi sunt, ut diei Bissextilis habeatur ratio. Vel si subducas tantum 365 dies, ut in anno Bissextili colliguntur, sumendi sunt, ut in exemplo proposito subductis 365 ex 479 supersunt 114, qui etiam est nonus Kalendas Maii in anno Bissextili, ut 113 in communi.
units.tr: 3. It should be noted in passing that whenever, in computing both fixed and wandering Egyptian years, a transition is made from a common Julian year to a bissextile year after February 24, 366 days must be subtracted from the sum collected, so that account is taken of the bissextile day. Or, if you subtract only 365 days, as they are counted in a bissextile year, that is to be taken; thus in the example proposed, with 365 subtracted from 479, 114 remains, which is also the ninth day before the Kalends of May in the bissextile year, just as 113 is in the common year.

units.la: XI. Annus Æthiopicus nihilo discrepat ab Ægyptiaco fixo præterquam in mensium nominibus quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: XI. The Ethiopian year differs in nothing from the fixed Egyptian year except in the names of the months, which follow.

Tyr. | Tybi. | Decem. 27. Jacatit. | Mecchir. | Jan. 26. Magabit. | Phamenoth. | Feb. 25. Mijazia. | Pharmuthi. | Mart. 27. Ginbat. | Pachon. | April. 26. Syne. | Pauni. | Maii, 26 Hamle. | Epiphi. | Jun. 25. Nahase. | Mesori. | Julii, 25. Pagomen. | Epagomenæ. | Aug. 29.
