units.la: I. In hoc laterculo menses tam Ægyptiacos fixos quàm Æthiopicos descriptos habes, unà cum diebus in anno Juliano quibuscum ineunt: qui tamen ubitate sunt augendi usque ad Feb. quoties annus ab Aug. 30 incipiat. Hoc est cùm annus quilibet Ægyptiacus vel Æthiopicus propositus intercalarem proximus excipiat. Tum enim Mascaram & Thoth Aug. 30. Tykymt & Paophi Sept. 29. incipiet, & sic deinceps usque ad Februarium inclusum. Nam Magabit & Phamenoth ineunt Feb 26. at Mijazia & Pharmuthi in Martii 27. & sic deinceps, ut in laterculo describuntur, ob diem Februario intercalatum.
units.tr: I. In this table you have the months of both the fixed Egyptian and the Ethiopian calendars, set out together with the days of the Julian year on which each begins. These dates, however, must be increased by one, up to February inclusive, whenever the year begins on August 30. That is, this happens when any Egyptian or Ethiopian year under consideration follows a leap year. For then Mascaram and Thoth will begin on August 30, and Tykymt and Paophi on September 29, and so on through February. Magabit and Phamenoth then begin on February 26, but Mijazia and Pharmuthi on March 27, and so on as they are described in the table, because of the day intercalated in February.

units.la: 2. Dies quos Ægyptii Græcè Ἐπαγόμεναι vocant, Æthiopes corruptè Pagomen. Hæc igitur est anni forma ab Æthiopibus eitamnum usitata, quæ cùm eadem sit omnino quæ Actiaca sive Ægyptiaca fixa, ulteriori explicatione non indiget.
units.tr: 2. The days which the Egyptians call Epagomenae [Ἐπαγόμεναι] in Greek, the Ethiopians corruptly call Pagomen. This, then, is the form of the year still in use among the Ethiopians to this day. Since it is entirely the same as the Actian or fixed Egyptian year, it needs no further explanation.

units.la: CAP. XI. De anno Persico.
units.tr: CAP. XI. On the Persian year.

units.la: Annus Persicus est Solaris.
units.tr: The Persian year is solar.

units.la: II. Estque vel vagus vel fixus, iste Yezdegerdicus, hic Gelalens vocatur.
units.tr: II. It is either wandering or fixed. The former is called Yezdegerdic, the latter Gelalean.

units.la: III. Annus Yezdegerdicus ejusdem est formæ atque Nabonazareus, ut diebus constans 365 Mensibus 12 τεταρτ. ἡμέραις, & epagomenis quinque.
units.tr: III. The Yezdegerdic year has the same form as the Nabonassarean, consisting of 365 days: 12 months and 5 epagomenal days.

units.la: I. Yezdegird filius Shahriar ultimus erat Persarum Rex, à Saracenis interfectus; à cujus obitu Persæ suos deducunt annos, qui nihilo discrepant à Nabonazareis, præterquam Epochâ, & mensium nominibus.
units.tr: I. Yezdegird, son of Shahriar, was the last king of the Persians, killed by the Saracens. From his death the Persians date their years, which differ from the Nabonassarean only in the epoch and the names of the months.

units.la: IV. Menses Persici sic se habent. Menses | D. M. | Dies Col. PERSICI. | | Fervardin mah. | 30 | 30 Ardabahesht mah. | 30 | 60 Chordad mah. | 30 | 90 Tyr. mah. | 30 | 120 Mordad mah. | 30 | 150 Sharivar mah. | 30 | 180 Mcher mah. | 30 | 210 Aban mah. | 30 | 240 Adar mah. | 30 | 270 Di mah. | 30 | 300 Beheman mah. | 30 | 330 Esphandarmod mah. | 30 | 360 Musteraka. | 5 | 365
units.tr: IV. The Persian months are as follows. Months | Days | Cumulative total. Persian names: Fervardin mah, 30, 30; Ardabahesht mah, 30, 60; Chordad mah, 30, 90; Tyr mah, 30, 120; Mordad mah, 30, 150; Sharivar mah, 30, 180; Mcher mah, 30, 210; Aban mah, 30, 240; Adar mah, 30, 270; Di mah, 30, 300; Beheman mah, 30, 330; Esphandarmod mah, 30, 360; Musteraka, 5, 365.

units.la: I. Sin1. Singulis, ut vides, mensibus vocula mah adjicitur, quæ Persicè mensem significat: propterea quòd aliquis cujusque mensis dies eodem nomine, quo ipse mensis, gaudet; ut 17 Fervardin mah, dicitur Fervardin: 3 Ardibahesht vocatur Ardabahesh, &c. Quocirca ut ipse mensis à die isto distinguatur, voculam istam mah sibi adscriptam habet. Quas Græci ἡμέρας ἡμερῶν; Persæ Musteraka q. d. Dies Furtivos vocant. Fervardin est mensis primus in anno Persico ut Thoth in Nabonasareo: ultimus Esphandarmod post quem completum Musteraka frequentiss ineunt, aliquando post Aban mah.
units.tr: I. As you see, the word mah is added to each month; in Persian it means "month". This is because some day of each month bears the same name as the month itself: the 17th day of Fervardin mah is called Fervardin, the 3rd day of Ardibahesht is called Ardabahesh, and so on. So that the month may be distinguished from that day, the word mah is attached to it. The Greeks call these the "days of days" [ἡμέρας ἡμερῶν]; the Persians call the Musteraka, as it were, "furtive days". Fervardin is the first month of the Persian year, as Thoth is in the Nabonassarean year. The last is Esphandarmod, after which the completed Musteraka most often begin, sometimes after Aban mah.

units.la: V. Ut neomeniam Fervardin invenias annum Yezdeger- dicum per 4 dividos, quotum subtrahas ex 167, & rel- iquus sit dies à Kal. Jan. quo Fervardin init.
units.tr: V. To find the new moon of Fervardin in a Yezdegerdic year, divide the year by 4, subtract the quotient from 167, and the remainder is the day counted from January 1 on which Fervardin begins.

units.la: 1. Nimirum ut annus primus Nabonasareus cœpit Feb. 26. sic Yezdegerdicus primus à Junii 16 incepit, qui à Kal. Jan. est 167, anno Christi 632. Nabonasareo 1380. Thoth iniit Martii 18. Ghoiac igitur isto anno unà cum Fervardin Persico cœpit Jun. 16, is est ut dixi 167 à Kal. Januariis. Et hinc est quod quotus divisionis ex 167 subtrahendus est, ut neomeniam Fervardin assequamur.
units.tr: 1. Indeed, just as the first Nabonassarean year began on February 26, so the first Yezdegerdic year began on June 16, which is the 167th day from January 1, in the year of Christ 632, Nabonassarean 1380. Thoth began on March 18. Therefore Choiac of that year, together with Persian Fervardin, began on June 16, which, as I said, is the 167th day from January 1. And this is why the quotient of the division must be subtracted from 167 to reach the new moon of Fervardin.

units.la: 2. Ex. gr. Proponatur annus Yezdegerdicus 246; ut ejus initium ernamus, 246 partimur per 4, quotus 6, subductus è 167 relinquit 106. Ergo isto anno neomenia Fervardin incidit in diem 106 à Kal. Jan. sive in April. 16.
units.tr: 2. For example, let the Yezdegerdic year 246 be proposed. To find its beginning, divide 246 by 4: the quotient is 6, and subtracting it from 167 leaves 106. So in this year the new moon of Fervardin falls on day 106 from January 1, that is, on April 16.

units.la: 3. Si nihil post divisionem supererit, unitatem è quoto subducas; & residuum ex 167. Sic anni 292 per 4 divisi in quoto dant 73, in residuo 0, aufer igitur unitatem è quoto, & residuum 72 subduc ex 167, & relinquetur 95. Ergo annus Yezdegerdicus 292 iniit April. 5.
units.tr: 3. If nothing remains after the division, subtract one from the quotient, and then subtract the result from 167. Thus the year 292, divided by 4, gives a quotient of 73 and a remainder of 0. Take one from the quotient, leaving 72, and subtract it from 167, which leaves 95. Therefore the Yezdegerdic year 292 began on April 5.

units.la: 4. Post annum Yezdegerdicum 433, Christi 1064, si vel nihil vel unitas post divisionem restiterit, unitas è quoto subducenda est. Et quotus iste, unitate, si opus sit, mutilatus, si major sit quàm qui ex 167 subduci queat, ad 167 addantur 365 & è summâ 532 subtrahatur. Hoc anno Christi 1667 Yezdegerdicus 1037 init, qui per 4 divisus in in quoto dat 259 in residuo; i. e. Annus hic post Yezdegerdicum 433 venit; abjiciendum est igitur unitatem è quoto propter unitatem in residuo, & residuum 258 ex 532 subtrahendum, & reliquus fit dies 274 à Kal. Jan. Is est Oct. 1. Ergo hoc anno Christi 1667, Yezdegerdicus 1037 incipit oct. 1. Adeo ut neomenia Fervardin Persici, & Choiac Ægyptiaci & Kalendæ Octob. Juliani concurrunt.
units.tr: 4. After the Yezdegerdic year 433, which is the year of Christ 1064, if either nothing or one remains after the division, one must be subtracted from the quotient. If that quotient, reduced by one where necessary, is too large to be subtracted from 167, add 365 to 167 and subtract the quotient from the sum, 532. In this year of Christ 1667 the Yezdegerdic year 1037 begins. Divided by 4, it gives a quotient of 259 and a remainder of 1. That is, this year falls after the Yezdegerdic year 433. Therefore one must be taken from the quotient on account of the one in the remainder, and the 258 that remains subtracted from 532. The remainder is day 274 from January 1, which is October 1. So in this year of Christ 1667 the Yezdegerdic year 1037 begins on October 1. Thus the new moon of Persian Fervardin, the Egyptian Choiac and the Julian Kalends of October coincide.

units.la: VI. Annus Gelaleus est solaris Tropicus.
units.tr: VI. The Gelalean year is a tropical solar year.

units.la: 1. Nomen sortita est hæc anni forma à Sultan Gelal. Eddin Melickshah Arselan Saljuki, ut eum vocat Ulug Beig: hic Mesopotamiæ erat imperator: Menses eosdem habet quos Yezdegerdica, viz. 12 tricenarios & 5 Musteraka, in anno communi, sex in intercalari ut annus Actiacus. Sed primo instituto menses verè solares erant, à transitu solis per singula signa numerati.
units.tr: 1. This form of year took its name from Sultan Gelal Eddin Melikshah Arselan Seljuk, as Ulugh Beg calls him; he was emperor of Mesopotamia. It has the same months as the Yezdegerdic year, namely twelve months of thirty days and 5 Musteraka in a common year, and six in an intercalary year, as in the Actiac year. But at its first institution the months were truly solar, numbered from the sun's passage through the individual signs.

units.la: VII. Constat hic annus diebus 365 & scrupulis diurnis 14'. 33''. 7'''. 32''''. i. e. horis 5 49'. 15''. 0'''. 48''''.
units.tr: VII. This year consists of 365 days and 14′ 33″ 7‴ 32″″ of daily scruples, that is, 5 hours 49′ 15″ 0‴ 48″″.

units.la: VIII. Methodus hujus anni in hoc fere consistit, ut cum sexies vel septies quadriennio quovis vertente facta fuerit intercalatio, semel ad quintum annum proroge- tur.
units.tr: VIII. The method of this year consists roughly in this: when, in every period of four years, intercalation has been made six or seven times, it is postponed to the fifth year.

units.la: 1. Est igitur annus hic, si quis alius, verè Tropicus, motibus solaribus quàm exactissimè respondens. Embolismus enim sextus & nonnunquam septimus in annum quintum delatus æquinoctia & solstitia iisdem perpetuo mensium diebus affigit.
units.tr: 1. This year, then, is truly tropical, if any other is, corresponding as exactly as possible to the motions of the sun. For the sixth, and sometimes the seventh, intercalary day, carried over into the fifth year, fixes the equinoxes and solstices to the same days of the months perpetually.

units.la: 2. Inventa fuit hæc anni forma, ut panegyris Neurus eodem perpetuo die celebraretur, non secus ac Gregoriana anni forma ob paschatis celebritatem instituta fuit. Sed quoniam, vix vel ne vix quidem in Historicis legendis, occurrat hæc anni forma, non est ut in eâ explicandâ diutius immoremur.
units.tr: 2. This form of the year was devised so that the festival of Neurus (the panegyris) would be celebrated on the same day forever, just as the Gregorian form of the year was instituted for the sake of the celebration of Easter. But since this form of the year hardly, or scarcely at all, occurs in reading the historians, there is no need for us to linger longer over explaining it.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: De anno Syriaco.
units.tr: On the Syriac year.

units.la: Annus Syriacus est Solaris fixus, ejusdem quantitatis atque Julianus.
units.tr: The Syriac year is a fixed solar year, of the same length as the Julian.

units.la: I. HUnc annum Arabes, Persæque Rumeum sive Græcum appellant, quo Syrogræci, Antiocheni, cæterique Orientales in æra Seleucidarum utuntur. Quoad iam anni quàm mensium quantitatem singulorum à Juliano nihilo differt: Constat enim diebus 365 horis 6. & mensibus duodecim ejusdem, cujus Juliani, quantitatis.
units.tr: I. This year the Arabs and Persians call Rumeum, or Greek, and the Syro-Greeks, Antiochenes and other Orientals use it in the era of the Seleucids. As to the length of the year and of its months, it differs in no way from the Julian: for it consists of 365 days and 6 hours, and of twelve months of the same length as the Julian ones.

units.la: II. A Juliana dissentit hæc anni forma
units.tr: II. This form of year differs from the Julian in the following respects.

units.la: III. Primò, Epochà non enim à Kal. Januariis, sed Octobribus computatur.
units.tr: III. First, the epoch: it is reckoned not from the Kalends of January but from the Kalends of October.

units.la: IV. Secundò, mensium nominibus, quæ sequuntur. Menses SYRIACI. | Menses Juliani. Tishrin prior. | October. Tishrin posterior. | November. Canun prior. | December. Canun posterior. | Januarius. Shabat. | Februarius. Adar. | Martius. Nisan. | Aprilis. Aiyar. | Maius. Haziran. | Junius. Tamuz. | Julius. Ab. | Augustus. Elul. | September.
units.tr: IV. Second, the names of the months, which follow. Syriac months | Julian months. Tishrin prior | October. Tishrin posterior | November. Canun prior | December. Canun posterior | January. Shabat | February. Adar | March. Nisan | April. Aiyar | May. Haziran | June. Tamuz | July. Ab | August. Elul | September.

units.la: I. Tishrin prior, ut in laterculo vides, est primus anni mensis, una cum Kalendis Octobris iniens. Singuli menses eundem dierum numerum colligunt quem Juliani iis respondentes. Adeo ut Shabat non secus ac Februarius in anno communi dies 28, in Bissextili 29 sibi vendicat. Quocirca cognita anni Juliani forma haec simul innotescit, quippe quae prorsus Juliana est, atque ideo satis explicata.
units.tr: I. Tishrin prior, as you see in the table, is the first month of the year, beginning with the Kalends of October. Each month has the same number of days as the Julian month corresponding to it, so that Shabat, like February, has 28 days in a common year and 29 in a bissextile year. Hence, once the form of the Julian year is known, this form is at the same time known as well, since it is wholly Julian, and therefore sufficiently explained.

units.la: 2. Hujus anni formae frequens est in Ulug Beigo, Albatenio, Eutichio sive Said Ebn Batrick annalium Alexandrinorum scriptore, aliisque scriptoribus Orientalibus usus.
units.tr: 2. This form of year is frequently used by Ulug Beg, Albatenius, Eutychius, that is Said ibn Batrik, the writer of the Alexandrian annals, and by other Oriental writers.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: De anno Graeco.
units.tr: On the Greek year.

units.la: Annus Graecus est vel Atticus vel Macedonicus, vel Syromacedonicus, vel Paphiorum vel Bythymorum.
units.tr: The Greek year is either Attic, Macedonian, Syro-Macedonian, or that of the Paphians or the Bythymians.

units.la: II. Annus Atticus est Lunaris fixus.
units.tr: II. The Attic year is a fixed lunar year.

units.la: 1. GRÆCI antiquitus ab oraculo mandatum acceperunt, τὸ ᾱ̈ ἔτος, ἡμέρας, μῆνας, ἡμέρας, ἔτη, ut sacrificarent secundum tria, videlicet Patria, menses, dies & annos. Quae verba ita sunt interpretati, ut annus eorum solis, menses, & dies Lunae motibus consentirent; ut refert Gemin. Elim. Astron. c. 6. Annus igitur eorum Solaris, menses & dies Lunares sint necesse fuit, unde & totum annum nos Lunarem fixum, sive intra cardines Solares cohibitum nuncupamus.
units.tr: 1. The Greeks of old received a command from an oracle, [τὸ πρῶτον ἔτος, ἡμέρας, μῆνας, ἡμέρας, ἔτη, as printed], that they should sacrifice according to three things, namely fatherland, months, days and years. They interpreted these words to mean that their year should agree with the motions of the sun, and their months and days with the motions of the moon, as Geminus reports in his Elements of Astronomy, ch. 6. Their year therefore had to be solar and their months and days lunar, which is why we also call the whole year "lunar fixed," or confined within the limits of the sun.

units.la: 2. Porro prius quam exactam syderum scientiam assecuti sunt Athenienses, annum suum in 12 menses tricenarios dispertiti sunt, Lunam diebus 30 periodum suam absolvere pro concesso habentes, quem tamen solis etiam motibus ut accommodarent, alteri cuique vertenti anno mensem alium tricenarium adjiciebant. Et haec quidem anni forma nonnullis Græciæ civitatibus diu prævaluisse videtur, usque dum annuas menstruásque syderum conversiones magis perspectas habentes, eam in modo describendam immutabant.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, before the Athenians attained an exact knowledge of the stars, they divided their year into twelve months of thirty days each, taking it as given that the moon completed its course in thirty days. To make this agree with the motions of the sun, however, they added another thirty-day month to every alternate year. This form of year seems to have long prevailed in several Greek states, until they, having a clearer grasp of the annual and monthly revolutions of the stars, changed the way of reckoning it.

units.la: III. Estque vel communis vel Embolimeus.
units.tr: III. It is either common or embolismic.

units.la: IV. Annus communis 12, Embolimeus 13 mensibus Lunaribus constat, à novilunio viso computatis.
units.tr: IV. A common year consists of twelve lunar months, and an embolismic year of thirteen, counted from the sighting of the new moon.

units.la: I. Nimirum Græci non à novilunio vero nec medio sed viso, hoc est, ἀπὸ τῆς φάσεως τῆς σελήνης, ab isto vid. tempore quo Luna post coitum se primò videndam præbet, menses suos deducebant.
units.tr: I. The Greeks reckoned their months not from the true new moon nor from the mean one, but from the sighted one, that is, [ἀπὸ τῆς φάσεως τῆς σελήνης], from the moment when the moon first shows itself visible after conjunction.

units.la: V. Mensium Atticorum nomina, quantitatem ac ordinem hoc laterculum exhibet. Menses | D. M. | Dies Coll. units.la: I. Mensis Lunaris est dierum 29 hor. 12. 44'. Ex horis istis 12 bis collectis completur dies, hinc menses omnes alternis sunt cavi & pleni sive 29 & 30 dierum; annus communis 354. In anno embolimæo alius mensis post posideonem inseritur, adeo ut duplex sit Posideon, prior & posterior, unde Ptolemæus, "Ἀεχεῖ ἈΔίνηση Εὐάτρχε μηνὸς Ποσιδεῶνος ὁ ἐπίλοιπ, Almag. l. 4. p. 106. Anni autem Embolimæi sunt 3. 5. 8. 11. 14. 16. 19. cycli decemnovalis: reliqui communes.
units.tr: I. A lunar month is 29 days, 12 hours and 44 minutes. When these 12-hour portions are collected twice, a whole day is completed; hence the months alternate between hollow and full, that is, 29 and 30 days, and the common year has 354. In an embolismic year another month is inserted after Posideon, so that there are two Posideons, the former and the latter. Whence Ptolemy says (Almagest, bk. 4, p. 106): [Greek as printed, garbled in the scan]. The embolismic years are the 3rd, 5th, 8th, 11th, 14th, 16th and 19th of the nineteen-year cycle; the rest are common.

units.la: 2. Prima dies cujuslibet mensis vocatur νουμηνία, ultima ἑνη ἡ νέα, Vetus & nova, propterea quòd partim ad veterem partim ad novam Lunam spectat. Totus autem mensis in tres partes distribuitur, quarum prima ἱσταμένου, secunda ἐπὶ δεκα, tertia ἐπὶ Σιροῦ putà σύνοδος appellatur. Ut prima dies vocatur νουμηνία vel φθὶν ἱσταμένου, secunda δευτέρα ἱσταμένου. Et sic usque ad ἑικάδην quam excipit φθὶν ἐπὶ δεκα, δευτέρα ἐπὶ δεκα, & sic deinceps usque ad ἐνάτην vigesimam, post quam dies retrorsum numerantur, ut Kalendæ, nonæ, & Idus in anno Juliano. Nam si plenus sit annus, ἐνάτη sequitur. Decima desinentis mensis, tunc ἑννάν φθιροῦ, ὀγδόη φθιροῦ, & sic deinceps ordine retrogrado usque ad ἑνην ἡ νέα; pro φθιροῦ nonnunquam legitur ἀπόλ, pro ἐπὶ δεκα, μεσοῦ. Si mensis sit cavus post ἐνάτη venit ἑννάν φθιροῦ, tunc ὀγδὸν φθιροῦ, &c. hinc Aristophanes in Nubibus, Act. 4. Πέμπτη, τετάρτη, τρίτη, μετὰ ταύτην δευτέραν, Ἐπὶ ἣν ἐγὼ μάλιστα πάντων ἡμερῶν Διάδικα, πόρρω, ἡ βδελυροῦμαι, Ἐνδὶς μετὰ ταύτην ἐπὶ ἑνη ἡ νέα. Quinta, quarta, tertia, post hanc secunda, Postea quam ego maxime omnium dierum Timeo, & horreo, & abominor, Statim post eam est vetus & nova.
units.tr: 2. The first day of any month is called noumenia [νουμηνία], and the last hene he nea [ἕνη ἡ νέα], "old and new," because it belongs partly to the old moon and partly to the new. The whole month is divided into three parts: the first is called histamenou [ἱσταμένου], the second epi deka [ἐπὶ δέκα], and the third epi Siro, that is, synodos [σύνοδος], conjunction. Thus the first day is called noumenia, or phthin histamenou, and the second deutera histamenou. So it goes on until the twentieth day, which is followed by phthin epi deka, deutera epi deka, and so on up to the ninth [ἐνάτη] of the last part, after which the days are counted backwards, as the Kalends, Nones and Ides are in the Julian year. For if the month is full, the ninth follows. The tenth of the waning month is then ennan phthirou, the eighth ogdoe phthirou, and so on in reverse order down to hene he nea. For phthirou one sometimes finds apol, and for epi deka, mesou. If the month is hollow, after the ninth comes ennan phthirou, then ogdoe phthirou, and so on. Hence Aristophanes in the Clouds, act 4: [Πέμπτη, τετάρτη, τρίτη, μετὰ ταύτην δευτέρα, ἐφ' ἣν ἐγὼ μάλιστα πάντων ἡμερῶν δέδοικα, καὶ βδελύττομαι, εἶτα μετὰ ταύτην ἕνη ἡ νέα]. Fifth, fourth, third, after that the second, which I fear and abhor most of all days; after that comes old and new.

units.la: Nimirum quinta φθιροῦ, quarta φθιροῦ, &c. Et quidem ut Romani per Kalendas nonas & Idus, sic Græci per descriptas hasce partes dies quoscunque exprimunt. Verum
units.tr: Namely, fifth phthirou, fourth phthirou, and so on. And just as the Romans express dates by Kalends, Nones and Ides, so the Greeks express any day by these divisions of the month.

units.la: ἐτη ἡ νέα nonnunquam vocatur Ἰεταρὶς, ut & Ἀπμηλεὰς in honorem Demetrii Macedonis; Ἐνη ἡ νέα à Solone primò vocata fuit.
units.tr: Hene he nea is sometimes called Ietaris, and also Apmeleas, in honour of Demetrius of Macedon. Hene he nea was first so called by Solon.

units.la: VI. Initium anni Attici ab isto novilunium deductum est, cujus plenilunium solstitium æstivum proximè sequebatur.
units.tr: VI. The beginning of the Attic year was reckoned from the new moon whose full moon was the next to follow the summer solstice.

units.la: 1. Veteres Græci, Metonis præsertim & Eudoxi temporibus, solstitium æstivum in octavo cancri gradu & Julii 8 fixum arbitrati sunt; postea ad Junii 27 deductum est, Timocharide præsertim & Hypparcho florentibus. Quapropter si detur annus quispiam Atticus cujus initium sive neomeniam Hecatombæonis quæras; si annum per. Jul. 4400 antecedit, ab isto novilunio propositum computes, cujus plenilunium Julii 8, si sequatur 4400, ab isto cujus plenilunium Junii 27 proximum excipiat.
units.tr: 1. The ancient Greeks, especially in the times of Meton and Eudoxus, judged the summer solstice to fall on the eighth degree of Cancer, that is, on July 8. Later it was moved back to June 27, especially when Timocharis and Hipparchus flourished. Therefore, if you seek the beginning of some Attic year, that is, its new moon of Hecatombaeon, and if that year falls within the Julian period 4400, you should count from the new moon that is proposed for it, whose full moon is July 8. If it falls after 4400, take the next new moon whose full moon is June 27.

units.la: 2. Ex. gr. Timocharis, ut refert Ptolemæus l. 7. c 3. p. 170, observabat spicam virginis exactè borealem Lunæ partem tangere super Horizontem Orientis anno Nabonassari 466, Pyanepsionis sexto Φᾶϊνοντος. Thoth septimo. Annus Nabonassari 466 iniit anno per. Jul. 4431 Nov. 2. hoc anno plenilunium accidit Julii 3, quod itaque proximum erat post Jun. 27. Novilunium medium commissum est Jun. 18. horâ 21. Visa fuit Luna Jun. 20 Anno igitur proposito neomenia Hecatombæonis in Junii 20 incurrit, is est 171 à Kal. Jan. A neomeniâ Hecatombæonis ad ineuntem Pyanepsionem in mensium laterculo colliguntur dies 118, Pyanepsionis sextus Φᾶϊνοντος est dies 24 ejusdem mensis, at 24 ad 118 additi efficiunt 142. Erat igitur Pyanepsionis 24, dies 142 à neomeniâ Hecatombæonis inclusive, quæ incidit in diem 171 à Kal. Jan. addas igitur 170 ad 142 aggregatum est 312. Sextus igitur Pyanepsionis Φᾶϊνοντος erat dies 312 à Kal. Jan. is est Nov. 8, qui erat & septimus dies menses Ægyptiaci Thoth, utpote qui, uti dictum est, incepit Nov. 2. Hoc igitur modo progrediendum est quotiescunque anni vel dies Attici ad Julianos occurrunt revocandi. VII. Annus Macedonicus est vel Lunaris vel Solaris. VIII: Annus Lunaris est ejusdem forme cujus Atticus. IX. Menses Macedonici sunt qui sequuntur. MENSES MACEDONICI Δῖῶ. | Απλλαῖῶ. | Αυδυναῖῶ. | Πεεῖνῶ. | Δύσρῶ. | Ξάνδικῶ. | Αξλςμάνῶ. | Δαύνῶ. | Πιγνέμῶ. | Λώ. | Γοξπαῦῶ. | Τπερβερεταῖῶ.
units.tr: 2. For example, Timocharis, as Ptolemy reports in book 7, chapter 3, page 170, observed that the Spike of Virgo touched exactly the northern part of the Moon above the eastern horizon in the year 466 of Nabonassar, on the sixth day of Pyanepsion, Phainontos. The seventh day of Thoth. The year 466 of Nabonassar began in the Julian period year 4431, on November 2. In this year the full moon fell on July 3, which was therefore the next after June 27. The mean new moon occurred on June 18 at the twenty-first hour. The moon was seen on June 20. So in the year in question the new moon of Hecatombaeon fell on June 20, which is the 171st day from January 1. From the new moon of Hecatombaeon to the beginning of Pyanepsion, counting by the table of months, there are 118 days. The sixth day of Pyanepsion, Phainontos, is the 24th day of that same month, and 24 added to 118 makes 142. So the 24th of Pyanepsion was the 142nd day counting inclusively from the new moon of Hecatombaeon, which fell on the 171st day from January 1. Add 170 to 142, and the sum is 312. So the sixth day of Pyanepsion, Phainontos, was the 312th day from January 1, that is, November 8, which was also the seventh day of the Egyptian month Thoth, since, as was said, that began on November 2. This is the method to follow whenever Attic years or days have to be converted to Julian dates. VII. The Macedonian year is either lunar or solar. VIII. The lunar Macedonian year has the same form as the Attic. IX. The Macedonian months are those that follow. MACEDONIAN MONTHS: Dios [Δῖος]; Apellaios [Απλλαῖος]; Audynaios [Αυδυναῖος]; Peritios [Πεεῖνος]; Dystros [Δύστρος]; Xanthikos [Ξανδικὸς]; Artemisios [Αρτεμίσιος]; Daisios [Δαίσιος]; Panemos [Πανήμος]; Lous [Λῷος]; Gorpiaios [Γορπιαῖος]; Hyperberetaios [Υπερβερεταῖος].

units.la: I. E mensibus hisce Macedonicis alternis 29 & 30 dierum primus, sive ΔΙῶ Attico Maimacterioni respondet. Annus enim Macedonicus non ut Atticus à solstitio æstivo computatur, sed ab æquinoctio Autumnali. Lous itaque in Hecatombeonem convenit, Gorpiæus: in Metagitnonem, Hyberbereteus in Boedromionem, & Dius primus Macedonicus in Maimacterion:m quartum mensem Atticum concurrit. Unde ‘Τπερβερεταῖῶ, πανεμῶ ἡ ἱσταμένου’ ut ait Zenobius, à Galeno cùm Septembri Juliano & mysteriis Atticis confertur, quæ mense Boedromione celebrata sunt. Gal. de sanit. tuend. l. 4. c. 8.
units.tr: I. Of these Macedonian months, the first, Dios, which has 29 and 30 days alternately, corresponds to the Attic Maimacterion. For the Macedonian year is not reckoned from the summer solstice as the Attic is, but from the autumnal equinox. Thus Lous falls in with Hecatombaeon, Gorpiaios with Metageitnion, Hyperberetaios with Boedromion, and Dios, the first Macedonian month, with Maimacterion, the fourth Attic month. Hence, as Zenobius says, "Hyperberetaios, the month of the ninth ... of the beginning," is compared by Galen with the Julian September and the Attic mysteries, which were celebrated in the month of Boedromion. Galen, On the Preservation of Health, book 4, chapter 8.

units.la: 2.Et hæc quidem antiqua fuit mensium Macedonicorum dispositio, quæ tandem aliquando mutata fuit, eò quòd Alexander <bl>Ἀξλωμιναν δυπεν</bl> agere mandavit, ut refert Plutarchus ; quo factum est, ut Artemisius in locum Dæfii, & sic Hyperberetæus in locum Dii translatus esset, & primus mensis evaderet. Et novam quidem hanc mensium Macedonicorum dispositionem inter alios Josephus antiquitatum Judaicarum auctor semper observat.
units.tr: 2. This was the ancient arrangement of the Macedonian months, which was at last changed, because Alexander ordered [the months] to be reckoned in another way, as Plutarch reports. As a result, Artemisios was moved into the place of Dystros, and so Hyperberetaios into the place of Dios, and the first month came to be another. Josephus, the author of the Jewish Antiquities, among others, always follows this new arrangement of the Macedonian months.

units.la: X. Annus Macedonicus solaris duplex est, Julianus, & Tropicus.
units.tr: X. The Macedonian solar year is of two kinds, the Julian and the tropical.

units.la: XI. Annus Macedonum Julianus ejusdem est formæ ac annus à Julio Cæsare constitutus.
units.tr: XI. The Julian Macedonian year has the same form as the year established by Julius Caesar.

units.la: XII. Menses iidem sunt qui in Lunari, hoc ordine procedentes.
units.tr: XII. The months are the same as in the lunar year, proceeding in this order.

units.tr: MACEDONIAN MONTHS (Julian equivalents): Audynaios [Αυδυναῖος] — January; Peritios [Πλειῶν] — February; Dystros [Δύστρος] — March; Xanthikos [Ξανδικὸς] — April; Artemisios [Αρτεμίσιος] — May; Daisios [Δαίσιος] — June; Panemos [Πανήμος] — July; Lous [Λῷος] — August; Gorpiaios [Γορπιαῖος] — September; Hyperberetaios [Υπερβερεταῖος] — October; Dios [ΔΙΟΣ] — November; Apellaios [Απελλαῖος] — December.

units.la: I. Hoc anno Macedonum Juliano scriptores Ecclesiastici saepius utuntur, ut Eusebius, Διὰ μηνὸς γεγονότος ἡμέρας ἰδῶν νοεμβρίου, Dii menfis 13, sive Idibus Novembris. Eusteb hist. Eccl. l. 8. c. 19. Et alibi χρ. ἐν τῇ μακεδόνων μηνὶ Δύστρῳ Ἰουλίῳ, ὡς ἐν ἀπίστῳ Ῥωμαίοις ἀπὸ ἐνδίκα καλανδῶν Ἀπειλλίου, ibid. l. 7. c. 26. ubi ut vides Dystri 22 cum Martii 22 confertur. Euagrius τῇ πρώτῃ τῶν ξανδικῶν ἡμέρᾳ Ἀπειλλίου μηνὸς, Euagr. hist. Eccl. l. 4. c. 9. E quibus aliisque quàm plurimis, quae produci possunt, veterum testimoniis, menses hosce Macedonicos verè Julianos fuisse constat.
units.tr: I. The Ecclesiastical writers often use the Macedonian year in the Julian form, as Eusebius does, writing: "in the month of Dios, on the thirteenth day before the Ides of November" [Διὰ μηνὸς γεγονότος ἡμέρας ἰδῶν νοεμβρίου], that is, on the 13th day of Dios, or the Ides of November. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 8, chapter 19. And elsewhere: "in the Macedonian month of Dystros, which is July" [χρ. ἐν τῇ μακεδόνων μηνὶ Δύστρῳ Ἰουλίῳ], as among the Romans "from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April" [ἀπὸ ἐνδίκα καλανδῶν Ἀπειλλίου], ibid., book 7, chapter 26, where, as you see, the 22nd of Dystros is compared with the 22nd of March. Evagrius: "on the first day of Xanthikos, in the month of Apellaios" [τῇ πρώτῃ τῶν ξανδικῶν ἡμέρᾳ Ἀπειλλίου μηνὸς], Evagrius, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 9. From these and very many other ancient testimonies, which could be brought forward, it is clear that these Macedonian months were truly Julian.

units.la: XIII. Annus Macedonicus Tropicus est, qui in 4 partes distributus erat, quarum singulae ab uno è ἔτρης sive punctis cardinalibus incipiebant.
units.tr: XIII. The tropical Macedonian year was divided into four parts, each of which began from one of the cardinal points.

units.la: I. Macedones enim nonnunquam annum suum in quatuor tuor æquales partes dispescebant, quarum singulæ tria signa dies 91 sibi vendicabant. Dius enim ab æquinoctio Autumnali, Peritius à solstitio Brumali, Artemisius ab æquinoctio verno, & Lous à solstitio æstivo computabatur; reliquique menses interjacentes ordine suo procedebant.
units.tr: I. The Macedonians sometimes divided their year into four equal parts, each of which contained three months, that is, 91 days. For Dios was counted from the autumnal equinox, Peritios from the winter solstice, Artemisios from the vernal equinox, and Lous from the summer solstice; and the months in between proceeded in their order.

units.la: XIV. Annus Syromacedonum, Paphiorum, & Bythynio- rum mensium solummodo nominibus à Macedonico Tro- pico discrepat, ut è subjecto laterculo videre est.
units.tr: XIV. The year of the Syromacedonians, Paphians, and Bithynians differs from the Macedonian year only in the names of the months, as can be seen from the table below.
