units.tr: Ali Ebn Abi Taleb, the fifth emperor of the Muslims, was inaugurated on Friday, the twenty-fifth of Dhu al-Hijjah in the year of the Hegira 35, according to Abulpharagius, Dynasties 9, p. 185. Let us first see in what year and on what day of the Christian era the year of the Hegira 35 began. The calculation proceeds thus: 35 × 7836 = 7836; 30)34(1, remainder 4; 1 × 7836 = 7836; 4 × 7836 = 31344; 31344 ÷ 30 = 1044; 7836 + 1044 = 8880; 8880 ÷ 8766 = 1, remainder 114; 114 ÷ 24 = 4, remainder 18. Completed years: 34. Subtract 1: 33. Days from 1 January: 196 minus 5, leaving 191. Sum 655.

units.la: 3. In hoc ; ut videre est, exemplo, primò unitatem aufero ex anno proposito 35. Et annos completos 34, divido per 30. quotus est, 1. residuum 4. Quotum 1. duco in 7836 & numerus etiam productus est 7836. deinde in eundem numerum multiplico 4, & productum 31344 divido per 30, quotum 1044 addo ad productum primæ multiplicationis 7836. Summam 8880 divido per 8766 quotus est, 1. residuum 114, quod per 24 divisum in quoto dat 4, in residuo 18. Jam quotum penultimæ divisionis, 1. ex annis Hegiræ completis 34 subduco, & relinquuntur 33, quibus addo 622. Summa 655 est annus Christi, quo annus Hegiræ 34 exiit. Deinde 4 ultimæ divisionis quotum unitate augeo, quoniam numerus residuus est plufquam 12, viz. 18. Summam 5 ex 196 aufero & relinquuntur 191. Annus igitur Hegiræ 34 exiit die 191 à Kal. Januariis; Is est Julii 10, ut è Kalendario Juliano patet. Proximus itaque live propositus Hegiræ annus 35 coepit Julii 11. anno Æræ Christianæ 655.
units.tr: 3. In this example, as can be seen, first I subtract the unit from the proposed year 35. I divide the completed years, 34, by 30: the quotient is 1 and the remainder 4. I multiply the quotient 1 by 7836, and the product is also 7836. Then I multiply 4 by the same number 7836, and divide the product 31344 by 30; the quotient 1044 I add to the product of the first multiplication, 7836. I divide the sum 8880 by 8766: the quotient is 1 and the remainder 114, which divided by 24 gives 4 in the quotient and 18 as remainder. Now I subtract the quotient of the penultimate division, 1, from the completed Hegira years, 34, and 33 remain, to which I add 622. The sum 655 is the year of Christ in which the Hegira year 34 ended. Then I increase the quotient 4 of the last division by one, since the remaining number, 18, is more than 12. I subtract the sum 5 from 196 and 191 remain. The Hegira year 34 therefore ended on day 191 from the Kalends of January; this is 10 July, as is clear from the Julian calendar. Hence the following year, or the proposed Hegira year 35, began on 11 July in the year of the Christian era 655.

Another example: Gawhar, minister of al-Muizz li-Din Allah, invaded Egypt in the year of the Hegira 358, on the seventeenth day of Shaban, a Tuesday, as Elmacinus testifies in his History of the Saracens, book 3, p. 227. Let us calculate the beginning of this year. 358 × 7836 = 7836; 30)357(11, remainder 27; 11 × 7836 = 86196; 27 × 7836 = 211572; 211572 ÷ 30 = 7052; 7052 + 7836 + 86196 = 93248; 93248 ÷ 8766 = 10, remainder 5588; 5588 ÷ 24 = 232, remainder 20. Completed years: 357. Days from 1 January: 561. Subtract 11: 346 remain; add 622: sum 968. Subtract 233: 328 remain.

units.la: Annus Hegiræ 257 finitus est anno Christi 968, die à Kal. Jan. 328, sive Nov. 24. Nam penultimæ divisionis quotus 10, unitate augendus est, propterea quòd ultimæ quotus 232 excedat 196. Quocirca anni 11 subtrahendi sunt ex annis Hegiræ completis 257, ut ad annos Christi reducantur. At 11 ex 357 subductis supersunt 346, qui cum 622 collecti dant 968. Quinetiam ultimæ divisionis quotus 232 unitate augendus est, quoniam residuum 20 excedat 12, ut fit 233, at 233 major est numerus quàm ut ex 196 subducatur, subtrahendus igitur ex 561, & reliquus fit dies 328 à Kal. Jan. quo annus Hegiræ 357 exiit, is est Nov. 24. Ergo annus Hegiræ 358 propositus incepit anno Christi 968 Nov. 25.
units.tr: The Hegira year 357 ended in the year of Christ 968, on the 328th day from the Kalends of January, that is, 24 November. For the quotient of the penultimate division, 10, must be increased by one, because the quotient of the last division, 232, exceeds 196. Accordingly, 11 years must be subtracted from the completed Hegira years, 357, to reduce them to years of Christ. When 11 is subtracted from 357, 346 remain, which added to 622 give 968. Moreover, the quotient of the last division, 232, must be increased by one, since the remainder 20 exceeds 12, which makes 233. But 233 is a larger number than can be subtracted from 196, so it must be subtracted from 561, and the remainder is day 328 from the Kalends of January, on which the Hegira year 357 ended, that is, 24 November. Therefore the proposed Hegira year 358 began in the year of Christ 968 on 25 November.

A third example: Aljunabius, as our most distinguished and learned Edward Pocock testifies, and Leunclavius assert that Constantinople was taken by Muhammad Khan in the year of the Hegira 857, on the twentieth of Jumada I, a Tuesday. Let us examine to which year of Christ this Hegira year 857 corresponds. 857 ÷ 30 = 856, quotient 28, remainder 6, ... 223587 ÷ 8766 = 25, remainder 4437; 4437 ÷ 24 = 184, remainder 21 ... Completed years: 856. Subtract 25: 831 remain. Add 622: the sum is the year of Christ 1453. Days from 1 January: 196. Subtract 185: 11 remain. Therefore the Hegira year 856 ended on the 11th day from the Kalends of January, that is, 11 January, in the year of Christ 1453. Thus the proposed Hegira year 857 began in the year of Christ 1453 on 12 January.

units.la: XII. Feria quâ annus init, ita calculetur. Annos Hegirae labentes per 210 dividas, & neglecto quoto numerum residuum per 30 dividas, & quotum in quinque ducas, quo seorsim reservato, annos completos de divisione residuos, Embolimaeos quidem in 5, communes in 4 multiplices, & utriusque multiplicationis productum numero prius reservato conjungas summam 6 auctam per 7 distribuas, residuum est Feria labentis anni.
units.tr: XII. The day of the week on which the year begins is calculated as follows. Divide the elapsed Hegira years by 210, and neglecting the quotient, divide the remainder by 30; multiply the quotient by five and keep this product apart. Subtract the completed years from the division's remainder; multiply the intercalary years by 5 and the common years by 4, and add the products together with the number kept apart. Divide the sum, increased by 6, by 7; the remainder is the weekday of the current year.

units.la: 1. Haec Feriae calculandae methodus ab Ulug Beigo traditur, nisi quòd nos multiplicationum & numeri reservati summae sex adjiciendum docemus, ille tantùm quinque. Et ratio est, quoniam ille primum Hegirae annum à feriâ quintâ, Astronomorum ad instar auspicatur, nos autem à feriâ sextâ; unde & anni Muhammedici vulgò computantur. Hisce praemissis methodum exemplis illustremus.
units.tr: 1. This method of calculating the weekday is handed down by Ulugh Beg, except that we teach that the sum of the multiplications and of the kept number must be increased by six, whereas he adds only five. The reason is that he begins the first Hegira year on Thursday, after the custom of the astronomers, whereas we begin on Friday, which is also the usual way of reckoning the Muhammedan years. With these things premised, let us illustrate the method by examples.

units.la: 2. Annum Hegirae 35 coepisse Julii 11, anno Christi 655 jam ostendimus, videamus in quotum hebdomadis feriam incidat. Anni 35 per 210 dividi nequeunt; neglectâ itaque primâ methodi parte, 35 distribuo per 30, quotus est 1. residuum 5. quotum 1. in 5 duco, & productum 5 reservo; Residuum est 5. Ergo hic quintus est annus triacontaeteridos, & quatuor sunt completi. E quibus unicus est Embolimaeus, & tres communes; itaque 1. multiplico in 5, & 3 in 4. prioris multiplicationis productum est 5 posterioris 12, hacque addas numero reservato 5 & ad summam 22 adjicias 6, aggregatum 28 per 7 divisum relinquit 0. Id est 7. nam quoties o sit in residuo feria 7 assumenda est. Coepit ergo hic annus Feriâ septimâ; Cyclus solis hoc anno Christi 655 erat 20. Litera Dom. D. character Julii 11. C. erat itaque Feria septima, & rectè procedit calculus. 12, ut sit 233, at 233 major est numerus quàm ut ex 196 subducatur, subtrahendus igitur ex 561, & reliquus sit dies 328 à Kal. Jan. quo annus Hegiræ 357 exiit, is est Nov. 24. Ergo annus Hegiræ 358 propositus incepit anno Christi 968 Nov. 25.
units.tr: 2. We have already shown that the Hegira year 35 began on 11 July in the year of Christ 655; let us see on which day of the week it falls. The years 35 cannot be divided by 210, so, leaving aside the first part of the method, I divide 35 by 30: the quotient is 1 and the remainder 5. I multiply the quotient 1 by 5 and keep the product 5 apart. The remainder is 5. So this is the fifth year of the thirty-year cycle, and four years are complete, of which one is intercalary and three are common. I multiply 1 by 5, and 3 by 4. The product of the first multiplication is 5, of the second 12; add to these the kept number 5, and to the sum 22 add 6. The total 28 divided by 7 leaves 0, that is, 7, for whenever the remainder is 0 the weekday 7 is to be taken. This year therefore began on Saturday. The cycle of the sun in the year of Christ 655 was 20, and the dominical letter was D, the character of 11 July being C. So the day was Saturday, and the calculation proceeds correctly. Then the other remaining part of the example: subtract the quotient of the penultimate division, 1, from the completed years; increase 12 ... the year of Christ 968 on 25 November. [The remaining sentences in this unit repeat the calculation of the Hegira year 358 as printed above, and are translated as they stand in the text.]

units.la: XII. Feria quâ annus init, ita calculetur. Annos Hegirae labentes per 210 dividas, & neglecto quoto numerum residuum per 30 dividas, & quotum in quinque ducas, quo seorsim reservato, annos completos de divisione residuos, Embolimaeos quidem in 5, communes in 4 multiplices, & utriusque multiplicationis productum numero prius reservato conjungas summam 6 auctam per 7 distribuas, residuum est Feria labentis anni.
units.tr: XII. The weekday on which the year begins is calculated thus. Divide the elapsed years of the Hegira by 210, and, disregarding the quotient, divide the remainder by 30. Multiply the quotient by 5 and keep this product apart. From the remainder of the division take the complete years: multiply the intercalary years by 5 and the common years by 4. Add the two products to the number kept apart, and add 6 to the sum. Divide the total by 7; the remainder is the weekday of the current year.

units.la: 1. Haec Feriae calculandae methodus ab Ulug Beigo traditur, nisi quòd nos multiplicationum & numeri reservati summae sex adjiciendum docemus, ille tantùm quinque. Et ratio est, quoniam ille primum Hegirae annum à feriâ quintâ, Astronomorum ad instar auspicatur, nos autem à feriâ sextâ; unde & anni Muhammedici vulgò computantur. Hisce praemissis methodum exemplis illustremus.
units.tr: 1. This method of calculating the weekday is handed down by Ulugh Beg, except that we teach adding six to the sum of the multiplications and the reserved number, whereas he adds only five. The reason is that he begins the first year of the Hegira on the fifth day (Thursday), following the astronomers, whereas we begin on the sixth day (Friday); and this is also why Muslim years are commonly reckoned from it. With these points premised, let us illustrate the method with examples.

units.la: 2. Annum Hegirae 35 coepisse Julii 11, anno Christi 655 jam ostendimus, videamus in quotum hebdomadis feriam incidat. Anni 35 per 210 dividi nequeunt; neglectâ itaque primâ methodi parte, 35 distribuo per 30, quotus est 1. residuum 5. quotum 1. in 5 duco, & productum 5 reservo; Residuum est 5. Ergo hîc quintus est annus triacontaeridos, & quatuor sunt completi. E quibus unicus est Embolimaeus, & tres communes; itaque 1. multiplico in 5, & 3 in 4. prioris multiplicationis productum est 5 posterioris 12, haec addas numero reservato 5 & ad summam 22 adjicias 6, aggregatum 28 per 7 divisum relinquit 0. Id est 7. nam quoties olit in residuo feria 7 assumenda est. Coepit ergo hic annus Feriâ septimâ; Cyclus solis hoc anno Christi 655 erat 20. Litera Dom. D. character Julii 11. C. erat itaque Feria septima, & rectè procedit calculus.
units.tr: 2. We have already shown that the year 35 of the Hegira began on July 11, anno Christi 655. Let us see on what day of the week it fell. The years 35 cannot be divided by 210, so, setting aside the first part of the method, I divide 35 by 30. The quotient is 1 and the remainder 5. I multiply the quotient 1 by 5 and keep the product 5 in reserve. The remainder is 5, so this is the fifth year of the thirty-year cycle, and four years are complete. Of these, one is an embolismic year and three are common. So I multiply 1 by 5 and 3 by 4. The product of the first multiplication is 5, and that of the second is 12. Add these to the reserved number 5, make the sum 22, and add 6, giving 28. Divided by 7, this leaves 0, which stands for 7, since whenever the remainder is 0 the day 7 is taken. This year therefore began on the seventh day. The solar cycle in the year anno Christi 655 was 20. The dominical letter was D, and the character of July 11 was C. So it was the seventh day, and the calculation is correct.

units.la: 3. units.tr: 3. Likewise, we found earlier that the year 358 of the Hegira began on November 25, anno Christi 968, and that the year 857 began on January 12, anno Christi 1453. Let us work out the day of the week for each. For 358: 358 divided by 210 gives 1, which counts for nothing, and the remainder is 148. For 857: 857 divided by 210 gives 4, with the remainder 17. The steps are set out in the layout below, as in the earlier example, and the working for each year is carried through in the same way.

units.la: Hic annum Hegiræ labentem 358 divido per 210, quotus 1. nullius est momenti, quoniam 210 numerum septenarium præcisè continet. Residuum 148 divido per 30, quorum 4 in 5 duco, & productum 20 subscribo, è residuo 28 unitatem aufero, completos ut haberem annos 27, è quibus 10 Embolimæos in 5 duco, & 17 communes in 4, & utriusque productum subscribo, ut videre est, deinde numeros ex tribus hisce multiplicationibus productos, viz. 20. 50. & 68 colligo, summæ 138 addo 6, & aggregatum 144 per 7 distribuo, & residuum est 4. Ergo hic annus cœpit Feriâ quartâ. Anno Christi 968 quo hic annus incepit, cyclus solis erat 25. Lit. Dom. E, D. character Nov. 25 G. Erat ergo Feria quarta sive dies Mercurii.
units.tr: Here I divide the elapsed year 358 by 210. The quotient is 1, which counts for nothing, since 210 is exactly a multiple of the seven-day week. I divide the remainder 148 by 30. The quotient is 4, which I multiply by 5, writing down the product 20. From the remainder 28 I take away 1, so that there are 27 complete years. Of these, 10 are embolismic, which I multiply by 5, and 17 are common, which I multiply by 4. I write down the product of each, as can be seen. Then I add the numbers from these three multiplications, namely 20, 50 and 68, making 138. I add 6 to the sum, and divide the total 144 by 7, leaving a remainder of 4. So this year began on the fourth day, Wednesday. In anno Christi 968, when this year began, the solar cycle was 25, the dominical letter was E, the dominical character D, and the character of November 25 was G. It was therefore the fourth day, that is, Wednesday.

units.la: 4. In ultimo exemplo, 857 per 210 divisi, relinquunt annos 17, qui per 30 dividi non possunt, & idcirco divisione non est opus, sed methodi explicandæ gratiâ describo, ac si divisionem admitterent. Divisi itaque 17 per 30 in quoto dant 0, in residuo 17,0 in 5 ductum producit 0. Residuum 17 unitate mutilatum est 16, è quibus sex sunt anni Embolimæi in 5,& 10 communes in 4 ducendi; utriusque multiplicationis productum conjungo (nam prior multiplicatio, uti dictum est, producit 0.) ad aggregatum 70 addo 6, summa 76 per 7 divisa relinquit 6. Hic itaque annus cœpit Feriâ sextâ. Anno Christi 1453 cyclus solis erat 6, Lit. Dom. G. character Jan. 12. E. Erat igitur Feria sexta sive dies veneris. Quod si dies iste primus anni propositi in feriam, hâc methodo inventam non quadret (quod quam rarissimè, si unquam accidit) per feriam regulâ perpetuâ castigandus est.
units.tr: 4. In the last example, dividing 857 by 210 leaves 17 years, which cannot be divided by 30, so no division is needed here. I set it out only for the sake of explaining the method, as if it could be divided. Dividing 17 by 30 gives 0 as the quotient and 17 as the remainder; 0 multiplied by 5 gives 0. Taking one from 17 leaves 16, of which six are intercalary years to be multiplied by 5 and 10 are common years to be multiplied by 4. I add together the products of these multiplications (the first, as said, gives 0), and to the total 70 I add 6, making 76. Divided by 7, this leaves 6. So this year began on the sixth day. In the year of Christ 1453 the solar cycle was 6, the dominical letter G, and the character of 12 January E. So the day was the sixth, that is, Friday. But if this first day of the year in question does not agree with the weekday found by this method (which happens very rarely, if ever), it must be corrected by the perpetual rule for the weekday.

units.la: XIII. Ut feriam quâ mensis propositus incipit, invenias, numerum mensium plenorum à Muharram ad quæsitum exclusivè, in 2 ducas, produćto numerum mensium ca- vorum & feriam Muharram sive characterem anni ad- jungas, aggregatum enim per 7 divisum reliquam faciet feriam mensis quæsiti.
units.tr: XIII. To find the weekday on which the stated month begins, take the number of full months from Muharram up to the one sought, exclusive; double it, adding the number of hollow months; then add the weekday of Muharram, or the character of the year. The sum divided by 7 leaves the weekday of the month sought.

units.la: 1. Hæc etiam methodus ab Ulug Beigo proponitur, in quâ menses pleni duplicandi sunt, propterea quod quilibet eorum, ut dier. 30, quatuor septimanas biduo excedit, menses cavi, uno tantum die, ut dier. 29. Sed mensis quæsitus non numerandus est, quoniam Feria Muharram calculo adjicitur.
units.tr: 1. This method too is set out by Ulugh Beg, in which full months are doubled, because each of them, having 30 days, exceeds four weeks by two days, while hollow months, having 29 days, exceed them by one day only. But the month sought is not counted, since the weekday of Muharram is added to the calculation.

units.la: 2. Quæramus in quotam hebdomadis feriam incidat neomenia Dulheggiæ anno Hegiræ 35. Character hujus anni sive Feria, quâ Muharram cœpit erat septima, ut ostensum est. A Muharram inclusivè ad Dulheggiam exclusivè, sex sunt menses pleni, cavi quinque. Bis sex sunt 12, quibus additis 5 propter quinque menses cavos, Summa est 17, adde feriam Muharram 7, & fit 24. quæ per 7 divisa residuum facit 3. Ergo Dulheggia hoc anno coepit Feriâ tertiâ, sive die Martis 5 & idcircò Dulheggiæ 25 erat feria sexta sive dies veneris, ut rectè scribit Abulpharagius.
units.tr: 2. Let us ask on what weekday of the week the new moon of Dhu'l-Hijjah falls in the 35th year of the Hijra. The character of this year, or the weekday on which Muharram began, was the seventh, as has been shown. From Muharram inclusive to Dhu'l-Hijjah exclusive there are six full months and five hollow ones. Twice six makes 12; add 5 for the five hollow months, which gives 17; add 7 for the weekday of Muharram, and the total is 24. Divided by 7, this leaves 3. Therefore Dhu'l-Hijjah began this year on the third day, that is Tuesday, the 5th; and so the 25th of Dhu'l-Hijjah was the sixth day, that is Friday, as Abulpharagius correctly writes.

units.la: 3. Annus 358 coepit Feriâ quintâ, à Muharram ad Shabanum sunt menses 4 pleni, 3 cavi, bis 4 est octo, adde 3 ob tres menses cavos, & 4 ob feriam Muharram, summa est 15, quæ per 7 divisa, relinquit 1. Shabân ergo hoc anno coepit Feriâ primâ, & idcircò Shabani 17 erat Feria tertia, ut asserit Elmacinus.
units.tr: 3. The year 358 began on the fifth day. From Muharram to Sha'ban there are 4 full months and 3 hollow ones. Twice 4 is 8; add 3 for the three hollow months and 4 for the weekday of Muharram; the sum is 15, which divided by 7 leaves 1. So Sha'ban began this year on the first day, and therefore the 17th of Sha'ban was the third day, as Elmacinus asserts.

units.la: 4. In ultimo exemplo, annum Hegiræ 857 Feriâ sextâ iniisse per calculum invenimus. Videamus in quotam feriam incidat Jomadæ prioris dies vigesimus. Inter Muharram inclusivè & Jomadam priorem duo sunt menses pleni, totidémque cavi; duo menses pleni duplicati fiunt 4 quibus si 2 propter duos menses cavos, & 6 ob feriam Muharram adjiciamus summa est 12, aufer 7, restant 5. Itaque Jomada prior incepit Feriâ quintâ sive die Jovis. Et ideo Jomadæ prioris dies 20 erat Feria tertia, sive dies Martis 3, ut auctores supra laudati rectè statuunt. Hic annus juxta calculum præcedentem iniit Jan. 12. anno Christi 1453. ab initio anni Muhammedici ad ineuntem Jomadam priorem dies colliguntur 118. adde dies 11 ante incœptum annum Muhammedicũ elapsos & fiunt 129. his rursum adjicias 20 pro vigesimo Jomadæ prioris, summa est 149. Ergo dies Jomadæ prioris vigesimus anno Hegiræ 857 in diem Julianum à Kal. Jan. 149, sive Maii 29 convenit, quæ etiam erat Feria tertia. Nam cyclus solis anno Christi 1453 erat 6. Lit. Dom. G. character Maii 29 B. Erat ergo Feria tertia. Et quidem Constantinopolim hoc anno Christi, hoc die mensis, & hâc Feriâ hebdomadis captam fuisse, in patriarchicâ Martinii Crusii historiâ confirmatur, his verbis Ἦταν χρόνοι ἀπὸ χρισῦ γενέσεως χίλιοι πεῤῥακόσιοι πεντήκοντα πέντε, μηνὶ ὑπὸσῇ ἰνδίζῃ, ἡμέρᾳ ὑπ᾽ ἐ. Annus igitur erat à Christi nativitate 1453, mensis Majus, dies 29, Feria 3. Quæ omnia per calculum hunc nostrum quàm exactissimè exuuntur.
units.tr: 4. In the last example we have found by calculation that the year 857 of the Hijra began on the sixth day. Let us see on what weekday the twentieth day of Jumada I falls. Between Muharram inclusive and Jumada I there are two full months and as many hollow ones. Two full months doubled make 4; if we add 2 for the two hollow months and 6 for the weekday of Muharram, the sum is 12; take away 7, and 5 remains. So Jumada I began on the fifth day, that is Thursday. Therefore the 20th day of Jumada I was the third day, that is Tuesday, the 3rd, as the authors cited above rightly state. This year, according to the preceding calculation, began on January 12 in the year of Christ 1453. From the beginning of the Muhammadan year to the start of Jumada I, the days come to 118; add the 11 days that had elapsed before the Muhammadan year began, and the total is 129; add again 20 for the twentieth of Jumada I, and the sum is 149. Therefore the twentieth day of Jumada I in the year 857 of the Hijra corresponds to the Julian day 149 from the first of January, that is May 29; this was also the third day. For the solar cycle in the year of Christ 1453 was 6, the Dominical letter G, and the character of May 29 is B. So it was the third day. And that Constantinople was taken in this year of Christ, on this day of the month and on this day of the week, is confirmed in Martin Crusius's patriarchal history, in these words: Ἦταν χρόνοι ἀπὸ χρισῦ γενέσεως χίλιοι πεῤῥακόσιοι πεντήκοντα πέντε, μηνὶ ὑπὸσῇ ἰνδίζῃ, ἡμέρᾳ ὑπ᾽ ἐ [There were years from the birth of Christ one thousand four hundred and fifty-five, in the month ..., on the day ...]. The year therefore was 1453 from the birth of Christ, the month May, the day 29, the weekday the third. All of which our calculation here agrees with most exactly.

units.la: XIV. Si proposito quolibet anno Christi currente, quaeratur, quotus Hegirae annus ei respondeat, hac utendum est methodo. Ab annis Christi labentibus aufer 621, residuum divides per 33, quotum dividendo addas, summa est annus Hegirae labens vel ei proximus, quod per calculum neomeniae istius anni discernendum est.
units.tr: XIV. If, for any given year of Christ, one asks which year of the Hijra corresponds to it, the following method must be used. From the elapsed years of Christ subtract 621; divide the remainder by 33; add the quotient to the remainder. The sum is the elapsed year of the Hijra, or the one nearest to it, which must be decided by calculating the new moon of that year.

units.la: 1. Annis circiter 33 vertentibus, annus unus Muhammedicus anticipatur, & dies preterea 4. 18. 48'. Nam anni Juliani 33 dies colligunt 12053 h. 6. o'. totidem Muhammedani dies 11694. hor. 2. 24'. Differentia est dies 359. h. 3. 36', aufer annum Muhammedicum sive dies 354. h. 8. 48'. & restant d. 4. 18. 48'. Annis itaque Julianis 33 vertentibus sive completis praeter unum annum Muhammedanum dies tantùm 4. hor. 18. 48'. retroaguntur. Ad inveniendum igitur annum Hegirae Juliano respondentem, nullus commodior occurrit numerus quam 33. utpote per quem anni Juliani à primo Hegirae fluentes, divisi in quoto dabunt annos Muhammedicos à tot Julianis retroversos, quique idcircò ad dividendum sive annorum Julianorum à primo Hegirae elapsorum numerum adjecti, annum conficient Muhammedanum Juliano labenti ferè respondentem.
units.tr: 1. In about 33 revolving years, one Muhammadan year is gained, together with a further 4 days, 18 hours and 48 minutes. For 33 Julian years make 12,053 days, 6 hours and 0 minutes; the same number of Muhammadan days is 11,694 days, 2 hours and 24 minutes. The difference is 359 days, 3 hours and 36 minutes. Subtract one Muhammadan year, that is 354 days, 8 hours and 48 minutes, and 4 days, 18 hours and 48 minutes remain. So when 33 Julian years have revolved, or been completed, except for one Muhammadan year, only 4 days and 18 hours and 48 minutes have fallen back. To find the year of the Hijra that corresponds to a Julian year, no more convenient number presents itself than 33: since the Julian years elapsed from the first year of the Hijra, divided by it, will give the number of Muhammadan years that have slipped back by that many Julian years. These, being therefore added to the number of Julian years elapsed from the first year of the Hijra, make a Muhammadan year that roughly corresponds to the Julian year that is running.

units.la: 2. Primus annus Hegirae coepit anno Christi 622. ex annis itaque Christi labentibus subduc 621, & reliquus erit annorum Julianorum à primo Hegirae fluentium numerus, quo, ut dixi, per 33 diviso, quotus exhibebit annos retroversos, atque ideo adjiciendos. Ex. gr. Si proponatur annus Christi 1582, ut quaeramus totus annus Hegirae in eum conveniat. Ergo ex 1582 subduco 621, & restant annis 961. quibus per 33 divisis quotus est 29. Ergo annis Julianis 961 anni totidem Muhammedani, & praeterea 29 propemodum effluxerunt. Ad dividendum itaque sive ad 961 addo 29, summa 990 est; vel ipse annus Hegirae qui anno Christi 1582 incepit, vel saltem ei proximus, ut certiores autem fiamus utrum annus iste Mudammedicus anno Christi 1582 currente cœpit necne, initium ejus calculandum est. Per methodum autem ante traditam annus Hegiræ 989 exiit anno Christi 1582. Jan. 25. Annus igitur Hegiræ 990 iniit eodem anno Christi Jan. 26. Eodem nimirum anno quem calculus noster repræsentat.
units.tr: 2. The first year of the Hijra began in the year of Christ 622. From the elapsed years of Christ, then, subtract 621; the remainder will be the number of Julian years that have passed since the first year of the Hijra. Dividing it by 33, as I have said, the quotient will show the years that have slipped back, which are therefore to be added. For example, if the year of Christ 1582 is proposed, and we seek which year of the Hijra as a whole falls in it: from 1582 I subtract 621, and 961 years remain. Divided by 33, this gives a quotient of 29. So, 961 Julian years, and as many Muhammadan years, plus about 29 more, have passed. Therefore, adding 29 to 961, the sum is 990: this is either the very year of the Hijra which began in the year of Christ 1582, or at least the one nearest to it. But to be more certain whether that Muhammadan year began during the year of Christ 1582 or not, its beginning must be calculated. By the method given above, the year 989 of the Hijra ended in the year of Christ 1582 on January 25. Therefore the year 990 of the Hijra began in the same year of Christ, on January 26, the very year our calculation represents.

units.la: 3. Annus, quo hæc meditor, est Æræ Christianæ 1667. Scire vellem quotus annus Hegiræ in eum conveniat. Igitur ex 1667 subduco 621, & residuum 1046 divido per 33, quotum 31 aggrego ad dividendum 1046, aggregatum est 1077. Ergo huic anno Christi 1667 annus Hegiræ 1077 partim respondet. Quando autem incepit dictus Hegiræ annus, per methodum superius traditam eruendum est; juxta quam annus Hegiræ 1077 incepit anno Christi 1666 Jun. 24. Quocirca posterior tantum istius pars in annum hunc 1667 incurrit. Hoc autem anno labente, annus Hegiræ proximus sive 1078 init, idque Jun. 13. Nam annus 1077 est communis, quod ex eo patet quòd si 1077 per 30 dividas, residuum erit 27, ast annus triacontaeteridos 27 est communis juxta propositionem sextam. Colligit igitur hic annus dies solummodò 354. Annus Hegiræ 1077 coepit Jun. 24. Is est dies à Kal. Jan. 175. Ergo ad 354 addas 175. summa est 529. aufer dies unius anni Juliani, sive 365, supersunt 164. Ergo hoc anno Christi 1667 annus Hegiræ 1078 init die 164 à Kal. Jan. sive Jun. 13. idque feriâ quintâ, quod & ex Methodo superius tradità pro feriâ Mustahal, sive neomeniæ Muharram inveniendâ, & è cyclo solis patet. Nam cyclus solis est 24 Lit.Dom. F. Character Junii 13.C. Est ergo Feria quinta, sive dies Jovis.
units.tr: 3. The year in which I am writing these things is the Christian Era 1667. I should like to know which year of the Hijra falls in it. So, from 1667 I subtract 621, and divide the remainder 1046 by 33; the quotient 31 I add to 1046, and the sum is 1077. Therefore the year of Christ 1667 corresponds in part to the year 1077 of the Hijra. When that year of the Hijra began must be worked out by the method set out above; by which the year 1077 of the Hijra began in the year of Christ 1666 on June 24. Hence only the latter part of that year falls into this year 1667. And with this year running, the next year of the Hijra, that is 1078, begins, on June 13. For the year 1077 is a common year, which is clear from the fact that if you divide 1077 by 30, the remainder is 27, and a year 27 in the thirty-year cycle is common, according to the sixth proposition. So this year gathers only 354 days. The year 1077 of the Hijra began on June 24, which is the 175th day from the first of January. Add 175 to 354, and the sum is 529; take away one Julian year, that is 365, and 164 remain. Therefore in this year of Christ 1667 the year 1078 of the Hijra begins on the 164th day from the first of January, that is June 13, and on the fifth day, Thursday; this is also clear from the method given above for finding the weekday of Muharram, the Mustahal, and from the solar cycle. For the solar cycle is 24, the Dominical letter F, and the character of June 13 is C. So it is the fifth day, that is Thursday.

units.la: 4. Dies quo hisce scribendis vaco est Sept. 26. Muharram, ut ostensum est, iniit hoc anno Christi Jun. 13. feriâ quintâ. Ergo Rabia posterior init Sept. 10. feriâ tertiâ: Et dies hæc Sept. 26 est Rabiæ posterioris dies 17, si à medâ media nocte computetur. Sed' Arabes ab occasu solis dies suos deducunt, ut ante monuimus. Jam vero Sol occidit, octavo enim post meridiem hora sonuit. Dies itaque Rabiæ posterioris 18 jam cœptus est & fluit. Nos summam igitur manum primo huic Institutionum Chronologicarum Libro imposuimus, anno Christi 1667 Sept. 26. anno autem Hegiræ 1078. Rabiæ poster. 18.
units.tr: 4. The day on which I am free to write these things is Sept. 26. As shown above, Muharram began this year of Christ on June 13, a Friday. Therefore Rabia posterior begins on Sept. 10, a Tuesday. This day, Sept. 26, is the 17th day of Rabia posterior, if the day is counted from midnight to midnight. But the Arabs reckon their days from sunset, as we noted before. Now the sun has set, for it sounded the eighth hour after noon. So the 18th day of Rabia posterior has already begun and is running on. We have therefore put the final touches to this first book of the Chronological Institutes, on the year of Christ 1667, Sept. 26, and in the year of the Hegira 1078, Rabia posterior 18.

units.la: Libri Primi.
units.tr: Of the First Book.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: INSTITUTIONUM. CHRONOLOGICARUM. LIBER SECUNDUS.
units.tr: INSTITUTIONUM. CHRONOLOGICARUM. LIBER SECUNDUS.

units.la: CAP. I. De Syzygiis & Eclipsibus.
units.tr: CHAP. I. Of Syzygies and Eclipses.

units.la: In primo Libro de χρονικῇ Chronologiæ parte actum est, quæ temporis natura, & partes explicantur: Sequitur Χρονο-λογικὴ. II. Pars Χρονολογικὴ est, quæ de Characteribus agit Chronologicis. III. Characteres sunt certæ quædam notæ quibus diversa tempora à se invicem distinguantur. IV. Suntque vel naturales vel instituti. V. Characteres naturales sunt, qui à naturalibus causis dependent. VI. Characteres naturales sunt tres, Syzygiæ, Eclipses, & puncta cardinalia. VII. Syzygiæ dicuntur novilunia, & plenilunia.
units.tr: In the first book on the chronological part of chronology, the nature of time and its divisions were explained. What follows is the chronological part [χρονολογικὴ]. II. The chronological part deals with chronological characters. III. Characters are certain marks by which different times are distinguished from one another. IV. They are either natural or instituted. V. Natural characters are those that depend on natural causes. VI. There are three natural characters: syzygies, eclipses, and the cardinal points. VII. Syzygies are new moons and full moons.

units.la: Yzygiæ inter temporum characteres recensetur, propterea quòd si quid circa novilunium aut plenilunium gestum tradatur, tempus ita definitum per tabulas Astronomicas quàm certissimè computetur. Quinetiam sine tabulis Astronomicis dies, quibus committuntur, per cyclum Lunæ, vel epactam inveniantur, uti posthæc ostendemus.
units.tr: Syzygies are counted among the characters of time, because if anything is recorded as having happened near a new moon or a full moon, the time so defined can be calculated as exactly as possible by astronomical tables. Moreover, even without astronomical tables, the days on which they fall can be found by the lunar cycle or the epact, as we shall show later.

units.la: VIII. Eclipsis in genere est privatio vel defectio lucis in corpore lucido, per corporis opaci interpositionem effecta.
units.tr: VIII. An eclipse in general is the privation or failure of light in a luminous body, brought about by the interposition of an opaque body.

units.la: 1. Eclipses certissima temporum κεφαλαια non immerito judicantur; utpote quæ diligenter observatæ, & fideliter posteritati traditæ tempora præterita à futuris exquisitissimè distinguunt. Tot enim ad deliquia tam Lunæ quàm solis occurrunt necessaria, ut duo per omnia similia, viz. quoad tempus, locum; digitos, &c. nunquam accidere possunt. Post elapsos fateor annos 18, eodem iterum die Luna deficiat, sed non eodem diei momento, nec iisdem circumstantiis quibus priores vestitæ sunt. At Solarium Eclipsium ἀποτελέσματα est veri multò dissimilior, cum per parallaxes tantopere varientur. Et hinc est quod si quispiam (quod sæpe factum legimus) Eclipses curiosius observet, & observatas scriptis mandet, per eas annus diésque, quo contigerunt, ab aliis quibuscunque secernatur. Quod exemplis statim patefiet.
units.tr: 1. Eclipses are rightly judged the most certain chief points [κεφάλαια] of time, since, when they are carefully observed and faithfully handed down to posterity, they distinguish past times from future times most exactly. For so many eclipses of the moon as well as of the sun occur that two in every respect alike, namely in time, place, digits, and so on, can never happen. I admit that after eighteen years the moon fails again on the same day, but not at the same moment of the day, nor under the same circumstances as the earlier ones. The effects [ἀποτελέσματα] of solar eclipses, however, are much more dissimilar, since they vary so greatly through parallax. Hence, if anyone (as we often read has been done) observes eclipses more carefully and commits his observations to writing, the year and day on which they occurred are distinguished from all others. This will be made clear at once by examples.

units.la: IX. Eclipses sunt vel Lunares vel Solares.
units.tr: IX. Eclipses are either lunar or solar.

units.la: X. Eclipsis Lunaris est privatio lucis Solaris in Lunâ per globum terrenum solem inter & Lunam positum effecta.
units.tr: X. A lunar eclipse is the privation of the sun's light in the moon, brought about by the earth's globe placed between the sun and the moon.

units.la: 1. Nimirum quicquid luminis à Lunâ in terram projicitur, à sole tanquam à fonte mutuatur; quo fit ut si terra, quam Lunæ ad instar corpus esse opacum nemo dubitat, solem & Lunam interjiciatur, Luna luce suâ mutuatitiâ, quâ fulget, privetur necesse est, & obtenebrescat: Terræ scilicet umbrâ pro solis radiis in eam transmissâ. Terra vero solem inter & Lunam nunquam interjacet, præterquàm in pleniluniis, quando Luna soli opponitur; & in iis tantùm interluniis, quibus Sol, Terra, & Luna in eâdem sunt lineâ rectâ, & Terra medium locum occupans, lucem à sole ad Lunam transmissam intercipit.
units.tr: 1. Clearly, whatever light is cast from the moon onto the earth is borrowed from the sun as from its source. Hence, if the earth, which no one doubts is an opaque body like the moon, is interposed between the sun and the moon, the moon must necessarily be deprived of the borrowed light by which it shines and be darkened, since the earth's shadow takes the place of the sun's rays sent toward it. The earth, however, is never interposed between the sun and the moon except at full moons, when the moon is opposite the sun, and only at those conjunctions in which the sun, earth, and moon lie on one straight line and the earth, occupying the middle place, intercepts the light passing from the sun to the moon.

units.la: . 2. In omnibus autem pleniluniis hoc non accidit, eò quòd Luna latitudine suâ ab Ecliptica, nunc versùs Austrum,nunc versùs Boream Terræ umbrā præterfugit. Cum Sol autem circa nodos sive caput & caudam Draconis versetur, quibus orbita Lunæ cum orbitâ solis connectitur, ( quod plerunque bis in anno contingit ) Luna ei directè opposita in umbram Terræ interjectæ plus aut minus (prout se habet Lunæ ad solem oppofitio) ad Austrum aut Boream Eclipticæ immergitur.
units.tr: 2. This does not happen at all full moons, because the moon, by its latitude from the ecliptic, passes by the earth's shadow sometimes toward the south and sometimes toward the north. But since the sun is situated near the nodes, that is the head and tail of the Dragon, where the orbit of the moon is joined with the orbit of the sun (which happens usually twice a year), the moon, directly opposite to it, is immersed in the earth's shadow interposed, more or less according as the opposition of the moon to the sun is situated, toward the south or north of the ecliptic.

units.la: XI. Eclipsis Lunaris est vel totalis vel partialis. XII. Eclipsis Lunæ totalis est, quâ tota Luna in umbram Terræ immersa luce suâ spoliatur.
units.tr: XI. A lunar eclipse is either total or partial. XII. A total lunar eclipse is one in which the whole moon, immersed in the earth's shadow, is deprived of its light.

units.la: 1. Cùm luminaria in ipsissimis adeò nodis existant, ut centrum Lunæ per umbræ Terrenæ centrum vel omnino vel ferè transeat, tota Luna sub umbrâ latitat, ibidémque scrupula aliqua horaria plerunque, nonnunquam duas etiam horas moratur. Et idcirco totalis Eclipsis meritò nuncupetur.
units.tr: 1. Since the luminaries stand so exactly at the nodes that the centre of the moon passes through the centre of the earth's shadow either altogether or nearly so, the whole moon lies hidden under the shadow, and it usually remains there for some scruples of an hour, and sometimes even for two hours. Therefore it is rightly called a total eclipse.

units.la: 2. Hujusmodi Eclipsis Lunæ totalis à Sulpitio Gallo prædicta, L. Paulo Æmilio, & Licinio Crasso Coss. accidit, ab horâ secundâ usque ad quartam horam noctis quam pridie nonas Septembris insecuta est dies; teste Livio Dec. 5. l. 4. Annus erat urbis conditæ 586. per. Jul. 4546. & nox quâ contigit hæc Eclipsis in Juliana anni formâ ista erat quæ inter Jun. 21. & 22 fluxit. Initium Eclipseos per tabulas Danicas erat Jun. 21. h. 6. 14'. post meridiem Macedoniæ, medium hor. 8. 18'. finis horâ 10. 22'. Digiti Ecliptici 15 2/12. Duratio moræ hor. 1. 32'. tota duratio Eclipseos horæ 4. 8'. Tota ergo Luna sub umbrâ latitare cœpit hor. 7. 32'. sive secundâ circiter noctis hora, adeo ut horâ quartâ ex umbrâ tota emersit. Et hæc quidem Eclipsis luculentissimus est character, non tam consulatûs L. Pauli Æmilii, & Licini Crassi sed & epochæ Urbis Conditæ, Cùm hæc enim Eclipsis acciderit anno Urbis Conditæ 586 & per. Jul. 4546, certissimo nobis sit argumento, epocham V. C. ab anno per. Jul. 3961 procedere, sive ab anno ante Christum 753.
units.tr: 2. A total lunar eclipse of this kind, foretold by Sulpicius Gallus, occurred in the consulship of L. Paulus Aemilius and Licinius Crassus. It began from the second hour of the night until the fourth hour, on the night which followed the day before the Nones of September, as Livy testifies in Dec. 5, book 4. This was the year 586 from the founding of the city, Julian period 4546. The night on which this eclipse occurred, in the Julian form of the year, was the one that ran between June 21 and 22. According to the Danish tables, the beginning of the eclipse was June 21 at 6 h. 14' p.m. Macedonian time, the middle at 8 h. 18', and the end at 10 h. 22'. The eclipse digits were 15 2/12. The duration of totality was 1 h. 32', and the whole duration of the eclipse was 4 h. 8'. The whole moon therefore began to lie under the shadow at 7 h. 32', that is, about the second hour of the night, so that at the fourth hour it had emerged wholly from the shadow. This eclipse is a most brilliant character, not only of the consulship of L. Paulus Aemilius and Licinius Crassus but also of the epoch of the founding of the city. For since this eclipse occurred in the year 586 from the founding of the city and in Julian period 4546, it is a most certain proof to us that the epoch of the year from the foundation of the city (V.C.) runs from the Julian period 3961, that is, from the year 753 before Christ.

units.la: XIII. Eclipsis Lunæ partialis est quâ pars tantum Lunæ deficit.
units.tr: XIII. A partial eclipse of the Moon is one in which only part of the Moon is darkened.

units.la: 1. Cùm luminaria nodis remotiora moventur, pars tantùm Lunæ, luce suâ per terram interpositam despoliatur, alterâ Lunæ parte lucem suam adhuc retinente, unde Eclipsis tantum partialis exurgit, quæ tamen major vel minor fit prout Luminarium à nodis distantia major vel minor, atque adeò ipsa Luna ab Umbræ terrenæ centro proprior, remotiorve fuerit.
units.tr: 1. When the luminaries are moving farther from the nodes, only a part of the Moon is stripped of its light by the Earth lying between, while the other part of the Moon still keeps its light. So a merely partial eclipse arises. It is larger or smaller according as the luminaries are farther from or nearer to the nodes, and according as the Moon itself is closer to or farther from the centre of the Earth's shadow.

units.la: 2. Hujusmodi defectiones Lunæ partiales apud antiquos frequenter occurrunt observatæ; nos unicam methodi gratiâ seligemus per quam de reliquis judicium feratur; Ptolemæus ait, Τῷ πίνυ ζ ἔτει Φιλομήτορος, ὃ ἐσὶ φᾶσ' ἀπὸ Ναβο-ναςάρου καὶ Αἰγυπτίως φαμενὼθ κζ', ἐς τὴν κα ἀπὸ ὥρας η ἀρχομένης, ἕως ι λήγούσης, ἐν Αλεξανδρείᾳ ἐξέλιπεν ὁ σελήνη τὸ πλεῖσον ἀπ' ἀρχῆς ἀκλούνως ζ. In 7 igitur anno Philometoris qui est 574 à Nabonasaro secundùm Ægyptios Phamenoth 27, sequente 28, ab horâ octavâ incipiente, usque ad decimâ desinentem, Alexandriæ defecit Luna plurimùm à septentrione digitos 7. Ptol. p.142. Anno Nabonasari 574 neomenia Thoth contigit Octob. 6. neomenia Phamenoth, April. 4. Dies itaque Phamenoth 28 erat Kal. Mai, anno per. Jul. 4540. Porro per tabulas Danicas anno ĩsto per. Jul. 4540. Mai. 1. defecit ad Septentrionem Lunâ digitos 7. 26′. Initium Eclipseos Alexandriæ h. 0. 57′, post mediam noctem, medium hor. 2. 22′. Finis hor. 3. 47′. Duravit ergo hor. 2. 50′. Sol in Tauri gradu 5. 29′. 54″. Addit Ptolemæus medium Eclipseos fuisse post mediam noctem horis temporalibus 2. 30′, æquinoctialibus 2. 20′. Differt itaque calculus nester ab observatione scrupulis tantùm 2′. Per hanc igitur Eclipsim non tantùm epochæ Nabonasaræ sed & Ptolemæi Philometoris initium certissimè adstruatur, Nam si septimus
units.tr: 2. Partial eclipses of the Moon of this kind were often observed among the ancients. For the sake of method I shall choose one case by which judgement may be made about the rest. Ptolemy says: "In the seventh year of Philometor, which is 574 from Nabonassar according to the Egyptians, on Phamenoth 27, the following 28th, beginning at the eighth hour and ending at the tenth, at Alexandria the Moon was eclipsed for the most part from the beginning, to the extent of 7 digits." [Τῷ πίνυ ζ ἔτει Φιλομήτορος, ὃ ἐσὶ φᾶσ' ἀπὸ Ναβο-ναςάρου καὶ Αἰγυπτίως φαμενὼθ κζ', ἐς τὴν κα ἀπὸ ὥρας η ἀρχομένης, ἕως ι λήγούσης, ἐν Αλεξανδρείᾳ ἐξέλιπεν ὁ σελήνη τὸ πλεῖσον ἀπ' ἀρχῆς ἀκλούνως ζ.] Ptolemy, p. 142. In the year 574 of Nabonassar the new moon of Thoth fell on October 6, and the new moon of Phamenoth on April 4. Phamenoth 28 was therefore May 1 in the year 4540 of the Julian period. Moreover, by the Danish tables, in that year 4540 of the Julian period, on May 1, the Moon was eclipsed to the north by 7 digits 26′. The beginning of the eclipse at Alexandria was at 0 h. 57′ after midnight, the middle at 2 h. 22′, the end at 3 h. 47′. It lasted therefore 2 h. 50′. The Sun was at 5° 29′ 54″ of Taurus. Ptolemy adds that the middle of the eclipse was after midnight by 2 h. 30′ in temporal hours, or 2 h. 20′ in equinoctial hours. Our calculation therefore differs from the observation by only 2′. By this eclipse, then, the beginning not only of the Nabonassarean epoch but also of Ptolemy's Philometor may be most certainly established. For if his seventh year was in the Julian year 4540, then the first year fell in 4534, [and began] 180 years before Christ.

units.la: . 2. In omnibus autem pleniluniis hoc non accidit, eò quòd Luna latitudine suâ ab Ecliptica, nunc versùs Austrum, nunc versùs Boream Terræ umbră præterfugit. Cum Sol autem circa nodos sive caput & caudam Draconis versetur, quibus orbita Lunæ cum orbitâ solis connectitur, (quod plerunque bis in anno contingit) Luna ei directè opposita in umbram Terræ interjectæ plus aut minus (prout se habet Lunæ ad solem oppositio) ad Austrum aut Boream Ecliptice immergitur.
units.tr: . 2. However, this does not happen at every full moon, because the Moon, by its latitude from the ecliptic, passes by the Earth's shadow sometimes to the south and sometimes to the north. But since the Sun lies near the nodes, that is the head and tail of the Dragon, where the orbit of the Moon meets the orbit of the Sun (which happens generally twice a year), the Moon, when directly opposite the Sun, is immersed in the shadow of the Earth lying between, more or less to the south or north of the ecliptic, according to how the opposition of the Moon to the Sun stands.

units.la: XI. Eclipsis Lunaris est vel totalis vel partialis.
units.tr: XI. A lunar eclipse is either total or partial.

units.la: XII. Eclipsis Lunæ totalis est, quâ tota Luna in umbram Terræ immersa luce suâ spoliatur.
units.tr: XII. A total eclipse of the Moon is one in which the whole Moon, immersed in the shadow of the Earth, is deprived of its light.

units.la: 1. Cùm luminaria in ipsissimis adeò nodis existant, ut centrum Lunæ per umbræ Terrenæ centrum vel omnino vel ferè transeat, tota Luna sub umbrâ latitat, ibidémque scrupula aliqua horaria plerunque, nonnunquam duas etiam horas moratur. Et idcirco totalis Eclipsis merito nuncupetur.
units.tr: 1. When the luminaries are so exactly at the nodes that the centre of the Moon passes wholly or nearly wholly through the centre of the Earth's shadow, the whole Moon lies hidden under the shadow, and it usually remains there for some scruples of an hour, and sometimes even for two hours. Therefore such an eclipse is rightly called total.

units.la: 2. Hujusmodi Eclipsis Lunæ totalis à Sulpitio Gallo prædicta, L. Paulo Æmilio, & Licinio Crasso Coss. accidit, ab horâ secundâ usque ad quartam horam noctis quam pridie nonas Septembris insecuta est dies; teste Livio Dec. 5. l. 4. Annus erat urbis conditæ 586. per. Jul. 4546. & nox quâ contigit hæc Eclipsis in Juliană anni formâ ista erat quæ inter Jun. 21. & 22 fluxit. Initium Eclipseos per tabulas Danicas erat Jun. 21. h. 6. 14'. post meridiem Macedoniæ, medium hor. 8. 18'. finis horâ 10. 22'. Digiti Ecliptici 15 2/11. Duratio moræ hor. 1. 32'. tota duratio Eclipseos horæ 4. 8'. Tota ergo Luna sub umbrâ latitare cœpit hor. 7. 32', sive secundâ circiter noctis horâ, adeo ut horâ quartâ ex umbrâ tota emersit. Et hæc quidem Eclipsis luculentissimus est character, non tam consulatus L. Pauli Æmilii, & Licini Crassi sed & epochæ Urbis Conditæ, Cùm hæc enim Eclipsis acciderit anno Urbis Conditæ 586 & per. Jul. 4546, certissimo nobis sit argumento, epocham [?] C. ab anno per. Jul. 3961 procedere, sive ab anno ante Christum 753.
units.tr: 2. A total eclipse of the Moon of this kind, predicted by Sulpicius Gallus, occurred in the consulship of L. Paulus Aemilius and Licinius Crassus, from the second to the fourth hour of the night, which followed the day before the Nones of September, as Livy witnesses (Dec. 5, bk. 4). It was the year 586 from the founding of the city, 4546 of the Julian period, and the night on which this eclipse fell, in the Julian form of the year, was the one that flowed between June 21 and 22. According to the Danish tables, the beginning of the eclipse was June 21 at 6 h. 14′ after noon, Macedonian time, the middle at 8 h. 18′, the end at 10 h. 22′. The digits of the ecliptic were 15 2/11. The duration of the totality was 1 h. 32′, and the whole duration of the eclipse 4 h. 8′. The Moon therefore began to be wholly hidden under the shadow at 7 h. 32′, that is, about the second hour of the night, and came out of the shadow entirely at the fourth hour. This eclipse is indeed a most brilliant mark, not only of the consulship of L. Paulus Aemilius and Licinius Crassus but also of the epoch of the founding of the city. For since this eclipse fell in the year 586 from the founding of the city and 4546 of the Julian period, it gives us a most certain proof that the epoch of the V.C. proceeds from the year 3961 of the Julian period, that is, from the year 753 before Christ.

units.la: XIII. Eclipsis Lunæ partialis est quâ pars tantum Lunæ deficit.
units.tr: XIII. A partial eclipse of the Moon is one in which only part of the Moon is darkened.

units.la: 1. Cùm luminaria nodis remotiora moventur, pars tantùm Lunæ, luce suâ per terram interpositam despoliatur, alterâ Lunæ parte lucem suam adhuc retinente, unde Eclipsis tantum partialis exurgit, quæ tamen major vel minor fit prout Luminarium à nodis distantia major vel minor, atque adeò ipsa Luna ab Umbræ terrenæ centro proprior, remotiorve fuerit.
units.tr: 1. When the luminaries are moving farther from the nodes, only a part of the Moon is stripped of its light by the Earth lying between, while the other part of the Moon still keeps its light. So a merely partial eclipse arises. It is larger or smaller according as the luminaries are farther from or nearer to the nodes, and according as the Moon itself is closer to or farther from the centre of the Earth's shadow.

units.la: 2. Hujusmodi defectiones Lunæ partiales apud antiquos frequenter occurrunt observatæ; nos unicam methodi gratiâ seligemus per quam de reliquis judicium feratur; Ptolemæus ait, [Greek text illegible, ~60 letters] In 7 igitur anno Philometoris qui est 574 à Nabonasaro secundum Ægyptios Phamenoth 27, sequente 28, ab horâ octavâ incipiente, usque ad decimâ definentem, Alexandriæ defecit Luna plurimùm à septentrione digitos 7. Ptol. [Greek illegible] p.142. Anno Nabonasari 574 neomenia Thoth contigit Octob. 6. neomenia Phamenoth, April. 4. Dies itaque Phamenoth 28 erat Kal. Mai, anno per. Jul. 4540. Porro per tabulas Danicas anno isto per. Jul. 4540. Mai. 1, defecit ad Septentrionem Lunâ digitos 7. 26'. Initium Eclipseos Alexandriæ h. 0. 57'. post mediam noctem, medium hor. 2. 22'. Finis hor. 3. 47'. Duravit ergo hor. 2. 50'. Sol in Tauri gradu 5. 29'. 54". Addit Ptolemæus medium Eclipseos fuisse post mediam noctem horis temporalibus 2. 30'. æquinoctialibus 2. 20'. Differt itaque calculus noster ab observatione scrupulis tantùm 2'. Per hanc igitur Eclipsim non tantùm epochæ Nabonasaræ sed & Ptolemæi Philometoris initium certissimè adstruatur. Nam si septimus ejus annus erat per Jul. 4540. Ergo primus incidit in 4534. ineuntem ; ante Christum 180.
units.tr: 2. Partial eclipses of the Moon of this kind were often observed among the ancients. For the sake of method I shall choose one case by which judgement may be made about the rest. Ptolemy says: "In the seventh year of Philometor, which is 574 from Nabonassar according to the Egyptians, on Phamenoth 27, the following 28th, beginning at the eighth hour and ending at the tenth, at Alexandria the Moon was eclipsed for the most part from the beginning, to the extent of 7 digits." [Greek text illegible in the scan.] Ptolemy, p. 142. In the year 574 of Nabonassar the new moon of Thoth fell on October 6, and the new moon of Phamenoth on April 4. Phamenoth 28 was therefore May 1 in the year 4540 of the Julian period. Moreover, by the Danish tables, in that year 4540 of the Julian period, on May 1, the Moon was eclipsed to the north by 7 digits 26′. The beginning of the eclipse at Alexandria was at 0 h. 57′ after midnight, the middle at 2 h. 22′, the end at 3 h. 47′. It lasted therefore 2 h. 50′. The Sun was at 5° 29′ 54″ of Taurus. Ptolemy adds that the middle of the eclipse was after midnight by 2 h. 30′ in temporal hours, or 2 h. 20′ in equinoctial hours. Our calculation therefore differs from the observation by only 2′. By this eclipse, then, the beginning not only of the Nabonassarean epoch but also of Ptolemy's Philometor may be most certainly established.

units.la: XIV. Eclipsis solaris est privatio lucis solaris in terrâ per Lunam, jolem inter & terram inter- jectam effecta.
units.tr: XIV. A solar eclipse is the privation of the sun's light on the earth, brought about by the Moon interposed between the sun and the earth.

units.la: 1. Eclipsis solaris dicitur non quòd ipse Sol luce suâ privetur, sed quòd oculis nostris privatus videatur. Ipse enim Sol lucem suam nunquam amittit, sed intactam perpetuò retinet & illibatam. Verùm Luna in Synodis inter solem & terram transiens, lucem solarem nobis terram habitantibus nonnunquam intercipit, unde Sol etiam Eclipsim pati nobis videatur, non minùs quàm Lunæ incolis, Si qui sint, cùm terra soli & Lunæ interponitur.
units.tr: 1. A solar eclipse is so called not because the Sun itself is deprived of its light, but because it appears to be deprived of it to our eyes. For the Sun never loses its light, but always retains it intact and unimpaired. Rather, the Moon, passing between the sun and the earth at conjunctions, sometimes intercepts the solar light from us who inhabit the earth; whence the Sun also seems to us to suffer an eclipse, no less than it would to the inhabitants of the Moon, if there are any, when the earth is interposed between the sun and the Moon.

units.la: XV. Eclipsis Solaris est etiam vel totalis vel partialis. XVI. Eclipsis Solis totalis est quâ totus Sol per Lunam in- terjectam nobis absconditur.
units.tr: XV. A solar eclipse is also either total or partial. XVI. A total solar eclipse is one in which the whole Sun is hidden from us by the Moon interposed.

units.la: 1. Eclipsis solis totalis ut rarò, sic ubique terrarum nunquam accidit, sed aliquâ tantùm illius parte. Nam globus lunæ eum minor sit quàm terra, non potest Umbram suam in totum terræ discum projicere, sed tantùm in aliquam illius partem. Unde fit ut cùm alicubi totalis sit solis desectio, alibi partialis sit tantùm, alibi nulla necesse est.
units.tr: 1. A total eclipse of the sun occurs as rarely as it occurs everywhere on earth never; it happens only in some part of it. For since the globe of the Moon is smaller than the earth, it cannot project its shadow over the whole disc of the earth, but only onto some part of it. Hence it comes about that where the solar obscuration is total in one place, it is only partial in another, and in others it is necessarily none.

units.la: 2. Hujusmodi solis deliquium Romæ contigit, cùm teste Livio, Luce inter horam tertiam fermè & quartam tenebræ obortæ fuerant. Liv. Dec. 4. l. 8. Coss. Livio Salinatore & M. Valerio Messala. Hæc Eclipsis per prædictas Longomontani tabulas accidit anno per. Jul. 4526. Urbis conditæ 566 Julii, 17. Initium Eclipseos erat h. 6. 51'. 49". post med. noct. medium h. 7. 51'. 40". Finis h. 8. 51'. 40". Duravit ergo h. 2. 0. Digiti Ecliptici 12 o'. Sol in Cancri gradu 19. 41'8.". Latitudo Romæ 42. 8'. Ortus est igitur Sol isto die hor. 4. 4c'. occidit h 7. 20'. dies erat horarum æquinoctialium 14. 40'. Quælibet hora [...] scrupulorum 73. Hora itaque tertia (juxta quam observatæ sunt hæ tenebræ) cœpit horâ a quinctiali 7, 6'. post med noctem. Inter horam itaque ᴡɛɪɛuᵻ tertiam & quartam summa fuit obscuratio. Et hæc etiam Eclipsis Solaris certissimus est character non tantum anni quo Livius Salinator & M. Valerius Messala Consules fuere, sed & epochæ U. C. Etenim cùm annus hic erat opus Urbis conditæ 566, & per. Jul. 4526. Urbem conditam fuisse anno per. Jul. 3961 manifestum est, quod & antea probatum.
units.tr: 2. An eclipse of this kind occurred at Rome when, according to Livy, "between the third and fourth hour, as near as may be, darkness had come on in the daylight." Livy, Dec. 4, bk. 8, in the consulship of Livius Salinator and M. Valerius Messala. This eclipse, by the aforementioned Longomontanus tables, took place in the year 4526 of the Julian period, 566 from the founding of the City, on 17 July. The beginning of the eclipse was at 6h 51' 49" after midnight, the middle at 7h 51' 40", the end at 8h 51' 40". It therefore lasted 2h 0'. Digits eclipsed 12° 0'. The Sun was at 19° 41' 8" of Cancer. Latitude of Rome 42° 8'. The Sun therefore rose on that day at 4h 4c', set at 7h 20'; the day was 14h 40' in equinoctial hours. Each hour [...] of 73 scruples. The third hour (by which these darkness was observed) therefore began at 7h 6' after midnight in equinoctial hours. Between the third and fourth hour, then, the obscuration was complete. And this eclipse of the Sun is a most certain mark not only of the year in which Livius Salinator and M. Valerius Messala were consuls, but also of the epoch of the year from the founding of the City. For since this year was the 566th from the founding of the City, and it is clear that the City was founded in the year 3961 of the Julian period, as 4526 is, this was also proved before.

units.la: XVII. Eclipsis solis partialis est, quâ pars tantùm solis nobis abscond" "itur.
units.tr: XVII. A partial solar eclipse is one in which only a part of the Sun is hidden from us.

units.la: 1. Quum Luminaria conjuncta exactè versentur in eodem nodo, putâ simul in capite vel simul in caudâ draconis tum demum creatur Eclipsis solis totalis. Quum verò Luna non in ipso, quo Sol, est nodo, sed aliquantulùm, vel minimùm ab eo transeat, totam solis lucem nobis velare nequit, sed aliquam tantùm illius partem. Unde partialis oritur Eclipsis.
units.tr: 1. When the luminaries, in conjunction, lie exactly in the same node, that is, together in the head or together in the tail of the dragon, then at last a total solar eclipse is produced. When, however, the Moon passes not exactly in the very node where the Sun is, but a little or very slightly away from it, it cannot veil the whole light of the sun from us, but only some part of it. Hence a partial eclipse arises.

units.la: 2. Hujusmodi (ut alias pretereamus) fuit ista solis desectio, quam Thucydides anno octavo belli Peloponesiaci contigisse refert, Τὰ ἐπιγενόμενα ... Initio statim insequentis ætatis Sol ex parte defecit, circa neomeniam. Thucyd. l. 4. p. 138. Ed. Steph. Nullus occurrit annus, ista circiter tempora, quo contingere potuit hæc Eclipsis, præterquam annus per. Jul. 4290. quo Martii, 21. h. 8. 35′. post med. noct. Athenis Sol defecit digit. 9½. juxta tabulas antea laudatas. Et hæc quidem Eclipsis infallibilis est character initii belli Peloponesiaci. Annum enim quo contigit hæc Eclipsis octavum fuisse istius belli, Thucydides ipse testatur; contigit autem anno per. Jul. 4290. Cœptum est igitur istud bellum anno per. Jul. 4283. E quibus exemplis satis patet quanti momenti sint Eclipses in temporibus quibuscunque distinguendis.
units.tr: 2. Of this kind (to pass over others) was that eclipse of the sun which Thucydides reports as having occurred in the eighth year of the Peloponnesian War: "At the very beginning of the following summer the Sun was partly eclipsed, about the new moon." Thucydides, bk. 4, p. 138, ed. Stephanus. No year occurs, around that time, in which this eclipse could have happened, except the year 4290 of the Julian period, on 21 March, at 8h 35' after midnight, when at Athens the Sun was eclipsed 9½ digits, according to the tables cited above. And this eclipse is an infallible mark of the beginning of the Peloponnesian War. For Thucydides himself testifies that the year in which this eclipse occurred was the eighth of that war; it occurred, however, in the year 4290 of the Julian period. That war therefore began in the year 4283 of the Julian period. From these examples it is sufficiently clear how great a value eclipses have for distinguishing times of any kind.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: De Æquinoctiis & Solstitiis.
units.tr: Of the Equinoxes and Solstices.

units.la: Puncta cardinalia sunt tempora quibus Sol cardinalia Zodiaci signa, viz. Arietem, Cancrum, Libram, & Capricornum ingreditur.
units.tr: The cardinal points are the times at which the Sun enters the cardinal signs of the Zodiac, namely Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn.

units.la: II. Suntque vel Æquinoctia vel Solstitia.
units.tr: II. They are either equinoxes or solstices.

units.la: III. Æquinoctium est tempus quo nox dici fit æqualis.
units.tr: III. An equinox is the time when night becomes equal to day.

units.la: IV. Esque vel Vernale vel Autumnale.
units.tr: IV. It is either vernal or autumnal.

units.la: V. Æquinoctium Vernale committitur cùm Sol Arietem, Autumnale cùm Libram ingreditur.
units.tr: V. The vernal equinox occurs when the Sun enters Aries, and the autumnal when it enters Libra.

units.la: I. THoc anno Christi 1667. Sol primum Arietis punctum invadit per tabulas Parisinas Mar. 10. h. 11. 9'. post meridiem noctē Lond. & eodem temporis articulo ver init, unde hoc Vernale dicitur Æquinoctium. Sol hoc anno Libram ingreditur nostro calculo Sept. 13. h. 5. 50'. Londini, tunc itaque temporis Autumnus incipit, & Autumnale conficitur Æquinoctium.
units.tr: I. This year, 1667 of Christ, the Sun first enters the point of Aries, according to the Parisian tables, on March 10 at 11h 9' after noon, London time, and at that same moment spring begins, whence this is called the vernal equinox. This year, by our calculation, the Sun enters Libra on September 13 at 5h 50' at London; then autumn begins, and the autumnal equinox is completed.

units.la: VI. Solstitium est tempus quo vel nox diem vel dies noctem longissime superat.
units.tr: VI. A solstice is the time when either night most greatly exceeds day, or day exceeds night.

units.la: I. Solstitium dicitur propterea quòd istis anni tempestatibus, Sol tardissimo motu progreditur, adeò ut Sol stare nobis quodammodo videatur.
units.tr: I. It is called a solstice because in those seasons of the year the Sun advances with the slowest motion, so that to us it seems almost to stand still.

units.la: VII. Solstitium duplex est, Æstivum & Brumale.
units.tr: VII. The solstice is twofold, summer and winter.

units.la: VIII. Solstitium æstivum est quo Sole Cancrum ingrediente dies fit longissima, & brevissima nox. Brumale quo Sole Capricornum invadente, nox è contra fit longissima, & brevissima dies.
units.tr: VIII. The summer solstice is when, with the Sun entering Cancer, the day becomes longest and the night shortest. The winter solstice is when, with the Sun entering Capricorn, conversely the night becomes longest and the day shortest.

units.la: I. Ut hoc anno Sol Cancrum invadit nostro quidem calculo Jun. 11. h. 4. 0'. post meridiem Londini, quo tempore Æstas init, unde Solstitium Æstivum appellatur. At Dec. 11. h. 4. 25. post meridiem Sol Capricornum ingrediens Brumam introducit, unde ista tempestas Brumale solstitium nuncupatur.
units.tr: I. Thus this year the Sun enters Cancer, by our calculation, on June 11 at 4h 0' after noon at London, at which time summer begins, whence it is called the summer solstice. But on December 11 at 4h 25' after noon, the Sun entering Capricorn brings in winter (Bruma), whence that season is called the winter solstice.

units.la: IX. In Æquinoctiis pariter ac Solstitiis duo occurrunt observanda, Anticipatio, & Caßulus.
units.tr: IX. In equinoxes as well as solstices two things are to be observed: anticipation and lapse.

units.la: X. Æquinoctiorum & Solstitiorum anticipatio, est annua eorum versus mensium initia retroversio in anno Juliano per excessum ejus supra annum Tropicum effecta.
units.tr: X. The anticipation of equinoxes and solstices is their annual backward shift against the beginnings of the months in the Julian year, brought about by the Julian year's excess over the tropical year.

units.la: 1. Annus Julianus præter dies 365. horas colligit 6. Tropicus autem horas tantum 5. 49'. plus minus. Adeò ut quilibet annus Julianus Tropicum excedat scrupulis circiter horariis 11. Quanta vero sit præcisa anni Tropici quantitas ac mensura, nondum inter ipsos convenit Astronomos. Nos Longomontanum, qui eam exquisitissimè venatus est, amplectentes sententiam annum hunc Tropicum diebus 365. h. 5. 48'. 55''. definimus. Aufer horas 5. 48'. 55''. ex horis 6. o'. residuum est h. o. 11'. 5''. Quocirca annus Tropicus quotannis Julianum anticipat, hoc est annuum suum orbem conficit, priusquam compleatur annus Julianus, hor. o. 11'. 5''. At anni 4. vertentibus hæc anticipatio fit hor. o. 44'. 20''. ut hoc anno Sol Arietem ingreditur Martii 10. hor. 11. 9'. o''. expletis quatuor annis, sive anno Christi 1671. Sol hoc tempus anticipabit hor. o. 44'. 20''. & idem Arietis punctum ingredietur hor. 10. 24'. 40''. Et sic paulatim æquinoctia, quibus annus Tropicus mensuratur, in anno Juliano totum diem retrocedendo peragrant.
units.tr: 1. The Julian year gathers 365 days and 6 hours, whereas the tropical year has only about 5h 49' more or less. So every Julian year exceeds the tropical year by about 11 minutes of hours. How great the precise quantity and measure of the tropical year is, the astronomers have not yet agreed among themselves. We, embracing Longomontanus, who hunted it out most exactly, define this tropical year as 365 days, 5h 48' 55''. Take 5h 48' 55'' from 6h 0'; the remainder is 0h 11' 5''. Therefore the tropical year anticipates the Julian year each year, that is, completes its annual circle before the Julian year is complete, by 0h 11' 5''. But after four years this anticipation amounts to 0h 44' 20''. So, whereas this year the Sun enters Aries on March 10 at 11h 9' 0'', when four years are complete, that is in the year of Christ 1671, the Sun will anticipate this time by 0h 44' 20'', and it will enter the same point of Aries at 10h 24' 40''. And so, little by little, the equinoxes, by which the tropical year is measured, travel through the Julian year, falling back a whole day.

units.la: 2. Ut Scias autem quot annis totus dies anticipetur, primò annuæ anticipationis scrupula 11'. 5''. reducas in scrupula secunda; multiplices ergo scrupula prima 11 in 60, producto 660 addas reliqua scrupula secunda 5, Summa est 665. Igitur Æquinoctia uno anno retrovertuntur scrupulis secundis 665''. Secundum hæc consideres etiam quot scrupula secunda in uno die continentur. Scrupula autem prima unius diei sunt 1440. quæ in 60 ducta producunt scrupula secunda 86400. hæc dividas per 665,quotus est 129 1/665. hoc est tantùm non 130. Annis ergo quam proximè 130 totus dies ab Æquinoctiis & Solstitiis anticipatur. Adeò ut idem Æquinoctium vernum quod hoc anno Christi 1667. committitur Martii 10. h. 11. 9'. post mediam noctem; post annos 130 expletos in Martii 9. h. 11. 9'. post med. noct. retrovertetur, nimirum si annus iste idem sit post Bissextilem ac præsens. At post annos 260. ad Martii 8. h. 11. 9'. retrocedet. Et sic annis quibusque 130. vertentibus, Anticipatio, sive πρόληψις hæc ὑπαρξις totum diem complet.
units.tr: 2. To know how many years it takes for a whole day to be anticipated, first reduce the annual anticipation of 11' 5'' to seconds: multiply the 11 minutes by 60, giving 660, and add the remaining 5 seconds; the sum is 665. So the equinoxes fall back 665'' in one year. Next, consider how many seconds are contained in one day. The minutes of one day are 1440, which multiplied by 60 give 86,400 seconds. Divide these by 665, and the quotient is 129 1/665, that is, scarcely 130. So in about 130 years a whole day is anticipated from the equinoxes and solstices. Thus the vernal equinox that falls on March 10 at 11h 9' after midnight in 1667 will, after 130 years are complete, fall back to March 9 at 11h 9' after midnight, provided that year stands in the same relation to the leap year as the present one does. After 260 years it will fall back to March 8. And so, as every 130 years pass, this anticipation (πρόληψις, this ὕπαρξις) completes a whole day.

units.la: XI. Æquinoctiorum & Solstitiorum calculus vel Astronomicus est, vel Arithmeticus. XII. Astronomicus est, qui per tabulas Astronomicas ad- ministratur. XIII. Calculus Arithmeticus est, qui per Arithmetices præ- cepta perficitur.
units.tr: XI. The calculation of the equinoxes and solstices is either astronomical or arithmetical. XII. The astronomical calculation is that which is carried out by means of astronomical tables. XIII. The arithmetical calculation is that which is accomplished by the precepts of arithmetic.

units.la: 1. Hoc novum fateor, & hactenus inauditum videatur, ut Æquinoctia, & Solstitia aliter quam per tabulas Astronomicas calculentur. At quoniam nobis facilis & expedita per Arithmeticem solam puncta cardinalia computandi methodus occurrit, non abs re erit, si novam hanc nostram calculandi methodum, ejusque rationes ac fundamenta paucis explicemus.
units.tr: 1. I admit that this is new, and it may seem hitherto unheard of, that equinoxes and solstices should be calculated otherwise than by astronomical tables. But since an easy and expedient method of computing the cardinal points by arithmetic alone has occurred to us, it will not be out of place to set out briefly this new method of calculating, together with its reasons and foundations.

units.la: 2. Annus, ut ostensum est, Julianus Tropico major est scrupulis horariis 11'. 5". Et anni consequenter Tropici 130 minores sunt quàm totidem Juliani toto die. Annis ergo 130 Æquinoctia & Solstitia versùs mensium initia solido die retroaguntur, sive quod idem est, post annos 130. uno die citiùs committuntur quam ante. Deligatur igitur Æquinoctium aliquod certissimis observationibus deprehensum, illudque pro Epochâ sive radice habeatur, à quâ alia quæcunque calculentur. Deinde propositio quovis anno cujus Æquinoctium quærimus, computemus quot anni
units.tr: 2. The Julian year, as has been shown, exceeds the tropical year by 11' 5'' of hours. Consequently 130 tropical years are less than the same number of Julian years by a whole day. So in 130 years the equinoxes and solstices are pushed back by a full day toward the beginnings of the months; or, what is the same thing, after 130 years they fall a day earlier than before. Let some equinox established by most certain observations be chosen and regarded as the epoch or root, from which all others are calculated. Then, for any year whose equinox we seek, let us compute how many years

units.la: Lib.II. Chronologicarum. 95
units.tr: Book II of the Chronology. 95

units.la: anni inter epocham istam & propositum intercedunt, si annus propositus epocham præcedat, quotiescunque 130 continentur in annis interfluentibus, toties unus dies addendus est, ut Æquinoctium quæsitum teneamus: eò quòd Æquinoctia isto temporis intervallo tot diebus retrocesserant. Sic propositus annus epocham sequatur, tot dies auferendi sunt, propterêa quòd ab epochâ ad annum propositum tot diebus retrovertentur. Et denique per regulam proportionis horæ etiam & scrupula anticipata vel anticipanda colligantur, quæ etiam vel addenda sunt vel auferenda (unde & Prostaphæretica non immerito nuncupentur) srout annus propositus epocham procedat aut lequatur.
units.tr: If the years that lie between this epoch and the year proposed are such that the proposed year comes before the epoch, then for every 130 years contained in the intervening span, one day must be added to find the equinox sought, because the equinoxes had gone back by that many days over that interval. If the proposed year follows the epoch, that many days are to be subtracted, because from the epoch to the proposed year they will have turned back by that many days. Finally, by the rule of proportion, the hours and scruples anticipated or to be anticipated are also gathered, and these are either added or subtracted, which is why they are not without reason called Prosthaphaeretic, according as the proposed year precedes or follows the epoch.

units.la: 3. Porrò nulla accuratiùs inventa sunt Æquinoctia quàm quæ Tycho Brahæ anno Æræ Christianæ 1584, & sequentibus Uraniburgi observavit. Quapropter Æquinoctia ab ipso observata, & Solstitia per ejus tabulas iisdem observationibus fundatas calculata, pro epochis nostris tam Æquinoctialibus quam Solstitialibus habeamus: è quibus alia quæcunque sive præcedentia sive consequentia certissimè pariter atque expeditissimè computemus.
units.tr: 3. Moreover, no equinoxes have been found more accurately than those which Tycho Brahe observed at Uraniborg in the year 1584 of the Christian era and in the years following. Therefore we take the equinoxes observed by him, and the solstices calculated from his tables, which rest on those same observations, as our epochs, both equinoctial and solstitial. From these we may calculate any others, whether earlier or later, with equal certainty and great ease.

units.la: XIV. Arithmeticus Æquinoctiorum, Solstitiorúmque calculus hisce regulis expediatur.
units.tr: XIV. The arithmetical calculation of the equinoxes and solstices is carried out by these rules.

units.tr: XV. First; the equinoxes and solstices set down below are to be noted as the epochs of the others.

units.la: XVI. Secundò ; Propósito quovis anno vel Æræ Christianæ, vel Periodi Julianæ cujus Æquinoctia vel Solstitia quæris, iste annus in hoc laterculo pro Epochâ tuâ seligatur, qui æque distat à Bissexto atque propositus.
units.tr: XVI. Secondly; For any proposed year, whether of the Christian era or of the Julian period, whose equinoxes or solstices you seek, let that year be selected from this table as your epoch which is equally distant from a leap year as the proposed year is.

units.la: XVII. Tertio; Hoc ut citiùs innotescat, scias, quòd in annis Christi hi sunt Bissextiles, 4. 8. 12. 16. 20. 24. 28. 32. 36. 40. 44. 48. 52. 56. 60. 64. 68. 72. 76. 80. 84. 88. 92. 96. 100. In annis Periodi Julianæ hi, 1. 5. 9. 13. 17. 21. 25. 29. 33. 37. 41. 45. 49. 53. 57. 61. 65. 69. 73. 77. 81. 85. 89. 93. 97. 101. reliqui communes.
units.tr: XVII. Thirdly; So that this may be learned more quickly, know that in the years of Christ these are the leap years: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, 60, 64, 68, 72, 76, 80, 84, 88, 92, 96, 100. In the years of the Julian period these: 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29, 33, 37, 41, 45, 49, 53, 57, 61, 65, 69, 73, 77, 81, 85, 89, 93, 97, 101. The rest are common years.

units.la: XVIII. Quarto ; Annum propositum ab anno Epochæ tuæ selectæ detrahas, residuum per 130 dividas & quoto reservato, residuum divisionis in 24 ducas, & productum per eundem numerum 130 distribuas, & quoto iterùm reservato residuum hujus divisionis in 60 multiplicatum etiam per 130 dividas. Primæ divisionis quotus dat dies, secundæ Horas, tertiæ Scrupula prima Prosthapheretica, Epochæ quidem addenda, si annus propositus eam præcedat, detrahenda si sequatur. Summa, vel residuum est Æquinoctium Solstitiumve quæsitum Uraniburgi.
units.tr: XVIII. Fourthly; Subtract the year of your chosen epoch from the proposed year, divide the remainder by 130, and keep the quotient. Multiply the remainder of this division by 24, and divide the product by the same number, 130. Again keep the quotient, and multiply the remainder of this division by 60, and divide that too by 130. The quotient of the first division gives days, that of the second hours, and that of the third the first scruples. These are the Prosthaphaeretic amounts, to be added to the epoch if the proposed year precedes it, and subtracted if it follows. The sum or the remainder is the equinox or solstice sought, at Uraniborg.

units.la: 1. Exempli gratiâ : hoc anno Christi 1667. quoniam præter complet at 64 erat Bissextilis, ut igitur assumas annum Ch reliqui sunt anni 80. Hi &ta itaque primâ divisio niam solidus dies nondu dit. 1667 1587 80 24 320 160 130) 1920 (14 Hor. 13 62 52 100 60 130) 6000 (46 Scru. 52 80 78 20
units.tr: 1. For example: in this year of Christ 1667, since 1664 was a leap year, and the year 1587 is taken as the starting point, the remaining years are 80. Here, as in the first division, since a whole day is not yet completed, the calculation proceeds as follows. 1667 − 1587 = 80; 80 × 24 = 1920; 1920 ÷ 130 = 14 (hours), remainder 100; 100 × 60 = 6000; 6000 ÷ 130 = 46 (scruples), remainder 20.

units.la: Ergo anno Christi 1667 tur Martii 10. h. 12.10'. ut autem tempus hoc ita Quæratur Æquinoctium vernum hic est annus tertius à Bissextili etas annorum centurias colligit 67, è regulâ tertiâ patet. Pro epochâ Christi 1587. Aufer 1587 ex 1667. per 130 dividi nequeunt. Neglene, sive primâ methodi parte, quom anticipatur, Calculus ita proce-
units.tr: Therefore in the year of Christ 1667 the vernal equinox falls on March 10, h. 12, 10'. This year is the third after a leap year. The ages of years gather into centuries, 67, as is clear from the third rule. For the epoch of Christ 1587, subtract 1587 from 1667; the quotient is not divisible by 130, so in the first part of the method, when the time is anticipated, the calculation goes forward as follows.
