units.la: 2. Hic, uti vides, subtractis 1587 ex 1667 residui sunt anni 80, quos in 24 (quot horæ in die continentur) multiplico, & productum 1920 divido per 130, quotus 14 dat horas anticipatas; deinde refiduum hujus divisionis quod est 100, duco in 60, & productum 6000 divido per 130, & quotiens est 46. Igitur ab anno Christi 1587 usque ad 1667, præter horas 14, scrupula 46. anticipata sunt. Porro Annus hic propositus epocham sequitur. Auferantur igitur horæ 14.46'.ab Æquinoctio verno 1587, quod accidit Mart. 11. h. 2. 56'. hoc modo Epocha | Mart. 11. 2. 56. Aufer | 0. 14. 46. Residuum | 10. 12. 10.
units.tr: 2. Here, as you see, when 1587 is subtracted from 1667 the remaining years are 80. I multiply these by 24 (the number of hours in a day) and divide the product, 1920, by 130; the quotient 14 gives the anticipated hours. Then I multiply the remainder of this division, which is 100, by 60, and divide the product, 6000, by 130; the quotient is 46. So from the year of Christ 1587 up to 1667, besides 14 hours, 46 scruples have been anticipated. Moreover, this proposed year follows the epoch. Therefore subtract 14 h. 46' from the vernal equinox of 1587, which fell on March 11, h. 2, 56'. Thus: epoch March 11, 2, 56; subtract 0, 14, 46; remainder March 10, 12, 10.

units.la: Æquinoctium vernum committipost mediam noctem Uraniburgi ; supputatum, ad alios meridianos O accomaccommodetur, Consulas regulam 5 & tabellam ei subjectam, in qua ubicunque occurrit A Tempus ibi notatum. Addendum est, ubi S. Subtrahendum Uraniburgi meridiano, ut ad urbium ibi descriptarum meridianos redigatur. Ut Londino subjicitur. S. o. 5'. id est, Subtrahe h. o. 50'. Ut tempus itaque quo Æquinoctium hoc Londini conficitur deprehendas, à Martii 10. h. 12. 10'. Subtrahe h. o. 50'. & relinquitur Mart. 10. h. 11. 20'. pro Æquinoctio verno Londini. Ad Romam scribitur A. o. 9'. Addas itaque h. o. 9'. ad tempus Uraniburgi inventum. Summa Mart. 10. h. 12.19'. post medium noctem est tempus quo commissum est hoc Æquinoctium Romæ.
units.tr: The vernal equinox falls after midnight at Uraniborg. To adapt the computed time to other meridians, consult rule 5 and the table appended to it, in which wherever A occurs, the time is noted there. Where S stands, the amount is to be added; where A stands, it is to be subtracted from the Uraniborg meridian, so that the time is reduced to the meridians of the cities described there. For London the table gives S. 0. 50', that is, you subtract 0 h. 50'. So to find the time at which this equinox occurs at London, subtract 0 h. 50' from March 10, h. 12, 10'; there remains March 10, h. 11, 20', for the vernal equinox at London. For Rome, A. 0. 9' is written, so you add 0 h. 9' to the time found at Uraniborg. The sum, March 10, h. 12, 19', after midnight, is the time at which this equinox occurs at Rome.

units.la: 3. Eodem modo Solstitium Æstivum calculetur, quod anno Christi sive Epochâ 1587 accidit Jun 12. 7. 37'. Auferatur tempus prosthaphæreticum h. 14. 46'. restat Jun. 11. h. 16. 51'. post med. noct. Uraniburgi pro solstitio æstivo, Æquinoctium Autumnale eodem anno Christi 1587 contigit Sept. 13. h. 21. 26'. Auferatur h. 14. 46'. Committitur hoc anno Christi 1667 Æquinoctium Autumnale Sept. 13. h. 6. 40': Uraniburgi. Londini h. 5. 50' post med. noct. Eodem modo procedit & Solstitii Hiberni calculus deductis h. 14. 46', ab Epochâ sive Solstitio Hiberno, anno Christi 1587.
units.tr: 3. In the same way the summer solstice is calculated. In the year of Christ, or epoch, 1587 it fell on June 12, 7, 37'. Subtract the Prosthaphaeretic time, 14 h. 46', and there remains June 11, h. 16, 51', after midnight at Uraniborg, for the summer solstice. The autumnal equinox in the same year of Christ 1587 fell on Sept. 13, h. 21, 26'. Subtract 14 h. 46', and in this year of Christ 1667 the autumnal equinox occurs on Sept. 13, h. 6, 40', at Uraniborg; at London, 5 h. 50' after midnight. The calculation of the winter solstice proceeds in the same way, with 14 h. 46' subtracted from the epoch, that is, the winter solstice of the year of Christ 1587.

units.la: 4. Si major adhuc ἀπειρία cuivis arriserit, calculum hunc nostrum ad scrupula secunda, tertia, &c. propagare licet. Nam si ultimæ divisionis residuum in 60 multiplices, productum per 130 divisum in quoto dabit scrupula secunda, in residuo numerum in 60 etiam ducendum & per 130 dividendum, ut scrupula etiam tertia computemus. Et sic quousque libitum fuerit. Ut in exemplo propositio, ultimæ divisionis residuum 20 in 60 multiplicatum producit 1200, numerus iste productus per 130 divisus, in quoto dat scrupula secunda 9". adeò ut tempus prosthaphæreticum exactius adhuc calculatum sit h. 14. 46'. 9". & sic deinceps.
units.tr: 4. If any still greater passion for minute detail [ἀπειρία] has taken hold of anyone, this calculation of ours may be extended to seconds, thirds and so on. For if you multiply the remainder of the last division by 60 and divide the product by 130, the quotient will give seconds; and in the same way, multiplying the remainder by 60 and dividing by 130 again, we may compute thirds too, and so on as far as one wishes. As in the proposed example, the remainder of the last division, 20, multiplied by 60, gives 1200; this product divided by 130 gives in the quotient 9 seconds. So the Prosthaphaeretic time is calculated more exactly still, as 14 h. 46' 9", and so on.

units.la: 5. Aliud exemplum. Sed exploremus novam hanc nostram Æquinoctia calculandi methodum, per antiqua ista Æquinoctia ab Hipparcho observata, ut certitudo ejus æquè ac facilitas innotescat. Ptolemæus igitur ait Hipparchum Æquinoctium Autumnale, ὡς ἀκριβῶς observâsse anno 32 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ, τῆ γ' τῶν ἐπιφυτῶν τῆ μην-ταῖς τῆς ἐις ἡμέραν πλήρη φθορᾶ, Tertiâ die Epagomenôn mediâ nocte diem quartam introducente, Ptol. Almag. l. 3. p. 62. Ed.Gr. Annus 32 tertiæ per Calippicæ erat annus per. Jul. 4567. Thoth hoc anno iniit Sept.29. Igitur tertia ἐπιφανῶν incidit in Sept. 26. observatum est igitur Æquinoctium mediâ nocte inter Sept.26. & 27, sive ineunte Sept. 27.c.c. Videamus quantùm Calculus noster ab antiquâ hâc observatione discrepet. Annus per. Jul. 4567. est secundus post ff.96.
units.tr: 5. Another example. But let us test this new method of ours for calculating the equinoxes against the ancient equinoxes observed by Hipparchus, so that its accuracy and ease may both become known. Ptolemy therefore says that Hipparchus observed the autumnal equinox exactly (ὡς ἀκριβῶς) in the 32nd year of the third Calippic period, τῆ γ' τῶν ἐπιφυτῶν τῆ μην-ταῖς τῆς ἐις ἡμέραν πλήρη φθορᾶ [on the third day of the Epagomenae, in the middle of the night, as the fourth day begins], Ptol. Almag. l. 3. p. 62. Ed. Gr. The 32nd year of the third Calippic period was the year 4567 of the Julian period. Thoth began in that year on September 29. Therefore the third of the ἐπιφανῶν fell on September 26. The equinox was therefore observed in the middle of the night between September 26 and 27, that is, at the beginning of September 27. Let us see how far our calculation departs from this ancient observation. The year 4567 of the Julian period is the second after the ff.96.

units.la: Bissextilem. Assumendum est igitur pro epochâ Æquinoctium Autumnale anno per. Jul. 6299. Et calculus sic procedit. Subductis 4567 ex 6299, reliqui sunt anni 1732, qui per 130 divisi in quoto dant dies prosthaphæreticos 13, & residuum est 42, quod in 24 ductum, & per 130 divisum dat horas prosthaphæreticas 7, & residuum facit 98 quod in 60 ductum, & per 130 divisū dat scrupula 45'. Igitur ab anno per. Jul. 4567, usque ad annum 6299 Æquinoctiorum anticipatio fuit dier. 13. h. 7. 45'. Annus propositus epocham præcedit, Addatur itaque tempus hoc prosthaphæreticum ad epocham 6299 / 4567 / 130) 1732 (13 dies. / 13 / 43 / 39 / 42 / 24 / 168 / 84 / 130) 1008 (7 Horæ. / 91 / 98 / 60 / 130) 5880 (45 Scrupula. / 52 / 68 / 65 / 30 epocham tuam, hoc est ad Æquinoctium Autumnale anno per Iul. 6299. d. h. Epocha | Sept. 13. 15. 38. Adde | 13. 7. 45. Summa | Sept. 26. 23. 23.
units.tr: Leap year. We must therefore take as the epoch the autumnal equinox in the year 6299 of the Julian period. The calculation proceeds thus. Subtracting 4567 from 6299 leaves 1732 years, which divided by 130 gives 13 prosthaphaeretic days in the quotient, with a remainder of 42. This, multiplied by 24 and divided by 130, gives 7 prosthaphaeretic hours, with a remainder of 98, which multiplied by 60 and divided by 130 gives 45 minutes. Therefore from the year 4567 of the Julian period to the year 6299, the anticipation of the equinoxes was 13 days, 7 hours, 45 minutes. The year proposed comes before the epoch, so this prosthaphaeretic time is added to the epoch 6299, that is, to the autumnal equinox in the year of the Julian period 6299: Epoch Sept. 13, 15h 38m; add 13d 7h 45m; sum Sept. 26, 23h 23m.

units.la: Accidit igitur hoc Æquinoctium Sept. 26 h. 23. 23'. post mediam noctem Uraniburgi, pro Alexandriæ meridiano, cui accommodata fuit hæc observatio. Adde h. 1. 35'. Et exactum Æquinoctii tempus Alexandriæ fit Sept. 27. h. 0. 58'. Distat ab observatione scrupulis tantùm horariis 58. At tabulæ Alphonsinæ idem hoc Æquinoctium repræsentant Sept. 26. h. 16.26'. Danicæ Sept. 27. 4. 0'. Parisinæ Sept. 26. 17. 45'. adeò ut primæ tabulæ ab observatione dissentiant h. 7. 34'. secundæ h. 4. 0'. tertiæ h. 6. 15'. noster calculus h. 0. 58'. multùm igitur ad observationem propiùs accedit, quàm tabulæ istæ, quæ tamen omnium habentur præstantissimæ.
units.tr: This equinox therefore fell on September 26 at 23h 23m after midnight at Uraniburg, reckoned by the meridian of Alexandria, to which this observation was adapted. Add 1h 35m, and the exact time of the equinox at Alexandria comes to September 27, 0h 58m. It differs from the observation by only 58 minutes of an hour. But the Alphonsine Tables represent the same equinox as September 26, 16h 26m; the Danish as September 27, 4h 0m; the Parisian as September 26, 17h 45m. So the first tables differ from the observation by 7h 34m, the second by 4h 0m, the third by 6h 15m, while our calculation differs by 0h 58m. It therefore comes much nearer the observation than those tables, which are nevertheless held to be the most excellent of all.

units.la: 6. Sed hoc idem expertus sum in aliis quamplurimis veterum observationibus, quod Æquinoctia nimirum, & Solstitia ab iis mirâ diligentiâ observata, exactiùs per nostram methodum, quam per tabulas, penè dixeram, quascunque repræsentantur. Non quidem diffiteor quin tabulæ Astronomicæ singulare aliquod Æquinoctium aliquando propiùs attingant, sed omnes tabulæ, quas mihi videre contigit, ab observatione in universum remotius & sæpius aberrant, quàm methodus nostra. Nam ex. gr. Hipparchus aliud observavit Æquinoctium Autumnale Sept. 27. 12.0'. anno per. Iul. 4556. Hoc tabulæ Alphonsinæ exhibent Sept. 26. 21. 10'. Prutenicæ Sept. 27. 22, 17'. Parisinæ Sept. 27. 1.37'. methodus nostra Sept. 27. 8. 59'. Adeò ut methodus ab observatione distet horis tantùm 3. 1'. Cum omnes tabulæ prædictæ plusquam horis 10. aberrant. At tabulæ Danicæ hoc Æquinoctium exactè cum observatione repræsentant Sept. 27. 12. o'. quæ tamen in priori exemplo ab observatione dissonant h. 4. atque idcirco plusquàm nostra methodus vel ab eâ vel hâc.
units.tr: 6. I have found the same thing in very many other ancient observations, namely that equinoxes and solstices observed with remarkable care are represented more exactly by our method than by the tables, I was almost going to say than by any tables. I do not deny that the astronomical tables sometimes come closer to some particular equinox, but all the tables that I have had occasion to see depart from observation, on the whole, further and more often than our method does. For example, Hipparchus observed another autumnal equinox on September 27 at 12h 0m in the year 4556 of the Julian period. The Alphonsine Tables give this as September 26, 21h 10m; the Prutenic as September 27, 22h 17m; the Parisian as September 27, 1h 37m; our method as September 27, 8h 59m. So our method differs from the observation by only 3h 1m, whereas all the aforementioned tables differ by more than 10 hours. The Danish Tables represent this equinox exactly as the observation, September 27, 12h 0m, yet in the previous example they differ from the observation by 4 hours; so they are no more reliable than our method, or rather less so.

units.la: 7. Denique Æquinoctium vernum ab Hipparcho observatum fuit anno per. Jul. 4568 Martii 24. h. 11. o'. Hoc Æquinoctium juxta tabulas Alphonsinas incidit in Martii 24. 0. o'. per Danicas in Martii 24. 21. 38'. juxta Prutenicas in Martii 24. 5. 41'. Per Parisinas in Martii 24. 8. 9'. at per methodum nostram in Martii 24. h. 12. 16'. observationem igitur Hipparcheam calculus noster excedit horâ tantùm 1. 16'. Cum calculus è tabulis Danicis eam excedat h. 10. 38'. Et reliquæ tabulæ multùm deficiunt plusquàm noster calculus excedit.
units.tr: 7. Finally, the vernal equinox observed by Hipparchus fell in the year of the Julian period 4568, on March 24 at 11h 0m. According to the Alphonsine Tables this equinox falls on March 24 at 0h 0m; according to the Danish on March 24 at 21h 38m; according to the Prutenic on March 24 at 5h 41m; according to the Parisian on March 24 at 8h 9m; but according to our method on March 24 at 12h 16m. Our calculation therefore exceeds the Hipparchan observation by only 1h 16m, whereas the calculation from the Danish tables exceeds it by 10h 38m; and the remaining tables fall far short, by more than our calculation exceeds it.

units.la: 8. Sed me reprimo: Alii in aliis observationibus methodi nostræ experimentum faciant, quæ non tantùm adeò certa est, ut nec accuratissimis cedat tabulis Astronomicis, verùm & adeò facilis & expedita, ut ipse per eam tria prædicta Hipparchi Æquinoctia cum duobus aliis, iisdemque ex antiquissimis, in universum quinque, quartâ horæ parte calculavi, quo temporis spatio neminem per tabulas quasvis Astronomicas plusquàm unicum posse Æquinoctium Solstitiúmve calculare pro quovis pignore contendam.
units.tr: 8. But I restrain myself. Let others try the experiment of our method on other observations. It is not only so certain that it yields to the most accurate astronomical tables in no respect, but it is also so easy and quick that I myself, by means of it, calculated the three aforesaid equinoxes of Hipparchus together with two others from the most ancient times, five in all, in a quarter of an hour. In that space of time I maintain that no one could calculate by any astronomical tables more than a single equinox or solstice, whatever wager is offered.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: De Cyclo solis & litera Dominicali.
units.tr: On the Solar Cycle and the Dominical Letter.

units.la: Characteres instituti sunt, qui à naturalibus non dependent causis, sed ab hominibus instituuntur.
units.tr: Characters are instituted; they do not depend on natural causes but are established by men.

units.la: II. Suntque vel in orbem redeuntes vel fixi.
units.tr: II. They are either recurring or fixed.

units.la: III. Characteres in orbem redeuntes sunt, qui post certam annorum seriem evolutam iterum incipiunt.
units.tr: III. Recurring characters are those which, after a certain series of years has run its course, begin again.

units.la: IV. Suntque vel cycli vel periodi.
units.tr: IV. They are either cycles or periods.

units.la: V. Cycli sunt quatuor, cyclus Solis, cyclus Lunæ, Indictio, & Epacta.
units.tr: V. There are four cycles: the cycle of the sun, the cycle of the moon, the indiction, and the epact.

units.la: I. HIsce annumerari poterant & cycli Judæorum, & Cathaiorum. Cycli Judæorum duo sunt, Annus Sabbaticus & Jubilæus, quorum ille septimo quovis anno, hic septies septimo sive quadragesimo nono recurrit. Cyclus Cathaiorum etiam duplex est, Simplex & Compositus, Simplex est cyclus annorum 60. Compositus è tribus simplicibus conflatus annis 180 constat, quorum primus vocatur Shanec ven; Secundus Junec ven; Tertius Cha ven. Sed hosce prætereo, ut raro si unquam occurrentes. Anni enim Sabbatici & Jubilæi divinitus licèt instituti, nuspiam tamen per sacrum textum à Judæis leguntur observati. Et Cathaiorum cycli ad Astronomos præcipuè spectant.
units.tr: I. To these could be added the cycles of the Jews and of the Cathayans. The Jewish cycles are two: the Sabbatical year and the Jubilee, of which the former recurs every seventh year and the latter every seven times seventh year, that is, every forty-ninth. The Cathayan cycle is also twofold: simple and compound. The simple cycle is a series of sixty years. The compound cycle, made up of three simple cycles, consists of 180 years, of which the first is called Shanec ven, the second Junec ven, and the third Cha ven. But I pass these over, as they rarely if ever come up. For although the Sabbatical and Jubilee years were instituted by God, the Jews are nowhere read in the sacred text to have observed them. And the Cathayan cycles concern chiefly the astronomers.

units.la: VI. Cyclus solis est Series annorum 28, quâ peractâ dies solis ad eandem literam Dominicalem revertitur, & feriæ consequenter reliquæ eâdem literâ, quâ priùs, designantur.
units.tr: VI. The cycle of the sun is a series of 28 years, at the end of which the day of the sun returns to the same Dominical letter, and the remaining weekdays are consequently marked by the same letter as before.

units.la: I. Vocatur itaque Cyclus solis, non quod annis 28, solis ipsius aliqua fiat ἀποκατάστασις, sed propter diem Solis sive Dominicam, quæ tot annis evolutis eâdem literâ Dominicali rursùm indigitatur. Annus enim communis Julianus dies colligit 365, qui per 7 divisi dant septimanas 52, & unum praeterea diem superfluum, quo fit ut annus quilibet communis ab eâdem desinat feriâ, quâ coepit, & proximus à sequenti: Quocirca septem annis evolutis quaelibet anni dies, eadem iterum hebdomadis esset Feria, nisi dies Bissextilis quarto cuilibet anno insertus obstaret. Hic autem efficit ut annus quilibet Bissextilis dies colligens 366, praeter completas septimanas, duos relinquat dies superfluos, qui communem feriarum cursum perturbant. Et quoniam haec feriarum series, quae septem alioquin annis absolveretur, quarto quovis interpellatur, hinc fit quòd annis quater septem sive 28, totus iste feriarum circuitus, omni sublatâ varietate, praecisè compleatur. Annis itaque 28 cyclus hic solis totus absolvitur.
units.tr: I. The cycle is therefore called the cycle of the sun, not because some restoration [ἀποκατάστασις] of the sun itself is completed in 28 years, but on account of the day of the Sun, that is, Sunday, which after so many years have elapsed is again marked by the same Dominical letter. For the ordinary Julian year gathers 365 days, which divided by 7 give 52 weeks and one extra day over. So it happens that every common year ends on the weekday on which it began, and the next year begins on the following weekday. Hence, if seven years had run out, each day of the year would again fall on the same day of the week, were it not for the intercalary day inserted in every fourth year. This makes each leap year, gathering 366 days, leave, beyond its complete weeks, two superfluous days, which disturb the common course of the weekdays. And since this series of weekdays, which would otherwise be completed in seven years, is interrupted at every fourth year, it follows that after four times seven, or 28 years, the whole circuit of the weekdays, with all variation removed, is exactly completed. Thus the cycle of the sun is wholly completed in 28 years.

units.la: VII. Litera Dominicalis est una vel duae è literis, A. B. C. D. E. F. G. quae per totum cycli solaris decursum Domi- nicam quotannis indigitat.
units.tr: VII. The Dominical letter is one or two of the letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, which through the whole course of the solar cycle marks the Sunday of each year.

units.la: 1. Nimirum in Kalendario Juliano singulis anni diebus una è septem istis primis Alphabeti literis adscribitur, quibus omnes hebdomadis cujusque per totum annum feriae designantur, unde & Characteres audiunt. Sicut primae Januarii diei apponitur litera A. Si ista itaque dies sit Dominica, A per totum annum communem Dominicam indicabit, B diem Lunae, C Martis; & sic deinceps. Communem dico, nam in anno Bissextili ob diem post Feb. 23 intercalatum, duae sint literae Dominicales necesse est, quarum prior fungatur ab initio anni, ad Feb. 24. exinde ad finem anni posterior; ut quando Litera Dominicalis est GF. tunc G Dominicam designat usque ad Bissextum sive Feb. 24, reliquo anno F. Et quandoquidem annis 28 vertentibus septies intercalatur, hinc in cyclo solis currente Litera Dominicalis septies duplex est.
units.tr: 1. Namely, in the Julian calendar one of the first seven letters of the alphabet is assigned to each day of the year, by which all the weekdays of the whole year are marked; hence they are also called characters. Thus the letter A is placed against the first day of January. If that day is a Sunday, A will mark every Sunday of the common year, B Monday, C Tuesday, and so on. I say common, for in a leap year, because of the day intercalated after February 23, there must be two Dominical letters: the first serves from the beginning of the year to February 24, and the second from then to the end of the year. So when the Dominical letters are GF, G marks Sunday until the leap day, or February 24, and F for the rest of the year. And since, in the course of 28 years, the intercalation occurs seven times, in the cycle of the sun the Dominical letter is therefore double seven times.

units.la: VIII. Literae Dominicales ordine retrogrado procedunt, sic G. F. E. D. C. B. A.
units.tr: VIII. The Dominical letters proceed in retrograde order, thus G, F, E, D, C, B, A.

units.la: 1. Ut si hoc anno Lit. Dom. sit G. proximo erit F. tertio E. & sic deinceps usque ad A, quam G iterum sequitur. Et sic in anno Bissextili quo duplex est Lit. Dominicalis, eodem ordine collocantur. Ut si F & G, sint Dominicales, non F. sed G primum locum obtinet, hoc modo GF. sic FE. ED. DC. CB. BA. AG.
units.tr: 1. So if this year the Dominical letter is G, next year it will be F, the third year E, and so on down to A, which is followed again by G. Likewise in a leap year, where there are two Dominical letters, they are arranged in the same order. If F and G are the Dominical letters, G, not F, holds the first place, in this way: GF, then FE, ED, DC, CB, BA, AG.

units.la: IX. Literam Dominicalem in Juliana anni formâ per to- tum cyclum solarem hoc pinacidium exhibet.
units.tr: IX. In the Julian form of the year this table shows the Dominical letter through the whole solar cycle.

units.la: Cyclus Solaris cum litera Dominicali.
units.tr: Cycle of the Sun with the Dominical letter.

units.la: I. Etiam si totus annorum 28 circuitus proprie dicatur cyclus solis, cyclus solis tamen dicitur quilibet etiam annus in isto circuitu; Ut annus primus cycli solaris vocatur cyclus solis primus, Annus secundus cyclus solis 2, & sic deinceps. Primus autem annus cycli solaris Literam Dominicalem habet duplicem GF. Secundus E. tertius D. quartus C. Quintus ut Bissextilis BA. & sic deinceps, ut in laterculo videre est. Ultimus annus cycli solaris habet A, & tertius est à Bissextili, primus itaque sequentis cycli ad GF iterum regreditur.
units.tr: I. Although the whole circuit of 28 years is properly called the cycle of the sun, any single year within that circuit is also called a cycle of the sun. Thus the first year of the solar cycle is called the first cycle of the sun, the second year the second cycle of the sun, and so on. The first year of the solar cycle has the double Dominical letter GF, the second E, the third D, the fourth C. The fifth, being a leap year, has BA, and so on, as can be seen in the table. The last year of the solar cycle has A, and since the third year after a leap year is the first of the next cycle, it returns to GF.

units.la: X. Ut cyclum solis & ex eo dependentem literam Dominicalem invenias, annum per Jul. currentem dividas per 28, vel ad annum Christi labentem adjicias 9, & summam dividas per 28, si quid ex utràvis divisione supererit, numerus residuus, si nihil, 28 est cyclus solaris istius anni.
units.tr: X. To find the cycle of the sun, and the Dominical letter that depends on it, divide the current Julian year by 28, or add 9 to the current year of Christ and divide the sum by 28. If anything remains from either division, that residue is the number. If nothing remains, 28 is the cycle of the sun for that year.

units.la: 1. Ex gr. Annus quo hæc meditor, est per Jul. 6380. Si cyclum solis hoc anno deprehenderem 6380 divido per 28, quotiens 227 ostendit quot cycli ab initio hujus periodi ad annum propositum completi sunt. Numerus residuus est 24. Ergo hic annus est cycli currentis 24, sive, uti vulgò loquimur, Hoc anno cyclus solis est 24. Est etiam annus hic Ærae Christianae 1667, adde 9, summa est 1676 quae divisa per 28 relinquit etiam 24, pro cyclo solari hujusce anni, cui in tabulâ supra scriptâ respondet Litera Dominicalis F.
units.tr: 1. For example, the year in which I am writing these things is 6380 by the Julian reckoning. If I wish to find the cycle of the sun for this year, I divide 6380 by 28; the quotient, 227, shows how many cycles have been completed from the beginning of this period up to the year in question. The remainder is 24. So this year is the 24th year of the current cycle, or, as we commonly say, this year the cycle of the sun is 24. This year is also 1667 of the Christian era. Add 9, the sum is 1676, which divided by 28 also leaves 24 for the solar cycle of this year, to which in the table above the Dominical letter F corresponds.

units.la: 2. At si cyclum solis anno Christi 1671 quaeras, ad 1671 addas 9, summam 1680 dividas per 28, quotus est 60, residuum 0. Ergo 28 est cyclus solis. Ad annos Christi addimus 9 propterea quòd Æra Christiana cyclo solis 10 incepit, adeò ut cycli 9 completi fuerint.
units.tr: 2. But if you seek the cycle of the sun for the year of Christ 1671, add 9 to 1671, obtaining 1680. Divided by 28 this gives 60 with no remainder. So 28 is the cycle of the sun. We add 9 to the years of Christ because the Christian era began in the tenth year of the solar cycle, so that nine cycles had been completed.

units.la: XI. Ut in quotam hebdomadis feriam incidat quaelibet anni dies invenias, primò cyclum solis & per eum literam Dominicalem notam habeas, deinde observes quisnam sit character diei propositi, sive quamnam habet literam in Kalendario sibi affixam, numerus dierum à Dominicali ad hunc diei Characterem inclusive est Feria diei propositi.
units.tr: XI. To find on which day of the week any day of the year falls, first learn the cycle of the sun and, through it, the known Dominical letter. Then observe the character of the day in question, that is, which letter is attached to it in the calendar. The number of days from the Dominical letter to this character of the day, counted inclusively, is the weekday of the day in question.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Hoc anno Christi 1667, Scirem in quotam hebdomadis feriam incidat Mart. 16. Cyclus solis, uti dictum est, hoc anno est 24. Lit. Dom.F, in Kalendario character Martii 16 est E, quae est litera Septima ab F inclusive, ordine directo numerando F. G. A. B. C. D. E. Ergo Martii 16 est Feria Septima sive dies Sabbati. Sic character April. 15 est G. Ergo hoc anno fuit Feria secunda, sive dies Lunae.
units.tr: 1. For example, in the year of Christ 1667 I want to know on which weekday March 16 falls. The cycle of the sun, as said, this year is 24. The Dominical letter is F; in the calendar the character for March 16 is E, which is the seventh letter counting from F inclusive, reckoning forward F, G, A, B, C, D, E. Therefore March 16 was the seventh day, that is, Saturday. Likewise the character for April 15 is G. Therefore this year it was the second day, that is, Monday.

units.la: 2. Idem etiam efficiatur, neglecto diei Characterc, à litera Dominicali simpliciter numerando quot dies ad propositum etiam inclusum restant; ut ad Aug. 18 adscribitur litera F, quae hoc anno est Dominicalis. Ergo Aug. 18 est Dominica, Aug. 23 est sexta ab 18 inclusive: Est igitur Feria sexta sive Dies Jovis. Sed haec satis sunt aperta.
units.tr: 2. The same result can also be reached, ignoring the day's character, by counting simply from the Dominical letter how many days remain up to and including the date in question. Thus to Aug. 18 the letter F is assigned, which this year is the Dominical letter. Therefore Aug. 18 is a Sunday. Aug. 23 is the sixth day counting from the 18th inclusive, so it is Feria sexta, or Thursday (Dies Jovis). But these things are clear enough.

units.la: XII. Ut literam Dominicalem in anno Gregoriano invenias, in promptu habeas literam Dominicalem Julianam, à quâ exclusivè retrorsùm progrediendo detrahas literas tres, & relinquetur litera Dominicalis in anno Gregoriano communi. In Bissextili tres aufer literas à primâ Dominicalium, & litera residua est prima Dominicalis in anno Gregoriano, cui proxima est conjungenda.
units.tr: XII. To find the Dominical letter in the Gregorian year, have at hand the Julian Dominical letter. Counting backwards from it, excluding it, subtract three letters, and the letter that remains is the Dominical letter in the common Gregorian year. In a leap year, take three letters away from the first Dominical letter, and the letter that remains is the first Dominical letter in the Gregorian year, to which the next letter is to be joined.

units.la: 1. Gregorius, ut annum Julianum castigaret, decem dies ex anno Christi 1582 subduxit. Si septem tantùm detraxisset dies, Litera Dominicalis eadem mansisset in anno Gregoriano quæ in Juliano. Sed quoniam præter solidam septimanam tres insuper dies abstulit, hinc tres etiam literæ auferendæ sunt à Dominicali Juliana ut Gregorianam assequamur.
units.tr: 1. Gregory, to correct the Julian year, removed ten days from the year of Christ 1582. Had he removed only seven days, the Dominical letter in the Gregorian year would have remained the same as in the Julian. But since, besides the whole week, he dropped three further days, three letters must also be taken away from the Julian Dominical letter in order to arrive at the Gregorian one.

units.la: 2. Ex. gr. Hoc anno Christi 1667 Litera Dominicalis, ut dixi, in anno Juliano est F, à quâ, ordine quo procedunt Literæ Dominicales, hoc est retrogrado, numerando tres aufero literas E. D. C. & relinquitur B pro literâ Dominicali in anno Gregoriano. Sic anno 1670 cyclus solis erit 27, Litera Dominicalis in anno Juliano B, aufer tres literas A. G. F. proxima sive E Litera Dominicalis erit in Gregoriana anni formâ. At anno Christi 1668, ut Bissextili, cyclus solis erit 25, Litera Dominicalis E. D. ab E exclusive subduc tres literas D. C. B. & relinquitur A pro primâ literâ Dominicali in Anno Gregoriano; cui jungenda est proxima litera sive G. Ergo AG, erit Litera Dominicalis in anno Gregoriano, ut ED in Juliano.
units.tr: 2. For example: in this year of Christ 1667 the Dominical letter in the Julian year is F, as I said. Counting backwards, in the order in which the Dominical letters run, I take away the three letters E, D, C, and B remains as the Dominical letter in the Gregorian year. So in 1670 the solar cycle will be 27 and the Julian Dominical letter B. I take away the three letters A, G, F, and the next letter, E, will be the Dominical letter in the Gregorian form of the year. But in the year of Christ 1668, a leap year, the solar cycle will be 25 and the Dominical letter E, D. Counting back from E, excluding it, I subtract the three letters D, C, B, and A remains as the first Dominical letter in the Gregorian year, to which the next letter, G, is to be joined. Therefore AG will be the Dominical letter in the Gregorian year, as ED is in the Julian.

units.la: 3. Hæc regula valet à correctione tantùm ad annum Christi 1700, ut cui dies Bissextilis est expungenda, quæ tamen in anno Juliano retinetur. Atque idcò non tres sed duas tantùm literas ab anno 1700, ad 1800 auferendæ sunt à Dominicali Juliana, ut habeatur Gregoriana; ut anno Christi 1713, cyclus solis erit 14, Litera Dominicalis in anno Juliano D. Aufer duas literas C. B. & sequitur A pro literâ Dominicali Gregorianâ. 4.
units.tr: 3. This rule holds only from the correction up to the year of Christ 1700, at which the leap day, which is nevertheless retained in the Julian year, is to be dropped. Therefore from 1700 to 1800 not three but only two letters are to be taken away from the Julian Dominical letter to obtain the Gregorian one. Thus in the year of Christ 1713 the solar cycle will be 14 and the Julian Dominical letter D. Take away the two letters C, B, and A follows as the Gregorian Dominical letter. 4.

units.la: 4. Ab anno Christi 1800 ad 1900 ob aliam diem intercalarem omissam, una tantum litera à Dominicali Juliana subducenda est, ut Gregorianam assequamur. Ut anno 1839 cyclus solis est 28, Lit. Dom. A in anno Juliano. Auferunam literam puta G, & proxima sive F est Dominicalis in anno Gregoriano.
units.tr: 4. From the year 1800 to 1900, because another intercalary day has been omitted, only one letter is to be subtracted from the Julian Dominical letter in order to obtain the Gregorian. So in 1839 the solar cycle is 28 and the Dominical letter in the Julian year is A. Take away one letter, say G, and the next, F, is the Dominical letter in the Gregorian year.

units.la: 5. Ab anno 1900 ad 2100, quoniam unica dies intercalaris duabus hisce annorum centuriis negligitur, Litera Dominicalis Gregoriana proxima erit ad Julianam. Ut cùm cyclus solis sit 4, C erit Litera Dominicalis Juliana, B Gregoriana: cyclo solis 13 FE Juliana, ED Gregoriana.
units.tr: 5. From 1900 to 2100, since one intercalary day is neglected in these two centuries, the Gregorian Dominical letter will be the one next after the Julian. So when the solar cycle is 4, C is the Julian Dominical letter and B the Gregorian; with solar cycle 13, the Julian is FE and the Gregorian ED.

units.la: 6. Ab anno 2100 ad 2200 Litera Dominicalis Gregoriana eadem erit atque Juliana. At ab anno 2200 ad 2300 proxima litera post Dominicalem Julianam erit Gregoriana, ut si E sit Juliana, F erit Gregoriana. Si illa ED, hæc FE. Sequenti centuriâ secunda post Literam Dominicalem Julianam, ordine viz. directo, erit Gregoriana; ut si ista sit B, hæc erit D. Et hoc modo Litera Dominicalis in anno Gregoriano facillimè perpetuóque computetur.
units.tr: 6. From 2100 to 2200 the Gregorian Dominical letter will be the same as the Julian. But from 2200 to 2300 the letter next after the Julian Dominical letter will be the Gregorian, so that if E is the Julian, F will be the Gregorian; if the Julian is ED, the Gregorian is FE. In the following century the second letter after the Julian Dominical letter, in direct order, will be the Gregorian; so if the Julian is B, the Gregorian will be D. In this way the Dominical letter in the Gregorian year can be computed most easily and for all time.

units.la: CAP. IV. De cyclo Lunæ, sive Aureo numero.
units.tr: CHAP. IV. On the cycle of the Moon, or the Golden Number.

units.la: Cyclus Lunæ est series annorum 19, quâ revolutâ, novilunia, plenilunia, reliquique Lunæ χρυσαλίδες, ad eandem diem Julianam redeunt.
units.tr: The cycle of the Moon is a series of 19 years, at the end of which the new moons, full moons and the other phases of the Moon return to the same Julian day.

units.la: 1. ATHENIENSES olim dies & menses ad Lunæ, annos autem ad Solis motus accommodabant: Et idcirco quoniam annus solaris duodecim menses Lunares diebus 11 excedit, ut annum suum 12 mensibus Lunaribus constantem intra terminos Solares coërcerent, post aliquot annos mensibus suis duodecim communibus alium, Embolimæum dictum, interserebant. Annorum systema quo vertente Solis & Lunæ motus per hunc Embolismum, ad idem redire punctum putabant, Cyclum vocabant, sive Periodum.
units.tr: 1. The Athenians once arranged their days and months by the Moon, but their years by the motions of the Sun. Since the solar year exceeds twelve lunar months by 11 days, they therefore inserted, after some years, an extra month, called Embolimaeus, among their twelve common months, so as to keep their year of twelve lunar months within the limits of the solar year. The system of years at the end of which, with this intercalation, the motions of the Sun and Moon returned, as they thought, to the same point, they called a Cycle or Period.

units.la: 2. Porrò nondum exactè compertis Solis Lunæque motibus, hujusmodi cyclorum varii sunt instituti, ut Dieteris, Tetraeteris, Octaeteris, aliique, quorum errore tandem deprehenso Enneadecaeteridem, sive cyclum Decemnovalem instituebant, quo labente, mensem Embolimæum septies intercalabant, & eo modo solis Lunæque motus ad idem restituì punctum pro certo habuerunt. Et quidem isto annorum numero vertente, novilunia, plenilunia cœteraeque Lunæ configurationes ad eandem saltem diem solarem regrediuntur, ut si supponamus novilunium accidere hoc anno Jun. 21, post annos 19 completos eodem iterum die committetur.
units.tr: 2. However, since the motions of the Sun and Moon were not yet exactly known, various cycles of this kind were set up, such as the Dieteris, Tetraeteris, Octaeteris, and others. When their error was at last detected, they established the Enneadecaeteris, or nineteen-year cycle, in which they intercalated the Embolimaean month seven times as the cycle passed, and by this means held it for certain that the motions of the Sun and Moon were restored to the same point. Indeed, when this number of years has run its course, the new moons, full moons and the other configurations of the Moon return at least to the same solar day. For example, if we suppose a new moon to fall this year on Jun. 21, after the 19 years are complete it will again fall on the same day.

units.la: II. De hoc Cyclo notetur:
units.tr: II. Concerning this cycle, note the following:

units.la: III. Primò; Cyclus Lunæ Decemnovalis annis Julianis 19, minor est h. 1. 27'. 31''. 55'''.
units.tr: III. First; The nineteen-year lunar cycle is shorter than 19 Julian years by 1 h. 27' 31" 55'''.

units.la: 1. Hoc ex utriusque collectione demonstretur. Nam mensis Lunaris juxta peritissimos Astronomorum, est dier. 29 h. 12. 44'. 3". 11'''. quæ duodecies multiplicata producunt anni communis quantitatem d. 354. h. 8 48'. 38". 12". hæc in 19 ducta producunt dies 6732. h. 23. 24'. 5". 48'''. Addantur 7 menses Embolimæi (toties enim annis 19 vertentibus intercalatur) sive dies 206. h. 1,7. 8'. 22". 17'''. Summa est dies 6939. h. 16. 32'. 28". 5". At anni Juliani 19 dies colligunt 6939 hor. 18. o. aufer d. 6939. h. 16. 32'. 28". 5'''. ex 6939. h. 18. o. residuum est d. o. h. 1. 27'. 31". 55'''. minor igitur est Cyclus Lunæ quàm 19 anni Juliani h. 1. 27'. 31". 55'''. adeò ut si novilunium hoc anno conficeretur, Jan. 21. h. 10. post mediam noctem, post annos 19 elapsos, novilunium eâdem iterum die committeretur, sed non eâdem dici horâ, viz. decimâ, sed horâ 8. 32'. 28", 5'''. Et hinc fit quod cyclis 16 sive annis 304 hæc fit horarum 23. 20'. 30". 40". At annis circiter 312.
units.tr: 1. This is shown from the sum of both. For a lunar month, according to the most skilled astronomers, is 29 days, 12 h. 44' 3" 11'''; multiplied twelve times, these make the length of a common year, 354 days, 8 h. 48' 38" 12"; multiplied by 19, these give 6732 days, 23 h. 24' 5" 48'''. Add 7 Embolimaean months (for so many are intercalated as the 19 years turn), that is 206 days, 17 h. 8' 22" 17'''. The sum is 6939 days, 16 h. 32' 28" 5". But 19 Julian years make 6939 days, 18 h. 0'. Subtract 6939 d. 16 h. 32' 28" 5''' from 6939 d. 18 h. 0'; the remainder is 0 d. 1 h. 27' 31" 55'''. The cycle of the Moon is therefore shorter than 19 Julian years by 1 h. 27' 31" 55'''. So if a new moon were occurring this year on Jan. 21 at 10 o'clock after midnight, after 19 years have elapsed the new moon would again fall on the same day, but not at the same hour, namely the tenth, but at the hour 8 h. 32' 28" 5'''. And hence it comes about that over 16 cycles, or 304 years, the difference is 23 h. 20' 30" 40"; over about 312 years

units.la: sol idus dies anticipatur, adeò ut idem novilunium quod hoc anno committitur, Jan. 21. h. decimâ, post annos 312 expletos ad Jan. 20. h. 10. retrovertetur, & post alios annos 312 ad Jan. 19. h. 10. retrocedet.
units.tr: the difference amounts to a whole day, so that the same new moon which falls this year on Jan. 21 at the tenth hour will, after 312 years have been completed, fall back to Jan. 20 at the tenth hour, and after another 312 years will recede to Jan. 19 at the tenth hour.

units.la: IV. Secundò; Per cyclum Lunæ dies in quos novilunia, & plenilunia quotannis incidunt, inveniantur.
units.tr: IV. Secondly; By the cycle of the Moon, the days on which the new moons and full moons fall each year are found.

units.la: 1. Hæc unica videtur methodus, quâ veteres sine tabulis Astronomicis novilunia quotannis computare solebant. Cùm annis enim 19 vertentibus novilunia ad eandem diem revertri observâssent, anno primo quo hanc methodum introducebant (quisnam iste fuit nihil refert, eò quòd in circulo nullum est principium φύσει, sed tantùm θέσει) observabant novilunia commissa Jan. 23. Feb. 21. Mart. 23. & sic deinceps ad anni finem, ad hos itaque dies in Kalendario adscribebant 1. Secundo anno commissa deprehendebant novilunia Jan. 12. Feb. 10. Mart. 12. April. 10. &c. unde ad istos dies appingebant 2. & ob eandem rationem anno tertio ad Jan. 1. & 31. ad Mart. 1. & 31. ad April. 29. & sic usque ad exitum anni adnotabant 3. & eodem modo percurrebant annos 19, observantes in quemnam diem, incidebant novilunia quovis cycli istius decemnovalis anno, & diei cuilibet quo confecta sunt novilunia unam è figuris 1. 2. 3. 4. 5,&c. usque ad 19 affigebant, viz.diebus quibus primo cycli anno commissa sunt apponebant 1, quibus secundo 2, quibus tertio 3, quibus quarto 4, & sic deinceps usque ad 19, adeò ut hæ figuræ diebus quibus adscribuntur commissa fuisse novilunia, per totum cyclum Decemnovalem indigitabant.
units.tr: 1. This seems to be the only method by which the ancients, without astronomical tables, used to compute the new moons each year. For when they had observed that, as nineteen years turned, the new moons returned to the same day, in the first year in which they introduced this method (who that was matters little, since in a circle there is no principle by nature, but only by convention) they noted that the new moons fell on Jan. 23, Feb. 21, Mar. 23, and so on to the end of the year. To these dates in the calendar they therefore attached the figure 1. In the second year they found that the new moons fell on Jan. 12, Feb. 10, Mar. 12, Apr. 10, etc., and to these dates they attached 2. For the same reason, in the third year they attached 3 to Jan. 1 and 31, to Mar. 1 and 31, and to Apr. 29, and so on to the end of the year. In the same way they went through the 19 years, observing on which day a new moon fell in each year of this nineteen-year cycle, and they attached to each day on which new moons had occurred one of the figures 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and so on up to 19. That is, to the days on which new moons occurred in the first year of the cycle they attached 1; to those of the second year, 2; to those of the third, 3; to those of the fourth, 4; and so on up to 19. Thus these figures, by the days to which they were attached, indicated the new moons throughout the whole nineteen-year cycle.

units.la: 2. Quocirca propositó quolibet anno cycli decemnovalis cujus novilunium aliquod invenirent, Kalendarium hisce figuris instructum consulebant, & diem in mense propósito quærebant, cui numerus istius anni in cyclo Decemnovali affixus fuit. Ex. gr. Si quærendus esset dies Martii quo commissum est novilunium anno Christi 354, hic annus erat cycli Decemnovalis 13. Itaque numerum 13 quærentes in mense Martio, eúmque diei undecimo adscriptum invenientes, isto anno novilunium in Martii undecimum incidere pronunciabant. Hosce porrò numeros Aureos appellitabant, vel ob aureum eorum in noviluniis investigandis usum, vel quòd in Kalendariis auro depingi solebant.
units.tr: 2. Accordingly, when they wished to find the new moon in any given year of the nineteen-year cycle, they consulted a calendar furnished with these figures and sought, in the month in question, the day to which the number of that year in the nineteen-year cycle was attached. For example, if one wished to find the day in March on which a new moon fell in the year of Christ 354, this year was year 13 of the nineteen-year cycle. Seeking the number 13 in the month of March and finding it attached to the eleventh day, they pronounced that in that year the new moon fell on the eleventh of March. These numbers they called golden numbers, either because of their golden usefulness in finding new moons, or because they were customarily painted in calendars in gold.

units.la: 3. Et hi quidem Aurei numeri Synodi Nicenæ temporibus, quibus in Kalendariis primò descripti sunt, diem, quo novilunia contingebant, accuratè satis indicabant: Non item post aliquot annorum centurias ob ἀποκύνην σλαvαϊκὴν, jam explicatam: nisi pro quibúlvis annis 312, qui ab istis temporibus sunt elapsi, solidus dies auferatur. Hoc autem observato, nunc etiam dierum novilunia per Aureos numeros comperiamus. Ex. gr. Hoc anno Christi 1667. Scire vellem quonam Januarii die commissum sit novilunium. Synodus Nicena celebrata est anno Christi 325. Igitur ex 1667, subduco 325, supersunt anni 1342 quos divido per 312, quotiens est 4, residuum 94. Novilunia quatuor diebus retroversa quotus ostendit; præterea hoc anno cyclus Lunæ est 15. Kalendarium igitur ad calcem hujus Libri descriptum consulens, quæro numerum istum 15 in mense Januario, eúmque ad Jan. 19 affixum invenio, ab isto quatuor solidos subduco dies, viz. 18.17.16. 15. & relinquitur Dies Januarii 14, quo novilunium hoc anno confectum esse tabulæ Astronomicæ fidem faciunt. Et hoc modo novilunia per aureos numeros etiam Nicenos quotannis inveniantur; ut & plenilunia dies tantùm 15, ad novilunii diem addendo, sic ad 14 addo 15, summa 29 diem indicat quo Luna plena videtur. Et hæc quidem methodus solido die nunquam aberrabit.
units.tr: 3. Now these golden numbers, in the time of the Synod of Nicaea, when they were first set down in calendars, indicated with sufficient accuracy the day on which new moons occurred. Not so after some centuries had passed, owing to the [ἀποκύνην σλαβαϊκὴν] already explained, unless a full day is subtracted for each of the 312 years that have elapsed since those times. With this observed, we can now also find the days of new moons by the golden numbers. For example, in this year of Christ 1667 I should like to know on which day of January the new moon occurred. The Synod of Nicaea was held in the year of Christ 325. Subtracting 325 from 1667, there remain 1342 years, which I divide by 312; the quotient is 4, the remainder 94. The quotient shows that the new moons have been carried back four days. Moreover, this year the cycle of the Moon is 15. Consulting the calendar described at the end of this book, I seek the number 15 in the month of January and find it attached to Jan. 19. From this I subtract four whole days, namely 18, 17, 16, 15, and there remains January 14, on which day astronomical tables testify that the new moon occurred this year. In this way new moons are found each year by the golden numbers, even the Nicene ones; and full moons likewise, by adding 15 days to the day of the new moon: thus 14 plus 15 gives 29, the day on which the Moon is seen to be full. This method will never err by a full day.

units.la: V. Tertiò; Per aureum hunc numerum paschatis cele- brandi dies juxta Synodi Nicenæ decretum quotannis inveniatur.
units.tr: V. Thirdly: By this golden number the day of celebrating Easter is found each year according to the decree of the Synod of Nicaea.

units.la: 1. Hanc propono regulam, propterea quòd paschali celebritate nonnunquam annus unus ab aliis secernatur, atque ita temporum sit character. Quam tamen ut intelligas, tenendum est Synodum Nicenam de paschali celebritate hæc tria decrevisse, primò ut post Æquinoctium vernum, ut tunc temporis commissum, vid. Martii 21; secundò ut post quartam decimam proximam isti Æquinoctio; tertiò ut die Dominicâ quartam decimam istam consequente perageretur: Eandémque Synodum (ut D. Ambrosius asserit Epist. l. 10. ep. 83. quæ est ad Episcopos Æmiliæ) aureos hosce numeros, ut perpetuos terminorum paschalium indices, instituisse.
units.tr: 1. I propose this rule, because the paschal celebration sometimes distinguishes one year from another, and so is a mark of the times. In order to understand it, it must be held that the Synod of Nicaea decreed three things about the paschal celebration: first, that it be after the vernal equinox, which at that time was fixed on March 21; second, that it be after the fourteenth day of the moon nearest to that equinox; third, that it be kept on the Sunday following that fourteenth day. And that same Synod (as St. Ambrose asserts, Epist. book 10, ep. 83, which is addressed to the bishops of Aemilia) instituted these golden numbers as perpetual indicators of the paschal limits.

units.la: 2. Si diem itaque quo paschalis hæc festivitas sit celebranda, secundùm Oecumenicæ istius Synodi decreta (quibus nostra etiam Ecclesia Anglicana religiosissimè insistit) invenires, Kalendarium nostrum Julianum consulas cum anni propositi cyclo decemnovali, sive aureo numero, ibidémque novilunium istud quæras cujus quarta decima dies Martii 21 proximè sequitur, & Litera Dominicalis anni tui quæ quartam decimam istam excipit, est character paschalis tuæ celebritatis.
units.tr: 2. If, therefore, you wish to find the day on which this paschal festival is to be celebrated, according to the decrees of this ecumenical Synod (to which our English Church also adheres most scrupulously), consult our Julian calendar for the cycle of nineteen years, or golden number, of the year in question, and look there for the new moon whose fourteenth day most nearly follows March 21; the Dominical Letter of your year, which falls on the Sunday following that fourteenth day, is the mark of your paschal celebration.

units.la: 3. Ex. gr. Hoc anno Christi 1667 cyclus Lunæ sive aureus numerus est 15. Igitur in mense Martio quæro numerum istum 15, quem ad Martii 19. adscriptum invenio. Hoc novilunium est paschale quoniam ejus quartadecima Martii 21 sequitur, incidítque in April. 2. Litera Dominicalis hoc anno est F, quæ etiam ad April. 7 apponitur, igitur April. 7 est Dominica quâ paschalis celebritas est peragenda.
units.tr: 3. For example: in this year of Christ 1667 the cycle of the moon, or golden number, is 15. So in the month of March I look for this number 15, which I find written against March 19. This new moon is the paschal one, since its fourteenth day falls on March 21, and it falls on April 2. The Dominical Letter this year is F, which is also placed against April 7; therefore April 7 is the Sunday on which the paschal celebration is to be kept.

units.la: VI. Ut cyclum Lunæ invenias, annum per Jul. dividas per 19, vel ad annum Christi currentem addas 1, & summam dividas per 19. Si quid ex utrâvis divisione reliterit, numerus iste residuus, si nihil, 19 est cyclus Lunæ quæsitus.
units.tr: VI. To find the cycle of the moon, divide the year by the Julian reckoning by 19, or add 1 to the current year of Christ and divide the sum by 19. If anything remains from either division, that residual number is the cycle sought; if nothing remains, 19 is the cycle of the moon sought.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Annus hic est per Jul. 6380. Quopropter 6380 divido per 19, & residuum fit 15, sic etiam ad annum Christi 1667 addo unitatem, summam 1668 distribuo per 19, quotus est 87, numerus residuus itidem 15. Utroque igitur modo cyclus Lunæ, sive aureus numerus hoc anno est 15.
units.tr: 1. For example: this year, by the Julian reckoning, is 6380. Therefore I divide 6380 by 19, and the remainder is 15. Likewise, I add one to the year of Christ 1667, divide the sum 1668 by 19, the quotient is 87 and the remainder again 15. By either method, therefore, the cycle of the moon, or golden number, this year is 15.

units.la: 2. Verùm annus Christi 1671 auctus unitate & divisus per 19, in quoto dat 88 & nihil relinquit: Ergo 19 erit cyclus Lunæ istius anni. Annis Christi unitatem addimus eò quòd Æra Christiana cyclo Lunæ 2 cœpit, uno anno cycli jam elapso.
units.tr: 2. But the year of Christ 1671, increased by one and divided by 19, gives 88 as the quotient and leaves nothing; therefore 19 will be the cycle of the moon of that year. We add one to the years of Christ because the Christian Era began in the second year of the lunar cycle, one year of the cycle having already elapsed.

units.la: CAP. V. De Indictione.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On the Indiction.

units.la: Indictio est Series annorum 15 in orbem rediens.
units.tr: An indiction is a series of 15 years returning in a circle.

units.la: QUando Indictiones primò sunt institutæ nondum constat: hoc tantùm constat eas post Constantini tempora, sive ab anno Christi 312 vulgarem in usum receptas fuisse. Eas Græci Ἐπιβολὰς largitiones, sive distributiones appellant: Quamvis & Ἰνδικτιῶν vocabulum ab iis retentum sæpe legimus.
units.tr: When indictions were first instituted is not yet settled. It is certain only that they came into common use after the time of Constantine, that is, from about the year of Christ 312. The Greeks call them epibolas [Ἐπιβολὰς], that is, largesses or distributions, though we often read that they also retained the word indiktiōn [Ἰνδικτιῶν].

units.la: II. Indictio est vel Græca vel Romana.
units.tr: II. The indiction is either Greek or Roman.

units.la: 1. Hic enim Indictionem Cæsaream ab 8 Kal. Octob. ineuntem, ut & Antiochenam à Mense Maio juxta quosdam numeratam prætereo, quippe quæ nullius sunt momenti, nec usquam, ni fallor, occurrunt usitatæ.
units.tr: 1. I pass over the Caesarean indiction, which begins on 8 Kalends of October, and the Antiochene indiction, which some reckon from May. These are of no importance and, unless I am mistaken, are nowhere found in use.

units.la: III. Indictiones Græcæ à Kal. Septembribus ineunt.
units.tr: III. Greek indictions begin on the Kalends of September.

units.la: 1. Harum usus in Actis Conciliorum & Imperatorum novellis præcipuè consignandis obtinuit; ut in Manuelis Comneni novellâ de Immobilibus magnæ Ecclesiæ, Τοῦ μάνου ... Dat. Mense Augusto, Indictione primâ, anno mundi 6661.
units.tr: 1. Their use was chiefly established in recording the Acts of Councils and the imperial novels. So in the novel of Manuel Comnenus concerning the immovable property of the Great Church, [Τοῦ μάνου ...] Given in the month of August, in the first indiction, in the year of the world 6661.

units.la: IV. Si Græcam invenires Indictionem, annum mundi currentem juxta computum Græcum divides per 15, si quid restat, numerus residuus, si nihil, 15 est Indictio anni propositi.
units.tr: IV. If you find a Greek indiction, divide the current year of the world, reckoned by the Greek computation, by 15. If something remains, the remainder is the indiction of the year in question; if nothing remains, 15 is the indiction of the year proposed.

units.la: 1. Sic annum prædictum, quo edita est ista Manuelis Comneni novella, viz. 6661 divido per 15; Quotiens est 444, residuum 1. Ergo iste primus erat Indictionis annus. At si anno mundi juxta computum Constantinopolitanum civilem 6600, indictionem scirem; divisis 6600 per 15, quotus est 440, residuum 0. Ergo 15 fuit indictio. Quod etiam confirmatur à rescripto Alexii, quo novellam suam de nup-
units.tr: Thus, dividing the aforesaid year, in which this novella of Manuel Comnenus was published, namely 6661, by 15: the quotient is 444 and the remainder 1. So that year was the first year of the indiction. But if I knew the indiction for the year of the world according to the civil Constantinopolitan reckoning, 6600, then dividing 6600 by 15 gives a quotient of 440 and a remainder of 0. So the indiction was 15. This is also confirmed by the rescript of Alexius, by which he ordered his novella on marriages to be ratified, and at the foot of which we read these words:

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] tiis ratam esse jussit ⁊ ut ad cujus calcem hæc legimus, Γεγονώτα χῷ ἴδν Μάγνον μὲν ἀπὸ ὅτ... Dat. mense Martio, præsenti indictione 15, anno 6600.
units.tr: ...ordered that his novel concerning marriages be valid; and at its foot we read, Γεγονώτα χῷ ἴδν Μάγνον μὲν ἀπὸ ὅτ... Given in the month of March, in the present indiction 15, in the year 6600.

units.la: V. Indictiones Romanæ à Kal. Jan. ineunt.
units.tr: V. The Roman indictions begin on 1 January.

units.la: 1. Nimirùm Annus Græcus sive Constantinopolitanus à Kal. Septembribus proficiscitur, & idcirco Indictiones etiam ab eâdem Epochâ numerantur. Annus autem Romanus à Kalendis Januariis exordium sumit, & consequenter Indictiones; ab eodem videlicet atque annus initio deducuntur. Harum usus in Pontificum Romanorum bullis, diplomatibus, aliisque eorum scriptis adhuc valet.
units.tr: 1. The Greek or Constantinopolitan year begins on the Kalends of September, and so the indictions are also counted from that same epoch. The Roman year, however, takes its beginning from the Kalends of January, and consequently the indictions are reckoned from the same starting point as the year. Their use still holds in the bulls, diplomas and other writings of the Roman pontiffs.

units.la: VI. Si Indictionem Romanam scire cupias, annum per. Jul. currentem divide per 15, vel etiam Anno Christi aggreges 3, & aggregatum dividas per 15, si quid ex utraque divisione relinquatur, numerus iste residuus, si nihil 15 est Indictio quaesita.
units.tr: VI. If you wish to know the Roman indiction, divide the current year of the Julian period by 15, or add 3 to the year of Christ and divide the sum by 15. If something remains from either division, that remainder is the indiction sought; if nothing remains, 15 is the indiction sought.

units.la: 1. Ex, gr. Hoc anno Christi 1667 Indictionem haberem. Itaque ad 1667 addo 3, summa 1670 per 15 distributa in quoto dat 111, in residuo 5. Ergo hic est annus quintus Indictionis 112, sive ut vulgò loquimur, Hoc anno Indictio est 5. Est etiam hic annus per. Jul. 6380 qui per 15 divisus praeter Indictiones completas 425, relinquit 55 Utroque igitur modo computetur Indictio.
units.tr: 1. For example, in this year of Christ 1667 I would have the indiction. So I add 3 to 1667; the sum 1670 divided by 15 gives 111 as quotient and 5 as remainder. Therefore this is the fifth year of the indiction 112, or, as we commonly say, this year the indiction is 5. This year is also 6380 of the Julian period, which divided by 15 gives 425 complete indictions and leaves 55 over. Either way, therefore, the indiction is computed.

units.la: 2. Ad annos Christi adjiciendum est 3, propterea quòd primus annus Æræ Christianæ coepit Indictione quartâ, tribus jam completis.
units.tr: 2. 3 must be added to the years of Christ, because the first year of the Christian Era began in the fourth indiction, with three already completed.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAP. VI.

units.la: De Epactis.
units.tr: On the Epacts.

units.la: Epacte sunt dies ad feriam vel etatem Lune inveniendam adjecti.
units.tr: Epacts are days added to find the weekday or the age of the moon.

units.la: I. EPACTARVM naturam ipsa vocis etymologia demonstrat. Nam ἐπάγεσι ἐπακταὶ dicuntur, propterea quòd ἐπάγεται; i. e. Adjiciuntur ut Hebdomadis feriam vel ætatem Lunæ consequamur. II. Epacte sunt vel Solis vel Lune. III. Epacte Solis sunt dies adjectitii ad inveniendam hebdomadis feriam sive πρῶτα τῆς ἐβδομάδος. IV. Sunt que vel menstrue vel Annue. V. Epacte Solis menstrue sunt dies mensis cujuflibet qui 28 excedunt.
units.tr: I. The nature of epacts is shown by the etymology of the word itself. For they are called epaktai [ἐπακταί] because they are brought on [ἐπάγεται], that is, they are added so that we may reach the weekday of the week or the age of the moon. II. Epacts are either solar or lunar. III. Solar epacts are days added to find the weekday of the week, or the first [πρῶτα τῆς ἐβδομάδος]. IV. They are either monthly or annual. V. Monthly solar epacts are the days of any month that exceed 28.

units.la: 1. In quovis mense, dempto Februario in anno communi, plures quàm 28 colliguntur dies, & consequenter plusquam completæ septimanæ. Dies itaque mensis cujuflibet post 28 exactos residui, dicuntur Epacte, quæ sequentis mensis Kalendis sunt adjiciendæ ut feriam earum habeamus. Sic Januarius dies habet 31, aufer omnes hebdomades sive 28, & relinquuntur 3, qui cum Februarii Kalendis collecti dant 4, Februarius igitur in Feriam quartam incidet à Kal. Januariis, inclusive; ut si Januarius incat Feriâ secundâ, Februarius Feriâ quintâ inibit, & sic in reliquis. VI. Epacte Solis annue sunt dies post exactas omnes anni septimanas relicti.
units.tr: 1. In any month, except February in a common year, more than 28 days are counted, and so more than complete weeks. The days of any month that remain after 28 have been passed are therefore called epacts, and they are to be added to the calends of the following month so that we have its weekday. Thus January has 31 days. Take away all the weeks, that is 28, and 3 remain; these, added to the calends of February, give 4. So February falls on the fourth day counting from the calends of January inclusive. Hence, if January begins on the second feria, February will begin on the fifth, and so on for the rest. VI. Annual solar epacts are the days left over after all the weeks of the year have been completed.

units.la: 1. Sic annus communis dies colligit 365, qui per 7 divisi dant Septimanas 52, & unum relinquunt diem superfluum, qui Kalendis anni proximi Januariis adjectus eas secundam esse post Kalendas Januarias anni precedentis feriam indicat. Ut si annus quilibet propositus incipiat Feriâ prima, hic post exactas omnes septimanas unam relinquens diem quæ etiam est Feria prima, primam sequentis anni diem in Feriam secundam rejiciet. At annus Bissextilis, ut diebus constans 366, post completas omnes septimanas duos facit dies residuos, eadem addendos methodo, feriam anni sequentis ut habeamus.
units.tr: 1. Thus a common year contains 365 days, which divided by 7 give 52 weeks and leave one superfluous day. Added to the calends of January of the next year, this day shows that the first day of that year falls one day later in the week than the first day of the year before. So if any given year begins on the first feria, it will leave one day over after all the weeks have run out, and that day is also the first feria; it will therefore push the first day of the following year to the second feria. A bissextile year, however, having 366 days, leaves two days over after all the weeks are completed, and these are to be added by the same method, so that we have the weekday of the next year.

units.la: 2. Has Solis Epactas Concurrentes Solis veteres computistæ nuncupare solent, quæ cum regularibus collectæ quotam feriam, sive πηλίκη τῆς ἑβδομάδος indigitabant. Solis regulares vocabant ferias Kalendarum mensium per totum annum primum Kalendarii, sive quando Litera Dominicalis fuit G. Nam cum Litera Dominicalis est G, Kalendæ Januariæ in feriam secundam incidunt: Ergo regulares Januarii perpetuò sunt 2. Kalendæ Februariæ in feriam quintam, ergo 5 sunt regulares Februarii, & sic in reliquis; post omnes exactas septimanas istius anni, unus superest dies sequentis anni Kalendis adjiciendus, ut earum habeatur Feria: Ut Epacta Solis sit 1, hanc componas cum regularibus Januarii sive 2, Summa 3 dat Feriam in quam Kalendæ Januarii isto anno incidunt. Hic autem annus post omnes elapsas hebdomades unum itidem diem relinquit, ut sequentis anni concurrentes, sive Epactæ Solis sint 2, quæ cum regularibus Januarii 2 collectæ Kalendas Januarias hoc anno Feriam esse quartam indicant.
units.tr: 2. The veteran computists were accustomed to call these solar epacts the concurrents of the sun. When these were added to the regulars, they indicated the day of the week, or which day it was [πηλίκη τῆς ἑβδομάδος]. They called the regulars of the sun the weekdays of the calends of the months throughout the whole first year of the calendar, or when the Dominical Letter was G. For when the Dominical Letter is G, the calends of January fall on the second feria (Monday); so the regulars of January are always 2. The calends of February fall on the fifth feria, so the regulars of February are 5, and so on for the rest. After all the complete weeks of that year have run out, one day remains, to be added to the calends of the next year so that its weekday is obtained. Thus, if the solar epact is 1, compare this with the regular of January, which is 2; the sum, 3, gives the weekday on which the calends of January fall in that year. This year too leaves one day over after all the weeks have elapsed, so that the concurrents of the following year, or the solar epacts, are 2. When these are added to the regular of January, which is 2, they show that the calends of January of this year fall on the fourth feria.

units.la: 3. Hæ Solis Epactæ jam penitus obsoluerunt, eò quòd Feriæ, sive πηλίκη τῆς ἰσδομάδος per Literas Dominicales facilius pariter atque expeditius quotannis inveniantur. Quapropter nec opus est, ut iis explicandis ulterius incumbamus.
units.tr: 3. These solar epacts have now gone wholly out of use, because the weekday, or which day it is [πηλίκη τῆς ἑβδομάδος], is found each year more easily and quickly by means of the Dominical Letters. Therefore there is no need for us to labour further over explaining them.

units.la: VII. Epactæ Lunares sunt dies post exactas Syzygias de mensibus aut annis civilibus residui.
units.tr: VII. Lunar epacts are the days left over, in civil months or years, after the complete syzygies.

units.la: VIII. Sùntque vel menstruæ vel annuæ.
units.tr: VIII. And they are either monthly or annual.

units.la: IX. Epactæ Lunares menstruæ sunt dies mensium qui post integras Syzygias relinquuntur.
units.tr: IX. Monthly lunar epacts are the days of the months that remain after complete syzygies.

units.la: 1. Mensis Lunaris diebus constat 29. h. 12.44'.3''. Menses autem civiles, Juliani præsertim, nunc 30 nunc 31 dierum fiunt, Unico dempto Februario; quo fit ut si supponamus novilunium committi Kalendis Martiis ineuntibus, atque ideo mensem Lunarem & Julianum simul inire, integrâ Syzygiâ sive diēb. 29.h.12.44'.3''. elapsis, dies una, & horæ 12 de mense Martio, adhuc relinquerentur, adeò ut Kalendis April, ineuntibus Luna secunda, sive secunda novæ Syzygiæ dies laberetur. Et quoniam unus dies solidus de mense priori relictus fuit, hinc Kalendis Aprilibus unitas addenda est ut ætatem Lunæ consequamur. Quapropter Epacta Aprilis est 1. Aprilis præterea 30 tantùm dies colligens solidum diem post d. 29, h. 12 non relinquit, sed tantùm horas 12, quæ tamen cum horis 12 quæ mense Martio supra diem solidum excurrebant, diem alium constituunt, adeò ut Kalendis Junii duo dies aggregandi sunt, Lunæ ætatem ut teneamus. Unde Junii Epacta fit 2. Et sic usque ad anni exitum Epactæ menstruæ progrediuntur, ut ultimo mense completo undecim dies in Epactam insequentis anni colligantur.
units.tr: 1. A lunar month consists of 29 days, 12 hours, 44 minutes and 3 seconds. Civil months, however, especially the Julian, are now 30 or 31 days long, with the single exception of February. It follows that if we suppose the new moon to fall on the first day of March, and so the lunar and Julian months to begin together, then when a complete syzygy of 29 days, 12 hours, 44 minutes and 3 seconds has elapsed, one day and 12 hours of March would still remain. Thus on 1 April the moon would be in its second day, that is, the second day of the new syzygy would have slipped by. And since one full day was left over from the previous month, one must be added on 1 April to reach the age of the moon. Therefore the epact of April is 1. Moreover, April has only 30 days, so after 29 days and 12 hours it leaves no full day, only 12 hours; but these 12 hours, together with the 12 hours that ran over a full day in March, make another day. Thus two days must be added on the first of June so that we keep the age of the moon. Hence the epact of June becomes 2. And so the monthly epacts progress until the end of the year, so that when the last month is completed, eleven days are carried over into the epact of the following year.

units.la: X. Epactæ Lunares annuæ sunt dies anni solaris, qui post exactum annum Lunarem excurrunt.
units.tr: X. The annual lunar epacts are the days of the solar year that run over once the lunar year is complete.

units.la: 1. Epactæ annuæ, ut è præcedentibus patet, ex Epactis menstruis colliguntur. Et quoniam post exactas omnes Syzygias undecim dies de anno Juliano restant percurrendi, hinc evenit, ut Epactæ annuæ per undecim perpetuò progrediantur, idque per totum cyclum Lunarem. Ex gr. Primus annus cycli Lunaris juxta computum vulgarem, Epactam habet 11. Secundus igitur annus habebit bis 11, sive 22, quibus si rursum addas 11 fiunt 33, sed ultra 30 nunquam procedant; aufer itaque 30, restant 3, in Epactam tertii anni cycli Lunaris. Quartus autem adjectis iterum rum 11 Epactam habebit 14,& sic usque ad ultimum cycli Lunaris annum, cui competit Epacta 19. Et primo iterum Epacta 11, ut anteá. Et sic Epactæ unà cum cyclo Lunari post annos 19 expletos in orbem redeunt.
units.tr: 1. As is clear from what has gone before, the annual epacts are gathered from the monthly epacts. Since eleven days of the Julian year remain to be run through after all the syzygies are complete, it follows that the annual epacts advance by eleven each year, and this continues through the whole lunar cycle. For example, the first year of the lunar cycle, by the common reckoning, has epact 11. The second year therefore has twice 11, that is 22; if you add 11 again to these you get 33, but epacts never go beyond 30, so take away 30, leaving 3, which is the epact of the third year of the lunar cycle. The fourth, with 11 added again, has epact 14, and so on to the last year of the lunar cycle, to which epact 19 belongs. Then the first year again has epact 11, as before. So the epacts, together with the lunar cycle, return to the beginning after the 19 years are completed.

units.la: XI. Epactæ Lunares annuæ vel in anno Juliano, vel Gregoriano quærantur.
units.tr: XI. Annual lunar epacts are to be sought either in the Julian year or in the Gregorian year.

units.la: XII. Epactam Lunarem in anno Juliano si quæras, cyclum Lunarem anni propositi undecies multiplices, numerus productus si minor sit quàm 30 est Epacta anni propositi, sin major, dividatur per 30 & numerus residuus est Epacta quæsita.
units.tr: XII. If you seek the lunar epact in the Julian year, multiply the lunar cycle of the year in question by eleven. If the product is less than 30, it is the epact of the year in question; if greater, divide it by 30, and the remainder is the epact sought.

units.la: 1. Exempli gratiâ: Sit cyclus Lunæ 2, si Epactam ei congruentem haberes, 2 ducas in 11, productum est 22. Ergò cùm cyclus Lunæ est 2, Epacta est 22.
units.tr: 1. For example: let the lunar cycle be 2. If you wished to have the epact corresponding to it, multiply 2 by 11; the product is 22. Therefore, since the lunar cycle is 2, the epact is 22.

units.la: 2. Hoc anno Christi 1667 cyclus Lunæ est 15. Ut Epactam invenirem, multiplico 15 in 11, numerus productus 165 per 30 divisus in quoto dat 5, in residuo 15; Ergò hoc anno Epacta Lunaris est 15.
units.tr: 2. In this year of Christ 1667 the lunar cycle is 15. To find the epact I multiply 15 by 11; the product, 165, divided by 30 gives a quotient of 5 and a remainder of 15. Therefore the lunar epact this year is 15.

units.la: XIII. Si Epactam Gregorianam cupias, eam ex Juliana facillimè formes. Nam si Epacta Juliana major sit quàm 10, ex eâ subtrahas 10, si minor, ei addas 30, & è summâ subtrahas 10, numerus residuus ex utráv is subtracti one est Epacta Gregoriana quæsita.
units.tr: XIII. If you want the Gregorian epact, you can easily form it from the Julian. If the Julian epact is greater than 10, subtract 10 from it; if less, add 30 to it and subtract 10 from the sum. The remaining number, in either case, is the Gregorian epact sought.

units.la: 1. Exempli gratiâ: Cùm cyclus Lunæ est 2, Epacta Juliana est 22, subtrahe 10, restant 12, ergò 12 est Epacta Gregoriana. Hoc anno Christi 1667 Epacta Juliana est 15, deme 10 restant 5 pro Epactâ Gregoriana. At anno Christi 1666 cyclus Lunæ erat 14 Epacta Juliana 4, quæ minor est quàm 10, ei itaque addas 30, è summâ 34 subduc 10, numerus residuus 24 est Epacta Gregoriana.
units.tr: 1. For example: when the lunar cycle is 2, the Julian epact is 22; subtract 10, and 12 remains, so 12 is the Gregorian epact. In this year of Christ 1667 the Julian epact is 15; take away 10, and 5 remains as the Gregorian epact. But in the year of Christ 1666 the lunar cycle was 14 and the Julian epact 4, which is less than 10; so you add 30 to it, making 34, and subtract 10 from that; the remaining number, 24, is the Gregorian epact.

units.la: 2. Ex Epactâ Juliana subduco 10, propterea quòd Gregorius pontifex, ut annum Julianum castigaret, mensi Octobri anno Christi 1582 dies 10 subduxit.
units.tr: 2. I subtract 10 from the Julian epact because Pope Gregory, to correct the Julian year, removed 10 days from the month of October in the year of Christ 1582.

units.la: 3. Hæc regula valebit tantùm ad annum Christi 1700 ineuntem incuntem, exinde enim usque ad annum 1900 ineuntem ex Epacta Juliana subtrahendum est 11, ut Gregorianam assequamur. Ex. gr. anno Christi 1730 cyclo solis 2 competit Epacta Juliana 22, aufer 11, restant 11. pro Epacta Gregoriana: Anno Christi 1848 cyclus Lunae est 6, Epacta Juliana 6, cui addas 30. e summa 36 deme 11. residuum 25 est Epacta Gregoriana istius anni; ab anno Christi 1900 ad 2200 ex Epacta Juliana 12 subducendum est. Et sic deinceps numerus subducendus unitate augendus est.
units.tr: 3. This rule holds only up to the beginning of the year of Christ 1700. From then until the beginning of 1900, 11 must be subtracted from the Julian epact to arrive at the Gregorian. For example, in the year of Christ 1730, the solar cycle 2 has Julian epact 22; take away 11, and 11 remains as the Gregorian epact. In the year of Christ 1848 the lunar cycle is 6 and the Julian epact 6, to which you add 30; from the sum, 36, take 11; the residue, 25, is the Gregorian epact of that year. From the year of Christ 1900 to 2200, 12 must be subtracted from the Julian epact, and so on, the number to be subtracted increasing by one each time.

units.la: XIV. Si dies quo novilunium committitur per Epactam computares, numero mensium a Martio inclusio addas Epactam anni currentis; summa si minor sit quam 20, ex 30 subducatur, si maior ex 60, & reliquus sit dies mensis propositi quo fiet novilunium.
units.tr: XIV. If you wish to compute the day on which the new moon falls by means of the epact, add the epact of the current year to the number of months counted from March inclusive. If the sum is less than 20, subtract it from 30; if greater, subtract it from 60. The remainder is the day of the proposed month on which the new moon occurs.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Hoc anno Christi 1667 Epacta est 15. Scire vellem in quotam Junii diem incidat novilunium. Junius est mensis quartus a Martio inclusive; Igitur ad Epactam 15 addo 4, summam 19 subtraho ex 30, residuum est 11. Ergo novilunium accidit Junii undecimo. Si scirem quota sit Luna die Junii 26, computo quot dies a novilunio usque ad propositum elapsi sunt, sunt autem 15, Ergo Junii 26 est Luna decima quinta; sive plenilunium.
units.tr: 1. For example: in this year of Christ 1667 the epact is 15. I want to know on which day of June the new moon falls. June is the fourth month counting from March inclusive; so I add 4 to the epact 15, and subtract the sum, 19, from 30. The remainder is 11. So the new moon falls on June 11. If I wanted to know what day of the moon June 26 is, I count how many days have elapsed from the new moon to the date proposed; there are 15. Therefore June 26 is the fifteenth day of the moon, that is, full moon.

units.la: 2. Si mense Januario vel Martio novilunium quaeratur, nihil ad Epactam anni addendum est. Mense Februario, ut & Aprili unitas tantum. Ut si diem Martii vel etiam Januarii cognoscerem quo Luna Soli conjungitur, hoc anno, ad Epactam 15 addo nihil: Nam ipsa Epacta diem ostendit. Epacta est 15, ergo die 15 Januarii vel Martii novilunium conficitur.
units.tr: 2. If the new moon is sought in January or March, nothing is to be added to the epact of the year; in February and April, only one. For example, if I wanted to know the day of March, or even January, on which the moon is conjoined with the sun, in this year I add nothing to the epact 15, since the epact itself shows the day. The epact is 15, therefore the new moon occurs on the 15th of January or March.

units.la: 3. Haec regula valet in annis Gregorianis aeque ac Julianis; dummodo Epactam Gregorianam Julianae loco adhibeas.
units.tr: 3. This rule holds for Gregorian years as well as Julian, provided you use the Gregorian epact in place of the Julian.

units.la: 4. Vulgaris aetatem Lunae per Epactas inveniendi methodus sic se habet. Si propositio die quolibet in anno Juliano quota sit Luna cognoscceres,hos tres numeros in unam summam colligas,Epactam anni currentis, numerum mensium à Martio inclusive, & diem mensis propositum: Summa è tribus hisce numeris collecta, si minor sit quàm 30, ipsa est ætas Lunæ, sin major ex eâ 30 subtrahatur, & numerus residuus ætatem Lunæ quæsitam ostendit. Ex. gr. Scirem quota sit Luna hoc anno Sept. 12. Epacta est 15, September à Martio 7, dies propositus 12, hos tres numeros 15, 7, 12, in unam summam colligo, quæ est 34, subtrahe 30, residuum est 4. Ergò Septembris duodecima est quarta à novilunio.
units.tr: 4. The common method of finding the age of the moon by means of the epacts is as follows. If you wish to know what age the moon is on a given day in the Julian year, add together three numbers into one sum: the epact of the current year, the number of months from March inclusive, and the day of the proposed month. If the sum of these three numbers is less than 30, it is the age of the moon; if greater, subtract 30 from it, and the remaining number shows the age of the moon sought. For example, I wish to know the age of the moon this year on September 12. The epact is 15, September is the seventh month from March, and the proposed day is 12. I add these three numbers, 15, 7 and 12, into one sum, which is 34; subtract 30, and the remainder is 4. Therefore September 12 is the fourth day after the new moon.

units.la: 5. Etiamsi ætas Lunæ per Epactas præcisè definiri nequit, hæc tamen methodus solido die nunquam aberrabit, adeò ut tutò satis vulgarem in usum adhibeatur.
units.tr: 5. Even though the age of the moon cannot be defined exactly by epacts, this method will never be wrong by a full day, so it may safely enough be used for ordinary purposes.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: De periodo Metonicâ & Calippicâ.
units.tr: On the Metonic and Callippic Period.
