units.la: Periodi sunt vel Ethnicæ vel Christianæ.
units.tr: Periods are either Gentile or Christian.

units.la: II. Periodi Ethnicæ sunt quæ ab Ethnicis instituuntur.
units.tr: II. Gentile periods are those instituted by the Gentiles.

units.la: III. Suntque Metonica & Calippica.
units.tr: III. These are the Metonic and the Callippic.

units.la: IV. Periodus Metonica est Systema annorum 19, quibus evolutis annum Atticum solari ad amussim convenire statuit Meton.
units.tr: IV. The Metonic period is a system of 19 years, after which Meton determined that the Attic year would agree exactly with the solar year.

units.la: 1. METON celeberrimus erat Athenien-sium Astronomus, qui annis plùs minùs 430 ante Christum natum floruit. Hic trieteridos, ut & ogdoeteridos ab Athenien-sibus institutæ errores deprehendens, aliam adinvenit periodum, putà Enneadecaeteridem sive annorum 19, quibus labentibus mensem Lunarem septies intercalavit, quâ ratione Lunarem eorum annum solares intra cardines exactissimè constitutum putavit. Enimvero solarem definivit annum dieb. 365. h. 6. 18'. 56''. 50'''. 31'''. 34''''. mensem Lunarem d. 29.h. 12. 45'. 47''. 26''. 48'''. 30''''. Annum Lunarem d. 354. h. 9. 11'. 29''. 21'''. 42'''. 0''''. unde annos Lunares 19 cum mensibus Embolimis 7, æquè ac annos solares 19 dies usque ad scrupulum 6940 colligere, atque ita annis 19 vertentibus Solis Lunæque motus quàm exactissimè concordare docuit.
units.tr: 1. Meton was a most celebrated astronomer of the Athenians, who flourished about 430 years, more or less, before the birth of Christ. He detected the errors both of the trieteris and of the ogdoeteris instituted by the Athenians, and devised another period, namely the enneadecaeteris, or a period of 19 years. In it, by intercalating a month seven times, he thought their lunar years were fixed most exactly within the limits of the solar year. He defined the solar year as 365 days, 6 hours, 18 minutes, 56 seconds, 50 thirds, 31 fourths and 34 fifths; the lunar month as 29 days, 12 hours, 45 minutes, 47 seconds, 26 thirds, 48 fourths and 30 fifths; and the lunar year as 354 days, 9 hours, 11 minutes, 29 seconds, 21 thirds, 42 fourths and 0 fifths. From this he showed how 19 lunar years with 7 embolismic months could be made to equal 19 solar years, in days, to the scruple, 6940, and so taught that as the 19 years run their course the motions of Sun and Moon agree as exactly as possible.

units.la: 2. Ab hâc Metonis periodo vulgaris cyclus Lunaris sive aureus numerus originem duxit, qui quidem cum eâ convenit, annorum numero, & Embolismorum situ, non item Epochâ, nec anni solaris nec Lunaris quantitate.
units.tr: 2. From this period of Meton the common lunar cycle, or golden number, took its origin. It agrees with it in the number of years and in the position of the embolismic months, but not in the epoch, nor in the length of either the solar or the lunar year.

units.la: 3. Hæc periodus à Censorino, aliisque Metoni auctori attribuitur, sed à Gemino Euclemon, Philippus, & Calippus institutores ejus perhibentur, Gemin. Elem. Astron. cap. 6.
units.tr: 3. This period is attributed by Censorinus and others to Meton as its author, but Geminus says that Euclemon, Philip and Callippus are reported to have been its institutors: Gemin. Elem. Astron. cap. 6.

units.la: V. Periodus Calippica quatuor Metonicis, sive annis 76 constat.
units.tr: V. The Callippic period consists of four Metonic periods, that is, of 76 years.

units.la: 1. Calippus post Metonem centum annis plùs minùs claruit. Hic anni præcipuè solaris quantitatem à Metone falsò constitutam assecutus, periodum Metonicam quater multiplicavit, atque ita novam instituit periodum annis 76 constantem, Calippicam ab eo vocatam.
units.tr: 1. Callippus flourished about a hundred years, more or less, after Meton. Chiefly by correcting the length of the solar year, which Meton had wrongly fixed, he multiplied the Metonic period four times and so instituted a new period of 76 years, called the Callippic after him.

units.la: 2. Hæc periodus ab Astronomis ut omnium exactissima recepta fuit, adeò ut ipse Ptolemæus eâ non rarò sit usus. Et Geminus loco prædicto ait, Καὶ ἀχῆ μάλιστα πάντων ἡ αὐτὴ περίοδος τῆς φαινομένης συμπτώσεως, Eadémque periodus apparentiis omnium maximè consonare videtur. Gem. ibid. VI. Periodus hæc Calippica cœpit anno per. Jul. 4384 solstitio æstivo.
units.tr: 2. This period was received by the astronomers as the most exact of all, so much so that Ptolemy himself often used it. Geminus, in the passage cited, says: "And the same period agrees most of all with the apparent conjunctions" [Καὶ ἀχῆ μάλιστα πάντων ἡ αὐτὴ περίοδος τῆς φαινομένης συμπτώσεως]. Gem. ibid. VI. This Callippic period began in the year 4384 of the Julian period, at the summer solstice.

units.la: VII. Ergò si propositio quovis anno per. Calippicæ annum per. Jul. ei congruentem haberes, periodos Calippicas completas in 76 ducas, numerum productum anno currenti auctum ad 4383 adjicias, aggregatum est annus per. Jul. quo quaesitus annus per. Calip. iniit circa solstitium æsti- vum.
units.tr: VII. Therefore, if you have a given year of the Callippic period and want the Julian year that corresponds to it, multiply the completed Callippic periods by 76, add the current year of the period to the product, and then add 4383. The sum is the Julian year in which the sought Callippic year begins, near the summer solstice.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Ptolemæus tradit Lunam defecisse τῷ λζ ἔτει τῆς πρίτης χαλ Καλίππου περιόδου, ὁ ἐτη χζ ἀπὸ Ναβονασάρου, καὶ Αἰγυπτίως τῷ ἰ ἐς τὴν γ Anno 37 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ, anno Nabonasari 507 secundum Ægyptios Tybi 2, sequente 3. Ptol. l. 6. p. 142. ed. gr. Hic annus erat 37 per.Calip. 3. duæ itaque periodi completæ sunt, & tertia fluit. Quocirca multiplicees 2 in 76, productum 152 anno propositio currentis periodi, puta 37 augeas, summam 189 ad 4383 addas, aggregatum 4572 est annus per. Jul. quo currente, annus per. Calip. quæsitus init, exiit igitur anno per. Jul. 4573 circa solstitium æstivum, à quo anni Attici numerantur.
units.tr: 1. For example, Ptolemy relates that the Moon was eclipsed in the 37th year of the third period of Callippus [τῷ λζ ἔτει τῆς τρίτης καὶ Καλίππου περιόδου], in the 507th year of Nabonassar, according to the Egyptians on the second of Tybi, the following day being the third. Ptol. l. 6, p. 142, Greek ed. This year was the 37th of the third Callippic period. Two periods are therefore complete, and a third is running. So multiply 2 by 76, giving 152; add the current year 37, giving 189; add 4383, giving 4572. This is the Julian year in which the Callippic year began. It follows that the Callippic year 37 began in Julian year 4573, near the summer solstice, from which the Attic years are counted.

units.la: VIII. Si è contra periodum Julianam ad Calippicam reduceres, ex anno propositio per. Jul. subtrahe 4383, residuum per 76 divisum in quoto dabit periodos Calippicas jam elapsas, in residuo annum periodi currentis quæsitum.
units.tr: VIII. If on the contrary you wish to reduce a Julian year to the Callippic period, subtract 4383 from the proposed Julian year. The remainder divided by 76 gives in the quotient the Callippic periods already elapsed, and in the remainder the sought year of the current period.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. proponatur annus prædictus per. Jul. 4572, ut eruamus quotus annus per. Calip. in eum conveniat. Igitur ex 4572 aufer 4383, residuum 189 per 76 divisum in quoto dat 2, in residuo 37. Ergò anno per. Jul. 4572 annus 37 tertiæ per. Calip. iniit.
units.tr: 1. For example, let the aforesaid Julian year 4572 be proposed, so that we may find which Callippic year it corresponds to. From 4572 take away 4383; the remainder 189, divided by 76, gives 2 in the quotient and 37 in the remainder. Therefore in the Julian year 4572 the 37th year of the third Callippic period began.

units.la: 2. Annus quo hæc scribo est per. Jul. 6380, aufer 4383 residuum 1997 per 76 distributum, in quoto dat 26, in residuo 21. Est igitur hic annus 21 per.Calippicæ 27. iniens circa solstitium æstivum.
units.tr: 2. The year in which I am writing this is Julian 6380. Take away 4383; the remainder 1997, divided by 76, gives 26 in the quotient and 21 in the remainder. So this year is the 21st year of the 27th Callippic period, beginning near the summer solstice.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: De periodo Dionysiana..
units.tr: On the Dionysian period.

units.la: Periodi Christianæ sunt quæ à Christianis sunt instituta. II. Súntque duæ, Dyonysiana & Juliana.
units.tr: Christian periods are those that were instituted by Christians. II. There are two: the Dionysian and the Julian.

units.la: I. IN hâc periodorum Christianarum divisione Cyrilliam à Cyrillo institutam omitto, quæ quinque cyclis Lunaribus sive annis 95 constabat. Hæc enim Chronologum exerceat, sed temporibus distinguendis nihil conducit. Quin etiam ipse Cyrillus eam è majori Theophili cyclo annorum 427 formavit. Sed deprehensis harum periodorum, viz. 437 & 95 annorum erroribus, in earum locum alia tandem institu​ta fuit, quam Dionysianam nuncupamus.
units.tr: I. In this division of the Christian periods I omit the Cyrillian period, instituted by Cyril, which consisted of five lunar cycles, or 95 years. It occupies the chronologer, but it contributes nothing to distinguishing times. Indeed, Cyril himself formed it from the greater cycle of Theophilus, of 427 years. But when the errors of these periods, namely of 437 and of 95 years, were detected, other periods were at last instituted in their place, which we call the Dionysian.

units.la: III. Periodus Dionysiana est series annorum 532, è cyclo solari in Lunarem, hoc est 28 in 19, multiplicato contexta, quâ peracta iidem cycli solis & Lunæ iisdem annis itemum concurrunt.
units.tr: III. The Dionysian period is a series of 532 years, formed by multiplying the solar cycle into the lunar cycle, that is, 28 into 19; when it is completed, the same cycles of the sun and moon coincide again in the same years.

units.la: 1. Hæc periodus Dionysiana vulgò nuncupatur, tanquam à Dionysio exiguo concinnata, quamvis non desunt qui Victorium Aquitanum eam instituisse tradunt, unde & Victoriana nonnunquam audit.
units.tr: 1. This period is commonly called the Dionysian, as if it had been devised by Dionysius Exiguus, although there are not lacking those who report that Victorius of Aquitaine instituted it, whence it is sometimes also called the Victorian.

units.la: 2. Conflatur hæc periodus ex cyclis Solis & Lunæ in se ductis. Nam si 28 in 19 multiplices, productum est 532. Adeò ut primo anno hujus periodi cyclus Solis sit 1, & cyclus Lunæ itidem 1. Anno secundo cyclus Solis 2, & cyclus Lunæ 2, & sic deinceps, anno vigesimo cyclus solis 20, Lunæ 1. Et per totum hujus periodi contextum hi cycli eundem in annum iterum non convenient, usque dum tota fit evoluta, & de novo incipiat.
units.tr: 2. This period is made up of the cycles of the Sun and Moon multiplied together. For if you multiply 28 by 19, the product is 532. So that in the first year of this period the solar cycle is 1 and the lunar cycle likewise 1; in the second year the solar cycle is 2 and the lunar cycle 2; and so on, so that in the twentieth year the solar cycle is 20 and the lunar 1. And throughout the whole course of this period these cycles do not agree again in the same year until the whole period has run its course and begins anew.

units.la: IV. Si proposito anno quolibet hujus periodi cyclum Solis & Lunæ in eum Concurrentes invenires, annum propositum dividas per 28, & per 19, residuum prioris divifionis est cyclus Solis, posterioris cyclus Lunæ, vel fi nihil supererit, cyclus Solis est 28, Lunæ 19.
units.tr: IV. If for any year of this period you wish to find the cycles of the Sun and Moon, and the year in which they coincide, divide the given year by 28 and by 19; the remainder of the first division is the solar cycle, and of the second the lunar cycle; or if nothing is left over, the solar cycle is 28 and the lunar 19.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Proponatur annus hujus periodi 326 ut ejus cyclos inveniam, 326 distribuo per 28, residuum 18 est cyclus solis, deinde 326 divido etiam per 19, & residuum 3 est cyclus Lunæ isti anno competens. Sic annus hujus periodi 143 per 28 divisus relinquit 3, per 19 distributus refiduum facit 10, ergò cyclus solis est 3, & Lunæ 10.
units.tr: 1. For example, let the year 326 of this period be proposed, so that I may find its cycles. I divide 326 by 28, and the remainder 18 is the solar cycle; then I also divide 326 by 19, and the remainder 3 is the lunar cycle belonging to that year. So too the year 143 of this period, divided by 28, leaves 3, and divided by 19 the remainder is 10; therefore the solar cycle is 3 and the lunar 10.

units.la: V. Si propositis cyclis quibusvis Solis & Lunæ, annum periodi Dionyfianæ tenerés in quem conveniunt, cyclum Solis datum multiplices in 57, & cyclum Lunæ datum in 476, productorum summa divisa per 532 residuum faciet annum quæsitum.
units.tr: V. If, given any cycles of the Sun and Moon, you wish to find the year of the Dionysian period in which they coincide, multiply the given solar cycle by 57 and the given lunar cycle by 476; the sum of the products, divided by 532, leaves a remainder which is the year sought.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Proponantur cyclus Solis 18, & Lunæ 3, ut annum per. Dionyfianæ eruamus in quem hi duo cycli confluunt, primò cyclum Solis 18 multiplicamus in 57; & productum 1026 reservamus, deinde cyclum Lunæ datum 3, multiplicamus in 476 & producto 1428 addimus productum prioris multiplicationis reservatum, summa 2454 per 532 divisa residuum facit 326, ergò annus periodi Dionyfianæ quæsitus est 326, ut qui per 28 divisus relinquit 18, per 19 divisus residuum facit 3.
units.tr: 1. For example, let the solar cycle 18 and the lunar cycle 3 be given, so that we may find the year of the Dionysian period in which these two cycles meet. First I multiply the solar cycle 18 by 57, and I keep the product 1026; then I multiply the given lunar cycle 3 by 476, and to the product 1428 I add the reserved product of the first multiplication, making the sum 2454. Divided by 532, this leaves 326, so the year of the Dionysian period sought is 326, which, divided by 28, leaves 18, and divided by 19 leaves 3.

units.la: 2. Aliud exemplum: Cyclus solis datus fit 3, Lunæ 10, cyclus Solis 3 in 57 ductus producit 171, cyclus Lunæ 10 in 476 ductus producit 4760, cui addas 171, summa est 4931, quæ per 532 divisa reliquum facit 143. Ergò annus quæsitus est periodi Dionyfianæ 143.
units.tr: 2. Another example: let the given solar cycle be 3 and the lunar cycle 10. The solar cycle 3 multiplied by 57 gives 171; the lunar cycle 10 multiplied by 476 gives 4760; add 171 to this, and the sum is 4931, which divided by 532 leaves 143. Therefore the year sought of the Dionysian period is 143.

units.la: Hanc annum periodi Dionyfianæ ex datis cyclis Solis & Lunæ inveniendi methodum à nobis institutam, alibi Deo volente demonstratam, dabimus.
units.tr: We shall give the method, which I have instituted for finding the year of the Dionysian period from the given cycles of the Sun and Moon, and which I shall demonstrate elsewhere, God willing.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: De Periodo Juliana.
units.tr: On the Julian Period.

units.la: Periodus Juliana est series annorum 7980, ex indictione 15 in periodum Dionysianam 532 multiplicatâ productâ, quâ solùm evolutâ iidem cycli Solis, Lunæ & indictionis in eundem annum iterum congrediuntur.
units.tr: The Julian Period is a series of 7980 years, formed by multiplying the indiction cycle of 15 by the Dionysian period of 532, and when this series has run its course the same cycles of the Sun, the Moon and the indiction come together again in the same year.

units.la: 1. EGregiam hanc periodum quâ nihil unquam in Chronologiâ præstantius inventum fuit, Josepho Scaligero acceptam habemus. Hic enim animadvertens quantùm conducunt Cyclus Solis, & Lunæ; & Indictiones ad annum unum ab aliis quibuscunque secernendum, istos tres cyclos in se invicem multiplicavit, primò quidem cyclum Solis 28 in cyclum Lunæ 19, & productum 532 in Indictionem 15, duxit, cujus productum 7980 periodum Julianam nominavit, propterea quòd annis Julianis accommodatur.
units.tr: 1. We have received this outstanding period, the most excellent thing ever discovered in chronology, from Joseph Scaliger. For he saw how greatly the cycles of the Sun and Moon and the indictions help to distinguish one year from all others. He multiplied these three cycles together: first he multiplied the cycle of the Sun, 28, by the cycle of the Moon, 19, and then multiplied the product, 532, by the indiction, 15. The product, 7980, he named the Julian period, because it is adapted to Julian years.

units.la: 2. Maxima hujus periodi præstantia in eo consistit, quòd per totum ejus contextum quilibet annus propriis suis cyclis gaudet, quos omnes nullus alius sibi vendicare potest. Ex. gr. Primus annus cyclo Solis 1, cyclo Lunæ 1, & Indictione 1 præditus est. Et nullus alius annus per totam periodum omnes eosdem cyclos possidebit, usque dum tota fit peracta. Sic annus hujus periodi 4714, cui primus Æræ Christianæ respondet, cyclum Solis habuit 10, Lunæ 2, Indictionem 4, omnes qui cycli nullum in alium convenient annum, nisi post annos 7980 expletos; unde iste annus ab omnibus aliis tam retrò quàm posteà putatis certissimis characteribus distinguitur. Idem de omnibus, per totam hanc periodum, annis statuendum est; adeò ut utilitates hujus periodi in temporibus distinguendis opinionem superant. Et hinc est quòd nos per totas hasce Institutiones Chronologicas hujus periodi toties mentionem facimus, utpote quæ infallibilis est temporum character.
units.tr: 2. The great value of this period lies in this, that throughout its whole course every year has its own cycles, which no other year can claim. For example, the first year has the cycle of the Sun 1, the cycle of the Moon 1 and the indiction 1. And no other year in the whole period will have all these same cycles until the whole period is completed. Thus the year 4714 of this period, to which the first year of the Christian Era corresponds, had the cycle of the Sun 10, the cycle of the Moon 2 and the indiction 4. These cycles do not agree with any other year except after the 7980 years are complete. Hence this year is distinguished from all other years, both earlier and later, by marks that are most certain. The same must be said of every year throughout this whole period, so that the usefulness of this period in distinguishing times exceeds its reputation. And for this reason we make mention of this period so often throughout these Chronological Institutions, since it is an infallible mark of time.

units.la: II. Si dato anno Æræ Christianæ annum per Jul. ei respondentem desideres, anno Christi proposito addas 7143, summa est annus per Jul. quæsitus. 4713
units.tr: II. If, given a year of the Christian Era, you wish to know the year of the Julian period that corresponds to it, add 4713 to the proposed year of Christ; the sum is the year of the Julian period sought. 4713

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Hic est annus Christi 1667, addes 4713, summa est 6380. Igitur annus Christi 1667 est annus per Jul. 6380. Annis Christi addimus 4713, eò quòd Æra Christiana coepit anno per. Jul. 4714, adeò ut anni 4713 jam expleti suerunt.
units.tr: 1. For example. Here is the year of Christ 1667. Add 4713; the sum is 6380. Therefore the year of Christ 1667 is the year 6380 of the Julian period. We add 4713 to the years of Christ because the Christian Era began in the year 4714 of the Julian period, so that the 4713 years have already been completed.

units.la: III. Si è contrà ex anno per. Jul. annum Christi erueres, aufer 4713, & reliquus fit annus Christi.
units.tr: III. If conversely you wish to draw the year of Christ from a year of the Julian period, subtract 4713, and what remains is the year of Christ.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Hic est annus, ut dictum est, per Jul. 6380 aufer 4713, residuum est 1667. Ergò annus Christi 1667, jam fluit unà cum anno per. Jul. 6380.
units.tr: 1. For example. Here is the year 6380 of the Julian period, as was said. Subtract 4713; the remainder is 1667. Therefore the year of Christ 1667 is running together with the year 6380 of the Julian period.

units.la: IV. Si ex anno per. Jul. Æram Christianam antecedenti dato, quot ad istam Æram supersunt anni cognoscere, annum datum deduc è 4714, & reliqui sunt anni quæsiti.
units.tr: IV. If from a given year of the Julian period you wish to know how many years remain before the Christian Era, subtract the given year from 4714, and the remainder is the years sought.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Olympiades computantur ab anno per. Jul. 3939. Aufer 3939 ex 4714, restant 776. Olympiades itaque numerari coeperant anno 776 ante Æram Christianam.
units.tr: 1. For example, the Olympiads are reckoned from the year 3939 of the Julian period. Subtract 3939 from 4714; 776 remain. Therefore the Olympiads began to be counted in the year 776 before the Christian Era.

units.la: V. Si dato quovis anno per. Jul. cyclos ejus solis, Lunæ, & Indictionis invenires, annum datum per 28; per 19, & per 15 partiaris, prima divisionis residuum est cyclus Solis, secundæ cyclus Lunæ, tertiæ Indictio, sive cyclus Indictionis; vel si nihil supererit 28 est cyclus Solis, 19 cyclus Lunæ, & 15 Indictio.
units.tr: V. If, given any year of the Julian period, you wish to find its cycles of the Sun, the Moon and the indiction, divide the year by 28, by 19 and by 15. The remainder of the first division is the cycle of the Sun, of the second the cycle of the Moon, and of the third the indiction, or cycle of the indiction; or if nothing remains, 28 is the cycle of the Sun, 19 the cycle of the Moon, and 15 the indiction.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Annus hic per. Jul. 6380 per 28 divisus relinquit 24, per 19 distributus residuum facit 15, per 15 divisus relinquit 5, ergò 24 est cyclus Solis, 15 cyclus Lunæ, & 5 Indictio Romana. At annus ultimus per. Jul. sive 7980 per hosce numeros divisus nihil relinquit, ergo 28 est cyclus Solis, 19 cyclus Lunæ, & 15 Indictio.
units.tr: 1. For example. This year 6380 of the Julian period, divided by 28, leaves 24; divided by 19, the remainder is 15; divided by 15, it leaves 5. Therefore 24 is the cycle of the Sun, 15 the cycle of the Moon, and 5 the Roman indiction. But the last year of the Julian period, that is 7980, divided by these numbers leaves nothing; therefore 28 is the cycle of the Sun, 19 the cycle of the Moon, and 15 the indiction.

units.la: VI. Si datis cyclis Solis, Lunæ, & Indictionis annum Periodi Juliane quaris in quem conveniunt, Multiplica Cyclum { Solis / Lunæ / Indictionis } in 4845 / 4200 / 6916
units.tr: VI. If, given the cycles of the Sun, the Moon and the indiction, you seek the year of the Julian Period to which they belong, multiply the cycle of the { Sun / Moon / Indiction } by 4845 / 4200 / 6916.

units.la: Summam productorum dividas per 7980, & residuus fiet annus periodi Juliane quæsitus datis cyclis præditus.
units.tr: Divide the sum of the products by 7980, and the remainder will be the year of the Julian period sought, having the given cycles.

units.la: Ex. gr. Proponantur cyclus Solis 18, Lunæ 3, Indictio 6, ut annum periodi Juliane investigemus ad quem pertinent, cyclum Solis 18 multiplicamus in 4845, & producto 87210 reservato, multiplicamus cyclum Lunæ 3 in 4200, & producto 12600 etiam reservato, multiplicamus Indictionem 6 in 6916, & producto 41496 addimus duo priora producta reservata. 87210 12600 41496 141306
units.tr: For example, let the cycle of the Sun be 18, the cycle of the Moon 3, and the indiction 6, so that we may find the year of the Julian period to which they belong. We multiply the cycle of the Sun 18 by 4845, and, keeping the product 87210, we multiply the cycle of the Moon 3 by 4200, and keep the product 12600 also; we multiply the indiction 6 by 6916, and add the product 41496 to the two earlier products kept. 87210 12600 41496 141306

units.la: Hæc productorum summa 141306 divisa per 7980 residuum est 5646, qui est annus periodi Julianæ ad quem dati cycli pertinent.
units.tr: This sum of the products, 141306, divided by 7980, leaves 5646, which is the year of the Julian period to which the given cycles belong.

units.la: Aliud exemplum: Anno hoc Christi 1668, quo hæc meditor, cyclus solis est 25, cyclus Lunæ 16, Indictio 6. Equibus datis annus per Jul. sic invenitur. Cyclus Solis 25 × 4845 = 121125 Lunæ 16 in 4200 producit 67200 Indictio 6 × 6916 = 41496 Summa 229821
units.tr: Another example. In this year of Christ 1668, in which I am writing these things, the cycle of the Sun is 25, the cycle of the Moon 16, and the indiction 6. With these given, the year of the Julian period is found thus: cycle of the Sun 25 × 4845 = 121125; Moon 16 in 4200 gives 67200; indiction 6 × 6916 = 41496; sum 229821.

units.la: Hæc summa 229821 per 7980 divisa, residuum facit 6381, Præsens ergo annus, ut datis cyclis præditus, est periodi Julianæ 6381.
units.tr: This sum, 229821, divided by 7980, leaves 6381. The present year, therefore, having these cycles, is year 6381 of the Julian period.

units.la: Hæc methodus annum periodi Julianæ ex datis cyclis Solis, Lunæ & Indictionis inveniendi ab aliis non ita pridem inventa, à nobis alibi demonstratur.
units.tr: This method of finding the year of the Julian period from the given cycles of the Sun, the Moon and the indiction was discovered not long ago by others, and is demonstrated by us elsewhere.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: De Æra Christiana & Diocletiana.
units.tr: On the Christian and Diocletianic Eras.

units.la: Hactenus de characteribus temporum institutis, qui in orbem redeunt, actum est, sequuntur Fixi.
units.tr: So far we have dealt with the characters of time that were instituted and return in a cycle. Next come the fixed ones.

units.la: II. Characteres fixi sunt, quorum capita certis quibusdam annis fixa manent & immota; quales sunt Æra sive Epochæ.
units.tr: II. Fixed characters are those whose beginnings remain fixed and unmoved at certain set years. Such are the eras, or epochs.

units.la: FIxos hujusmodi Characteres Græci Ἐπόχας Terminos vocant, idcirco quòd illis sistantur ac terminentur temporum intervalla, & ab iis tanquam à terminis anni sequentes computentur. Arabibus Tarich idem denotat, à verbo Arach, quod in secundâ conjugatione, Adscripto tempore notare significat; cui non multùm dissonat Latinum vocabulum Æra, sive Era, ut subinde scribitur.
units.tr: Greeks call such fixed characters epochs [Ἐπόχας], that is, termini, because the intervals of time are halted and bounded by them, and the following years are counted from them as from termini. For the Arabs, tarich [Tarich] means the same, from the verb arach [Arach], which in the second conjugation means to note by an assigned time. The Latin word aera, or era, as it is sometimes written, does not differ much from this.

units.la: III. Æra sunt vel Christianæ, vel Judaicæ, vel Ethnicæ, vel Muhammedicæ.
units.tr: III. Eras are either Christian, or Jewish, or Ethnic, or Muhammedan.

units.la: I. Nulla est gens tam fera, nulla tàm barbara quæ non aliquem admittit Deum, eundémque aliquali religione excipiat. Sed, proh dolor! Tanta est hominum Vesania, ut olim præsertim, tot propemodùm religiones, quot regiones erant: quæ tamen omnes ad hasce quatuor revocentur, Christianam scilicet, Judaicam, Ethnicam & Muhammedicam. Et quoniam nonnulli omnium harum religionum excultores, sua ediderunt Chronica, Chronologi inprimis interest omnes omnium eorum Epochas ad unguem habere, ut in quemcunque incidat historicum, tempora ab eo descripta recte distinguat. Et hinc oritur nostra Epocharum divisio, quarum singulas, Deo volente, cum situ suo in periodo Juliana, cyclo Solis, cyclo Lunæ & Indictione describam; ut initium earum certissimis characteribus distinguatur.
units.tr: I. There is no nation so savage, none so barbarous, that does not acknowledge some God and worship him with some religion. But, alas, such is the madness of men that in former times especially there were almost as many religions as regions. Yet all of them can be traced back to these four: the Christian, the Jewish, the Ethnic, and the Muhammedan. And since some adherents of all these religions have published their chronicles, it is of the greatest concern to the chronologer to know all the eras of all of them exactly, so that whatever historian he comes upon, he may correctly distinguish the times described by him. Hence arises our division of the eras, each of which, God willing, I will describe with its position in the Julian period, the cycle of the Sun, the cycle of the Moon, and the indiction, so that its beginning may be distinguished by the most certain marks.

units.la: IV. Æra Christiana vel ab ipsius Christi Nativitate, vel ab imperatore Diocletiano, vel à mundi primordio deducuntur.
units.tr: IV. Christian eras are derived either from the Nativity of Christ himself, or from the emperor Diocletian, or from the beginning of the world.

units.la: V. Æra à Christi Nativitate computata, quæ καὶ ἐξοχὴν Christiana vocatur, cœpit Kal. Januariis anno per Jul. 4714, cyclo Solis 10, cyclo Lunæ 2, Indictione 4.
units.tr: V. The era reckoned from the Nativity of Christ, which is called Christian par excellence [καὶ ἐξοχὴν], began on 1 January in the year 4714 of the Julian period, cycle of the Sun 10, cycle of the Moon 2, indiction 4.

units.la: 1. De verâ Christi sospitatoris nostri Nativitate vehementer inter Chronologos agitatur controversia. Nonnulli biennio, alii quadriennio, nec desunt qui quinquennio natalem ejus ante vulgarem Epocham accidisse contendunt. Sed non nostri est propositi in institutionibus hisce Chronologicis in arenam descendere, nec quidem Chronologi multum refert, quonam anno natus fuit Christus, dummodo de Epochâ ab ejus Nativitate vulgò deductâ certus fiat. De hâc autem inter omnes convenit, atque in controversiam vocari nequit. Quis enim non novit annum hunc vulgaris Æræ Christianæ 1667 esse per Jul. 6380? Aufer 1667 ex 6380, restant 4713. Anni igitur 4713 de periodo Juliana elapsi sunt, priusquam Æra hæc Christiana cœpit. Cœpit ergò anno ejusdem periodi 4714 ineunte.
units.tr: 1. About the true birth of Christ our Saviour there is a fierce controversy among chronologers. Some hold that he was born two years earlier, others four, and there are not lacking those who contend that his birth fell five years before the common era. But it is not my purpose in these chronological institutes to enter this arena, nor indeed does it matter much to the chronologer in what year Christ was born, provided he is certain about the era commonly reckoned from his Nativity. About this, however, all agree, and it cannot be called into question. For who does not know that the year 1667 of the common Christian era is 6380 of the Julian period? Take 1667 from 6380, and 4713 remain. So 4713 years of the Julian period had elapsed before this Christian era began. It therefore began at the start of year 4714 of that period.

units.la: 2. Æræ hujusce Christianæ institutor Dionysius perhibetur cognómento Exiguus (à quo & Æra Dionysiana nonnunquam dicitur) qui Justiniano imperante, annis post Christum natum plus minùs 530 florint. Hucusque enim ipsi etiam Christiani in annis supputandis Ethnicorum Epochis contenti fuerunt; exceptis Ægyptiis qui post tres circiter annorum centurias à Christo nato computatas Æram Dioclatianeam sibi propriam habuerunt; de quâ postea. Et juxta eandem quidem Æram Dioclatianeam Cyrillus cyclum suum 95 annorum instituit, primum suum cyclum ab anno Diocletiani 153 incipiens, & ultimum in 247 terminans: ut ipse scribit Dionysius, addens præterea, Nos à 248 anno ejusdem tyranni potius quàm principis inchoanter, noluimus circulis nostris memoriam impii & persecutoris innectere, sed magis elegimus ab incarnatione Domini nostri Jesu Christi annorum tempora prænotare, quatenus exordium spei nostræ notius nobis existeret, & causa reparationis humanæ, i. e. passio redemptoris nostri evidentius eluceret. Dionys. Exig. Epist. 1 Dionysius ergo Exiguus Epocham hanc à Christi Nativitate deductam primus instituit; sed paulò aliter quàm hodie usitatur. Vulgaris enim Epocha quæ hodie in usu est supponit Christum natum anno per. Jul. 4713, cyclo Solis 9, Lunæ 1, Indict. 3; & circumcisum Kal. Januariis anno sequente cyclo Solis 10, Lunæ 2, Indict. 4, & ab hujus circumcisionis die Epocha nostra computatur, ut anni Juliani primo. Dionysius autem Exiguus cyclum suum decemnovalem ab aureo numero 19 auspicatus est, & primum Æræ hujusce annum in secundo istius cycli collocavit; qui igitur aureo numero 1. præditus fuit, atque ideò annus hic erat periodi Julianæ 4713, cui aureus iste numerus 1 competit, non 4714 ut qui aureo numero 2 insignitus est.
units.tr: 2. The founder of this Christian era is said to be Dionysius, surnamed Exiguus (from whom it is sometimes called the Dionysian era), who flourished under the emperor Justinian, about 530 years after the birth of Christ. For up to that time even Christians themselves were content to reckon years by the eras of the Gentiles, except the Egyptians, who, after about three centuries had been counted from the birth of Christ, had their own Diocletianic era, of which more later. And indeed according to that same Diocletianic era Cyril established his cycle of 95 years, beginning his first cycle from year 153 of Diocletian and ending the last at 247, as Dionysius himself writes, adding: We, beginning from the 248th year of that tyrant rather than of the prince, have been unwilling to attach the memory of an impious persecutor to our cycles, but have rather chosen to note the years from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the beginning of our hope might be better known to us, and the cause of human restoration, that is, the passion of our Redeemer, might shine more clearly. Dionysius Exiguus, Epist. 1. Dionysius Exiguus therefore was the first to institute this era derived from the birth of Christ, but somewhat differently from what is used today. For the common era now in use supposes that Christ was born in the year 4713 of the Julian period, cycle of the Sun 9, Moon 1, indiction 3, and was circumcised on 1 January of the following year, cycle of the Sun 10, Moon 2, indiction 4; and from the day of this circumcision our era is counted, so that it is the first year of the Julian era. Dionysius Exiguus, however, began his nineteen-year cycle from golden number 19 and placed the first year of this era in the second of that cycle. So this year had golden number 1, and so was the year 4713 of the Julian period, to which golden number 1 belongs, not 4714, which is marked with golden number 2.

units.la: 3. Sed ut ut fit, usus à Bedâ introductus olim obtinuit, & etiamnum valet, ut Æræ hujus annos ab anno per. Jul 4714 cyclis prædictis notato ineunte numeremus. Et quoniam hic annus cyclis istis insignitus est, hinc ad cyclum Solis inveniendum anno Christi currenti addimus 9, ad aureum numerum 1, ad Indictionem 3, propterea quòd anni cycli Solaris 9, Lunaris 1, Indictionis 3 effluxissent, cùm vulgaris hæc Æra coepit à Christi Nativitate computata; ut in capitibus de istis cyclis dictum est. Quomodo autem anni per. Jul. ad annos hujus Æræ, & è contrà anni hujus Æræ ad annos per. Julianæ revocentur, capite præcedenti demonstratum est.
units.tr: 3. But however it may be, the usage introduced by Bede has long prevailed, and still holds, that we count the years of this era from the beginning of year 4714 of the Julian period, marked with the aforesaid cycles. And since this year is marked with these cycles, to find the cycle of the Sun for the current year of Christ we add 9, to find the golden number we add 1, and to find the indiction we add 3. This is because the years of the solar cycle 9, lunar 1, and indiction 3 had run out when this common era, reckoned from the Nativity of Christ, began, as was said in the chapters on those cycles. How the years of the Julian period are converted to the years of this era, and conversely the years of this era to those of the Julian period, was demonstrated in the preceding chapter.

units.la: VI. Æra ab imperatore Diocletiano deducta cœpit Aug. 29. anno Æræ Christianæ 284 per Jul. 4997, cyclo Solis 13, Lunæ 19, indict. 2.
units.tr: VI. The era derived from the emperor Diocletian began on August 29 in the year of the Christian era 284, which is Julian period 4997, solar cycle 13, lunar cycle 19, indiction 2.

units.la: 1. Diocletianus unà cùm Maximiano rerum Romanarum potitus, sub imperii finem diras in Christianos persecutiones exercuit, usque adeò ut multa Christianorum millia martyrio subjecit. Et quoniam truculenta hæc persecutio, in Ægypto gravissimè grassata fuit, superstites ibi Christiani in fratrum suorum memoriâ, qui gloriosissimâ Christi causâ barbarû istud passi sunt Martyriû, annos suos ab isto tempore computabant, quo primo Diocletianus iste ad imperiû provectus est, quod incidit in annû Æræ Christ. 284.
units.tr: 1. Diocletian, who shared the government of Roman affairs with Maximian, carried out savage persecutions against the Christians toward the end of his reign, so much so that he subjected many thousands of Christians to martyrdom. Since this brutal persecution raged most severely in Egypt, the Christians who survived there, in memory of their brothers who suffered that barbarous martyrdom for the most glorious cause of Christ, counted their years from the time when this Diocletian was first raised to the throne. That fell in the year of the Christian era 284.

units.la: 2. Hæc Æra sic instituta ab impio Martyrii istius auctore vocatur Diocletianea, ab ipsis Martyribus, Æra Martyrum, à regione quâ usitata fuit Arabicè Tarich Elkuphti Æra Ægyptiorum nuncupatur.
units.tr: 2. This era, thus established by the impious author of that martyrdom, is called Diocletianea. The martyrs themselves called it the Era of the Martyrs, and from the region where it was in use it is called in Arabic Tarich Elkuphti, the Era of the Egyptians.

units.la: 3. Hujus Æræ frequens apud veteres scriptores occurrit mentio, ac usus, ut apud Epiphanium, Ambrosium, Evagrium, Bedam, Hermannum Contractum, item apud Theonem in magnam Ptolemæi syntaxin Μεγαλη συνταξις, auctorem, Eutychium annalium Alexandrinorum, & Elmacinum historiæ Saraceniræ conditorem, ut & nonnunquam in Actis Conciliorum. Et Ægyptiis quidem Christianis vulgari in usu fuit non secus ac nobis Æra Christiana, usque dum Dionysius Exiguus Æram Christianam introduxisset, hoc est, annis circiter 249. verùm post annum Christi 532, extinctâ hâc Æra Christiana locum ejus occupavit, ab ipsis Ægyptiis non minùs quàm cæteris Christianis usitata.
units.tr: 3. This era is frequently mentioned and used by the ancient writers, as by Epiphanius, Ambrose, Evagrius, Bede and Hermannus Contractus; likewise by Theon in his commentary on Ptolemy's great syntaxis, Μεγαλη συνταξις [Megale syntaxis]; by Eutychius, author of the Alexandrian annals; by Elmacinus, founder of the history of the Saracens; and sometimes in the Acts of the Councils. Among the Christian Egyptians it was in common use, no less than the Christian era is for us, until Dionysius Exiguus introduced the Christian era, that is, about 249 years later. But after the year of Christ 532, when this Christian era had been extinguished, the Diocletianic era took its place, used by the Egyptians no less than by other Christians.

units.la: 4. Æthiopes autem in computis Ecclesiasticis hâc Æra Diocletianeâ (quam Annos Gratiæ vocant) etiamnum utuntur, sed in periodos Dionysianas distributa. Nam primum annum periodi Dionysianæ à primo Diocletianeo computant, sed expletâ annorum 532 serie, non ab initio Diocletiani rursùm incipiunt, sed ab initio periodi Dionysianæ secundæ: ut annum 534 non vocant annum Æræ Diocletianeæ 534, sed annum Gratiæ secundum, propterea quòd secundus est annus secundæ periodi. Sic hunc annum Christi 1667 qui est Æræ Diocletianeæ 1384 Æthiopes appellant annum Gratiæ 320, ut trecentesimum vigesimum tertiæ periodi; nam aufer duas periodos Dionysianas ex 1384, residuum est 320.
units.tr: 4. The Ethiopians, however, still use this Diocletianic era in their ecclesiastical reckonings (which they call the Years of Grace), but distributed into Dionysian periods. For they reckon the first year of a Dionysian period from the first Diocletianic year; but when the series of 532 years is complete, they do not start again from the beginning of Diocletian's era, but from the beginning of the second Dionysian period. So they do not call the year 534 the year 534 of the Diocletianic era, but the second year of Grace, because it is the second year of the second period. Thus they call this year of Christ 1667, which is the year 1384 of the Diocletianic era, the year of Grace 320, as the three hundred and twentieth of the third period; for if you take two Dionysian periods away from 1384, the remainder is 320.

units.la: 5. Hoc autem computo in rebus tantùm Ecclesiasticis usi videntur Æthiopes, in politicis Æra Christianâ; ex eo quòd Claudius Rex Æthiopiæ fidei suæ confessione anno à Christi Nativitate 1554 signat, qui erat annus gratiæ 207.
units.tr: 5. The Ethiopians seem to use this reckoning only in ecclesiastical matters, and the Christian era in civil ones. This is shown by the fact that Claudius, King of Ethiopia, dates his confession of faith in the year 1554 from the Nativity of Christ, which was the year of Grace 207.

units.la: VII. Si proposito anno Æræ Diocletianeæ, annum Christi ei congruentem invenires, ad annum Diocletiani curren- tem adjice 283, summa est annus Christi quæsitus.
units.tr: VII. If you found the year of Christ corresponding to a proposed year of the Diocletianic era, add 283 to the current year of Diocletian; the sum is the year of Christ sought.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Divus Ambrosius ait, Rursus nonagesimo & tertio à die imperii Diocletiani, cùm incidisset quarta decima Luna in quartam decimam diem Pharmutii mensis, quæ est quarto Idus Aprilis, quæ erat Dominicâ die, celebratum est pascha Dominicâ Pharmutii vigesimo & primo die qui fuit secundum nos sexto decimo Kalendas Maii, Ambrof. Epist. l. 10. ep. 83. Si in hunc patris locum incidens annum Diocletiani 93 ad annos Christi reducerem, ad 93 addo 283, summa est 376. Ergò annus Diocletiani 93 incepit anno Christi 376. Aug. 29. Initium enim Æræ Diocletianeæ ab Aug. 29 deducitur, eò quòd istud vulgare fuit annorum Ægyptiacorum principium.
units.tr: 1. For example, the divine Ambrose says: "Again, in the ninety-third year from the day of Diocletian's reign, when the fourteenth moon fell on the fourteenth day of the month Pharmuthi, which is four days before the Ides of April, which was a Sunday, Easter was celebrated on Sunday, the twenty-first day of Pharmuthi, which for us is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May." Ambros. Epist. l. 10, ep. 83. If I apply this passage of the Father and reduce Diocletian's year 93 to years of Christ, I add 283 to 93, and the sum is 376. Therefore Diocletian's year 93 began in the year of Christ 376, on August 29. For the beginning of the Diocletianic era is taken as August 29, because that was commonly regarded as the beginning of the Egyptian years.

units.la: VIII. Si Æram è contrà Christianam ad Diocletianeam revocares, ex anno Christi propositofubduc 283, & reli- quus erit annus Diocletianeus.
units.tr: VIII. If conversely you were to revert from the Christian era to the Diocletianic, subtract 283 from the proposed year of Christ, and the remainder will be the Diocletianic year.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Estò hic annus Christi 1667, aufer 283, & residuum est 1284. Ergò hoc anno Christi 1667 annus Diocletianeus 1384, iniit Aug. 30.
units.tr: 1. For example, let this year of Christ be 1667; take away 283, and the remainder is 1384. Therefore in this year of Christ 1667 the Diocletianic year 1384 began, on August 30.

units.la: 2. Annis Christi adjicimus pariter ac abjicimus 283, propterea quòd annus primus Æræ Diocletianeæ, uti dicum. stum est, coepit Aug. 29. anno Christi 284, adeo ut anni 283 à Christo juxta computum vulgarem completi sunt, priúsquam instituta fuit Æra Diocletianea.
units.tr: 2. We add 283 to years of Christ, and likewise subtract it, because the first year of the Diocletianic era, as has been said, began on August 29 in the year of Christ 284. So the years 283 of Christ, according to the common reckoning, were completed before the Diocletianic era was instituted.

units.la: CAP. XI. De annis mundi, sive Græcorum computis.
units.tr: CHAP. XI. On the years of the world, or the reckonings of the Greeks.

units.la: Æris à mundi conditu supputatis orientales utuntur Christiani, esque Annos mundi nuncupant.
units.tr: Eastern Christians use eras counted from the creation of the world, and they call these the Years of the World.

units.la: I. DE annis ab initio rerum computandis, tot ferè sunt sententiæ, quot computatores. Ut varios autem textum Hebraicum sequentium computos modò præteream, quippe qui nunquam in Epochas sive terminos temporum vulgò recepti sunt, Orientales propemodum omnes, Græci præsertim, ex 70 virorum auctoritate tempora sua digeruﬅ, & annos ab origine mundi, sic collectos pro Epochis habent, vocántque uti dictum eﬅ, Annos mundi, ut & ἔτη ἀπὸ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ Ἀδὰμ, aliquando ἔτη ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης τοῦ Ἀδὰμ, & subinde simpliciter Annos.
units.tr: I. There are almost as many opinions about the years to be counted from the beginning of things as there are computists. Setting aside for the moment the various reckonings that follow the Hebrew text, which were never generally received as Epochs, or fixed terms of time, nearly all the Orientals, and the Greeks especially, have arranged their times on the authority of the Seventy men. They hold as Epochs the years collected in this way from the origin of the world, and call them, as has been said, Years of the World; also years from the creation of Adam [ἔτη ἀπὸ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ Ἀδὰμ], sometimes years from the first of Adam [ἔτη ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης τοῦ Ἀδὰμ], and at times simply Years.

units.la: II. Hæ Æra à mundi conditu supputatæ, tres numerantur, quarum una Historica, altera Ecclesiastica, tertia civilis nuncupetur.
units.tr: II. These eras counted from the creation of the world are reckoned as three: one is called Historical, another Ecclesiastical, and the third civil.

units.la: III. Æra Græcorum historica est quæ ab initio rerum ad Christi natalem, annos putat completos 5500.
units.tr: III. The Greek historical era is the one which holds that 5500 years were completed from the beginning of things to the birth of Christ.

units.la: 1. Hanc idcirco Historicam appello Epocham, quòd è sacris & profanis Historiis ab Africano collecta fuit; quem à mundi primordiis ad incarnationem Dominicam annos 5500 computásse testatur Georgius Monachus.
units.tr: 1. I call this Historical Epoch for this reason: it was collected by Africanus from sacred and profane histories. George the Monk testifies that Africanus computed 5500 years from the first beginnings of the world to the Lord's incarnation.

units.la: 2. Hanc Africanum secuti, prædictus ille Georgius Monachus, Theophanes, Nicephorus cum aliis usurpant, quos inter Eutychius sive Said Ebn Batrik Arabicus Annalium Alexandrinorum scriptor, & Dorotheus Monembasiae metropolita, in Synopsi Miscellaneâ Græcobarbarè conscriptâ, à Seldeno laudatâ.
units.tr: 2. Following Africanus, the aforementioned George the Monk, Theophanes and Nicephorus, along with others, use this era. Among these are Eutychius, or Said Ebn Batrik, the Arabic writer of the Alexandrian Annals, and Dorotheus, metropolitan of Monemvasia, in the Miscellaneous Synopsis written in a Greco-barbarous style, which Selden praises.

units.la: IV. Historica hæc Orientalium Æra Christi natalem in an- num octavum post vulgarem Epocham incidisse supponit, sive in annum per. Jul. 4721.
units.tr: IV. This Oriental history supposes that the birth of Christ fell in the eighth year after the common era, that is, in the Julian year 4721.

units.la: 1. Hoc diligenter observandum est, aliter enim in historicis hâc Æra utentibus legendis pessimè hallucinemur. Ex gr. Eutychius, quem hanc Æram secutum fuisse supradictum est, à Christo nato ad imperium Diocletiani incœptum annos fluxisse 276 scribit, Annal. Alex. tom. 1 p. 401. Si vulgarem Epocham à Christo nato computatam hic admittas, imperium, Ærámque Diocletiani octennio antevertes. Sed ad 276, adde 8, summa 284 est annus Æræ vulgaris Christianæ, quo Diocletianus imperare, & Æra ab eo denominata numerari coepit. Sed hæc alibi fusiùs, Deo volente, demonstrare nitemur. Hic autem à nobis, ut ab aliis Chronologis, non penitùs prætermissa fuisse sufficiat.
units.tr: 1. This must be observed carefully, for otherwise we will go badly astray when reading historians who use this era. For example, Eutychius, who is said above to have followed this era, writes that 276 years ran from the birth of Christ to the beginning of Diocletian's reign (Annals of Alexandria, vol. 1, p. 401). If you accept here the common epoch, counted from the birth of Christ, you will place Diocletian's reign and era eight years too early. But add 8 to 276 and the sum is 284, the year of the common Christian era in which Diocletian began to reign and the era named after him began to be counted. We shall try, God willing, to demonstrate this more fully elsewhere. For now it is enough that it has not been wholly passed over here, as by other chronologers.

units.la: V. Æra Græcorum Ecclesiastica est quæ Christum anno mundi 5494 currente natum statuit.
units.tr: V. The ecclesiastical era of the Greeks is the one that places the birth of Christ in the year 5494 of the world.

units.la: 1. Hanc æram Ecclesiasticam appello, propterea quòd rebus Ecclesiasticis præsertim inservisse videtur; videlicet ad paschatis celebritatem juxta Ecclesiæ Alexandrinæ computum quotannis inveniendam. Enimvero juxta Paschalem Theophili computum; anno Christi 279 ab Aug. 29, cyclus Lunæ primus incepit. Addas 379 ad 5493, summa 5872 per 19 divisa eundem cyclum Paschalem exhibet, putà primum. Et sic per hanc Æram cyclum Paschalem quotannis computabant.
units.tr: 1. I call this the ecclesiastical era because it seems to have served chiefly ecclesiastical matters, namely to find each year the celebration of Easter according to the reckoning of the Church of Alexandria. Indeed, according to the Paschal computation of Theophilus, the first lunar cycle began in the year of Christ 279, from August 29. Add 379 to 5493 and the sum, 5872, divided by 19, shows the same Paschal cycle, namely the first. And so by this era they computed the Paschal cycle each year.

units.la: 2. Auctor hujus Æræ Panodorus perhibetur, qui Arcadio imperante, & Ecclesiam Alexandrinum prædicto Theophilo regente claruit. Usitatur etiam ab Elmacino in historiâ Saracenicâ Arabicè conscriptâ, sub annorum Solarium mundi nomine, ut ab annis Hegiræ Lunaribus distinguatur.
units.tr: 2. The author of this era is said to be Panodorus, who flourished under the emperor Arcadius, when Theophilus ruled the Church of Alexandria. It is also used by Elmacinus in his Saracen history, written in Arabic, under the name of solar years of the world, so that it may be distinguished from the lunar years of the Hegira.

units.la: VI. Anni in hac Ærâ computati ab Aug 29 procedunt.
units.tr: VI. The years counted in this era run from Aug. 29.

units.la: 1. Abeâ nimirùm die computantur, in quam neomenia Thoth in annis Ægyptiacis fixis quotannis incidit, quæ semper est Aug. 29, nisi quòd proximo post Bissextilem in Aug. 30 detruditur. Ab hoc autem initio deducuntur, propterèa quòd annis Actiacis accommodati erant, qui orientalibus Soli antiquitùs in usu fuere.
units.tr: 1. They are counted from that day on which the new moon of Thoth falls in the fixed Egyptian years each year. This is always Aug. 29, except that after a leap year it is moved to Aug. 30. This starting point is derived because the years were adapted to the Actian years, which the eastern peoples of old used in their solar reckoning.

units.la: VII. Annus igitur hujus Æræ 5494 incepit Aug. 29. anno primo Æræ vulgaris Christianæ, sive anno per. Jul. 4714 currente.
units.tr: VII. The year 5494 of this era therefore began on Aug. 29, in the first year of the common Christian era, or in the course of Julian period 4714.

units.la: 1. Cœpit hæc Æra ante periodum Julianam præsentem annis completis 780, adeò ut annus hujus Æræ 781, cum primo periodi Julianæ coincidat. Aufer 780 ex 7980 reliquus fit annus per. Jul. prolepticæ 7200. Ergò anno sequenti sive 7201 labenti caput hujus Æræ figendum est; vel ad 780 adjicias 4714 (quo anno per. Jul. labente cœpit primus Christi) summa est 5494. Ergo anno Christi primo annus hujus Æræ 5494 incepit Aug. 29. Adeò ut hæc Æra cœpit unà cum priori, nec ab eâ discrepat, nisi quòd mutelatur superfluis istis annis quibus prior Christi natalem prorogavit.
units.tr: 1. This era began 780 completed years before the present Julian period, so that year 781 of this era coincides with the first year of the Julian period. Take 780 from 7980 and the remainder is year 7200 of the proleptic Julian period. The beginning of this era is therefore to be fixed in the year after, that is, in the course of 7201. Or add 780 to 4714 (the year in whose course the first year of Christ fell in the Julian period) and the sum is 5494. So in the first year of Christ, year 5494 of this era began on Aug. 29. Thus this era began together with the earlier one and does not differ from it, except that it is curtailed by those superfluous years by which the earlier one postponed the birth of Christ.

units.la: VIII. Ut hanc Æram ad Christianam reducas, anno pro- positò deme 5493, residuus est annus Christi quo currente quæsitus iniit.
units.tr: VIII. To reduce this era to the Christian, subtract 5493 from the year proposed; the remainder is the year of Christ in whose course the year in question began.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Elmacinus hist. Sarac. l. 2, c. 7. ait Abu Abdalla Alamiaum diem obiisse elapsis annis Hegiræ 197, diebus 25, annis autem solaribus 6305, diebus 28. Mortuus est igitur anno hujus Æræ 6306 currente. Ex 6306 aufer 5493, & reliquus fit annus Christi 813. Igitur anno Christi 813 labente, Aug. 29, cœpit annus hujus Æræ 6306. Quod etiam ex annis Hegiræ confirmatur. Nam anni Hegiræ 197 dies 25 jam elapsi sunt, annus igitur 198 currebat. Verùm anno Hegiræ 198 neomenia Muharram incidit in Kalendas Septembris; anno Christi 813, adeò ut vigesimus quintus dies hujus anni, erat etiam Sept. 25. At Sept. 25 est duodetrigesimus etiam ab Aug. 29 inclusivé; unde hanc Æram unà cum neomeniâ Thoth incipere satis patet.
units.tr: 1. For example, Elmacin, History of the Saracens, book 2, chapter 7, says that Abu Abdalla Alamiaus died after 197 years of the Hegira and 25 days, that is, after 6305 solar years and 28 days. He therefore died in the course of year 6306 of this era. Subtract 5493 from 6306 and the remainder is the year of Christ 813. So in the year of Christ 813, on Aug. 29, year 6306 of this era began. This is also confirmed from the years of the Hegira. For 197 years and 25 days of the Hegira had already elapsed, so year 198 was running. But in year 198 of the Hegira the new moon of Muharram fell on the Kalends of September in the year of Christ 813, so that the 25th day of this year was Sept. 25. And Sept. 25 is also the 28th day counting inclusively from Aug. 29. Whence it is quite clear that this era begins together with the new moon of Thoth.

units.la: IX. Civilis Græcorum Æra, est quæ à mundi primordiis ad Christi Nativitatem annos 5508 completos numerat.
units.tr: The civil era of the Greeks is that which counts 5508 completed years from the beginning of the world to the Nativity of Christ.

units.la: 1. Æra Ecclesiastica historicæ octo annos abstulit, hæc totidem addit, & ut ablatio ista propter cyclum paschalem, sic & hæc additio propter Indictionem instituta fuit. Enimvero ut in rebus Ecclesiasticis cycli paschalis, sic in politicis Indictionis præcipuè ratio habenda fuit, utpote quæ post Theodosii tempora maximè frequentari, & ad edicta, diplomata, aliáque istiusmodi politica consignanda adhiberi cœpit; (unde & hanc Æram civilem appello) Ut igitur annus quisque currens per 15 divisus Indictionem rectè exhiberet, ad Æram historicam aggregabant octo, ut Christus natus diceretur anno mundi 5509, qui per 15 divisus relinquit Indictionem 4.
units.tr: 1. The ecclesiastical era of the historians removed eight years; this one adds as many. Just as that subtraction was made on account of the paschal cycle, so this addition was made on account of the indiction. Indeed, as in ecclesiastical affairs the paschal cycle was especially to be taken into account, so in civil affairs the indiction was, since after the time of Theodosius it came into very frequent use and began to be employed for sealing edicts, diplomas and other such public documents (whence I also call this the civil era). So that the current year, divided by 15, might correctly give the indiction, they added eight to the historical era, so that Christ is said to have been born in the year of the world 5509, which divided by 15 leaves indiction 4.

units.la: 2. Porrò è tribus hisce orientalium Æris, hæc maximè celebrata fuit, utpote quâ non tantùm Constantinopolitani, Moschovitæ, Albani, Illyrii, Georgiani, Bulgari, Græcique propemodùm omnes recentiores usi sunt, sed & ipsi imperatores novellas suas & edicta publica consignare soliti fuerunt.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, of these three eastern eras this one was the most celebrated, since it was used not only by the Constantinopolitans, Muscovites, Albanians, Illyrians, Georgians, Bulgarians and almost all the more recent Greeks, but the emperors themselves were accustomed to sign their novels and public edicts with it.

units.la: X. Annus hujus Æræ 5509 incipit anno primo Æræ Christianæ.
units.tr: The year 5509 of this era begins in the first year of the Christian era.

units.la: 1. Anni hujus Æræ 795 absoluti sunt, priúsquam periodus Juliana cœperit, adeò ut annus 796 in primum istius periodi incurrat.
units.tr: 1. The 795 years of this era were completed before the Julian period began, so that year 796 falls into the first year of that period.

units.la: 2. Anni verò in hac Æra usitati mensibus constant Julianis, atque ideò à neomeniâ Thoth nunquam incipiunt, quippe quæ nunquam in initium mensis cujusvis Juliani incidat, ei tamen ut quàm proximè exoriantur, à Kalendis Septembribus statim subsequentibus deducuntur.
units.tr: 2. The years of this era, however, are used with Julian months and so never begin at the new moon of Thoth, since it never falls on the beginning of any Julian month. Nevertheless, so that they may begin as nearly as possible to it, they are reckoned from the Kalends of September immediately following.

units.la: 3. Hæc Æra quamvis historicam octennio superet, non tamen illius ad instar Christi natalem loco suo detrudit, sed potius mundi primordium anticipat, adeo ut annus hujus Æræ 5509, non minus quam Ecclesiasticæ 5494 in primum Æræ Christianæ recte concurrat.
units.tr: 3. Although this era exceeds the historical one by eight years, it does not, like that one, push the birth of Christ back to its proper place. Rather, it anticipates the beginning of the world, so that year 5509 of this era, no less than year 5494 of the ecclesiastical era, rightly coincides with the first year of the Christian era.

units.la: XI. Anno hujus Æræ propósito subtrahe 5508, residuus est annus Æræ Christianæ quo currente cœpit.
units.tr: XI. Subtract 5508 from the year of this era proposed; the remainder is the year of the Christian era in whose course it began.

units.la: 1. Ex.gr. In tomo unionis Constantini & Romani temporibus facto, hæc legimus, Καὶ λοιπὸν ἀπὸ αὐτοῦ ... ἀλλ' ἴνα ἀπὸ βλίσεν παντλῶς, Ac proinde decernimus sententiâ, judicióque communi, ne ab anno hoc præsenti, qui est annus mundi 6428, indict. 8, quartas nuptias quispiam contrahat, sed ut ea prorsus rejiciantur. Si scire vellem in quotum annum Christi, hic mundi propositus conveniat, ex 6428 subduco 5508, residuum est 920. Ergo anno Christi 920, annus hic mundi 6428 incepit, à Kal. Sept. porro 6428 partiaris per 15, residuum est 8. Ergo indictio erat 8.
units.tr: 1. For example, in the tome of union made in the times of Constantine and Romanus we read these words: "And henceforth from it ... but in order that ... Accordingly we decree by sentence and common judgement that from this present year, which is the year of the world 6428, indiction 8, no one should contract a fourth marriage, but such marriages should be utterly rejected." [Καὶ λοιπὸν ἀπὸ αὐτοῦ ... ἀλλ' ἴνα ἀπὸ βλίσεν παντλῶς]. If I wished to know in what year of Christ this proposed year of the world falls, I subtract 5508 from 6428; the remainder is 920. Therefore in the year of Christ 920, this year of the world 6428 began, on the Kalends of September. Further, I divide 6428 by 15; the remainder is 8. Therefore the indiction was 8.

units.la: 2. Aliud exemplum: Manuelis Comneni novella de voluntariis homicidis, hisce verbis signatur, τῷ μηνὶ Απρίλιῳ, Ἰνδικτιῶνος ιδ', ἔτους ςχοδ', Dat. mense Aprili, Indictione 14, anno 6674. Aufer 5508 & reliquus fit annus Christi 1166, huic respondens. Dividas etiam 6674 per 15, residuum & consequenter Indictio est 14, atque ita eadem quæ Romana.
units.tr: 2. Another example: the novel of Manuel Comnenus concerning voluntary homicides is signed with these words: "Given in the month of April, in indiction 14, in the year 6674 [τῷ μηνὶ Απρίλιῳ, Ἰνδικτιῶνος ιδ', ἔτους ςχοδ']. Subtract 5508 and the remainder is the year of Christ 1166, which corresponds to it. Divide also 6674 by 15; the remainder, and consequently the indiction, is 14, and so it is the same as the Roman one.

units.la: CAP. XII. De Æra Judaica.
units.tr: CAP. XII. On the Jewish Era.

units.la: Hactenus de Æris Christianis quas excipit Judaica, à mundi conditu πχικὸς exurgens.
units.tr: So far concerning the Christian eras; the Jewish era follows, reckoned from the creation of the world, approximately.

units.la: 1. Udæi antiquitùs varias in temporibus suis computandis Epochas adhibebant, nonnunquam enim annos suos à Diluvio, subinde à linguarum divisione, alias ab ingressu, sæpius ab egressu ex Ægypto, aliquando ab edificatione templi, & nonnunquam ab ejus post captivitatem Babylonicam restauratione, post Alexandri tempora Æra Contractuum uti sunt, de quâ postea. Sed vulgaris eorum Epocha, quæ etiamnum & si ipsis fides sit habenda, mille abhinc annis iis in usu fuit, à mundi creatione computatur: non tamen revera sed πχικὸς, & methodi gratiâ. Nam uno plus anno ab orbis initio putant, quàm ipsi revera intercessisse credunt. Nam computus eorum à מולר תחו Neomeniâ Tohu exurgit, quæ anno solido mundi principium anticipat.
units.tr: 1. In ancient times the Jews used various epochs for reckoning their years. Sometimes they counted from the Flood, at other times from the division of tongues, at other times from the entry into Canaan, more often from the exodus from Egypt, sometimes from the building of the temple, and occasionally from its restoration after the Babylonian captivity; after the time of Alexander they used the Era of Contracts, of which more later. But their common epoch, which they still use (if they are to be trusted), and which has been in use among them for a thousand years, is computed from the creation of the world*. This is not strictly exact but approximate, and adopted for convenience of method. For they place the beginning of the world one year earlier than they actually believe it to have occurred, since their reckoning starts from the new moon of Tohu, which anticipates the beginning of the world by a full year.

units.la: 2. Hic autem diligenter animadvertendum est numerum millenarium in computo hoc Judaico sæpius omitti, ut annus Judaicus 5427 aliquando totus scribitur, שנת ה' חכו לבריאת עולם id est, Annus 5427 à creatione mundi, alias autem abjectis millenariis שנת חכו לפק Annus 427 Æræ minoris, nam לפק est abbreviatura pro לפרט קטון Æra sive computi minoris, viz. infra millenarium.
units.tr: 2. Here it must be carefully noted that the thousands are often omitted in this Jewish reckoning. Thus the Jewish year 5427 is sometimes written in full, שנת ה' חכו לבריאת עולם, that is, Year 5427 from the creation of the world; at other times, with the thousands dropped, שנת חכו לפק, Year 427 of the lesser Era, for לפק is an abbreviation of לפרט קטון, Era, or lesser reckoning, namely below the thousand.

units.la: II. Primus annus hujus Æræ cœpit Oct. 7. anno per. Jul. 953, cyclo Solis 1, Lunæ 3, Indict. 8.
units.tr: II. The first year of this Era began on 7 October, in the year of the Julian period 953, Solar cycle 1, Lunar cycle 3, Indiction 8.

units.la: III. Anno Æræ Christianæ primo currente cœpit annus Judaicus 3762 ab Autumno.
units.tr: III. In the first year of the Christian Era, the Jewish year 3762 began in autumn.

units.la: 1. Annus primus Æræ Christianæ erat per. Jul. 4714, auser 952, qui de periodo Juliana sunt elapsi, priusquam Æra cœpit Judaica, residuum est 3762. Ergò anno primo Æræ Christianæ currente annus Judaicus 3762 iniit, ita tamen ut maxima ejus pars in annum Christi secundum incurrat, quoniam ab Autumno cœpit, ut & maxima pars anni 3761 in Christi primum.
units.tr: 1. The first year of the Christian Era was year 4714 of the Julian period. Subtract 952, the years that had elapsed in the Julian period before the Jewish Era began, and the remainder is 3762. Therefore in the first year of the Christian Era the Jewish year 3762 began; yet most of it falls into the second year of Christ, since it began in autumn, just as most of the year 3761 falls into the first year of Christ.

units.la: IV. Propósito anno per. Jul. demas 952, vel anno Christi propósito adjicias 3761, & habebis annum Judaicum qui propósito currente cœpit.
units.tr: IV. To find the Jewish year beginning in a given year of the Julian period, subtract 952 from that year; or add 3761 to a given year of Christ, and you will have the Jewish year that begins in the given year.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Annus, quo hæc scribo, est per. Jul. 6380, aufer 952, residuum est 5428, est item annus Christi 1667, adde 3761, summa est 5428. Ergo utróque modo ab Autumno hujus anni Christi 1667, annus Judaicus 5428 exoritur.
units.tr: 1. For example, the year in which I am writing this is 6380 of the Julian period. Subtract 952 and the remainder is 5428; it is also the year 1667 of Christ, and adding 3761 gives 5428. So by either method, the Jewish year 5428 begins in autumn of this year 1667 of Christ.

units.la: V. Propósito è contra anno Judaico adde 952, & habebis annum per. Jul. vel abjice 3761, & habebis annum Christi quo currente annus Judaicus propósitus init.
units.tr: V. Conversely, to a given Jewish year add 952 and you will have the year of the Julian period; or subtract 3761 and you will have the year of Christ in which the given Jewish year begins.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Benjamin in præfatione ad itinerarium quæcunque in itinere memoratu digna observâsset in Castiliam secum detulisse refertur בשנה חמשלש anno 933. Neminem latet numerum millenarium more Judaico (de quo modò memini) penitùs hîc omitti. Sed æquè constat quatuor annorum millia de computo Judaico jam effluxisse. Addito igitur numero millenario hoc accidit בשנה ה׳ חמשלש Anno 4933. Aufer 3761, & reliquus fit annus Æræ Christianæ 1172, quo currente annus propósitus Æræ Judaicæ minoris 933 incepit.
units.tr: 1. For example, Benjamin, in the preface to his itinerary, is reported to have brought with him to Castile whatever he had noted as worth recording on his journey, dated בשנה חמשלש, in the year 933. It is well known that the thousands are wholly omitted here in the Jewish manner (of which I have just spoken). But it is equally certain that four thousand years had already passed in the Jewish reckoning. Adding the thousands, we get בשנה ה׳ חמשלש, in the year 4933. Subtract 3761, and the remainder is 1172, the Christian year in which the given year 933 of the lesser Jewish Era began.

units.la: 2. Verùm in annis Æræ minoris, omissis videlicet millenariis expeditiori calculo procedamus, dummodo annus propósitus annum Christi 240 non præcedat. Nam anno Christi 239 vertente, quatuor annorum millia de Æra Judaicâ completa sunt. Anno igitur Æræ minoris propósito adjice 239, summa est annus Christi quo currente propósitus exoritur: ut in prædicto exemplo ad 933, adde 239, summa est 1172 per hanc æquè ac priorem methodum.
units.tr: 2. But in years of the lesser Era, where the thousands are omitted, we may proceed by the quicker calculation, provided the given year does not precede the year 240 of Christ. For in the course of the year 239 of Christ, four thousand years of the Jewish Era were completed. So add 239 to the given year of the lesser Era, and the sum is the year of Christ in which the given year begins. Thus in the example above, adding 239 to 933 gives 1172, by this method as well as by the former.

units.la: VI. Si cyclum Solis aut Lunæ in anno Judaico desideres, annum currentem dividas per 28, & 19, residuum pri- oris divisionis est cyclus Solis, posterioris cyclus Lunæ.
units.tr: VI. If you wish to find the Solar or Lunar cycle in a Jewish year, divide the current year by 28 and by 19. The remainder of the first division is the Solar cycle, that of the second the Lunar cycle.

units.la: 1. Primus, ut ante monui, computi Judaici annus incipit cyclo Solis 1, Lunæ 3, quo fit ut idem perpetuo sit cyclus Solis in annis Julianis ac Judaicis, ab initio videlicet anni Judaici usque ad proximas Kalendas Januarias, quo tempore cyclus Solis Julianus unitate augetur, at Judaicus idem manet, usque ad proximum Autumnum. Ex.gr. Hoc anno Christi 1667 cyclo Solis 24, cœptus est annus Judaicus 5428, qui per 28 divisus, residuum facit 24. Sed cyclus Julianus incipit à Kal. Jan. Judaicus ab Autumno sive neomeniâ Tisri; adeò ut à Kal. Jan. ad annum hunc Judaicum ineuntem cyclus Judaicus erat 23, ut ad annum antecedentem 5427 pertinens.
units.tr: 1. As I noted before, the first year of the Jewish reckoning begins with Solar cycle 1 and Lunar cycle 3. It follows that the Solar cycle is always the same in Julian and Jewish years from the beginning of the Jewish year until the next 1 January, when the Julian Solar cycle increases by one, while the Jewish one stays the same until the next autumn. For example: in this year 1667 of Christ the Solar cycle is 24, and the Jewish year 5428 began with it; divided by 28, its remainder is 24. But the Julian cycle begins on 1 January, while the Jewish begins in autumn, at the new moon of Tishri. So from 1 January until the Jewish year beginning now, the Jewish cycle was 23, belonging to the preceding Jewish year 5427.

units.la: 2. At cyclus Lunæ Judaicus nunquam idem est atque Julianus, propterèa quòd primus annus Judaicus, cyclo Lunæ Juliano 3 labente consurgit; unde qui Judaicus primus est, idem Romanis tertius est cyclus Lunæ ab Autumno ad Kal. Jan. qui istis 2, hisce 4, & sic deinceps: ut si 5428 dividas per 19, numerus residuus est 13, Ergò anno Judaico 5428, cyclus Lunæ 13 competit. At hic annus Judaicus ab Autumno hujus anni Christi 1667, cyclo Lunæ 15 prædiți procedit; adeò ut ab Autumno ad Kal. Jan. sequentes cyclus Judaicus 13 cum Juliano 15 concurrit, at à Kal. Jan. ad proximum Autumnum, cyclus Judaicus idem manebit, & Julianus erit 16, & sic in reliquis.
units.tr: 2. The Jewish Lunar cycle, however, is never the same as the Julian, because the first Jewish year arises while the Julian Lunar cycle is 3. Hence the first Jewish year is the third Lunar cycle of the Romans. From autumn until 1 January, the Jewish cycle is two behind the Julian, and four behind the Roman, and so on. Thus if you divide 5428 by 19, the remainder is 13, and so the Lunar cycle 13 belongs to the Jewish year 5428. This Jewish year, which began in autumn of this year 1667 of Christ, proceeds with Lunar cycle 15. So from autumn until 1 January the Jewish cycle agrees with the Julian 15 in sequence, but from 1 January until the next autumn the Jewish cycle remains the same, while the Julian becomes 16, and so on for the rest.

units.la: 2. Cœtera ad computum hunc Judaicum spectantia è Libro primo petantur.
units.tr: 2. Other matters relating to this Jewish reckoning should be sought in the first book.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XIII.

units.la: De Epocha Trojæ captæ. U. C. & Antiochena.
units.tr: On the Era of the Capture of Troy, the A.U.C., and the Antiochene Era.

units.la: Epochæ Ethnicæ sunt quæ ab Ethnicis instituuntur. II. Hæ omnes vel à locis, vel à rebus, vel à personis deducuntur. III. Loca celebriora à quibus Epochæ deducuntur Ethnicæ, sunt Troja, Roma, & Antiochia. IV. Epocha à Trojâ deducta in excidio Trojano terminatur, quod accidit anno per. Jul. 3531, cyclo Solis 3, Lunæ 16, Indict. 6.
units.tr: Gentile eras are those established by the Gentiles. II. All of these are derived either from places, from events, or from persons. III. The more famous places from which Gentile eras are derived are Troy, Rome, and Antioch. IV. The era derived from Troy ends with the fall of Troy, which happened in Julian period 3531, solar cycle 3, lunar cycle 16, indiction 6.

units.la: 1. HÆC antiquissima videtur Ethnicorum Epocha, de cujus tamen termino, veteres pariter ac recentiores mirè dissentiunt. Nos juxta Diodori Siculi, & Dionysii Halicarnassensis sententiam eam definimus. Nam Diodorus ait annum primum Olymp. 94 definentem esse, ὑφ' ὧν ... ἐπὶ τὴν Τροίας ἅλωσιν; annum 780 post Trojæ excidium. Annus primus olymp. 94, erat per. Jul. 4310. Aufer annos 780 qui à Trojæ excidio effluxerunt, & reliqui fiunt 3530. Ergò primus ex istis 780 annis sive primus annus Epochæ Trojanæ erat per. Jul. 3531.
units.tr: 1. This seems to be the most ancient of the Gentile eras, though writers both ancient and modern differ remarkably about its end. We define it according to the opinion of Diodorus Siculus and Dionysius of Halicarnassus. For Diodorus says that the first year of the 94th Olympiad marks the end [ὑφ' ὧν ... ἐπὶ τὴν Τροίας ἅλωσιν], the 780th year after the fall of Troy. The first year of the 94th Olympiad was Julian period 4310. Subtract the 780 years that have elapsed since the fall of Troy, and 3530 remain. Therefore the first of those 780 years, or the first year of the Trojan era, was Julian period 3531.

units.la: 2. Præterea Dionysius Halicarnassensis ex Eratosthenis canonibus refert, Ilium captum fuisse, Ἐπὶ Ἀλθ... ἡμέρας ... διέβησαν, diebus 17 ante solstitium æstivum, die 23 mensis Thargelionis. De præcisâ die hic non est disputandi locus. Ex his autem verbis satis liquet excidium Trojanum accidisse circa solstitium æstivum, unde consequenter & Epocha hæc est computanda.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, Dionysius of Halicarnassus reports, from the canons of Eratosthenes, that Ilium was taken [Ἐπὶ Ἀλθ... ἡμέρας ... διέβησαν], seventeen days before the summer solstice, on the 23rd day of the month Thargelion. The exact day is not a matter for discussion here. From these words, however, it is clear enough that the fall of Troy occurred around the summer solstice, and this era is therefore to be computed accordingly.

units.la: 3. Verùm quamvis anni ab hâc Epochâ in antiquis scriptoribus nonnunquam occurrant numerati, nihil tamen certi ac indubitati de eâ definiri potest. Non igitur inter institutiones, sed disputationes potiùs Chronologicas locum meretur.
units.tr: 3. But although years counted from this era sometimes occur in ancient writers, nothing certain and indubitable can be established about it. It therefore deserves a place not among the institutions but rather among the chronological disputations.

units.la: V. Ut Epocha Trojana à Trojæ excidio, sic Romana à Romæ conditu supputatur, quæ vulgò nuncupatur Epocha sive anni V. C. id est Urbis Conditæ.
units.tr: V. As the Trojan era is reckoned from the fall of Troy, so the Roman era is reckoned from the founding of Rome; it is commonly called the era of the A.U.C., that is, of the year from the founding of the City.

units.la: VI. Epocha V. C. duplex est, Varroniana, & Capitolina.
units.tr: VI. The era of the A.U.C. is twofold: the Varronian and the Capitoline.

units.la: VII. Epocha V. C. Varroniana cœpit anno per. Jul. 3951, cyclo Solis 13, Lunæ 9, Indict. 1.
units.tr: VII. The Varronian era of the A.U.C. began in Julian period 3951, solar cycle 13, lunar cycle 9, indiction 1.

units.la: 1. Hæc Epocha Varroniana dicitur à M. Varrone quem Urbis Conditum in annum tertium olympiadis sextæ exeuntem retulisse testatur Plutarchus, cui congruit annus per. Jul. 3960. Quocirca Kalendis Januarius sequentibus, sive anno per. Jul. 3961 ineunte, cœpit hæc Epocha ab eo denominata. Non quòd Roma Kal. Jan. Condita fuit: Nam fundamenta ejus jacta fuisse 11 Kal. Maii, sive April. 21 (quæ & Palilia vocatur, propterea quòd festivitas quædam ita denominata, à pastoribus olim isto die celebrata fuit) testis est Plutarchus in vitâ Romuli: aliis etiam adstipulantibus. Sed à Kal. Jan. procedit, ut ab Epochâ anni Juliani, cujus formam plerique secuti sunt scriptores, qui annos suos ab Urbe Conditâ deducunt. Et hinc est quòd ubicunque occurrit annorum U. C. mentio, à Kal. Januariis computandi sunt, nisi aliter scriptorem eos incepisse certis conjecturis assequi possimus, non autem ab Urbis Palilibus eò quòd incertum est in quotam anni Juliani diem Romuli temporibus inciderint, quem longè aliam atque Julianam anni formam instituisse satis constat: Adeò ut etiamsi Palilia Romuli temporibus April. 21 celebrata sunt, num eadem tamen esset dies in anno Juliano admodum incertum est, vel potiùs certissimum est non fuisse. Sed omnes ferè in hoc conveniunt, quòd Romulus Urbis Conditum paulò ante Solstitium æstivum, sive ineuntem annum Atticum & olympiacum aggressus est.
units.tr: 1. This era is called Varronian after M. Varro, whom Plutarch testifies placed the founding of the City in the third year of the sixth Olympiad, as it was drawing to a close; the year Julian period 3960 agrees with this. Hence, on the following 1 January, that is, at the beginning of the year Julian period 3961, this era, named after him, began. Not that Rome was founded on 1 January: that its foundations were laid on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, that is, 21 April (which is also called the Palilia, because a certain festival of that name was once celebrated on this day by shepherds), Plutarch attests in his Life of Romulus, with others agreeing. But the reckoning proceeds from 1 January, as with the era of the Julian year, whose form most writers followed, who date their years from the Urbis Conditæ. And hence wherever a mention of years A.U.C. occurs, they are to be reckoned from 1 January, unless we can establish by certain conjectures that the writer began them otherwise; not from the Palilia of the City, because it is uncertain on what day of the Julian year the times of Romulus fell, since it is well established that he instituted a form of the year quite different from the Julian. So much so that even if the Palilia were celebrated on 21 April in the time of Romulus, it is quite uncertain whether that was the same day in the Julian year, or rather it is most certain that it was not.
