But nearly all agree on this, that Romulus began the founding of the City shortly before the summer solstice, that is, at the beginning of the Attic and Olympic year.

units.la: VIII. Epocha V. C. Capitolina coepit anno per. Jul. 3962, cyclo Solis 14, Lunae 10, Indict. 2.
units.tr: VIII. The Capitoline Era of the City begins in the year of the Julian period 3962, cycle of the Sun 14, cycle of the Moon 10, indiction 2.

units.la: I. Hanc Capitolinam vocamus Epocham, quippe quae in fastis Capitolinis observatur, qui à Verrio Flacco colleċti perhibentur, sed incerti potiùs sunt auƐtoris. Scaliger hanc Epocham Catonianam appellitat, acsi à M. Porcio Catone primò supputata fuisset. Sed nihil certè ex ejus computationibus de anno Urbis Conditae definiri potest. Quocirca nos cum Petavio Capitolinam eam nuncupare maluimus.
units.tr: I. We call this the Capitoline era, since it is observed in the Capitoline Fasti, which are said to have been collected by Verrius Flaccus, though their author is rather uncertain. Scaliger calls this era the Catonian, as if it had first been computed by Marcus Porcius Cato. But nothing certain about the year of the City's founding can be determined from his computations. For this reason, with Petavius, we preferred to name it the Capitoline.

units.la: IX. Anno V. C. proposito addas 3960, & habebis annum per. Jul. juxta computum Varronianum ei congruentem, vel si adjicias 3961, juxta Capitolinum.
units.tr: IX. Add 3960 to the proposed year AUC, and you will have the year of the Julian period agreeing with it according to Varro's reckoning; or if you add 3961, you have it according to the Capitoline.

units.la: I. Ex, gr. Cornelius Tacitus ait, Sexcentesimum & quadragesimum annum urbs nostra agebat, cùm primùm Cimbrorum audita sunt arma, Tacit. de Mor. German. Si quaeras in quotum annum per. Jul. annus U. C. 640 cõnveniat, ad 640, adjicias 3960, summa 4600 est annus per. Jul. quaesitus, juxta computum Varronianum, vel adjicias 3961, & efficies annum per. Jul. 4601 juxta Capitolinum.
units.tr: I. For example, Cornelius Tacitus says: Our city was in its six hundred and fortieth year when the arms of the Cimbri were first heard of. Tacitus, On the Manners of the Germans. If you ask in what year of the Julian period AUC 640 falls, add 3960 to 640; the sum, 4600, is the Julian year sought according to Varro's reckoning. Or add 3961, and you will get the Julian year 4601 according to the Capitoline.

units.la: 2. Plinius ait, Elephantos Italia primùm vidit Pyrrhi regis bello, & boves Lucas appellavit in Lucanis visos, anno Urbis quadringentesimo septuagesimo secundo, Plin. l. 8. c. 6. Annus, ut vides, erat U. C. 472, adde 3960, aggregatum 4432. Erat igitur annus per. Jul. 4432 juxta computum Varronianum, at juxta Capitolinum 4433. Caeterùm anni U. C. Varroniani Capitolinis plerùnque sunt praeferendi.
units.tr: 2. Pliny says: Italy first saw elephants in the war of King Pyrrhus, and the Lucanians called them oxen of Lucania, seen in the four hundred and seventy-second year of the City. Pliny, Book 8, chapter 6. The year, as you see, was AUC 472; add 3960, and the total is 4432. So the year of the Julian period was 4432 according to Varro's reckoning, but 4433 according to the Capitoline. Still, the Varronian years AUC are for the most part to be preferred to the Capitoline.

units.la: X. Proposito anno per. Jul. si annum Urbis Conditae ei respondentem haberes, ab anno proposito auser 396C, & residuus fit annus V. C. Varronianus.
units.tr: X. Given the proposed year of the Julian period, if you want the year of the City corresponding to it, subtract 3960 from the proposed year, and the remainder is the Varronian year AUC.

units.la: I. Ex gr. Annus primus Aerae Christianae fuit per. Jul. 4714, auser 3960, residuum est 754. Erat igitur annus Varronianus 754, vel abjectis 3961, fit annus Capitolinus 753. Annus praesens est per. Jul. 6380, auser 3960, & fit annus U. C. 2420.
units.tr: I. For example, the first year of the Christian Era was the Julian year 4714; subtract 3960, and the remainder is 754. So the Varronian year was 754, or, if you subtract 3961, the Capitoline year is 753. The present year is the Julian year 6380; subtract 3960, and the year AUC is 2420.

units.la: XI. Ab Urbe Antiochiâ deducitur Æra quæ ab eâ Antio- chena vocatur.
units.tr: XI. The Era called Antiochene is derived from the City of Antioch.

units.la: I. Hæc Æra non ut Trojana ab Urbis excidio, nec ut Romana ab Urbe condita, sed à recuperatâ Urbis libertate supputatur. Anni in hac Epochâ vocantur etiam τῶν χρηματιςμῶν τῆς Αντιοχίας, nonnunquam anni χρηματιζόντος τῆς πόλεως. Usurpatur hæc Æra ab Eusebio, Evagrio, Cedreno, Nicephoro, necnon in Chronico Alexandrino.
units.tr: I. This era is reckoned not from the fall of Troy, like the Trojan era, nor from the founding of the City, like the Roman, but from the recovery of the City's liberty. The years of this epoch are also called [τῶν χρηματισμῶν τῆς Αντιοχίας], the years of the oracles of Antioch, and sometimes [χρηματιζόντος τῆς πόλεως], the years of the city. This era is used by Eusebius, Evagrius, Cedrenus and Nicephorus, and also in the Alexandrian Chronicle.

units.la: XII. Hæc Æra Antiochena ab Autumno anno per. Jul. 4665, cyclo Solis 17, Lunæ 10, Indict. 15 procedit.
units.tr: XII. This Antiochene era begins from the autumn of the Julian year 4665, cycle of the Sun 17, cycle of the Moon 10, indiction 15.

units.la: XIII. Propositio igitur anno Æra Antiochenæ adjice 4664, summa est annus per. Jul. quo currente propositus iniit.
units.tr: XIII. Therefore, to the proposed year of the Antiochene era add 4664; the sum is the Julian year in whose course the proposed year began.

units.la: I. Ex. gr. Evagrius ait Justinianum imperatorem declaratum fuisse, Πρώτῃ τῆ ξανϑικῆ ἡμέρᾳ Αὐδυναίου μηνὸς, ἀνὰ τὴν πεμπτὴν καὶ ἐβδομηκοστὴν, ᾗ Πενταχοσιοστῷ ἔτῳ τῶν χρηματιζων τῆς Αντιοχείας: Die primo mensis Xanthici sive Aprilis anno quingentesimo, septuagesimo quinto Æra Antiochena. Evagr. Hist. Eccles. l. 4. c. 9. Si situm hujus anni in periodo Juliana deprehenderes, ad 575 adde 4664, summa 5239 est annus per. Jul. quo currente annus propositus 575 iniit, ab Autumno. Sed mensis Xanthicus sive Aprilis, quo ineunte renunciatus est imperator incurrit in annum per. Jul. 5240, aufer 4713, & habes annum Christi 527, quo currente hæc gesta sunt.
units.tr: I. For example, Evagrius says that Justinian was declared emperor on the first day of the month Xanthicus, that is April, in the five hundred and seventy-fifth year of the Antiochene era [Πρώτῃ τῇ ξανθικῇ ἡμέρᾳ Αὐδυναίου μηνὸς, ἀνὰ τὴν πεμπτὴν καὶ ἐβδομηκοστὴν, ᾗ Πενταχοσιοστῷ ἔτῳ τῶν χρηματιζων τῆς Αντιοχείας]. Evagrius, Ecclesiastical History, Book 4, chapter 9. If you find the place of this year in the Julian period, add 575 to 4664; the sum, 5239, is the Julian year in whose course the proposed year 575 began, from autumn. But the month Xanthicus, or April, in whose first days the emperor was announced, falls in the Julian year 5240. Subtract 4713, and you have the year of Christ 527, in whose course these things were done.

units.la: XI. Ab Urbe Antiochiâ deducitur Æra quæ ab eâ Antiochena vocatur.
units.tr: XI. The Era called Antiochene is derived from the City of Antioch.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAP. XIV.

units.la: De olympiadibus, & agonibus Capitolinis.
units.tr: On the Olympiads and the Capitoline games.

units.la: Res à quibus deducuntur Epochæ, sunt vel institutæ vel gestæ. II. Res institutæ sunt Agones. III. Agones sunt vel olympiaci, vel Capitolini. IV. Agones olympiaci, sive olympiades ab Iphito instituebantur.
units.tr: The events from which eras are reckoned are either instituted or accomplished. II. Instituted events are the games. III. Games are either Olympic or Capitoline. IV. The Olympic games, or Olympiads, were instituted by Iphitus.

units.la: 1. A Nte Iphitum, fateor, Hercules non Poeticus Jovis & Alcmenæ filius, sed qui ex Idæis Dactylis erat, ut & Æthlius, aliique Agones olympiaces celebrâsse perhibentur. Anni tamen ab iis computari priùs non coeperunt, quàm ab Iphito vel instituti vel saltèm restituti sunt, postquam diù fuissent intermissi. Ex hujus autem instituto quadriennio quolibet vertente, vel quod idem est, quinto quovis redeunte anno celebrata sunt hæc certamina de quibus non inepte Pindarus Od. I.
units.tr: 1. Before Iphitus, I admit, Hercules (not the poetic son of Jupiter and Alcmena, but the one who was among the Idaean Dactyls), and also Aethlius and others, are said to have celebrated Olympic games. Yet years were not begun to be reckoned from these games until they had been either instituted or at least restored by Iphitus, after being discontinued for a long time. From his institution these contests were celebrated every four years, or, what comes to the same thing, in every fifth year as it returns. Pindar aptly speaks of them in Ode 1:

units.la: Οὐτ' ὀλυμπίας 'Αγῶνα ἀμείνονʼ ἀνδρῶν ἀγῶνα. Neque ullum certamen olympiaco Præstantius tanemus.
units.tr: Οὐτ' ὀλυμπίας 'Αγῶνα ἀμείνονʼ ἀνδρῶν ἀγῶνα. [Neither do we sing of any contest more excellent than the Olympic contest of men.]

units.la: Rectè quidem. Hæc enim certamina totius Græcorum historiæ sunt basis unica & fundamentum; unde tempora hæc præcedentia μυθ non immeritò appellavit Varro.
units.tr: Rightly so. For these contests are the one basis and foundation of the whole history of the Greeks; hence Varro not unfittingly called the times preceding them mythical.

units.la: 2. Peracta sunt hæc certamina in campis Olympiæ, (unde denominantur) quæ Eleæ regionis urbs est, vicinis juxta Alphæum flumen, ubi Græciæ juventus pentathlo, nimirùm Cœstibus, Cursu, disco, saltu, & palestrâ decertabat.
units.tr: 2. These contests were held in the plains of Olympia, which gave them their name. Olympia is a city of the region of Elis, near the river Alpheus, where the youth of Greece competed in the pentathlon, namely boxing, running, the discus, leaping and wrestling.

units.la: Victor, olympionices dictus oleastro tandem coronatus fuit, quod iis majus judicabatur, quàm Romæ triumphare. Primus qui stadio vicit erat Coræbus Elæus, primus autem, quem Consulto priùs Apolline coronabant, Diocles Messenius, septimus ordine olympionices.
units.tr: The victor, called an olympionices, was at last crowned with wild olive, which was judged greater than triumphing at Rome. The first to win the foot race was Coroebus of Elis. The first whom they crowned, by the prior counsel of Apollo, was Diocles of Messene, the seventh in order of Olympic victors.

units.la: V. Prima olympias celebrata fuit anno per. Jul. 3938, cy- clo Solis 18, Lunæ 5, Indict. 8, plenilunio Solstitium æstivum subsequente.
units.tr: V. The first Olympiad was celebrated in the year of the Julian period 3938, solar cycle 18, lunar cycle 5, indiction 8, with the summer solstice following the full moon.

units.la: 1. Olympiaca hæc certamina quinque dies perdurabant, juxta quinque Gymnasticorum exercitiorum numerum, quibus certatum est; quorum ultimus in plenilunium incidebat, & proximo die judicium de victoriâ ferebatur, unde Scholiastes in Pindari oden 3. Ἐπὶ δὲ τῇ πανσελήνῳ ἡ ὀλυμπιακὸς ἀγὼν ἄγεται, ᾧ τῇ ἱκανωτάτῃ γνῶσιν ... Quippe in plenilunio agon olympiacus celebratur, & decimâ sextâ Lunâ judicium committitur.
units.tr: 1. These Olympic contests lasted five days, corresponding to the number of the five gymnastic exercises in which they competed. The last of these fell on the full moon, and on the next day the judgment of the victory was pronounced, whence the scholiast on Pindar's third ode says: [Ἐπὶ δὲ τῇ πανσελήνῳ ἡ ὀλυμπιακὸς ἀγὼν ἄγεται...]. For the Olympic contest is held at the full moon, and on the sixteenth day of the moon the judgment is committed.

units.la: 2. Istud autem plenilunium hisce celebritatibus observatum fuit, quod Solstitium æstivum dies Jul. 8 tunc temporis fixum, proximè sequebatur, utpote à cujus Neomeniâ annus eorum deductus fuit. At anno per. Jul. 2938, ista Neomenia Jul. 9. commissa est; cœptus est ergò primus agon Jul. 19, finitus Jul. 23, & proximâ die, ut sextadecimâ Lunâ, sententia pronunciabatur. Et ad eundem modum omnes olympiades succedentes proximis post Solstitium æstivum plenilunis celebratæ sunt, unde & anni olympiaci supputandi.
units.tr: 2. Now this full moon was observed in these festivities because it closely followed the summer solstice, which at that time was fixed on July 8, since their year was reckoned from its new moon. But in the year 3938 of the Julian period, that new moon fell on July 9; the first contest therefore began on July 19 and ended on July 23, and on the next day, the sixteenth day of the moon, the sentence was pronounced. In the same way all the following Olympiads were celebrated at the full moons next after the summer solstice, and from this the Olympic years are also reckoned.

units.la: VI. Propositio quolibet anno olympiaco, olympiades completas multiplices in 4, productò addas propositum olympiadis currentis annum, aggregato adjicias 3937, summa est annus per. Jul. quo currente quæsitus init.
units.tr: VI. For any Olympic year, multiply the completed olympiads by 4, add to the product the year of the current olympiad, and to the sum add 3937; the result is the Julian period year in which the year sought begins.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Phlegon Trallianus Hadriani libertus, teste Eusebio in Chron. Gr. p. 188. ait, Τῷ δὲ ἔτει τῆς σθ' ὀλυμπιάδος ἐγένετο ἔκλειψις ἡλίου μεγίστη τῶν ἐγνωσμένων πρότερον, ᾗ τῆς ἡμέρας ἐγένετο ... ὥστε ᾗ ἀπέχει ἐν ἐγγὺς φαίνεται; l. c. ut transfert transfert Hieronymus, Quarto autem anno olympiadis 202, Magna & excellens inter omnes quæ ante eam acciderant, defectio Solis facta, dies horâ sextâ ita in tenebrosam noctem versus, ut stellæ in Cælo visæ sunt: (unde patet pro τῷ Ν ἔτει, ut in exemplari Græco legitur, nos rectè substituisse τῷ δ' ἔτι) Si scire cupias in quotum annum per. Jul. annus hic quartus olymp. 202 concurrat, olympiades completas 201 ducas in 4, producto 804, addas annum currentis olympiadis sive 4, aggregato adjicias 3937, summa 4745 est annus per. Jul. quo currente quartus hic annus olymp. 202 incepit.
units.tr: 1. For example, Phlegon of Tralles, freedman of Hadrian, according to Eusebius in the Greek Chronicle, p. 188, says: [Τῷ δὲ ἔτει τῆς σθ' ὀλυμπιάδος ἐγένετο ἔκλειψις ἡλίου μεγίστη τῶν ἐγνωσμένων πρότερον...]. Jerome translates it: "But in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad, a great and remarkable eclipse of the sun occurred, greater than all those that had happened before it: at the sixth hour of the day, the day turned into dark night, so that the stars were seen in the sky." From this it is clear that, for the Greek reading "in the 50th year" (as it is read in the Greek copy), we rightly substituted "in the fourth year." If you wish to know in which year of the Julian period this fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad falls, multiply the completed 201 olympiads by 4, giving 804; add the year of the current olympiad, that is 4, giving 808; to this add 3937. The sum, 4745, is the Julian period year in which this fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad began.

units.la: 2. Josephus contra Apion. l. 1. hæc habet; ᾿Αλεξανδρέων δὲ πάντως ὁμολογεῖται ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκλείψεως πεπληρωκέναι ὀλυμπιάδα, Alexandrum verò profitentur omnes mortuum suisse olympiade 114, viz. ineunte, adeò ut olympiades 113 elapsæ sunt, & primus annus olymp. 114 currebat. Ergo 113 multiplices in 4, producto unitate auctô ob annum primum currentem, putâ 453 adjice 3937, aggregatum 4390 est annus per. Jul. quo olympias 114 celebrata fuit.
units.tr: 2. Josephus, in Against Apion, book 1, has this: all the Alexandrians agree that Alexander died in the 114th Olympiad, at its beginning. So 113 Olympiads had elapsed, and the first year of the 114th Olympiad was running. Therefore multiply 113 by 4, giving 452; increase this by one for the current first year, making 453; add 3937. The sum, 4390, is the Julian period year in which the 114th Olympiad was celebrated. [Ὁμολογεῖται ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκλείψεως πεπληρωκέναι ὀλυμπιάδα.]

units.la: 3. Bellum Peloponesiacum, ut testantur Diodorus & Thucydides, cœpit anno secundo olymp. 87, ducas 86 in 4, producto 344, addas 2, propter annum currentis olympiadis propositum, summæ 346 adjice 3937, aggregatum 4283 est annus per. Jul. quo currente propositus incepit, à Solstitio circiter æstivo.
units.tr: 3. The Peloponnesian War, as Diodorus and Thucydides attest, began in the second year of the 87th Olympiad. Multiply 86 by 4, giving 344; add 2 for the year of the current olympiad in question, giving 346; add 3937. The sum, 4283, is the Julian period year in which the war began, at about the summer solstice.

units.la: 4. Anni olympiaci nonnunquam non per olympiades sed collecti numerantur, ut quando pro olympiade unâ scribuntur anni quatuor, pro olympiadibus 15 anni 60, pro olymp. 18 anno secundo, annus olympiacus 70. Hæc dicitur Æra Iphiti, sive anni Iphitei, propterea quòd ab olympiade primâ ab Iphito restaurata incipiunt, & in hisce quidem annis multiplicatione non opus est, ut qui nobis multiplicantur. Numerus igitur annorum propositus addendus est tantùm ad 3937, ut annum per. Jul. consequamur. Ex. gr. Censorinus c. 21. scribit se scripsisse anno ab olympiade primâ millesimo & quartodecimo. Igitur ad 3937, addas 1014, summa 4951 est annus per. Jul. quo scribebat.
units.tr: 4. Olympic years are sometimes numbered not by olympiads but as a collected total: for example, four years for one olympiad, 60 years for 15 olympiads, or the second year of the 18th olympiad as Olympic year 70. This is called the Era of Iphitus, or the years of Iphitus, because they begin from the first olympiad restored by Iphitus. In these years no multiplication is needed, as we have just seen. So the stated number of years need only be added to 3937 to reach the Julian period year. For example, Censorinus, chapter 21, writes that he wrote in the 1014th year from the first Olympiad. Add 1014 to 3937; the sum, 4951, is the Julian period year in which he was writing.

units.la: VII. Si proposito anno per. Jul. annum olympiacum ei respondentem invenires, ex anno dato subduc 3937, annos reliquos divide per 4, quotus olympiades elapsas, residuum annum currentis olympiadis exhibebit.
units.tr: VII. If, for a given Julian period year, you wish to find the corresponding Olympic year, subtract 3937 from the given year, divide the remaining years by 4; the quotient shows the olympiads elapsed, and the remainder shows the year of the current olympiad.

units.la: I. Ex. gr. Proponatur annus per. Jul. 4714, qui primus erat Æræ Christianæ, ex annis 4714, subduc 3937, reliquos 777 per 4 divide, quotiens est 194, residuum 1. Ergo olympiades 194 completæ sunt, & primus annus olymp. 195 currebat.
units.tr: 1. For example, let the Julian period year 4714, which was the first year of the Christian Era, be proposed. Subtract 3937 from 4714; divide the remaining 777 by 4. The quotient is 194, the remainder 1. Therefore 194 olympiads were completed, and the first year of the 195th Olympiad was running.

units.la: 2. Annus quo hæc commentor est per. Jul. 6380, aufer 3937, reliqui 2443 per 4 divisi in quoto dant 610, in residuo 3. Ergo hoc anno tertius olymp. 611 incipit à Solstitio circiter æstivo.
units.tr: 2. The year in which I write this is Julian period 6380. Take away 3937; the remainder, 2443, divided by 4, gives 610 as quotient and 3 as remainder. Therefore in this year the third year of the 611th Olympiad begins, at about the summer solstice.

units.la: VIII. Agones Capitolini à Domitiano sunt instituti.
units.tr: VIII. The Capitoline games were instituted by Domitian.

units.la: I. De hoc Domitiani instituto sic Suetonius, Instituit & quinquennale certamen Capitolino Jovi, triplex Musicum, Equestre, Gymnicum, & aliquanto plurium quàm nunc est coronatorum. Certabatur etiam & prosâ oratione, Græce, Latinéque, ac præter Citharædos, Chorocitharistas quoque. & Psallocitharistas. Suet. in Fl. Domit. c. 4. Fuerunt igitur hæc certamina olympiadum ad instar quarto quovis anno completo, vel ineunte quinto celebrata. Quinetiam Imperatores Romanos hisce celebritatibus præsidere solitos testis est Herodianus l. 1.
units.tr: 1. Suetonius describes this institution of Domitian thus: "He also instituted a contest every five years for Jupiter Capitolinus, in three parts: musical, equestrian and gymnastic, with somewhat more crowned victors than now. There was also a contest in prose oratory, in Greek and in Latin, and besides cithara singers, there were also choral citharists and psalm citharists." (Suetonius, Domitian, ch. 4.) These contests were therefore celebrated like the Olympiads, every fourth year completed, or beginning the fifth. Herodian, book 1, also attests that Roman emperors were accustomed to preside over these festivities.

units.la: IX. Primus Agon Capitolinus institutus est anno per. Jul. 4799, Christi 86, cyclo Solis 11, Lunæ 11, Indict. 14.
units.tr: IX. The first Capitoline games were instituted in the year of the Julian period 4799, the year of Christ 86, solar cycle 11, lunar cycle 11, indiction 14.

units.la: X. Proposito igitur anno Capitolino adde 4798, Summa est annus per. Jul. in quem concurrit, vel addas 85, & habebis annum Christi.
units.tr: X. Therefore, to a given Capitoline year add 4798; the sum is the Julian period year in which it falls. Or add 85, and you have the year of Christ.

units.la: I. Ex. gr. Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. h. 1. dicit, Ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης ἀγῶνος ἐπὶ τὴν Κομμόδου πεντηκοστὴν ἐπὶ ἑκατὸν ἑπτὰ, A primo mo autem certamine (viz. Capitolino) usque ad Commodi mortem anni sunt centum undecim. Ad iii adde 4748, summa 4909 est annus Per. Jul. quocum init annus hic descriptus, viz. à Kal. Jan. vel ad iii adde 85, & habebis annum Christi 196 ei respondentem.
units.tr: 1. For example, Clement of Alexandria, Stromata book 1, says: "From the first contest (namely the Capitoline) to the death of Commodus there are one hundred and eleven years." [Ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης ἀγῶνος ἐπὶ τὴν Κομμόδου πεντηκοστὴν ἐπὶ ἑκατὸν ἑπτὰ.] Add 4798 to 111; the sum, 4909, is the Julian period year with which this year, reckoned from 1 January, begins. Or add 85 to 111, and you have the year of Christ 196 corresponding to it.

units.la: 2. Si agones, non anni collecti, describuntur, eodem modo procedendum est, quo in Olympiadibus. Ex. gr. Censorinus ait, Itaque hoc nunc anno qui celebratus est Agon, undequadragesimus numeratur, viz. Agon Capitolinus, de quo loquitur Cens. c. 18. Si ex hoc charactere annum Christi quo Censorinus haec scribebat, investigare libitum fuerit, multiplices Agones completos 38 in 4, producto unitate aucto (propterea quòd undequadragesimus jam Agon celebratus est, vel quod idem est, primus Agonis 39 iniit) addas 85, summa 238 est annus Christi quaesitus.
units.tr: 2. If contests, rather than collected years, are described, the same method must be followed as with the Olympiads. For example, Censorinus says: Therefore in this year, in which the games have been celebrated, it is counted as the thirty-ninth, namely the Capitoline games, of which Censorinus speaks in chapter 18. If you wish to find from this mark the year of Christ in which Censorinus wrote these words, multiply the 38 completed contests by 4, add 1 to the product (because the thirty-ninth contest has already been celebrated, or, what is the same, the first year of the thirty-ninth contest has begun), and add 85. The sum, 238, is the year of Christ sought.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: De Annis Julianis, Æra Hispanica, & Actiaca Victoria.
units.tr: On the Julian Years, the Spanish Era, and the Victory at Actium.

units.la: Res gestæ, quæ Epochis constituendis occasionem præbuerunt, sunt Juliana anni correctio, & Actiaca Victoria.
units.tr: The events which provided occasion for fixing epochs are the Julian correction of the year and the victory at Actium.

units.la: II. A Juliana anni correctione duplex exurgit epoch, Editio Juliana, & Æra Hispanica.
units.tr: II. From the Julian correction of the year arise a double epoch: the Julian Edition and the Spanish Era.

units.la: III. Editio Juliana (qui & Anni Juliani appellantur) coepit Kal. Jan. anno Per. Jul. 4669, ante Christum 45, cyclo Solis 21, Lunæ 14, Indict. 4.
units.tr: III. The Julian Edition (which are also called the Julian Years) began on 1 January in the year of the Julian Period 4669, before Christ 45, solar cycle 21, lunar cycle 14, indiction 4.

units.la: I. ANnus quo Julius Cæsar Dictator anno Romano castigando operam locavit, erat Per. Jul. 4668, qui & Annus Confusionis vocatur, ut dier. 445. Anni vero juliani non ab ipso Confusionis anno procedunt, sed à proximo ineunte.
units.tr: I. The year in which Julius Caesar the Dictator undertook the work of correcting the Roman year was the year 4668 of the Julian Period, which is also called the Year of Confusion, as of 445 days. The Julian years, however, do not proceed from the Year of Confusion itself, but from the next year, which begins.

units.la: IV. Proposito anno Juliano adde 4668, & habebis annum Per. Jul. ei congruentem: vel abjice 45, & numerus residuus est annus Christi.
units.tr: IV. To a given Julian year add 4668, and you will have the year of the Julian Period corresponding to it; or subtract 45, and the remainder is the year of Christ.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Censorinus egregium suum de die natali libellum commentatus est, se teste c. 21. anno Juliano 283 adde 4668, summa 4951 est annus Per. Jul. ei respondens. Vel abjice 45, & reliquus fit annus Christi 238, quo Censorinum scripsisse consentiunt universi.
units.tr: 1. For example, Censorinus, as he testifies in c. 21, was working on his excellent little book on birthdays in the Julian year 283. Add 4668 to 283, and the sum 4951 is the corresponding year of the Julian Period. Or subtract 45, and the remainder is the year of Christ 238, which everyone agrees is the year in which Censorinus wrote.

units.la: V. Æra Hispanica cæpit anno Per. Jul. 4676, ante Chri- stum 38, cyclo Solis 28, Lunæ 2, Indict. II.
units.tr: V. The Spanish Era began in the year of the Julian Period 4676, before Christ 38, solar cycle 28, lunar cycle 2, indiction 2.

units.la: 1. Anni hujus epochæ iidem prorsus sunt atque Juliani, nisi quòd in Hispaniam septem annis completis serius quàm Romæ sunt introducti.
units.tr: 1. The years of this epoch are exactly the same as the Julian years, except that they were introduced into Spain seven years later than at Rome.

units.la: 2. Hæc æra frequens occurrit in antiquis Hispaniæ monumentis, & à Conciliis Hispanicis usitata. Aliquoties simpliciter vocatur Æra, sive Era.
units.tr: 2. This era frequently occurs in ancient Spanish monuments and is used by the Spanish Councils. Sometimes it is simply called Era, or Era.

units.la: VI. Proposito anno Æræ Hispanicæ adjice 4675 summa est annus Per. Jul. vel abjice 38, & reliquus fit annus æræ Christianæ, quo cum init.
units.tr: VI. To a given year of the Spanish Era add 4675; the sum is the year of the Julian Period. Or subtract 38, and the remainder is the year of the Christian era in which it begins.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. In Præfatione ad Concilium Carthaginiense quartum hæc invenies; Concilium Carthaginiense nomine & temporis ordine quartum, habitum ab episcopis 214, æra 436. v. Bin. Concil. tom. 1. p. 587. edit. Col. Agrip. Si annum Per. Jul. vel Christi huic respondentem desideres, ad 436 adde 4675, summa 5111 est annus Per. Jul. quæsitus. Vel ex 436 abjice 38, & reliquus fit annus æræ Christianæ 398; à cujus initio, viz. Kal. Jan. annus hic procedit.
units.tr: 1. For example, in the preface to the Fourth Council of Carthage you will find this: The Council of Carthage, fourth in name and in order of time, held by 214 bishops, in the era 436. See Binius, Councils, vol. 1, p. 587, Cologne edition. If you wish the year of the Julian Period or of Christ corresponding to this, add 4675 to 436; the sum 5111 is the year of the Julian Period sought. Or subtract 38 from 436, and the remainder is the year 398 of the Christian era, from whose beginning, namely 1 January, this year proceeds.

units.la: VII. Æra Actiacæ Victoriæ cæpit Aug. 29. anno Per. Jul. 4684, ante Christum 30, cyclo Solis 8, Lunæ 10, Indict. 4.
units.tr: VII. The Actian Victory era began on 29 August in the year of the Julian Period 4684, before Christ 30, solar cycle 8, lunar cycle 10, indiction 4.

units.la: 1. Hæc æra denominatur à victoriâ quâ Antonius & Cleopatra ab Augusto navali certamine victi sunt, ad Acti-um um Epiri promontorium, ubi Augustus urbem condidit, & Nicopolin ab eâdem victoriâ denominavit.
units.tr: 1. This era is named from the victory by which Antony and Cleopatra were defeated by Augustus in the naval battle off Actium, a promontory of Epirus, where Augustus founded a city and named Nicopolis after the same victory.

units.la: 2. Non inchoatur autem hæc æra ab ipso die nec anno quo parta fuit hæc victoria, sed ab anno subsequente, & quidem Aug. 29. in quem in anno Nabonasareo neomenia Thoth incidit, à quo die Anni Actiaci perpetuò computantur, istis exceptis qui annos Ægyptiacos intercalares sex epagomenis præditos statim excipientes, Aug. 30. incipiunt. Vocantur autem hi anni Actiaci, etiam Ægyptiaci, ut & Augustorum anni.
units.tr: 2. This era does not begin from the very day or year in which the victory was won, but from the following year, namely on 29 August, on which day the new moon of Thoth fell in the Nabonassarean year; from this day the Actian years are reckoned continuously, except for those Egyptian years with six intercalary epagomenal days, which begin on 30 August immediately after them. These years are called Actian, also Egyptian, and also years of the Augusti.

units.la: VIII. Anno Actiaco proposito adjungas 4683; summa est annus Per. Jul. vel demas 30, & reliquus fit annus æræ Christianæ quo currente cœpit.
units.tr: VIII. To a given Actian year add 4683; the sum is the year of the Julian Period. Or subtract 30, and the remainder is the year of the Christian era in whose course it began.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Censorinus libello suo incubuit scribendo, se teste, Augustorum anno 267, Cens. c. 21. ad 267 adde 4683, summa 4950 est annus Per. Jul. vel abjice 30, residuus 237 est annus Christi, quo currente cœpit annus ille Actiacus 267 ab Aug. 29. desiit autem Aug. 28. anno proximo, sive Per. Jul. 4951, Christi 238.
units.tr: 1. For example, Censorinus, as he testifies, was busy writing his book in the 267th year of the Augusti, Cens. c. 21. Add 4683 to 267, and the sum 4950 is the year of the Julian Period; or subtract 30, and the remainder 237 is the year of Christ in whose course that Actian year 267 began on 29 August. It ended on 28 August of the following year, that is, the Julian Period year 4951, Christ 238.

units.la: 2. Josephus etiam his annis aliquoties utitur, qui tamen cum aliis nonnullis, ab ipso anno Per. Jul. 4683, quo superatus est ad Actium Antonius eos computat, quod admonendum censui, nè anni Actiaci cum annis ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν Ἀκτίῳ μάχης numeratis confunderentur.
units.tr: 2. Josephus also uses these years several times, but he, along with some others, reckons them from the year of the Julian Period 4683, in which Antony was defeated at Actium. I thought this worth noting, lest the Actian years be confused with years counted from the battle at Actium, ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν Ἀκτίῳ μάχης.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: De Epocha Nabonasarea, Philippea, Ale- xandrea, & Yezdegirdica.
units.tr: On the Nabonassarean, Philippean, Alexandrian and Yezdegirdic Epochs.

units.la: Epochæ à Personis denominatæ sunt Nabonasarea, Philippea, Alexandrea, & Yezdegirdica.
units.tr: Epochs are named after persons: the Nabonassarean, the Philippean, the Alexandrian and the Yezdegirdic.

units.la: II. Epocha Nabonasarea computatur à Nabonasaro primo Babyloniorum rege.
units.tr: II. The Nabonassarean epoch is reckoned from Nabonassar, the first king of the Babylonians.

units.la: I. IN mathematico regum Babyloniorum canone Nabonasarus familiam ducit, à cujus imperio ineunte Chaldæi & Ægyptii annos suos numerabant, sed Ægyptiacos vagos, dierum præcisè 365 sine horis appendicibus, quo fit ut anni Nabonasarei 1461 Julianos efficiant tantum 1460.
units.tr: I. In the mathematical canon of the kings of Babylon, Nabonassar heads the list. From the beginning of his reign the Chaldeans and Egyptians counted their years. The Egyptian years, however, were wandering years of exactly 365 days, without the extra hours, so that 1461 Nabonassarean years make only 1460 Julian years.

units.la: 2. Hæc quidem Epocha nihil in totâ chronologiâ celebrius, nihil cognitu magis necessarium, utpote qui exactissimus est temporum character, fallere nescius.
units.tr: 2. This epoch is indeed the most celebrated of all in chronology and the most necessary to know, since it is the most exact mark of time and cannot deceive.

units.la: III. Cœpit hæc æra Feb.26. anno Per. Jul. 3967, cyclo Solis 19, Lunæ 15, Indict. 7.
units.tr: III. This era began on 26 February in the year of the Julian period 3967, solar cycle 19, lunar cycle 15, indiction 7.

units.la: IV. Si dato igitur anno Nabonasareo annum Per. Jul. quo currente iniit haberes, ab anno Nabonasareo primo usque ad 127 adjice 3966, summa est annus Per. Jul. quæsitus.
units.tr: IV. So if, given a Nabonassarean year, you want the Julian period year in which it began, add 3966 to the Nabonassarean year, for years from the first up to 127; the sum is the Julian period year sought.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Ptolemæus ait lunam defecisse πῆ ἐτῇ Ναβο-πολασσάρου ὀ ἔκτῳ, ἐν ᾧ ἐτει Ναβονασάρου, Quinto anno Nabopollasari, qui est 127 à Nabonasaro. Ptol.l.5. p.125. ed Gr. Si annum Per.Jul. quæras, quo currente annus hic Nabonasareus 127 incepit, ad 127 adde 3966, summa 4093 est annus Per.Jul. quæsitus. Verùm quoto anni hujusce die cœpit propositus iste Nabonasareus, è primo harum institutionum libro, cap.10. petendum est.
units.tr: 1. For example, Ptolemy says that the moon was eclipsed in the sixth year of Nabopolassar, which is the year of Nabonassar [πῆ ἐτῇ Ναβοπολασσάρου ὀ ἔκτῳ, ἐν ᾧ ἐτει Ναβονασάρου], that is, in the fifth year of Nabopolassar, which is the 127th from Nabonassar. Ptol. lib. 5, p. 125, Greek edition. If you seek the Julian period year in which this 127th Nabonassarean year began, add 3966 to 127; the sum, 4093, is the Julian period year sought. But on what day of the year this Nabonassarean year began, one must look in chapter 10 of the first book of these Institutions.

units.la: V. Anno Nabonasareo proposito à 227, ad 1688 adjice 3965, vel ab 1688 ad 3149 adde 3964, & summa erit annus Per. Jul. quo cœptus est.
units.tr: V. For a proposed Nabonassarean year from 227 up to 1688, add 3965; or for a year from 1688 up to 3149, add 3964. The sum will be the Julian period year in which it began.

units.la: 1. Annus, ut dixi, primus Nabonasareus cœpit Feb. 26. at quoniam neomenia Thoth, sive initium anni Ægyptiaci per totum annum Julianum vagatur, & propter omissam quadriennio quolibet vertente diem intercalarem toto die retroagitur. Hinc annus Nabonasareus 227 ad Jan. 1. retroversus est, & annis proximis 1461, viz usque ad annum Nabonasari 1688, alius annus retrò peragratur. Nam annus 228 incepit Dec. 31. annus 232 Dec. 30. annus 236 Dec.29,& sic paulatim ad Kal.Jan. annis 1461 regreditur, & neomenia Thoth anno Nabonasari 1688 in Kal. Jan. iterum incidit. Et eâdem ratione annus etiam Nabonasari 3149 ibidem incipiet, ut qui annus est 1461 post 1688. Et hinc est quod annis quibuslibet 1461 vertentibus, annus unus à primo anno Per. Jul. quo Nabonasarei cœperunt, eximendus est, ut annorum Nabonasareorum in Periodo Juliana sedem inveniamus.
units.tr: 1. The first Nabonassarean year, as I said, began on 26 February. But since the new moon of Thoth, that is, the beginning of the Egyptian year, wanders through the whole Julian year, and because of the intercalary day omitted every four years, it is pushed back by a whole day. Hence the Nabonassarean year 227 is turned back to 1 January, and through the following 1461 years, that is, up to the Nabonassarean year 1688, another year is traversed backwards. For year 228 began on 31 December, year 232 on 30 December, year 236 on 29 December, and so gradually it returns to 1 January after 1461 years, and the new moon of Thoth again falls on 1 January in Nabonassarean year 1688. By the same reasoning the year 3149 also begins on that day, since it is the 1461st year after 1688. And hence it is that, whenever 1461 years have passed, one year must be removed from the Julian period year in which the Nabonassarean years began, so that we may find the places of the Nabonassarean years in the Julian period.

units.la: 2. Ex. gr. Ptolemæus refert lunam defecisse anno Nabonasari 366, Thoth 27. Ptol.l.4. p.105. videamus in quotum annum Per. Jul. neomenia Thoth hoc anno proposito inciderit. Annus 366 inter 227 & 1688 fluebat. Igitur ad 366 adjice 3965, summa 4331 est annus Per. Jul. quæsitus.
units.tr: 2. For example, Ptolemy reports that the moon was eclipsed in Nabonassarean year 366, Thoth 27. Let us see in what Julian period year the new moon of Thoth fell in this proposed year. Year 366 falls between 227 and 1688. So add 3965 to 366; the sum, 4331, is the Julian period year sought.

units.la: 3. Si proponatur annus Nabonasari 2350, adjiciendum est tantùm 3964, propterea quòd annus hic propositus sequatur annum 1688, & præcedit 3149. Porrò 2350 & 3964 collecti dant annum Per.Jul. 6314, quo currente annus propositus inivit, cujus neomenia Thoth methodo primo libro tradita inveniatur.
units.tr: 3. If the Nabonassarean year 2350 is proposed, only 3964 need be added, because this year follows 1688 and precedes 3149. Moreover, 2350 and 3964 together give the Julian period year 6314, in which the proposed year began. Its new moon of Thoth is found by the method given in the first book.

units.la: VI. Si annos Per. Jul. ad Nabonasareos è contra revoca- res, hàc utaris methodo. Si numerus annorum in Per.Jul major sit quàm 3967, & minor quàm 4193,
units.tr: VI. If you wish to convert Julian period years back into Nabonassarean ones, use this method. If the number of years in the Julian period is greater than 3967 and less than 4193,

units.la: de anno proposito subtrahas 3966 ; si major quàm 4193, & minor quàm 5653, demas 3965 ; si major quàm 5653, & minor quàm 7112, abjicias 3964, numerus è quâvis subtractione residuus est annus Nabonasari quaesitus.
units.tr: subtract 3966 from the year proposed; if it is greater than 4193 and less than 5653, take away 3965; if it is greater than 5653 and less than 7112, cast off 3964. The number left over from whichever subtraction applies is the Nabonassarean year sought.

units.la: 1. Haec methodus reducendi annos Per. Jul. ad Nabonasareos ex iisdem petitur principiis, ac prior quâ Nabonasari ad Julianos revocantur.
units.tr: 1. This method of reducing Julian period years to Nabonassarean ones rests on the same principles as the earlier method by which Nabonassarean years are turned into Julian ones.

units.la: 2. Ex.gr. Esto annus Per. Jul. 4714, qui primus est aerae Christianae. Hic annorum numerus major est quàm 4193, minor quàm 5653 ; quocirca ex 4714 subduc 3965, reliduum est 749. Ergò anno Per. Jul. 4714 annus Nabonasareus 749 exortus est.
units.tr: 2. For example, let the Julian period year be 4714, which is the first of the Christian era. This number is greater than 4193 and less than 5653; therefore subtract 3965 from 4714. The remainder is 749. Therefore in the Julian period year 4714 the Nabonassarean year 749 arose.

units.la: 3. Quaeramus etiam quotus annus Nabonasareus hoc anno Christi 1667 incipiat. Hic est annus Per. Jul. 6380, qui major est 5653, minor 7113 ; auser itaque 3964 ex 6380, & reliquus sit annus Nabonasari 2416, anno praesenti oriturus.
units.tr: 3. Let us also ask which Nabonassarean year begins in this year of Christ 1667. This is the Julian period year 6380, which is greater than 5653 and less than 7113. Subtract 3964 from 6380, and the remainder, the Nabonassarean year 2416, will begin in the present year.

units.la: 4. Ob eandem etiam rationem post annum Per. Jul. 7113 usque ad 8573, anni tantùm 3963 ex anno Per. Jul. propositio subducendi sunt, ut annus Nabonasareus habeatur. Reliqua ad annos hosce Nabonasareos spectantia libro primo cap. 10. traduntur.
units.tr: 4. For the same reason, after the Julian period year 7113 up to 8573, only 3963 need be subtracted from the proposed Julian period year to obtain the Nabonassarean year. The rest concerning these Nabonassarean years is handed down in book 1, chapter 10.

units.la: VII. Epocha Philippea a Philippo Aridaeo Alexandri Magni fratre cognominatur.
units.tr: VII. The Philippean era takes its name from Philip Arrhidaeus, brother of Alexander the Great.

units.la: 1. Post excessum Alexandri Magni, Aridaeus Philippi Amintae filii & Alexandri patris, filius ex pellice, atque adeò frater Alexandri Macedonum consensu in imperium provectus est, & Philippus etiam cognominatus. Ab hoc Philippo deducuntur anni qui vulgò Philippei vocantur, non à Philippo Alexandri Magni patre. Caeterùm anni hi Philippei sunt omnimodò Nabonasarei tardiùs incepti.
units.tr: 1. After the death of Alexander the Great, Arrhidaeus, the son of Philip, son of Amyntas, and the son of a concubine, and therefore the brother of Alexander, was raised to the throne by the consent of the Macedonians, and he was also called Philip. The years commonly called Philippean are dated from this Philip, not from Philip, the father of Alexander the Great. These Philippean years, however, always began later than the Nabonassarean.

units.la: VIII. Primus annus Philippeus iniit Nov. 12, anno Per. Jul. 4390, cyclo Solis 22, Lunae 1, Indict. 10. una cum anno Nabonasareo 425. 1. Anniv. Anni Philippei ab excessu Alexandri Magni supputantur. Obiit ille anno Per. Jul. 4390, mense Julio, anno Nabonasareo 424 currente, Nov. 12. sequente annus Nabonasareus 425 iniit, & unà cum eo primus Philippeus.
units.tr: VIII. The first Philippean year began on 12 November, in the Julian Period year 4390, solar cycle 22, lunar cycle 1, indiction 10, together with the Nabonassarean year 425. 1. The years of Philip are reckoned from the death of Alexander the Great. He died in the Julian Period year 4390, in July, while the Nabonassarean year 424 was running. On 12 November the following Nabonassarean year 425 began, and with it the first Philippean year.

units.la: IX. Ad annum igitur Philippeum propositum adjice 424, summa est annus Nabonasarcus, cui respondet & concurrit.
units.tr: IX. Therefore, add 424 to the Philippean year in question; the sum is the Nabonassarean year to which it corresponds and with which it coincides.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Censorinus refert se libellum suum exarasse anno Philippeo 562 hisce verbis; Item Philippi, qui ab excessu Alexandri Magni numerantur, & ad hunc usque perductì annos quingentos, sexaginta duos consummant. Censor. c. 21. Igitur ad 562 adjicias 424, summa 986 est annus Nabonasareus ei congruus: quem methodo superius tradita ad annum Per. Jul. revocare licet. Hic enim annus sequitur 227, & praecedit 1688; igitur ad 986 adjice 3965, summa 4951 est annus Per. Jul. quo annus Nabonasareus 986, & Philippeus 562, simul inierunt.
units.tr: 1. For example, Censorinus reports that he wrote his little book in the Philippean year 562, in these words: Likewise the years of Philip, which are counted from the death of Alexander the Great and extend down to this point, make up five hundred and sixty-two. Censorinus, ch. 21. So add 424 to 562; the sum, 986, is the corresponding Nabonassarean year. By the method given above, this can be converted to the Julian Period. This year follows 227 and precedes 1688; so add 3965 to 986, and the sum, 4951, is the Julian Period year in which the Nabonassarean year 986 and the Philippean year 562 began together.

units.la: 2. Albatenius celeberrimus Arabum Astronomus ab eadem epochâ, viz. Morte Alexandri Annos Ægyptiacos fixos aliquando deducit, & quidem à Kal. Octob. quod non praetereundum censui.
units.tr: 2. Albategnius, the most celebrated of the Arab astronomers, sometimes reckons Egyptian fixed years from this same epoch, namely the death of Alexander, and indeed from 1 October. I did not think this should be passed over.

units.la: X. Æra Alexandrea ab Alexandro Magno nomen sortita est.
units.tr: X. The Alexandrine era took its name from Alexander the Great.

units.la: 1. Haec æra diu videtur usitata fuisse, sed sub diversis nominibus; nam vulgò vocatur Æra, sive Anni Seleucidarum, à Seleuco Babyloniæ rege, ut à cujus exordio computatur. Arabes hanc æram vocant Tarich Dhilkarnaïm, hoc est Epocham bicornis, quo nomine Arabes Alexandrum Magnum appellare solent. Quinetiam ipsi quoque Judæi hanc æram usurpare coacti sunt, eámque vocarunt Æram Contractuum, propterea quòd Contractus civiles ea consignabant. Sed in libris Macchabæorum Graecorum anni nuncupantur.
units.tr: 1. This era seems to have been in use for a long time, but under different names. It is commonly called the Era, or the Years of the Seleucids, from Seleucus, king of Babylon, since it is reckoned from the beginning of his reign. The Arabs call this era Tarikh Dhulkarnain, that is, the era of the two-horned, which is the name the Arabs usually give to Alexander the Great. Indeed, the Jews too were obliged to use this era, and they called it the Era of Contracts, because civil contracts were dated by it. In the books of the Maccabees, however, it is called the years of the Greeks.

units.la: XI. Cæpit hæc æra Kal. Octob. anno Per. Jul. 4402, cyclo Solis 6, Lunæ 13, Indict. 7.
units.tr: XI. This era began on 1 October, in the Julian Period year 4402, solar cycle 6, lunar cycle 13, indiction 7.

units.la: 1. Quamvis enim hæc æra ab Alexandri successoribus Alexandrea nuncupatur, non tamen ab Alexandri obitu, ut precedens Philippea, deducitur, sed ab anno duodecimo post ejus excessum. Obiit enim Alexander Magnus anno Per. Jul. 4390, at orta est hæc æra anno 4402.
units.tr: 1. Although this era is called Alexandrine by Alexander's successors, it is not reckoned from the death of Alexander, as the preceding Philippean era is, but from the twelfth year after his departure. For Alexander the Great died in the Julian Period year 4390, but this era began in the year 4402.

units.la: XII. Proposito anno Alexandreo adjice 4401, summa est annus Per. Jul. quo currente cœpit à Kal.Octob.
units.tr: XII. To the Alexandrine year in question add 4401; the sum is the Julian Period year in which it began on 1 October.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Albatenius in libro de scientia stellarum desectum Solis à se observatum refert, anno Dhilkarnaim 1202, qui est annus 1214 ab Alexandri obitu, mense Ab. Albat. c.30. Si scire cupias in quotum annum Per. Jul. annus hic Dhilkarnaim sive Alexandreus 1202 conveniat, ad 1202 adde 4401, summa 5603 est annus Per. Jul. quæsitus, à cujus Kalendis Octobribus iniit. A 5603 abjice 4713, reliquus fit annus Christi 890. Menses hic usitati sunt Syriaci, juxta quos Tishrin prior unà cum Kal. Octobribus init. Mensis igitur Ab quo observata fuit hæc eclipsis in mensem Aug. anno Chr. 891 concurrit. Et quidem anno Christi 891, Aug.8. Solem exactè juxta observationem defecisse tabulæ Astronomicæ confirmant. In hoc autem exemplo annum Philippeum 1214 æquè ac Alexandreum 1202 designatum observes licet, & utramque ab eâdem epochâ, puta Kal.Octob. computatum; unde patet annos Ægyptiacos fixos, non minùs quàm vagos æræ quoque Philippeæ applicatos fuisse, quod antè notavi.
units.tr: 1. For example, Albategnius, in his book On the Science of the Stars, reports an eclipse of the sun that he observed in the year 1202 of Dhulkarnain, which is the year 1214 from the death of Alexander, in the month of Ab. Albategnius, ch. 30. If you wish to know in which Julian Period year this Dhulkarnain or Alexandrine year 1202 falls, add 4401 to 1202; the sum, 5603, is the Julian Period year sought, beginning on 1 October. Subtract 4713 from 5603, and the remainder is the Christian year 890. The months used here are Syrian, according to which Tishri, the first month, begins together with 1 October. The month Ab in which this eclipse was observed therefore coincides with August of the Christian year 891. And indeed, astronomical tables confirm that on 8 August of the year 891 the sun was eclipsed exactly as observed. In this example you may note that the Philippean year 1214 and the Alexandrine year 1202 are both given, and both are reckoned from the same epoch, namely 1 October. From this it is clear that fixed Egyptian years were applied to the Philippean era no less than the vague ones, as I noted before.

units.la: 2. Aliud exemplum: In primo Macchab. libro, c.7.1. hæc occurrunt; Ἔτος ἑνδὲ ἡ πντικοστὴ ἡ ἑκαλοστὴ ἐξῆλθε Δημήτριος ὁ υἱὸς Σελεύκου ἐκ Ῥώμης. Anno centesimo quinquagesimo primo (vid. Græcorum) exivit Demetrius filius Seleuci ex Româ. Si anni hujus situs in Periodo Juliana obtineres ad 151 adjice 4401, summa 4552 est annus Per. Jul. quo currente propositus Alexandreus 151 incepit. Sed à Nisan, unde omnes anni Græcorum in primo Macchabæorum libro memorati procedunt, ut qui in secundo libro à Tisri sequente; quo fit ut Anni Graecorum in priore libro descripti senis mensibus prius incipiant, quàm qui in posteriore occurrunt: quod diligenter est observandum.
units.tr: 2. Another example: In the first book of the Maccabees, chapter 7, verse 1, the following occurs: In the hundred and fifty-first year (of the Greeks) Demetrius, son of Seleucus, went out from Rome. [Ἔτους ἑκατοστοῦ πεντηκοστοῦ πρώτου ἐξῆλθε Δημήτριος ὁ υἱὸς Σελεύκου ἐκ Ῥώμης.] If you wish to know where this year falls in the Julian Period, add 4401 to 151; the sum, 4552, is the Julian Period year in which the Alexandrine year 151 began. But the years of the Greeks in the first book of the Maccabees run from Nisan, whereas in the second book they run from the following Tishri. As a result, the years of the Greeks described in the former book begin six months earlier than those in the latter. This must be carefully observed.

units.la: 3. Æræ huic Alexandreæ „Dhilkarnaim, contractum, sive Graecorum, Judaei annos suos lunares fixos, sive lunaefolares accommodabant. At Syromacedones sive Antiocheni post admissam anni Juliani formam, ei plerunque solares eque Julianos, sed antea, & subinde postea Ægyptiacos fixos applicabant.
units.tr: 3. The Jews adapted their fixed lunar years, or lunisolar years, to this Alexandrine era, which they called Dhulkarnain, the contract era, or of the Greeks. The Syro-Macedonians, or Antiochenes, after the Julian form of the year had been adopted, generally applied it to solar years, and these were Julian; but earlier, and sometimes later, they applied fixed Egyptian years.

units.la: XIII. Æra Yezdegirdica à Yezdegirdo ultimo Persarum rege nomen obtinuit.
units.tr: XIII. The Yezdegirdic era took its name from Yezdegird, the last king of the Persians.

units.la: 1. Cùm Saraceni sive Muslimi Yesdegirdum filium Shahriari ultimum Persarum regem prælio Jululensi (ut Arabicè vocatur) victum interfecissent, Persæ, Arabésque, Astronomi praesertim, ab eo novam hanc epocham instituebant. Anni in eâ usitati sunt Ægyptiaci vagi dier. 365 praecisé. Vocatur & Æra Persica sive anni Persici.
units.tr: 1. When the Saracens, or Muslims, had defeated and killed Yesdegird, son of Shahriar, the last king of the Persians, in the battle of Jululah (as it is called in Arabic), the Persians and Arabs, especially the astronomers, began this new epoch from him. The years used in it are the Egyptian wandering years of exactly 365 days. It is also called the Persian era, or the era of the Persian years.

units.la: XIV: Cæpit hæc æra Jul. 16. anno Per. Jul. 5345 Christi 632, cyclo Solis 25, Lunæ 6, Indict. 5.
units.tr: XIV: This era began on July 16, in the year of the Julian period 5345 of the Persians, which is the year of Christ 632, solar cycle 25, lunar cycle 6, indiction 5.

units.la: XV. Anno igitur Yesdegirdico proposito si præcedat annum 670 adjice 631, si sequatur, tantùm 630, summa est annus Christi quo propositus init.
units.tr: XV. Therefore, for a given Yezdegirdic year: if it is preceded by the year 670, add 631; if it follows, add only 630. The sum is the year of Christ in which the given year begins.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Detur annus Yesdegirdicus 436 ut quaeramus in quotum annum æræ Christianæ caput ejus sive neomenia Fervardin incidat. Igitur ad 436 (ut minorem numerum quàm 670) adjicias 631, summa 1067 est annus Christi, quo currente Yesdegirdicus propositus incepit.
units.tr: 1. For example. Let the Yezdegirdic year 436 be given, and let us find in which year of the Christian era its beginning, the new moon of Farvardin, falls. So add 631 to 436 (since it is a smaller number than 670). The sum, 1067, is the year of Christ in which the given Yezdegirdic year 436 began.

units.la: 2. Aliud exemplum. Anonymus scriptor Persicus à Jacobo Capello Graecè editus, refert anno mundi 6952 æquinoctium vernale deprehensum fuisse. Mar. 11. h. 8.29. ab ortu Solis, & addit Ηεγεπ ἡ ἴωαν ἐπι ακυ ματαλησωμευα, Anni autem Persici 813 completi sunt. Annus igitur 814 currebat. Hic annorum numerus major est quàm 670, eúmque consequenter sequitur, adjiciendum est igitur annos tantùm 630 ad 814, summa 1444 est annus Christi quo currente annus propositus 814 incepit, dies autem quo iniit methodo primo libro tradita inveniendus est. Hunc autem ipsum fuisse annum, quo currente propositus incepit, ex adjuncto anno mundi juxta politicum Graecorum computum satis patet. Erat enim annus mundi 6952, aufer 5508, & relinquitur annus Christi 1444.
units.tr: 2. Another example. An anonymous Persian writer, edited in Greek by Jacob Capellus, reports that the vernal equinox was observed in the year of the world 6952, on March 11, at 8:29 after sunrise [Mar. 11. h. 8.29.], and he adds: "The Persian years were completed as 813" [Ηεγεπ ἡ ἴωαν ἐπι ακυ ματαλησωμευα]. So the year 814 was running. This number of years is greater than 670, and it follows that only 630 must be added to 814. The sum, 1444, is the year of Christ in which the given year 814 began. The day on which it began is to be found by the method taught in the first book. That this was the very year in which the given year began is quite clear from the added year of the world according to the Greek civil reckoning. For the year of the world was 6952; take away 5508, and the year of Christ 1444 remains.

units.la: XVI. Si annus Christi proponatur ad Yesdegirdicum revo- candus, si minor sit quam 1300 aufer 631, si major au- fer 630, & numerus residuus erit annus Yesdegirdicus quaesitus.
units.tr: XVI. If a year of Christ is proposed to be converted to the Yezdegirdic reckoning: if it is less than 1300, subtract 631; if greater, subtract 630. The remaining number will be the Yezdegirdic year sought.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Proponatur annus Christi 924, ut quotus annus Yesdegirdicus eo currente coepit calculemus. 924 minor est numerus quam 1300; aufer itaque 631, & relictus est annus Yesdegirdicus 293.
units.tr: 1. For example. Let the year of Christ 924 be proposed, so that we may calculate which Yezdegirdic year began in it. Since 924 is less than 1300, subtract 631, and the Yezdegirdic year 293 remains.

units.la: 2. Annus hic Christi 1667 major est quam 1300, vel quod idem est; sequitur annum 1300, aufer itaque 630 ex 1667, numerus residuus est 1037. Hoc igitur anno Christi 1667 annus Yesdegirdicus 1037 ingreditur. In quotum autem anni hujusce diem neomenia Fervardin invenire, libro primo H. c. 11. traditur.
units.tr: 2. This year of Christ, 1667, is greater than 1300, or, what is the same, it follows the year 1300. So subtract 630 from 1667; the remaining number is 1037. So in this year of Christ 1667 the Yezdegirdic year 1037 begins. The day of this year on which the new moon of Farvardin falls is taught in book 1, chapter 11.

units.la: 3. Aliae nonnullae praeter hic numeratas nonnunquam occurrunt Ethnicorum epochae, ut Dionysii Mathematici, Aera Astronomica a primo Ptolemaei Philadelphi, anno Per. Jul. 4429 coepta: Aera Tyriorum ab anno Per. Jul 4589, Laodicenorum ab anno 4666, Edessenorum ab anno primo Seleucidarum, Ascalonitarum ab Augusti exordio anno Per. Jul. 4671. A caede Julii Caesaris anno 4670, idibus Martii. Ab Augusti consulatu anno praedicto 4671, Sept 22. Anni Augustorum Romani ab anno Per. Jul. 4687. Et ab Encaeniis Constantinopolitanis anno Christi 330. Maii 11. Verum has Ethnicorum epochas nos penitus non celasse satis est, utpote quae quam rarissime occurrunt, Epocharum nomine prorsus indignae.
units.tr: 3. Some other epochs of the Gentiles, besides those enumerated here, occasionally occur: the astronomical era of Dionysius the Mathematician, begun from the first year of Ptolemy Philadelphus, in the Julian period year 4429; the era of the Tyrians, from the Julian period year 4589; of the Laodiceans, from year 4666; of the Edessenes, from the first year of the Seleucids; of the Ascalonites, from the beginning of August in the Julian period year 4671. From the murder of Julius Caesar, in the year 4670, on the Ides of March. From the consulship of Augustus, in the said year 4671, on September 22. The years of the Roman Augusti, from the Julian period year 4687. And from the Encaenia at Constantinople, in the year of Christ 330, on May 11. But it is enough that we have not wholly passed over these epochs of the Gentiles, since they occur very rarely and are wholly unworthy of the name of epochs.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: De Æra Muhammedica.
units.tr: On the Muhammedan Era.

units.la: Æra Muhammedica ab hegirâ sive fugâ Muhammedis pseu- doprophetæ à Mecca ad Medinam supputatur.
units.tr: The Muhammedan era is reckoned from the hegira, or flight, of Muhammed the pseudo-prophet from Mecca to Medina.

units.la: 1. MUhammedes pseudopropheta primus Islamismi sive religionis Muhammedicæ institutor, Mecce natus est, quæ urbs est Arabiæ fœlicis. Pater ejus erat Abdalla, mater Emina avus Abdolmutaleb. Obiit autem pater ejus duobus mensibus priusquam Muhammedes nasceretur, juxta Elmacinum, at juxta Abulpharagium antequam secundum ætatis annum transegisset. Excessit etiam & mater ejus cùm sex annorum esset: quâ defunctâ, eum ad se recepit avus ejus Abdolmutaleb, quo etiam post annos duos mortuo, filius ipsius & Muhammedis patruus Abutalib eum educavit.
units.tr: 1. Muhammedes the pseudo-prophet, the first founder of Islamism, or the Muhammedan religion, was born at Mecca, a city of Arabia Felix. His father was Abdalla, his mother Emina, and his grandfather Abdolmutaleb. His father died two months before Muhammed was born, according to Elmacinus, but according to Abulpharagius before he had completed his second year. His mother also died when he was six years old. After her death his grandfather Abdolmutaleb took him in, and when he too died two years later, his son and Muhammed's uncle Abutalib brought him up.

units.la: 2. Hic cùm annum quadragesimum attigisset, novam quandam, qualis qualis fuit, religionem cudere, & monarchiam sibi usurpare molitus est. Hoc Koreishitæ procerésque Meccenses quibuscum versatus est, tandem animadvertentes eum solum vertere cogebant. Hic igitur nolens volens Meccâ migrare coactus Medinam fugit, urbem Yatreb antea vocatam, & decem dierum itinere Meccâ distantem. Medina verò dicta est ὡς ἐξοχὴν, quasi ἡ πόλις Nam Medina lingua Arabica urbem significat. Vocatur & Medinatalnabbi, urbs prophetæ, propterea quòd asylum fuit expulsi Meccâ Muhammedis.
units.tr: 2. When he reached the age of forty, he set about devising a new religion, of whatever kind it was, and seizing a monarchy for himself. The Koreishites and the leading men of Mecca, among whom he lived, at last perceived this and forced him to leave the region. Thus, unwilling but compelled, he left Mecca and fled to Medina, a city formerly called Yatreb, which lies ten days' journey from Mecca. Medina was called [ὡς ἐξοχήν] "the city" as it were by preeminence, [ἡ πόλις] as it were "the city"; for Medina in the Arabic tongue means city. It is also called Medinatalnabbi, the city of the prophet, because it became the refuge of Muhammed when he was driven out of Mecca.

units.la: 3. Ab hâc Muhammedis à Meccâ ad Medinam fugâ Omar tertius Muslimicorum imperator annos primus supputavit, literásque subsignavit, teste Elmacino hist. Sarac. l. 1. c.3. Post quam semel introductam, Muhammedis cultores nullam aliam temporis epocham adhibuerunt. Et quoniam Fuga Arabicè dicitur Hegira à verbo Hajara, quod in tertia conjugatione Fugere significat, hinc Epocha hæc Æra, sive anni Hegiræ; i.e. Fugæ nuncupatur.
units.tr: 3. From this flight of Muhammed from Mecca to Medina, Omar, the third emperor of the Muslims, began to count the years and to date his documents, as Elmacinus attests (Hist. Sarac. l. 1. c. 3). After this was once introduced, the followers of Muhammed used no other epoch of time. And since Fuga in Arabic is called Hegira, from the verb Hajara, which in the third conjugation means Fugere (to flee), hence this epoch is called the Era, or the years of the Hegira, i.e. of the Flight.

units.la: II. Æra hæc Muhammedica sive Hegiræ cœpit Jul. 16. anno Per. Jul. 5335, Christi 622, cyclo Solis 15, Lunæ 15, Indict. 10.
units.tr: II. This Muhammedan or Hegira era began on July 16 in the year of the Julian Period 5335, in the year of Christ 622, solar cycle 15, lunar cycle 15, indiction 10.

units.la: 1. Ab hoc tempore Arabes & universi religionis Islamiticæ sive Muhammedicæ cultores annos suos computare gaudent, qui planè lunares vagi sunt, duodecim mensibus lunaribus præcisè constantes. Et Saraceni quidem annis istiusmodi lunaribus ante Muhammedis nativitatem usi videntur, ut & iisdem mensibus quibus hodie.
units.tr: 1. From this time the Arabs and all the adherents of the Islamic or Muhammedan religion delight to reckon their years. These are purely lunar years, wandering through the seasons, consisting of exactly twelve lunar months. And the Saracens seem to have used such lunar years even before Muhammed's birth, and with the same months as they use today.

units.la: 2. De ipso autem die quo cœpit hæc æra, quamvis non de anno, nonnulla movetur controversia. Nam Astronomi à Julii 15, feriâ 5; alii à Julii 16, feriâ 6, annos hosce deducunt, pro confesso habentes Muhammedem eâ nocte quæ Julii 15 secuta est è Mecca ad Medinam profugisse. Nos Julii 16 initium hujus epochæ statuimus, utpote quòd apud Arabes Turcásque omnes vulgares solùm obtinuit. Et Astronomi soli, ut Alfraganius, Albatenius, Ulug Beig, & Alphonsus à Julii 15 eam deducant.
units.tr: 2. Yet there is some dispute about the very day on which this era began, though not about the year. For the astronomers count these years from July 15, a Thursday, while others count them from July 16, a Friday, taking it as certain that Muhammed fled from Mecca to Medina on the night following July 15. We have set the beginning of this epoch at July 16, since it has prevailed generally only among the Arabs and all the Turks. Only the astronomers, such as Alfraganius, Albatenius, Ulug Beig and Alphonsus, reckon it from July 15.

units.la: 3. At quoniam annus quilibet Muhammedicus ut merè lunaris minor sit quàm Julianus diebus circiter undecim, hinc fit quòd aliquantulùm operosior sit & difficilior horum annorum calculus quàm aliorum. Nos autem in priori harum institutionum libro methodum tradidimus, quâ etiam per Arithmetices præcepta tam annus Muhammedicus in Julianum, quàm Julianus in Muhammedicum reducatur. Ultimum igitur libri præcedentis caput consulat licet, qui plura de anno Muhammedico scisscitatur.
units.tr: 3. But because any Muhammedan year, being purely lunar, is shorter than a Julian year by about eleven days, it follows that the calculation of these years is somewhat more laborious and difficult than that of other years. In the earlier book of these Institutions, however, we gave a method by which a Muhammedan year may be reduced to a Julian year, and a Julian year to a Muhammedan, by the rules of arithmetic. The reader may therefore consult the last chapter of the preceding book, which treats more fully of the Muhammedan year.

units.la: KAlendarium hoc Julianum ut ad annum Julianum accommodatum sex constat versiculis, quorum primus Aureos numeros exhibet, putà Nicenos ; quorum ope novilunia & plenilunia, unà cum Paschatis celebrandi die (juxta Concilii Niceni decretum) quotannis computentur. v. l. 2. c. 4. Secundus dies mensis cujuslibet continet. Tertius Literas quarum singulæ, ordine quæque suo, sed retrograde, Dominicales sunt, ut Dominicam per totum annum indigitantes: quarum etiam ope feriæ hebdomadis cujuslibet inveniantur ; idque perpetuò, ut videre est l. 2. c. 3. Quartus partes repræsentat mensis cujuslibet Juliani, nimirùm Kalendas, nonas, & Idus ; de quibus actum est l. 1. c. 9. Quintus dies collectos exhibet in anno communi, & ultimus in bissextili ; quorum usus per totas hasce Institutiones Chronologicas frequens occurrit.
units.tr: This Julian calendar, as adapted to the Julian year, consists of six little verses. The first of them gives the Golden Numbers, namely the Nicene ones, by whose help the new moons and full moons are computed each year, together with the day for celebrating Easter (according to the decree of the Council of Nicaea); see book 2, chapter 4. The second gives the days of any month. The third gives the Letters, each of which, in its own order but running backwards, is a Dominical letter, indicating the Sunday throughout the whole year; by means of these the weekdays of any week are also found, and this always, as may be seen in book 2, chapter 3. The fourth represents the parts of any Julian month, namely the Kalends, the Nones, and the Ides; these were discussed in book 1, chapter 9. The fifth gives the collected days in a common year, and the last gives them in a leap year; their use occurs frequently throughout these Chronological Institutions.

units.la: E Tiamsi eorum gratia, qui linguis orientalibus non adeo sunt exercitati ab exoticis quibuscunque characteribus, per totas hasce Institutiones Chronologicas prudens abstinui; nè tamen iis qui linguas etiam doctas chronologicis suis addiderunt studiis, hic desideraretur; menses saltem orientales, aliáque nonnulla ad eos pertinentia, propriis suis characteribus exarata appendere, non operae pretium tantùm, sed & necessarium duxi. Menses igitur suos orientis incolae hunc in modum exprimunt.
units.tr: Although I have deliberately refrained, throughout these Chronological Institutes, from using exotic characters for the sake of those less practised in the oriental languages, I have nevertheless thought it not only useful but necessary to append here the oriental months and some related matters, written in their own characters, so that nothing is lacking for those who have added learned languages to their chronological studies. The inhabitants of the East express their months in the following way.

Æthiopes autem ἰωίρες ἰπποροφέας [?] vocant ጳጉሜን [?] Pagomen, ipso nimirùm Græco vocabulo depravato.
units.tr: The Persians call the intercalary days, or Epagomenae, Musteraka, that is, [καλοπιμὸς] "furtive" (Furtivus); and at the end of each month they usually add mah, that is, "month". So when they express Fervardin, they say Fervardin mah (the reason for which is given in the Institutes), and likewise for the other months. The Ethiopians, however, call them [ἰωίρες ἰπποροφέας [?]] Pagomen, the Greek word itself having been corrupted.

units.la: In diebus cujuslibet ex hisce mensibus dinumerandis Arabes sic procedunt. Primam mensis cujusque diem vocant مستهلّ Mustahalla, i. e. Neomeniam, novam lunam, a verbo هلّ Halla, Apparuit, sive splendere cœpit nova luna, unde & هلال Hilal τὴν τῆς σεληνης φαιν significat. Sic Elmacinus: Anno Hegiræ sexagesimo obiit Muavius filius Abufofiani في مستهل رجب In Mustahal Rajab, id est, τῇ νουμηνίᾳ τῇ Rajab. Elmac. hist. Sarac. l. 1. c. 7. A primâ die usque ad decimam quintam, (nonnunquam usque ad vigesimam) dies à Mustahal mensis elapsos sive præteritos numerant. Duo autem vocabula hoc sensu iis usurpantur, مضي Mada, Abiit, præteriit; & حلّ Rectissit, effluxit, ut in prædictâ historiâ Saracenicâ فلما كانت ليلة الجمعة لعشر مضين من المحرم Facta autem nocte diei veneris, decimâ Madeinâ, i. e. præteritorum de Muharram hist.Sar. l.1.c.8. Sic Abulpharagius, anno Hegiræ 248, Mortuus est Almontasser die Solis لخمس ليال quintâ noctium chalounâ, i. e. præteritarum de mense Rabia posteriori. Abulph. dynast. 9. p. 267. Diem mensis 15 appellant نصف Nasfph, q. d. Medium mensem, ut in loco Elmacini antè citato, in Mustahal, sive primâ die mensis Rajabi mortuus est Muavius. وقيل نصف رجب Et dictum est Nasfphi rajab, medio Rajab, i. e. die decimo quinto. Post diem 15 nonnunquam, post 20 perpetuò ordine retrogrado procedunt, non computantes quot dies ab initio mensis elapsi sunt, sed quot ad finem supersunt. Ut Elmacinus, Occisus est Abdalla, & capta Mecca manè, die martis لدلت عسرة ليلة بقيت عن Decimâ tertiâ nocte relictâ five superstite de Jomadâ priori, i.e. Jomadæ 18. Elmacin. l. 1. c. 12. Abulpharagius dynaft. 9. p. 227. وكان مودة في الملكرم Et accidit mors ejus (vid. Almohdi) in Muharram diebus five noctibus octo de eo relictis, i.e. Muharram 22. Elmacinus iterum, وكان بعدمه Et capta fuit Mecca decimo bakeina, i.e. reliquorum de mense Ramadân, hift. Sar. c. 1. Is est dies Muharram 21. Eutychius autem hunc 21 Ramadanis diem vocat & اول العسر الاخر من سهر رمضان Primum e decem ultimis diebus mensis Ramadân. Eutych. Annal. Alex. tom. 2. p. 342.
units.tr: In counting the days of any of these months, the Arabs proceed as follows. They call the first day of each month Mustahalla, that is, the neomenia, the new moon, from the verb halla, "it appeared", or "the new moon began to shine", whence also hilal signifies the appearance of the moon ([τὴν τῆς σελήνης φαίνωσιν]). Thus Elmacinus: "In the year of the Hegira 60, Muawiya son of Abu Sufyan died fi Mustahal Rajab", that is, "on the new moon day of Rajab" (Elmacinus, Historia Saracenica, book 1, ch. 7). From the first day up to the fifteenth (sometimes up to the twentieth), they count the days elapsed or past since the Mustahal of the month. Two words are used in this sense: mada, "he departed, he passed by", and halla, "he flowed away, he ran out", as in the Saracen history cited above: fa-lamma kanat laylat al-jum'a li-'ashr madayna min al-Muharram, "when it was the night of Friday, on the tenth [night] of the past [days] of Muharram" (Historia Saracenica, book 1, ch. 8). Likewise Abulpharagius, in the year of the Hegira 248: Almontasser died on Sunday li-khams layal chalouna, "on the fifth of the nights past", that is, of the days past of the month of Rabi' al-akhir (Abulpharagius, Dynastiae, dynasty 9, p. 267). They call the fifteenth day nisf, as if to say "the middle of the month", as in the passage of Elmacinus cited above: "in the Mustahal, or first day of the month of Rajab, Muawiya died", and "it is said nisf Rajab, the middle of Rajab", that is, on the fifteenth day. After the fifteenth, and sometimes after the twentieth, they proceed in a continuous backward order, not counting how many days have elapsed since the beginning of the month, but how many remain to its end. Thus Elmacinus: "Abdallah was killed, and Mecca was taken in the morning, on Tuesday", li-dalat 'ashara layla baqiyat 'an, "on the thirteenth night left over, or remaining, of Jumada al-ula", that is, the 18th of Jumada (Elmacinus, book 1, ch. 12; Abulpharagius, dynasty 9, p. 227). And again: "his death occurred (see al-Mahdi) in Muharram, on eight days or nights remaining of it", that is, the 22nd of Muharram. Elmacinus again: "Mecca was taken on the tenth bakiya", that is, "of the remaining [days] of the month of Ramadan" (Historia Saracenica, ch. 1). This is the 21st of Ramadan. Eutychius, however, calls this 21st day of Ramadan awwal al-'ashr al-akhir min shahr Ramadan, "the first of the last ten days of the month of Ramadan" (Eutychius, Annales Alexandrini, vol. 2, p. 342).

units.la: Ex his aliisque innumeris, quæ proferre possum, Arabicorum scriptorum testimoniis, satis abunde patet, Arabes non minus quam Athenienses post vigesimum saltem mensis cujusque diem (subinde post 15) retrorsum numerare, ut hi enim dicunt post diem 20, Δεύτερον φθίνοντος, τρίτην φθίνοντος, τέταρτον φθίνοντος, &c. sic & illi, Decimus bakin, nonus bakin, octavus bakin, & sic deinceps. Quod miror à chronologis antehac non observatum fuisse. Sed manum de tabulâ. De his enim aliisque, quæ ad annos præsertim menséque orientales pertinent, alibi (Deo volente) fusius agemus.
units.tr: From these and countless other testimonies of Arabic writers, which I could produce, it is quite clear that the Arabs, no less than the Athenians, count backwards after at least the twentieth day of each month (sometimes after the fifteenth). For just as the Athenians say deuteron phthinontos, triten phthinontos, tetarton phthinontos after the twentieth day, so the Arabs say tenth bakin, ninth bakin, eighth bakin, and so on. I am surprised that the chronologists have not observed this before now. But let me put down my pen from the table. For these and other matters, which pertain especially to the oriental years and months, I will (God willing) treat more fully elsewhere.
