units.la: TAntam Arithmetica cum Chronologiâ affinitatem, támque necessarium ad eam respectum habet ; ut nemo sine summâ temporis jacturâ libros vel evolvat Chronologicos, priusquam elementa saltèm Arithmetica imbiberit. Enimvèro nullum Theorema Chronologicum intelligi, nullum quaesitum inveniri, nullum problema deprehendi nulla controversia dirimi, nullus denique calculus administrari potest, sine variis numerorum inter sese compositionibus, quam Arithmeticam vulgò nuncupamus. Quapropter ad uberiorem rei Chronologicæ à nobis jam breviter explicatæ intelligentiam, nonnihil & de divinâ Arithmetices arte subnectere visum est. Non quòd omnia hujusce artis mysteria in nos suscepimus enucleanda, sed ea soluminodò (quod Titulus etiam ostendit) quæ Chronologo prorsùs requiruntur. Cùm autem partes Arithmeticæ duæ à nobis constituuntur, Characteristica & Practica, nos primæ præsertim parti, ut ab aliis intactæ, pertractandæ incubuimus. Cui quidèm illustrandæ tantam adhibuimus curam & diligentiam, ut nulli vel in libris impressis MSS. vel inscriptionibus quàcunque propemodum linguâ exaratis extant Characteres, quorum valor ex iis quæ hìc dictâ sunt non erutur. Ab antiquis (fateor) Romanis numeri per alias etiam ac à nobis descriptas notas nonnunquam repræsentati suerunt : at quæ non proprie ipsorum erant numerorum characteres, Tteres, sed potius ipsa verba numeralia characteristicè sive breviter scripta; ut ex his exemplis patet. Tres Sex Decem
units.tr: Arithmetic has such a close kinship with chronology, and such a necessary bearing on it, that no one can read chronological books without great loss of time unless he has at least absorbed the elements of arithmetic. Indeed, no chronological theorem can be understood, no question found, no problem grasped, no controversy settled, and in short no calculation carried out, without the various combinations of numbers among themselves, which we commonly call arithmetic. Therefore, for a fuller understanding of the chronological matter which we have already briefly explained, it seemed right to add something also about the divine art of arithmetic. Not that we have undertaken to unfold all the mysteries of this art, but only those (as the title also shows) which the chronologer absolutely requires. Since we divide arithmetic into two parts, the characteristic and the practical, we have set ourselves to treat especially the first part, since others have left it untouched. To illustrate it we have applied such care and diligence that there are almost no characters, in printed books or manuscripts or inscriptions written in almost any language, whose value cannot be drawn out from what is said here. Among the ancient Romans (I admit) numbers were sometimes represented by other signs too, which we have not described; but these were not properly characters of the numbers themselves, but rather the numeral words themselves written in shorthand, as the following examples make clear. Tres, Sex, Decem

units.la: Ubi in primâ figurâ prima & ultima litera vocis Tres, viz. T & S aliquo modo exprimuntur, unà cum vocali E puncto indigitatâ, per quam itaque non ipse numerus ternarius, sed vox tres indicatur. In alterâ notâ S & X clarè satis apparent, unà cum vocali puncto etiam notatâ, per quam itaque vox sex tota depingitur. In ultimâ d & c exprimuntur, unà cum duabus vocalibus per totidem puncta designatis, hæc igitur characteristica erat nota vocis decem. Verùm non tantùm numeralia, sed alia quamplurima, imò multa millia vocabulorum, characteristicis hujusmodi notis describpta sunt. Ut hæc pristina videatur Romanorum τυχηεια. Has notas M. Tullius Tyro Ciceronis libertus primus excogitavit. Unde Eusebius in Chron. ad an. MMXII. M. Tullius Tyro Ciceronis libertus qui primus notas commentus est, in Puteolano prædio usque ad centesimum annum consenescit. At Isidorus, Primus Tullius Tiro Ciceronis libertus commentus est notas, sed tantùm præpositionum, post eum Tertius Pesslaunius Philargyrus, & Aquila libertus Mæcenatis alius alias addiderunt. Dio, Πρῶτος ὁ Μαικήνας σημεῖά τινα γεγραμμάτων εἰς τὰς ἐξεύρε. Quinetiam Annæus Seneca alias etiam addidisse perhibetur. Hisce notis orationes in foro prolatas excipiebant, qui iis autem usi sunt notarii vocantur. D. Augustinus, Ex eo genere etiam sunt notæ, quas qui didicerunt Notarii appellantur. Ang. de doctr. Christ. Hinc illa Senecæ; Is multa disertè, quòd in foro vivat, dixit, quæ Notarius persequi non potuit, & ideò non refero, nè aliis verbis ponam quæ ab illo dicta sunt. Sen. in Αποφθεγμ. Ex quibus verbis liquet veteres Romanos notarios suos habuisse qui hujusmodi notarum ope, quæcunque in foro dicta sunt ἀντικτὸ ὑ scriptis mandarent. Quamplurimas harum notarum Janus Gruterus ad Inscriptionum calcem edidit, nos autem eas ut ad Arithmeticos proprie non pertinentes characteres, missas faciimus. Omnes autem proprie sic dictos characteres, vel in Romanâ, vel in aliâ quacunque linguâ nobis cognitâ, numeris indigitandis usitatos, pro virili explicare conati sumus; ut in quemcunque librum incidas, Arithmeticos ejus characteres æquè ac verba intelligas. In altera autem Arithmeticæ parte, quam Practicam appellamus; eam ut ab aliis quamplurimis expositam nos paucis expedimus, nec quicquam in eâ quod Chronologi non interest cognoscere adnotamus.
units.tr: In the first figure, the first and last letters of the word Tres, namely T and S, are expressed in some way, together with the vowel E indicated by a dot; so the sign does not stand for the number three itself but for the word tres. In the second sign, S and X are quite clearly visible, together with the vowel likewise marked by a dot, so the whole word sex is depicted by it. In the last, d and c are expressed, together with two vowels designated by two dots; this, then, was the characteristic sign of the word decem. Moreover, not only numerals but many other words, indeed many thousands of words, were described by signs of this kind. This was, as it were, the earlier fortune-telling of the Romans. Marcus Tullius Tiro, Cicero's freedman, first devised these signs. Hence Eusebius in his Chronicle, under the year 2012: "Marcus Tullius Tiro, Cicero's freedman, who first invented the signs, lived on into his hundredth year on his estate at Puteoli." But Isidore says: "Primus Tullius Tiro, Cicero's freedman, devised signs, but only for prepositions; after him Tertius Pesslaunius Philargyrus and Aquila, Maecenas's freedman, added others, each different ones." Dio says: "Maecenas was the first [πρῶτος ὁ Μαικήνας] to devise certain signs of letters for..." Moreover, Annaeus Seneca is said to have added still others. Speeches delivered in the forum were taken down by these signs, and those who used them are called notaries. St Augustine: "Of this kind also are the signs which those who have learned them are called notaries." (Augustine, On Christian Doctrine.) Hence Seneca's words: "He spoke many things eloquently, since he lives in the forum, which a notary could not follow, and so I do not report them, lest I set down in other words what was said by him." (Seneca, Apophthegms.) From these words it is clear that the ancient Romans had their own notaries, who by the aid of such signs committed to writing word for word whatever was said in the forum. Janus Gruter published a great many of these signs at the end of his Inscriptions, but we leave them aside as characters not properly belonging to arithmeticians. We have, however, tried to explain, as far as we could, all the characters properly so called, in Roman or any other language known to us, that are used to designate numbers, so that whatever book you come upon, you may understand its arithmetical characters as well as its words. In the other part of arithmetic, which we call practical, since it has been expounded by very many others, we dispose of it in a few words, and we note nothing in it that the chronologer need not know.

units.tr: Farewell.

units.la: Arithmetices Chronologicæ Liber Primus. CAP. I. De Arithmeticæ definitione & divisione.
units.tr: Book One of the Chronological Arithmetic. CHAPTER I. On the definition and division of arithmetic.

units.la: I. Arithmetica est ars rectè numerandi.
units.tr: I. Arithmetic is the art of counting correctly.

units.la: SUbjectum igitur Arithmeticæ est quantitas discreta, sive numerus. Numerus autem est multitudo ex unitatibus compositá. Unitas verò est secundùm quam unumquodque eorum quæ sunt unum dicitur. Numerorum porrò theoria ad Geometriam pertinet: Unde Euclides quæcunque propemodùm de numeris situ sunt necessaria in quinto, septimo, octavo, & nono Elementorum Geometricorum libro complexus est. Quocircà scientiâ numerorum Geometris, quorum interest naturam, species, ac proprietates eorum tradere; relictâ, nos varias tantùm numerorum inter se componendorum rationes explicandas suscipimus, & idcirco Arithmeticam ut à nobis traditam Artem rectè numerandi, sive numeros inter sese componendi non immeritò definimus.
units.tr: The subject of Arithmetic, then, is discrete quantity, or number. Number is a multitude composed of units, and a unit is that by which each of the things that are called one is called one. The theory of numbers belongs to Geometry, which is why Euclid included almost everything that is needed about numbers in the fifth, seventh, eighth and ninth books of his Elements of Geometry. Therefore, leaving aside the science of numbers, which it is the business of geometers to set out (their nature, kinds and properties), we undertake to explain only the various ways of combining numbers with one another. For this reason we define arithmetic, as we have presented it, not unfittingly as the art of counting correctly, that is, of combining numbers with one another.

units.la: II. Partes Arithmeticæ duæ sunt, Characterisitica & Practica.
units.tr: II. There are two parts of arithmetic, the Characteristic and the Practical.

units.la: III. Pars Characteristica est, quæ varios explicat Characteres quibus numeri exprimuntur.
units.tr: III. The Characteristic part is that which explains the various characters by which numbers are expressed.

units.la: IV. Pars Practica est, quæ praxes sive operationes docet. Arithmeticas.
units.tr: IV. The Practical part is that which teaches the procedures, or arithmetical operations.

units.la: 1. Qui rei Arithmeticæ operam locare sibi proponit, ut propositum assequatur, hæc duo perdiscat necesse est, primò mò quid sibi vellent varii isti characteres, quibus numeros describi usu venit; secundò ut numeros sic expressos sibi invicem addat, detrahat, multiplicet, dividat, vel aliter inter se conferat, prout occasio se præbuerit, aut studia postulaverint. Hinc est quòd nos, ut alios hanc Artem doceamus, Institutiones hasce nostras in prædictas partes, viz. Characteristicam & Practicam distribuimus. Primam Characteristicam propterea nuncupamus, quòd characteribus Arithmeticis exponendis tota designatur: Alteram verò Practicam, eò quod multifarias numerorum istiusmodi descriptorum characteribus compositiones, quas praxes vocant, sive operationes Arithmeticas, tradit.
units.tr: 1. Anyone who proposes to devote himself to the study of arithmetic must necessarily learn two things in order to reach his goal: first, (1) what those various characters mean by which numbers are commonly written; and second, (2) how to add, subtract, multiply, divide, or otherwise compare with one another numbers so expressed, as occasion offers or his studies require. Hence it is that, in order to teach this art to others, we divide these Institutes of ours into the aforesaid parts, namely the Characteristic and the Practical. We call the first Characteristic because it is wholly concerned with setting out the characters of arithmetic; the second we call Practical because it teaches the many compositions of numbers described by these characters, which are called procedures, or arithmetical operations.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De Characteribus Arithmeticis in genere.
units.tr: Of Arithmetical Characters in general.

units.la: I. Characteres Arithmetici sunt certa quædam notæ à variis gentibus, ad numeros breviter exprimendos usitatæ.
units.tr: I. Arithmetical characters are certain marks, in common use among various peoples, for expressing numbers briefly.

units.la: II. Súntque vel Figurativi, vel Literales.
units.tr: II. They are either figurative or literal.

units.la: III. Characteres Figurativi sunt certæ figuræ à literis diversæ, numeros ad indicandos inventæ.
units.tr: III. Figurative characters are certain shapes, different from letters, devised for indicating numbers.

units.la: IV. Literales sunt ipsæ linguæ cujusvis literæ usu numerali prædité.
units.tr: IV. Literal characters are the letters of any language, used with a numerical value.

units.la: I. EX Arithmeticis hisce characteribus Literales in usu primi fuisse videntur, idque in linguâ Hebraicâ. Cùm literæ enim Hebraicæ eodem perpetuò ordine, quo hodie, processerint, ut Aleph sit prima litera, Beth secunda da, & sic deinceps usque ad ultimam Thau, ut è Psalm. 112. & 119. Prov. 31. & Thren. 1. liquet, hinc tandem evenit, ut quotum in ordine Alphabeti locum litera quaeque sortita est, ejusdem & numerum indigitaret, ut ℵ 1, ℶ 2, ℷ 3, & sic deinceps usque ad ℸ, quae ut vigesima secunda litera etiam 22 forsitan indicabat. Quam per literas numerandi rationem apud Graecos etiam olim obtinuisse docet Hadrianus Amarotius.
units.tr: I. Of these arithmetical characters, the literal kind seems to have been used first, and this in the Hebrew language. For since the Hebrew letters have followed the same order ever since, as they do today, so that aleph is the first letter, beth the second, and so on in sequence to the last, tau, as is clear from Psalms 112 and 119, Proverbs 31 and Lamentations 1, it came about in the end that each letter indicated by its own value the number of the place it held in the order of the alphabet: aleph 1, beth 2, gimel 3, and so on to tau, which, as the twenty-second letter, perhaps also indicated 22. Hadrianus Amarotius teaches that this method of counting by letters was also once in use among the Greeks.

units.la: II. Cum res igitur huc provenerit; visae sunt tandem Alphabeti literae omnibus etiam numeris exprimendis satis idoneae. Et idcirco omnes Alphabeti literae in tres classes divisae sunt, quarum prima monadicos, altera denarios, tertia centenarios contineret numeros, ut mox patebit. Haec prima videtur numeros per literas exprimendi origo, quae consuetudo ex Hebraicâ in alias linguas tandem emanavit, ut protinus ostendemus.
units.tr: II. Since matters had therefore reached this point, the letters of the alphabet were at last seen to be quite suitable for expressing all numbers. And so all the letters of the alphabet were divided into three classes, of which the first would contain the units, the second the tens, and the third the hundreds, as will soon be clear. This first arrangement seems to be the origin of expressing numbers by letters, a custom which in the end spread from Hebrew into other languages, as we shall show presently.

units.la: 2. Quod ad Figurativos spectat, palam est eos ex oriente in occidentem, idque non ita pridem translatos esse, nunc autem dierum pluribus usitatos. Quamobrem ut numeros quomodocunque expressos legat quispiam pariter ac intelligat, utramque characterum speciem in promptu habeat, non expedit modo, sed & necesse est. Hoc autem ut citius acquiratur, priusquam singulos exponam characteres, non abs re erit Aureum hanc praemittere Tabellam, quâ omnes utriusque speciei characteres simul exhibentur.
units.tr: 2. As for the figurative characters, it is plain that they were carried from east to west, and that not very long ago, though they are now used by many people. Therefore, in order that anyone may read and understand numbers however they are expressed, it is not only useful but necessary to have both kinds of characters at hand. So that this may be learned more quickly, before I set out the individual characters, it will not be out of place to put in front this handy little table, in which the characters of both kinds are displayed together.

units.la: CAP. III. De Characteribus vulgaribus.
units.tr: CAP. III. Of Common Characters.

units.la: I. Characteres Figurativi sunt vel vulgares vel Indici. II. Vulgares sunt qui vulgò sunt in vsu.
units.tr: I. Figurative characters are either common or Indian. II. Common characters are those which are in common use.

units.la: INdicis propterea vulgares antepono characteres, non quòd hi primò sunt inventi, sed quòd vulgares sunt, & idcircò pluribus noti. Ab Indis enim numeros per figuras exprimendi ratio primò excogitata fuit, ut quibus ipsi Arabes eam acceptam referunt, non minùs quàm nos Arabibus, utì posthæc patebit. Nimirùm Indorum ingenio ingeniosissimam cifrarum inventionem debemus, quibus in infinitum numerare possumus, nusquam hæsitantes, nusquam confusi, nusquam figuris ad numeros quoslibet exprimendos destituti. Quod quidem egregium cifrarum inventum ab oriente in occidentem translatum, vulgò nobis etiamnum usitatur, & idcircò vulgarem per eas numerandi rationem primò exprimamus oportet, utpotè per quam reliquæ sunt explicandæ.
units.tr: That is why I put the common characters before the Indian ones: not because the common ones were invented first, but because they are common, and so better known to more people. For the method of expressing numbers by figures was first devised by the Indians, to whom the Arabs themselves credit it, no less than we credit the Arabs, as will appear later. We owe to the genius of the Indians the most ingenious invention of the cipher, by which we can count to infinity, never hesitating, never confused, never lacking figures to express any numbers whatever. This excellent invention of the cipher, carried from the East to the West, is still in common use among us. For this reason we must first set out the common method of counting by it, since the other methods are to be explained by reference to it.

units.la: III. Characteres vulgares sunt decem, viz. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0.
units.tr: III. The common characters are ten, namely 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0.

units.la: Decem horum characterum ope nullus detur numerus qui exactè non exprimatur, idque hac ratione. Novem priores figuræ sunt significativæ, & prima quidem 1 unitatem denotat, secunda 2 duas unitates, & sic usque ad 9, quæ ut nona novem designat. Ultima figura, Arabicè Cifra dicta, nihil per se significat, sed aliis ad dextram annexa notis earum valorem adauget, & quidem decuplâ perpetuò proportione. Nam una cifra o primo loco sive ad dextram (qui perpetuò primus vocatur locus) figuræ cujusvis appositâ, unitates istius figuræ in decades convertit, ut 2 valet duas unitates, sed 20 duas decades, 4 quatuor unitates, at 40 totidem decades. Si duæ cifræ cuilibet figuræ adjungantur, simplices istius figuræ unitates in decem decades, sive centurias crescunt, ut 100 valet decies decem sive centum unitates. 200 ducentas, &c. Eâdem quoque ratione 1000 significat decies centum sive mille: 10000 decies mille, 100000 decies decem mille, sive centum millia. Et sic usque in infinitum omnes figuræ significativæ, quotcunque cifras annexas habent, toties decuplâ proportione crescunt.
units.tr: By means of these ten characters no number can be given that is not expressed exactly, and this is how. The first nine figures have a meaning of their own: the first, 1, denotes one unit; the second, 2, two units; and so on up to 9, which as the ninth stands for nine. The last figure, called the cipher (in Arabic), means nothing in itself, but when annexed on the right to other figures it increases their value, always in a tenfold proportion. For when one cipher is placed after a figure in the first place, that is on the right (which is always called the first place), it turns the units of that figure into tens: 2 is worth two units, but 20 two tens; 4 is four units, but 40 is as many tens. If two ciphers are added to any figure, its simple units grow into ten tens, that is hundreds: 100 is worth ten tens, that is a hundred units; 200 two hundred, and so on. In the same way 1000 means ten hundreds, or a thousand; 10000 ten thousands; 100000 ten ten-thousands, or a hundred thousand. And so on to infinity: every significant figure grows in tenfold proportion for each cipher annexed to it.

units.la: 2. Et eodem quoque modo quot unitates quælibet figura per se sive primo loco ad dextram posita significat, tot secundo loco decades, tot tertio centurias, quarto tot millia valet; & sic deinceps loci cujusvis valor per decuplum incrementum etiam in infinitum progrediatur.
units.tr: 2. In the same way, however many units a figure denotes when it stands alone or in the first place on the right, it is worth that many tens in the second place, that many hundreds in the third, that many thousands in the fourth; and so on, the value of any place advancing in tenfold increase to infinity.

units.la: 3. Ut valor autem cujusvis loci citius innotescat, hanc tabellam subjicere visum est. Locus. | Valor. Primus | Unitates Secundus | Decades Tertius | Centuriæ Quartus | Millia Quintus | Decades millium Sextus | Centuriæ millium Septimus | Milliones Octavus | Decades millionum Nonus | Centuriæ millionum Decimus | Millia millionum Undecimus | Decades millium millionum Duodecimus | Centuriæ millium millionum Decimus tertius | Milliones millionum sive Biliones Decimus quartus | Decades Bilionum Decimus quintus | Centuriæ Bilionum Decimus sextus | Millia Bilionum Decimus septimus | Decades millium Bilionum Decimus octavus | Centuriæ millium Bilionum Decimus nonus | Milliones Bilionum sive Trihones.
units.tr: 3. So that the value of any place may be learned more quickly, it has seemed good to add the following table. Place: value. First: units. Second: tens. Third: hundreds. Fourth: thousands. Fifth: tens of thousands. Sixth: hundreds of thousands. Seventh: millions. Eighth: tens of millions. Ninth: hundreds of millions. Tenth: thousands of millions. Eleventh: tens of thousands of millions. Twelfth: hundreds of thousands of millions. Thirteenth: millions of millions, or billions. Fourteenth: tens of billions. Fifteenth: hundreds of billions. Sixteenth: thousands of billions. Seventeenth: tens of thousands of billions. Eighteenth: hundreds of thousands of billions. Nineteenth: millions of billions, or trillions.

units.la: Ex hâc Tabellâ valor cujusvis loci statim inveniatur. Dentur enim tres figuræ 532 sine commate interjecto : In hoc numero 2 stat primo loco ad dextram, 3 secundo, 5 tertio; ut autem è Tabellâ constat, tertius locus valet centurias unitatum, secundus decades; primus simplices unitates. In tertio autem loco figura est 5, quæ ibi igitur quinque centurias valet, sive quingentas unitates; 3 secunda loco ponitur, valet itaque tres decades unitatum, sive triginta; prima figura est 2, duas significans unitates. Figuræ igitur propositæ 532 valent quingentas triginta duas unitates. Proponatur numerus etiam major, puta 6548302: hic ultima figura ad sinistram sive 6 septimo loco ponitur, quæ itaque sex milliones valet, ut è tabellâ patet; proxima figura 5, ut sexto loco posita, quingenta millia significat; & sic deinceps, ut in tabulâ describuntur: ut numerus propositus sit sex milliones, quingenta, quadraginta octo millia, trecentæ duæ unitates. Nam etsi cifra nihil per se significat, inter 3 tamen & 2 interjecta, figuram 3 in tertium locum, qui est centuriarum, deducit.
units.tr: From this table the value of any place can be found at once. Let the three figures 532 be given, without a comma inserted. In this number 2 stands in the first place on the right, 3 in the second, 5 in the third. As the table shows, the third place is worth hundreds of units, the second tens, the first simple units. In the third place the figure is 5, which there is worth five hundred, or five hundred units. The 3 is placed in the second place, so it is worth three tens of units, or thirty; the first figure is 2, meaning two units. So the figures proposed, 532, are worth five hundred and thirty-two units. Take a larger number, say 6548302. Here the last figure on the left, 6, stands in the seventh place, so it is worth six million, as the table shows. The next figure, 5, placed in the sixth place, means five hundred thousand; and so on, as set out in the table. So the number proposed is six million, five hundred and forty-eight thousand, three hundred and two units. For although the cipher means nothing in itself, when placed between 3 and 2 it moves the 3 into the third place, which is that of hundreds.

units.la: 4. Ut majores autem numeros faciliùs enuncies, primò sex figuras pronunciare discas, quarum ultima à dextrâ centurias millium perpetuò designet, ut 536432 sic enuncies, Quingenta, triginta, sex millia, quadringenta, triginta duo. Deinde quemlibet datum numerum in membra minora redigas, supra septimam à dextrâ figuram ponendo virgulam unam, supra decimam tertiam virgulas duas, at supra undevigesimam tres, & sic quousque libet ad sextam quamlibet figuram virgularum unitate augeas. Denique, ad figuram quæ proxima quamlibet sequitur virgulam, legere incipias ac sex figuræ seorsim collocarentur, ut & in principio numeri ad sinistram si figuræ pauciores sint quàm sex. Ad figuram autem quæ unicam habet virgulam suprapositam pronuncies milliones, quæ duas habet virgulas, biliones, sive milliones millionum, quæ tres, trilliones, & sic deinceps, ut in hoc exemplo. 4254987653742603925
units.tr: 4. To pronounce larger numbers more easily, first learn to say six figures at a time, of which the last on the right always denotes hundreds of thousands. Thus 536432 you will say: five hundred and thirty-six thousand, four hundred and thirty-two. Then divide any given number into smaller groups, placing one dot above the seventh figure from the right, two dots above the thirteenth, three above the nineteenth, and so on as far as you like, adding one dot for each sixth figure. Finally, begin reading at the figure that follows each dot, and take the six figures separately, the same at the beginning of the number on the left if there are fewer than six figures. Over the group that has one dot you say millions; the group with two dots, billions, that is millions of millions; with three, trillions; and so on, as in this example: 4254987653742603925.

units.la: Numerum hìc datum sic pronuncies, Quatuor triliones, Ducenta, quingenta, quatuor millia, nongenti octoginta septem biliones, sexcenta quinquaginta tria millia, septingenti quadraginta duo milliones, sexcenta tria millia, nongenti viginti quinque. Et hoc modo quantuscunque proponatur numerus facillimè pronuncietur.
units.tr: You pronounce the number given here thus: four trillion, two hundred and five hundred and four thousand, nine hundred and eighty-seven billion, six hundred and fifty-three thousand, seven hundred and forty-two million, six hundred and three thousand, nine hundred and twenty-five. In this way any number proposed, however large, is most easily pronounced.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De Characteribus Indicis.
units.tr: On the Indian Characters.

units.la: I. Characteres Indici sunt quibus Indi, Turcæ, Arabes, Persæ, aliique populi orientales ad numeros exprimendos utuntur.
units.tr: I. The Indian characters are those which the Indians, Turks, Arabs, Persians and other eastern peoples use to express numbers.

units.la: 1. NOs vulgarem per figuras & cifram computandi rationem Arabibus acceptam ferimus, quod & ipsa vox cifra, ut Arabica, satis demonstrat. Arabicè enim Cifra, vacuum denotat, unde hæc nota iis cifra dicitur, quasi significationis vacua. Ipsi tamen Arabes non se sed Indos (quos [Arabic] Fodinam sapientiæ jure nuncupat Abulpharagius Dynast.1.) ingeniosissimam hanc per figuras numerandi rationem excogitâsse ferunt: quam itaque حساب أهل هند Computum populi Indiæ, sive Indorum Arithmeticam vocant. Et hinc est quòd etiamsi characteres isti ab aliis etiam usitantur, eos tamen Indicos à primis inventoribus denominamus.
units.tr: 1. We rightly credit the Arabs with the common method of computing by figures and the cipher, as the very word cifra, which is Arabic, shows well. For in Arabic cifra means empty, and so this mark is called cifra, as if it had an empty meaning. The Arabs themselves, however, say that it was not they but the Indians (whom Abulpharagius, Dynast. 1, rightly calls the mine of wisdom) who devised this most ingenious method of counting by figures. They therefore call it hisab ahl Hind, the reckoning of the people of India, or the Arithmetic of the Indians. And so, although these characters are also used by others, we name them Indian after their first inventors.

units.la: II. Characteres Indici sunt decem.
units.tr: II. There are ten Indian characters.

units.la: 1. Hi decem characteres Indici ejusdem prorsus sunt valoris, & naturæ, cujus vulgares ex iis deducti. Nam 1 significat unitatem, 2 duas unitates, & sic deinceps. Ultima item figura, quæ punctum est, idem valet ac vulgaris 0, sive cifra: quinetiam eodem modo atque vulgaris cifra, figuræ cujusvis valorem decuplâ proportione auget. Nam 1. valet 10, 0. 50, 9. 90, &c. ut & 1.. idem est atque 100, v.. idem quod 700, & sic in reliquis: adeò ut hi characteres nihilo discrepant à vulgaribus præterquam figurâ. Exempla horum characterum apud Geographos, Astronomos, Chronologos, aliósque scriptores Arabicos, Persicos, Turcicos, &c. passim occurrunt: ut Abulpheda in descriptione generali regionum Mawaralnahræ ait, وتوفي الحطيب سنة Et mortuus est Alhatibanno 516, viz. Hegiræ. Sic & Ulug Beig quàm doctissimus Indiæ princeps (Epoch. c.4.) Epocham Græcam asserit priorem esse Arabicâ diebus μγ.v.. i. e. 340700. Et in Grammaticâ quidem Turcicâ MS. quam nobis communicavit πολυσαωαδπ]Θ nostèr Amicus EDMUNDUS CASTELLUS, D.D. omnes hi characteres eodem quo supra modo describuntur, nisi quòd figura 2 hoc modo ⌐3 & 6 hoc ⌉ scribitur. Numerus autem Quinarius circello, & cifra puncto repræsentatur.
units.tr: 1. These ten Indian characters are of exactly the same value and nature as the common ones derived from them. For 1 signifies one unit, 2 two units, and so on. Likewise the last figure, which is a point, has the same value as the common 0, or cipher; and just as the common cipher, it increases the value of any figure tenfold. For 1· is 10, 0· is 50, 9· is 90, and so on; and 1·· is the same as 100, v·· the same as 700, and so with the rest. So these characters differ from the common ones in nothing but their shape. Examples of these characters occur everywhere in geographers, astronomers, chronologers and other Arabic, Persian and Turkish writers. Thus Abulfeda, in his general description of the regions of Mawaraalnahra, says: "And Alhatib died in the year 516" of the Hegira. Likewise Ulugh Beg, a most learned prince of India (Epoch. c. 4), asserts that the Greek era precedes the Arabic by 340700 days [μγ.v..]. And in a manuscript Turkish grammar, which our friend Edmund Castell, D.D., showed us, all these characters are described in the same way as above, except that the figure 2 is written thus ⌐3 and 6 thus ⌉. The number five is represented by a small circle, and the cipher by a point.

units.la: 2. At numerus quinarius & cifra aliter nonnunquam depinguntur, ille viz. per figuram 9, hæc per circellum, non aliter quàm cifra vulgaris, ut figuræ 100 orientalibus æquè ac nobis centum valeant: unde Alikoshgius Astronomus Persa, à Joanne Gravio laudatus, ait, صفر نوبسدن بر
units.tr: 2. But the number five and the cipher are sometimes drawn in another way: the former, namely, by the figure 9, and the latter by a small circle, just as the common cipher is, so that the figures for 100 have the value of one hundred for orientals as for us. Hence Alikoshgius, the Persian astronomer praised by John Greaves, says: "They write the cipher with the figure of a small circle" [sifr nevisdan bir; sürat dâyira-yi khurd].

units.la: صورات دايرة خرد Cifram figurâ circelli scribunt. Hisce figuris repræsentantur numerus quinarius & cifra in Arabico Ptolemæi Almagesto MS in Regia Bibliothecâ asservato, cujus videndi copiam nobis fecit doctissimus pariter & colendissimus noster amicus D. Thomas Rossius, Bibliothecarius Regius,& Ἐιμνάρχης: In hoc enim MS. circellus o cifram indicat, non numerum quinarium, qui perpetuò per dictam figuram 9 indigitatur; ut Almag. p. 8. edit. Gr. numerus Ptolemaicus ςϑϙ 4975 per ꟼqv9 transfertur. Quinetiam in MS. Alexandrino versionis 70, quod ut pretiosissimum ibidem reconditur, cujus folia Indicis hisce characteribus designantur, numerus quinarius non circello, sed dictâ figurâ, ut & cifra non puncto sed circello denotatur. Reliquæ figuræ modò descriptis similes sunt, nisi quòd figuræ ∧ linea sinistra sit brevior dextrâ, ut hoc modo ∧ descriptæ: quomodo & eam descriptam vidi in MS. Astrologico lingua Persica conscripto.
units.tr: These figures represent the number five and the cipher in the Arabic manuscript of Ptolemy's Almagest kept in the Royal Library, the sight of which was granted to us by the most learned and most esteemed friend of ours, Mr. Thomas Rossius, Royal Librarian and Ἐιμνάρχης. For in this manuscript the small circle indicates the cipher, not the number five, which is always marked by the said figure 9; as in the Almagest, p. 8 of the Greek edition, the Ptolemaic number ςϑϙ 4975 is rendered by ꟼqv9. Moreover, in the Alexandrian manuscript of the Septuagint, which is kept there as most precious, and whose leaves are marked with these Indian characters, the number five is denoted not by a small circle but by the said figure, and the cipher not by a point but by a small circle. The remaining figures are similar to those just described, except that the left line of the figure ∧ is shorter than the right, as in this form ∧; and I have seen it described in that way in a manuscript astrological work written in the Persian language.

units.la: 3. In impressis Avicennæ Arabicè ابن سينا Ibn Sina vocati, codicibus, numerus quinarius nunc figurâ 9, nunc circello repræsentatur, ut & cifra aliquando circello, aliàs puncto crassiori, qui tamen circellus videtur lituratus. Nam pagina 15 significatur his figuris 19, & pagina 20 his ᵠ. At in libro tertio pagina 505 sic notatur 909, cifrâ per circellum, ut antea per punctum notato; at pagina 350 per μ0. & 355 per μ00 signatur circello, viz. numerum quinarium indigitante. Et quidem circellus Indica videtur numeri quinarii figura, altera enim ϑ est tantùm litera Arabica ℊ inversa, quæ in Alphabeto Arabico eundem etiam numerum designat, atque ideò Arabibus forte solis circelli loco substituitur.
units.tr: 3. In the printed editions of Avicenna, called in Arabic Ibn Sina, the number five is sometimes represented by the figure 9, sometimes by a small circle; and the cipher sometimes by a small circle, at other times by a thicker point, though that circle seems to have been erased. For on page 15 it is marked by these figures, 19, and on page 20 by ᵠ. But in the third book, page 505, it is marked thus, 909, with the cipher denoted by a small circle, as before it was marked by a point; yet on page 350 it is marked by μ0., and on 355 by μ00, with a small circle, which indicates the number five. And indeed the small circle seems to be the Indian figure for the number five, for the other figure ϑ is only the Arabic letter ℊ inverted, which in the Arabic alphabet also designates the same number, and so it is perhaps substituted for the circle among the Arabs alone.

units.la: 4. Hujusmodi fuere characteres Arithmetici plurimis abhinc annorum centuriis ab Indis inventi, & per totum orientem usitati ; in occidentem autem translati varias subierunt mutationes. Majores enim nostri aliter quàm nos eos descripserunt: Sed utcunque scripti sunt, haud dubium est quin nostri ab Indicis efformantur. Quod ut clariùs pateat, non abs re erit omnes hujusmodi characteres in subjectâ tabellâ repræsentare.
units.tr: 4. Such were the arithmetical characters invented by the Indians many centuries ago and used throughout the East; but when they were carried to the West they underwent various changes. For our forefathers described them differently from us. Yet however they were written, there is no doubt that ours are formed from the Indian ones. To make this clearer, it will not be out of place to set out all such characters in the table below.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: De Characteribus Romanis.
units.tr: On the Roman Characters.

units.la: I. Hactenus de Characteribus Figuratis, sequuntur Literales.
units.tr: I. So far concerning the figured characters; the letter characters follow.

units.la: II. Characteres Literales sunt vel orientales vel occidentales.
units.tr: II. Letter characters are either eastern or western.

units.la: III. Characteres occidentales sive Romani sunt quinque, I, V, X, L, C.
units.tr: III. The western or Roman characters are five: I, V, X, L, C.

units.la: I. PEr hasce solas quinque literas Romani numeros omnes exprimere solebant, idque hoc modo. Prima litera I unitatem notat; V numerum quinarium, quoniam quinta est vocalis; X 10, ut decima Græci Alphabeti consonans, L verò 50; & C centum valet. Omnes alii numeri per hasce literas variè dispositas exhibentur: nam litera I bis posita valet 2, ter 3, &c. ut II 2, III 3; sic XX 20, XXX 30: Unde & in antiquis inscriptionibus hæc figura ⲴⲨ vel ⲭ 20 valeat, & hæc ⲭⲭ 30, ibi viz. literâ X bis, nec ter repetitâ. V & L nunquam repetuntur, ut nec I, X aut C plusquàm quater: nisi quòd I in antiquis quibusdam inscriptionibus sexies ponitur, ut in Ará oblongá Aquileiæ inventá, cui hæc inscripta sunt, ut ex Piglico notavit Gruterus.
units.tr: I. Using only these five letters, the Romans were accustomed to express all their numbers, and they did so in this way. The first letter, I, signifies unity; V signifies the number five, since it is the fifth vowel; X signifies ten, as the tenth consonant of the Greek alphabet; L is fifty; and C is worth a hundred. All other numbers are shown by these letters arranged in various ways: for I placed twice is worth 2, three times 3, and so on, as II is 2 and III is 3; so XX is 20 and XXX is 30. Hence in ancient inscriptions the figure XX is worth 20, and the figure XXX is worth 30, namely with the letter X used twice and not repeated three times. V and L are never repeated, nor are I, X or C used more than four times, except that in some ancient inscriptions I is placed six times, as on the oblong altar found at Aquileia, on which these words are inscribed, as Gruter noted from Pighius.

units.la: BELINO SEX CÆSERNIVS FAVSTVS IIIIII VIR V. S. L. M.
units.tr: TO BELINUS: SEXTUS CAESERNIUS FAUSTUS, SEVIR (SIX-FOLD MAN), HAS FULFILLED HIS VOW WILLINGLY AND DESERVEDLY.

units.la: Ubi vides ut litera I ante V I R sexies ponitur, ad significandum Sevir, vel Sextum vir, quod tamen vocabulum ita sæpius signatur V̄I V I R in ipsis etiam inscriptionibus. Alias autem cùm ad numerum quinarium deventum est, iste per figuram sibi propriam indicatur,ut 5 per V, 50 per L, 500 per Ɔ, & sic deinceps, uti mox patebit.
units.tr: Here you see that the letter I is placed six times before V I R, to signify Sevir, or Sextum vir; yet this word is more often abbreviated as V̄I V I R, even in the inscriptions themselves. Otherwise, when the number five is reached, it is indicated by its own special figure: 5 by V, 50 by L, 500 by Ɔ, and so on, as will soon become clear.

units.la: 2. Si litera I cuipiam è prædictis postponatur, tot ei unitates addit,quoties ipsa ponitur; ut VI 6, XII 12, LIII 53, CIII 103. Si verò I literæ V vel X præponatur, tot unitates ei detrahit; ut IV valet 4, quoniam I semel præmissa detrahit unitatem: sic & IX 9, IIX 8. Quinetiam X literis L & C præposita se iis adimit, ut XL 40, XC 90, XXC 80.
units.tr: 2. If the letter I is placed after any of the above, it adds as many units as it is repeated: VI 6, XII 12, LIII 53, CIII 103. But if I is placed before V or X, it takes away that many units: thus IV is 4, since one I placed in front takes away one unit; so too IX 9, IIX 8. Moreover, X placed before L and C subtracts itself from them: XL 40, XC 90, XXC 80.

units.la: 3. Porrò, ut una C valet 100, sic CC 200, CCC 300, CCCC 400. Cùm numerus autem quingentarius occurrit exprimendus, litera C (nè sæpius quàm par est, repeteretur) invertitur, eíque litera I præfigitur hunc in modum Ɔ, pro quo charactere corrupto nonnunquam scribunt D & Þ. Numerum verò millenarium ad exprimendum, quingentario aliam C præfigunt hunc in modum CIƆ, ex quo charactere depravato reliqui formantur millenarii, viz. ∞, M, &c. hinc CIƆ CIƆ vel ∞ ∞ 2000, & sic deinceps repetuntur.
units.tr: 3. Further, as a single C is 100, so CC is 200, CCC 300, CCCC 400. When the number five hundred has to be expressed, the letter C is reversed (lest it be repeated more often than necessary), and the letter I is prefixed to it, in this way: Ɔ. For this corrupted character some write D or Þ. To express the number one thousand, however, they prefix another C to the five hundred, in this way: CIƆ. From this corrupted character the remaining thousands are formed, namely ∞, M, and so on. Hence CIƆ CIƆ or ∞ ∞ is 2000, and so on in repetition.

units.la: 4. Porrò,ut 500 repræsentatur per I unicæ C, sic 5000 per eandem literam duabus C inversis præfixam, hunc in modum IƆƆ, quibus si præponas duas alias C directas sic CCIƆƆ characterem numeri 10000 habebis. Eâdem quoque ratione IƆƆ valet 50000 at CCCIƆƆƆ 100000, IƆƆƆƆ 500000, & CCCCIƆƆƆƆ 1000000, sive millionem. Et vereor ut hi characteres ulterius procedant, cùm sit contra ipsam eorum rationem & institutionem, ut eadem litera plusquam quater repeteretur.
units.tr: 4. Further, as 500 is represented by one reversed C with I, so 5000 is represented by the same letter with two reversed Cs prefixed, in this way: IƆƆ. If you put two other direct Cs before these, as in CCIƆƆ, you will have the figure for 10000. By the same reasoning IƆƆ is 50000, but CCCIƆƆƆ is 100000, IƆƆƆƆ is 500000, and CCCCIƆƆƆƆ is 1000000, or a million. I doubt whether these characters go any further, since it is contrary to their very principle and design that the same letter should be repeated more than four times.

units.la: 5. Hæc omnia ex tabellâ magis elucescent, quam subjiciam, postquam præmiserim numeros millenarios etiam per quinque prædictas literas cum lineâ transversâ nonnunquam depingi; ut I̅ 1000, V̅ 5000, X̅ 10000, L̅ 50000, C̅ 100000. Et quòd pro CIƆ CIƆ 2000 aliquoties scribunt IICIƆ vel IIM; sic etiam IVCIƆ 4000, VIICIƆ 7000, & sic in reliquis.
units.tr: 5. All this will become clearer from the table which I shall append, after first noting that the thousands are sometimes also marked by the five aforesaid letters with a transverse line: I̅ 1000, V̅ 5000, X̅ 10000, L̅ 50000, C̅ 100000. And since they often write IICIƆ or IIM for CIƆ CIƆ 2000, so also IVCIƆ is 4000, VIICIƆ is 7000, and so on for the rest.

units.la: 6. Hæc præcepta exemplis jam illustremus. Quintus Curtius l.7. ait, Quippe mediâ ferè nocte in castra redierunt, multis interfectis, pluribus captis, equôsque MDCCC abegêre, i. e. 1800. Varro de re rustica, l. 1. c. 28. Ut ver dies habeat XCI, æstas XCIV, autumnus XCI, hyems XXCIX: i. e. ver dies habeat 91, æstas 94, autumnus 91, & hyems 89; nam XX ante C, se, hoc est, 20 ei subtrahunt. Idem ibidem l. 3. c. 12. Ut cirtiter ꝏ ꝏ ꝏ ꝏ passuum locum inclusum habeat; ubi character millenarius quater positus quatuor millia significat. Velleius Paterculus l.1. Nam fermè ante annos DCCCCL floruit Homerus, intra ꝏ natus est: i.e. floruit ante annos nongentos quinquaginta, intra mille natus. Plinius hist.nat.l.36.c.13. Homo qui primus fabrus est ante annos (ut tradunt) IIIMDC, i. e. 3600. Cicero pro Roscio Comœdo, Proh deûm hominûmque fidem! qui H-S CCCIƆƆƆ CCCIƆƆƆ CCCIƆƆƆ quæstus facere noluit, (nam certè H-S CCCIƆƆƆ CCCIƆƆƆ CCCIƆƆƆ merere potuit & debuit, si potest Dionysio H-S. CCCIƆƆƆ CCCIƆƆƆ merere) is per summam fraudem & malitiam & perfidiam H S IƆƆƆ appetiit? Ubi characteres H-S CCCIƆƆƆ Sestertia centum millia valent, bis autem posita ducenta millia, & ter repetiti trecenta millia. At per IƆƆƆ quinquaginta millia significantur. Quæ omnia è tabellâ patent.
units.tr: 6. Let us now illustrate these rules with examples. Quintus Curtius, book 7, says: Indeed, they returned to camp almost at midnight, many having been killed, more taken, and they carried off 1800 horses, that is, 1800. Varro, On Agriculture, book 1, chapter 28: Let spring have 91 days, summer 94, autumn 91, and winter 89; that is, spring has 91 days, summer 94, autumn 91, and winter 89, for XX placed before C takes away 20 from it. The same author, book 3, chapter 12: Let Cirta have an enclosed area of ꝏ ꝏ ꝏ ꝏ paces, where the thousand-character, placed four times, signifies four thousand. Velleius Paterculus, book 1: For Homer flourished nearly nine hundred and fifty years ago, and was born within ꝏ, that is, he flourished more than 950 years ago and was born within 1000 years. Pliny, Natural History, book 36, chapter 13: The man who was the first smith lived, as they report, IIIMDC years ago, that is, 3600. Cicero, For Roscius the Actor: Good heavens, what a man! He who did not want to make a profit of H-S CCCIƆƆƆ CCCIƆƆƆ CCCIƆƆƆ (for surely he could and should have earned H-S CCCIƆƆƆ CCCIƆƆƆ CCCIƆƆƆ, if he could earn H-S CCCIƆƆƆ CCCIƆƆƆ from Dionysius) has sought H S IƆƆƆ by the utmost fraud, malice and treachery? Here the characters H-S CCCIƆƆƆ one hundred thousand sesterces have the value of 100,000; twice repeated they are 200,000, and three times repeated 300,000. But IƆƆƆ signifies fifty thousand. All this is evident from the table.

units.la: 7. Quod ad reliquos spectat in tabulâ descriptos Romanorum characteres, viz. numerorum 1000, 5000 & 10000, isti nullibi (ut opinor) extant, præterquam in antiquis quibusdam inscriptionibus, quarum unam & alteram in exemplum huc transferre non pigebit. Romæ apud Gentilem Delphinum extitit hæc antiquissima inscriptio ipsi Smetio visa.
units.tr: 7. As for the rest of the Roman characters described in the table, namely those for 1000, 5000 and 10000, these, as I think, are nowhere to be found except in certain ancient inscriptions. It will not be tedious to transfer one or two of these here as examples. At Rome, in the possession of Gentilis Delphinus, there existed this most ancient inscription, which Smetius himself saw.

units.tr: MINUCIA. M. L. HEDONE. OF THE SACRED RITES. LIVED 97 YEARS. BY HER WILL SHE ORDERED THIS TO BE MADE FROM 6200 SESTERCES.

units.la: Quid sibi vellent characteres hic insculpti satis è tabellâ constat viz. 6200. Nam primus character idem valet, vel potius idem est atque IƆƆ, cum hoc tantùm discrimine, quòd in charactere hic inscripto unaC inversa minor sit quàm altera, cùm in ↓IƆƆ utraque sit ejusdem quantitatis. Et ipse quidem nullus dubito quin omnes reliqui characteres ex iis qui in tabulâ primi describuntur, variè ob scribendi ceritritatem depravatis, efformantur. Quod tamen ut magis elucescat, aliam subjicere inscriptionem operæ pretium erit, quæ quidem fragmento tabulæ marmoreæ in domo medici civitatis inventa fuit.
units.tr: What the characters carved here signify is clear enough from the table, namely 6200. For the first character has the same value, or rather is the same as IƆƆ, with only this difference: in the character inscribed here, one inverted C is smaller than the other, whereas in IƆƆ both are of the same size. I myself have no doubt that all the other characters are formed from those described first in the table, variously corrupted through carelessness in writing. So that this may become clearer, it will be worth adding another inscription, which was found on a fragment of a marble tablet in the house of a physician of the city.

units.tr: P. DECIMIUS, SON OF P., OF THE FREEDMAN LINE OF EROS MERULA: PHYSICIAN, CLINICAL SURGEON, OCULIST, SIXVIR. FOR HIS FREEDOM HE GAVE 50,000 SESTERCES. FOR HIS SEVIRATE HE GAVE INTO THE PUBLIC TREASURY 2000 SESTERCES. FOR SETTING UP STATUES IN THE TEMPLE OF HERCULES HE GAVE 30,000 SESTERCES. FOR PAVING THE STREETS FOR PUBLIC USE HE GAVE 37,000 SESTERCES. FINALLY, THE DAY BEFORE HE DIED HE LEFT A PATRIMONY OF 19,000 SESTERCES.

units.la: Characteres hic inscriptos sic explicamus: Pro Libertate dedit Sestertia 50000; nam ista figura eadem est quæ IƆƆƆ, utpote quæ tres etiam C inversas ad dextram habet. Pro Seviratu dedit Sestertia 2000. In Statuas ponendas in ædem Herculis dedit Sestertia 30000; nam & iste character ⋔ idem est qui CCIƆƆ raptim scriptus. In vias sternendas dedit Sestertia 37000. Patrimonii denique reliquit Sestertia undeviginti millia, sive 19000; nam character millenarius ∞ reliquis præpositus se iis detrahit. Quod & in minoribus numeris antea observatum est.
units.tr: We explain the characters inscribed here as follows. For freedom he gave 50,000 sesterces; for this figure is the same as IƆƆƆ, since it likewise has three inverted C's on the right. For the sevirate he gave 2000 sesterces. For setting up statues in the temple of Hercules he gave 30,000 sesterces; for this character ⋔ is the same as CCIƆƆ, written hastily. For paving the streets he gave 37,000 sesterces. Lastly, he left a patrimony of nineteen thousand, that is 19,000 sesterces; for the thousand-mark ∞, placed before the other figures, subtracts itself from them. This was also observed earlier in smaller numbers.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: De Characteribus Hebraicis, & Samaritanis.
units.tr: On Hebrew and Samaritan Characters.

units.la: I. Characteres Orientales sunt Hebraici, Samaritani, Græci, Syriaci, Arabici, & Æthiopici.
units.tr: I. The Oriental characters are Hebrew, Samaritan, Greek, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic.

units.la: II. Hebraici sunt omnes Alphabeti literæ in tres classes novenarias distributæ, quarum prima monadicos, altera denarios, tertia centenarios continet, hunc in modum. Unitates. | Decades. | Centuriæ. א 1 | י 10 | ק 100 ב 2 | כ 20 | ר 200 ג 3 | ל 30 | ש 300 ד 4 | מ 40 | ת 400 ה 5 | נ 50 | ך 500 ו 6 | ס 60 | ם 600 ז 7 | ע 70 | ן 700 ח 8 | פ 80 | ף 800 ט 9 | צ 90 | ץ 900
units.tr: II. The Hebrew alphabet, all its letters, is distributed into three classes of nine. The first class contains the units, the second the tens, and the third the hundreds, as follows. Units. | Tens. | Hundreds. Aleph 1 | Yod 10 | Qof 100; Bet 2 | Kaf 20 | Resh 200; Gimel 3 | Lamed 30 | Shin 300; Dalet 4 | Mem 40 | Tav 400; He 5 | Nun 50 | Kaf final 500; Vav 6 | Samekh 60 | Mem final 600; Zayin 7 | Ayin 70 | Nun final 700; Het 8 | Pe 80 | Pe final 800; Tet 9 | Tsade 90 | Tsade final 900.

units.la: I. Omnes numeri infra millenarium per literas Hebraicas tribus hisce classibus (quarum ultima literas etiam finales introducit) dispositas exprimuntur. Ad numeros autem intermedios exprimendos literas primæ classis novenariæ subjiciunt secundæ, ut יא 11, יב 12, יג 13, & sic deinceps usque ad viginti; nisi quòd quindecim per יה i.e. 9 & 6, scribunt non per יו, utpote quòd unum è
units.tr: I. All numbers below a thousand are expressed by Hebrew letters arranged in these three classes (the last of which also takes in the final letters). To express intermediate numbers they add letters of the second class to those of the first, as Yod-Alef 11, Yod-Bet 12, Yod-Gimel 13, and so on up to twenty. The exception is fifteen, which they write not as Yod-Vav but as Yod-He, that is, 9 and 6, since Yod-Vav is one of the names of God. For that reason it is not to be pronounced when expressing any number, lest it be profaned.

units.la: Dei sit nominibus, & idcirco ad numerum quemlibet exprimendum non pronunciandum est, nè prophanetur. Eodem etiam modo נא valet 21, כג 23, לט 39, עו 76 ; & sic usque ad centenarios, quibus tertiá classe comprehensis subjiciuntur literæ primæ & secundæ, ut קיא III, רכ 230. At literæ quinque finales ad finem numeri juxta morem plerumque collocantur ; ut םמ vel םמ 644, ןב 932. Ubi notes quòd hosce numeros per Patha plerunque legunt, nisi desinant in ˋ vel ˋ; ut לאת lat 39, נג nag 53. Ipsis autem characteribus literas serviles aliquoties præponunt; ut מלה millah à 38, לקל lekal ad 130 : ubi etiam observes vellem, literas numerales ab aliis secerni virgulis supernè notatis, unam quidem unicâ, plures verò duabus.
units.tr: In the same way Nun-Alef is 21, Kaf-Gimel 23, Lamed-Tet 39, Ayin-Vav 76; and so on up to the hundreds, to which, when they are included in the third class, the first and second letters are added, as Qof-Yod-Alef 111 and Resh-Kaf-Lamed... more precisely Resh-Kaf 230. The five final letters, however, are commonly placed at the end of the number, as Mem-Mem (final) 644 and Nun-Bet 932. Note that these numbers are usually read with a patah, unless they end in a final letter, as Lamed-Alef-Tav (lat) 39 and Nun-Gimel (nag) 53. Sometimes they also prefix servile letters to the numeral characters themselves, as Mem-Lamed-He (millah) 38 and Lamed-Qof-Lamed (lekal) 130. Here I would also have you observe that numeral letters are set apart from the others by strokes marked above them: one stroke over a single letter, and two over several.

units.la: 2. Porrò ultra numerum 400 per literam ת perpetuò expressum, neglectis literis quinque finalibus, alios centenarios literæ ת nonnunquam adjungunt ; ut ףך 500, תך 600, םם 700 ; sic & תףך 800, תןך 900.
units.tr: 2. Beyond 400, which is always expressed by the letter Tav, the final letters being omitted, they sometimes add other hundreds to the letter Tav: as Pe-Kaf (final) 500, Tav-Kaf 600, Mem-Mem 700; and likewise Tav-Pe-Kaf 800 and Tav-Nun-Kaf 900.

units.la: 3. Si numeri millenarii occurrunt exprimendi eos, integris vocibus describere solent: ut mille per אלף Eleph, duo millia per אלפים Alpaijm, plura millia per אלפים Alaphim, cum literâ numerali præmissâ, ut ד אלפים quatuor millia, ל אלפים triginta millia, &c. Nonnunquam autem ipsi etiam millenarii per simplices Alphabeti literas repræsentantur, sequente præcipuè centenario, à quo tamen aliquantulùm separantur; ut תא 1430, הרמב 5242. Rarò etiam ante literam non centenariam ; אל 1030, עא 1070.
units.tr: 3. When thousands have to be expressed, they usually write them out in full words: a thousand by Eleph (אלף), two thousand by Alpaijm (אלפים), more thousands by Alaphim (אלפים), with a numeral letter placed before, as Dalet Alaphim, four thousand; Lamed Alaphim, thirty thousand; and so on. Sometimes, however, thousands themselves are represented by single letters of the alphabet, chiefly when a hundred follows, though these are set somewhat apart from it: as Tav-Alef 1430 and He-Resh-Mem-Bet 5242. Rarely they also stand before a letter that is not a hundred: Alef-Lamed 1030 and Ayin-Alef 1070.

units.la: 4. Totam hanc præcedentem characterum Hebraicorum doctrinam exemplis aliquibus jam illustremus, & primò quidem Biblicis. In Masoretharum notis Geneseos fini subjectis versus istius libri dicuntur esse אלה i.e. 1534 ; versus Exodi sunt אש i.e. 1209 ; Deuteronomii verò הנץ 955 : ubi videre e ut litera finalis ך fini vocis adjicitur: Sic & versus Samuelis sunt אוך 1506, ubi ה valet 1000, ו ut finalis ad finem rejecta 500, & 6. At versus Nehemiæ sunt תרפח 688; nam ק valet 400, & ר 200, qui numeri conjuncti efficiunt 600, & cum פח 688. Eadem numerandi ratio & in aliis libris observatur, ut in proœmio ad Benjamini Itinerarium, cum observationes suas in Castiliam detulisse traditur anno computi minoris Judaici חתקלג 933, In Seder Olam Zuta Moses excessisse dicitur anno mundi ב חפט 2489. In tractatu de inveniendo Moledoth & Tekuphoth à Munstero edito hæc legere est, הנרי קבלנו מרבותינו שחתרף חלקים יש בשער Ecce accepimus à Rabbinis nostris quod in horâ sint helakim 1080; nam ד ante תתרו est litera servilis, significans quòd: ibidem mensis constare dicitur, כט יב תשעו 29 d. 12 h. 793 hel. Verùm exempla hujusmodi passim occurrunt; hæc itaque præceptis nostris dilucidandis sufficiant.
units.tr: 4. Let us now illustrate this whole preceding doctrine of the Hebrew characters with some examples, first of all from the Bible. In the Masoretes' notes appended to the end of Genesis, the verses of that book are said to be Alah (אלה), that is, 1534. The verses of Exodus are Esh (אש), that is, 1209, and those of Deuteronomy Hanets (הנץ), 955; here you see that the final letter Kaf is added to the end of the word. Likewise the verses of Samuel are Uk (אוך), 1506, where He is 1000, Vav (as a final letter, rejected to the end) 500, and Kaf 6. The verses of Nehemiah are Tarpach (תרפח), 688: for Qof is 400 and Resh 200, which together make 600, and with Pe-He (פח) 688. The same method of counting is observed in other books too: in the preface to Benjamin's Itinerary, where his observations on Castile are said to have been reported in the year of the minor Jewish reckoning Hatkalag (חתקלג), 933. In the Seder Olam Zuta, Moses is said to have died in the year of the world Bechafat (ב חפט), 2489. In the tract on finding the Moledoth and Tekuphoth, published by Münster, one may read this: Ecce accepimus a Rabbinis nostris, quod in hora sunt helakim 1080 (הנרי קבלנו מרבותינו שחתרף חלקים יש בשער): that is, "Behold, we have received from our rabbis that there are 1080 helakim in an hour." Here Dalet before Tatru (תתרו) is a servile letter, signifying that the month is said to consist of 29 days, 12 hours, and 793 helakim (כט יב תשעו). But examples of this kind occur everywhere; these will suffice to clarify our rules.

units.la: 5. Sed non omittendum est Judæos in librorum præcipuè titulis, ad annum quo impressi sunt indigitandum, literas numerales alio atque quem tradidimus ordine collocare. Enimverò vocem unam vel plures, eásque vel seorsim, vel in sententiâ aliquâ Biblicâ comprehensas excogitant, quarum literæ ut ut dispositæ, numerum propositum valeant. Ex. gr. In Bibliis Sacris à Josepho Athia Amsteloda-mi editis, tria occurrunt frontispicia, unum ad Pentateuchum, ad Prophetas alterum, tertium ad Hagiographa. Primùm impressum dicitur שנת לשני עש ספר מהיר לפב Anno computi minoris lingua mea est stylus scribæ prompti, Psal. 45. ubi voces עש ספר ut virgulis supernè notatæ annum indigitant quo Pentateuchus impressus fuit. Quotus autem fuit annus computi Judaici minoris statim inveniatur, si omnes vocum istarum literas, unà cum numerico earum valore, itâ disponantur. ע 70 ט 9 ס 60 פ 80 ץ 200 Summa 419
units.tr: 5. But it must not be omitted that the Jews, especially on the title pages of books, to indicate the year in which they were printed, arrange the numeral letters in a different order from the one we have given. For they devise one or more words, either by themselves or included in some Biblical sentence, whose letters, however arranged, yield the number in question. For example, in the Bible printed at Amsterdam by Joseph Athias, three title pages occur: one for the Pentateuch, another for the Prophets, and a third for the Hagiographa. The first is said to have been printed in the words Anno computi minoris, lingua mea est stylus scribae prompti (Psalm 45), where the words Es sefer (עש ספר), marked above with strokes, indicate the year in which the Pentateuch was printed. The year of the minor Jewish reckoning is found at once if the letters of these words are arranged, together with their numerical values, as follows: Ayin 70, Tet 9, Samekh 60, Pe 80, Tsade final 200. Sum 419.

units.la: Ergò annus erat 419, juxta computum Judæorum minorem, de quo videfis Chronologicas nostras Institutiones. Sic & Prophetæ impressi dicuntur בשנת משא גי חוין לפ"ק Anno Onus vallis visionis computi minoris, Isai. 22. ubi literæ משא גי חוין valent 420. Frontispicium autem ad כתובים sive Hagiographa impressum est anno כתובים באצבע אלהים Scripta digito Dei; ubi primæ duæ literæ vocis כתובים viz. כח annum eundem 420 significant. Nam ח valet 400, & כ 20. Hunc etiam in modum Talmud Basiliæ impressum dicitur שנת פדות שלח לעמו Anno redemptionem misit populo suo, Pfal. 111. ubi literæ vocis שלח valent 338. Denique Seder Tepilloth Hispanensis sive Judæorum Hispanorum liturgia ingeniosissimè impressa dicitur, שנת הואר Hoc anno, i.e. anno 413, quem literæ הואר indigitant. Sed plura hujusmodi tibimet inter legendum observanda relinquo.
units.tr: So the year was 419 according to the minor Jewish reckoning, on which you may see our Chronologicae Institutiones. Likewise the Prophets are said to have been printed in the year of the minor computation, in the words Anno Onus vallis visionis (Isaiah 22), where the letters of Mesha Gi Chavin (משא גי חוין) make 420. The title page of the Hagiographa, however, was printed in the year of the words Scripta digito Dei (written with the finger of God), where the first two letters of the word Ketuvim (כתובים), namely Kaf and Tav, signify the same year, 420: for Kaf is 20 and Tav 400. In this way too the Talmud is said to have been printed at Basel in the year Anno redemptionem misit populo suo (Psalm 111), where the letters of the word Shelach (שלח) are worth 338. Finally, the Spanish Seder Tepilloth, or liturgy of the Spanish Jews, is said to have been printed very ingeniously in the words Hoc anno, that is, in the year 413, which the letters of Hoar (הואר) indicate. But I leave the observation of many more such things to you as you read.

units.la: III. Per Samaritanum sive antiquum Hebræorum Alphabe- tum ut literis finalibus destitutum, omnes numeri perpe- tuo hunc in modum exprimuntur.
units.tr: III. By the Samaritan or ancient Hebrew alphabet, which lacks final letters, all numbers are expressed in the following way.

units.la: א 1 | מ 10 | ף 100 ב 2 | י 20 | ק 200 ג 3 | ל 30 | ש 300 ד 4 | מ 40 | ת 400 ה 5 | נ 50 | ײ 500 ו 6 | ס 60 | ײא 600 ז 7 | ע 70 | ײב 700 ח 8 | פ 80 | ײג 800 ט 9 | צ 90 | ײד 900 Numeri millenarii eodem modo quo per literas recentiores sive Chaldaicas significantur, viz. ad monadicos, denarios, vel centenaries recurrendo: ut ͞ͅ1000, ͞230000, &c. Sed inter majorem & minores numeros literam ϸ interserunt; ut in versione Samaritanâ ad calcem libri Geneseôs dicitur ‎ Iste liber primus sectionum est 250. In reliquis Samaritani à vulgaribus Hebræorum characteribus non discrepant, ut diutiùs in iis explicandis immoremur non opus sit.
units.tr: Aleph 1 | Mem 10 | Pe 100; Beth 2 | Yod 20 | Qoph 200; Gimel 3 | Lamed 30 | Shin 300; Daleth 4 | Mem 40 | Tav 400; He 5 | Nun 50 | 500; Vav 6 | Samek 60 | 600; Zayin 7 | Ayin 70 | 700; Heth 8 | Pe 80 | 800; Teth 9 | Tsade 90 | 900. Thousands are expressed in the same way as by the later or Chaldean letters, namely by returning to the units, tens or hundreds: for example, 1000 (with a stroke above), 230000, and so on. But between the larger and smaller numbers they interpose a special mark. Thus in the Samaritan version at the end of the book of Genesis it is said: "This is the first book of sections," 250. In other respects the Samaritan letters do not differ from the common Hebrew characters, so there is no need to linger longer over them.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: De Characteribus Græcis.
units.tr: On the Greek Characters.

units.la: I. Characteres Græci sunt omnes Alphabeti literæ, & tres præterea figuræ, quarum singularum valor in hoc latercu- lo tribus novenariis constanti classibus exhibetur.
units.tr: I. The Greek characters are all the letters of the alphabet, together with three further figures. The value of each is shown in the following table, arranged in three classes of nine.
