units.la: Nobis autem haec figura à praedictâ Samaritanâ deducta, sed idcirco tantùm Σαν πι vocata videtur, quòd partim San sive Sigma conversum, partim verò πι Graecorum refert. Nonnunquam autem (ut in Eusebii Chronico) aliter depingitur, ut & in Tabulâ videre est.
units.tr: But this figure seems to have been derived from the Samaritan one mentioned above, and to have been called Σαν πι only because it partly resembles an inverted San or Sigma and partly the Greek πι. Sometimes, however, it is drawn differently, as in Eusebius's Chronicle, and as can be seen in the table.

units.la: 2. Graeci per Alphabetum suum tribus hisce figuris auctum numeros suos repraesentare soliti sunt; & quidem eodem fere modo quo Hebraei, majoris, viz. numeri characterere praecedente, ut ιαΙΙ, ϗ32, ϙ96, ρπ222. (At in antiquis nonnullis Inscriptionibus vidi numerum minorem praecedentem, ut ΑΙ 11, ΠΙ 13, in tabulâ extante apud Alphonsum Roiscium Messanae.) Ubi etiam observes ut linea transversa cuique numero superducatur: Ex. gr. Ptolemaeus Μαθματ. Συνταξ. l. 5. p. 125. ait, Πάλιν δὲ πρὸς ζ ἔτη Καμβύσου ἐβασίλευσε Ρ... Rursùm anno 7 Cambysis, qui est 225 à Nabonasaro, luna defecit. Et paucis interjectis, Καὶ συνάγει ὁ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐποχῆς χρίω ἔτη Αἰγυπτιακὰ ἀπὸ ἡμέρας ... Et tempus ab epochà colligit annos Ægyptiacos 224, & dies 196. Eusebius in chronico, p. 183. τὰ δ' μετὰ τοῦτο ἔτη τῶν ὑπὸ ... Inter hæc autem sunt anni 483. Si virgula cuivis ex hisce characteribus primo loco collocatis subjiciatur, tot per eos millenarii significantur, quot per se unitates valent: ut Ptolemæus libro prædicto, pag. 127. Συνάγλα ... Ubi characteres λϑ & ϛχμϛ 6644. Nonnunquam & linea transversa & virgula subjicienda millenaria omittitur; ut in novella imperatoris Alexii de nuptiis, τῆς γὰρ περιεχούσης ... 1. e. Indictione 7, anno 6592. Et mox, τῆς παρούσης ... præsenti Indictione 15, anno 6600. Geminus in Elem. Astron. c.6. ἑπτὰ ... fiunt ergo dies 292 1/3. Sed non omittendum est lineam transversam capiti ꝏ nonnunquam impingi, sic Ō vel ō; quæ quidem figura in demonstrationibus & calculis Astronomicis cifræ loco usurpatur; ut in Ptolemæi l.4. p.101. τὰ ἐκάστῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἐπιζάλλοντα ὁ ὁ ὁ ὁ ια μς λϑ Partes unicuique diei convenientes 0000 11, 46 39. Hujusmodi cifrarum exempla passim apud Ptolemæum occurrunt.
units.tr: 2. The Greeks, using their alphabet increased by these three figures, were accustomed to represent their numbers in almost the same way as the Hebrews, namely with the larger numeral placed before the smaller, as ιαΙΙ, ϗ32, ϙ96, ρπ222. (In some ancient inscriptions, however, I have seen the smaller number placed first, as ΑΙ 11, ΠΙ 13, in a table existing at Messina in the work of Alphonsus Roiscius.) Here you should also observe that a horizontal line is drawn over each number. For example, Ptolemy in his Mathematical Syntaxis, book 5, page 125, says: "Again, in the seventh year of Cambyses, which is 225 from Nabonassar, the moon was eclipsed" [Πάλιν δὲ πρὸς ζ ἔτη Καμβύσου ἐβασίλευσε Ρ...]. And a few lines later: "And he reckons the time from the epoch as 224 Egyptian years and 196 days" [Καὶ συνάγει ὁ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐποχῆς χρίω ἔτη Αἰγυπτιακὰ ἀπὸ ἡμέρας ...]. Eusebius in his Chronicle, page 183: "The years after this... Among these, however, are 483 years" [τὰ δ' μετὰ τοῦτο ἔτη τῶν ὑπὸ ...]. If a small stroke is placed under any of these characters when they stand first, they signify as many thousands as the units they stand for by themselves: as in the same Ptolemy, the aforementioned book, page 127, where the characters λϑ and ϛχμϛ stand for 6644. Sometimes the horizontal line and the thousands-stroke below are both omitted; as in the novel of the emperor Alexius on marriages: "For in the current indiction, 7, in the year 6592" [τῆς γὰρ περιεχούσης ...], and soon after, "in the present indiction 15, in the year 6600" [τῆς παρούσης ...]. Geminus in Elements of Astronomy, chapter 6: "Seven... therefore the days are 292 1/3" [ἑπτὰ ...]. But it should not be overlooked that the horizontal line is sometimes placed over the symbol for zero, as Ō or ō. This figure is used in demonstrations and astronomical calculations in place of a cipher, as in Ptolemy, book 4, page 101: "The parts falling to each day" [τὰ ἐκάστῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἐπιζάλλοντα], ὁ ὁ ὁ ὁ ια μς λϑ, "the parts belonging to each day," 0000, 11, 46, 39. Examples of such ciphers occur everywhere in Ptolemy.

units.la: 3. Si numerus quispiam major detur, quàm qui unicâ millenaria figurâ describatur, eum ad exprimendum duplici utuntur methodo, primo cuiqs characteri millenario virgulam suam subjiciunt. Et una quidem virgula millenariorum monades, altera decades, tertia centurias designat; ut numerus 26435 sic exprimitur κϛυλ. Ex. gr.
units.tr: 3. If a number is given that is larger than can be described by a single thousands figure, they use a twofold method to express it: first, they place a small stroke under each thousands character. One stroke marks the units of thousands, a second the tens, and a third the hundreds. For example, the number 26435 is expressed thus: κϛυλ.

units.la: Geminus in Elementis Astronomicis, cap. 15. ait. Παραπληλα δ ὁ ἑξηλισμὸς πεντ̀ηκοντα δυς μυρὰς χξθ, ἡμέρας ϛ ιϐϟνς, observatur autem evolutio continere menses 669, dies verò 19756. Et paucis interpositis, γινεται ὁ πὶς ἀειϑμὸς μοιρῶν ὀξγιβ, Fit ergo totus numerus graduum 260312. Et eâdem ratione hi characteres ͵Ϟϙξϛ valent 946894. Nonnunquam hâc utuntur figurâ ⟨ͻ⟩ cui ad dextram suprascribunt decades millium, ad sinistram centurias. Si alii minores numeri occurrunt exprimendi seorsim colloeantur, ut apud Ptol.l.4. p.100. Πάντ̀ς δ ἡμέρας ⟨ΛϞ⟩ ἡ ϛ↓τγ, omnes autem dies 310000,& 1783; sive conjunctim 311783.Et ib.p.102. ταῦτα ἐν ἐπιμεσὸν ἐλες εἰς τὸ πλῆρ ἡμ ἐν τῷ πεπλημμένῳ χρόνῳ συναχθέντα ἡμέρων ⟨ϗβ ϛχθ⟩, Hæc itaque partiti in multitudinem dierum ex dato tempore collectorum 224609. Ubi etiam observes literas huic figuræ suprascriptas monadicas quidem in denarias, denarias autem in centenarias promoveri; nam in ultimo exemplo litera ϐ suprascripta valet 20, & ϰ 200; cùm alibì illa tantùm 2, & hæc 20 significat: adeò ut eâdem ratione si characteres etiam centenarii præponantur, hi millenarii facti milliones etiam exprimerent.
units.tr: Geminus, in his Elements of Astronomy, chapter 15, says: "The period of the parallel cycle is 52 thousand 6? hundred... days, and the evolution is observed to contain 669 months and 19756 days" [Παραπληλα δ ὁ ἑξηλισμὸς πεντ̀ηκοντα δυς μυρὰς χξθ, ἡμέρας ϛ ιϐϟνς]. And a few lines later: "Therefore the whole number of degrees comes to 260312" [γινεται ὁ πὶς ἀειϑμὸς μοιρῶν ὀξγιβ]. By the same method, these characters ͵Ϟϙξϛ stand for 946894. Sometimes they use the figure ⟨ͻ⟩, with the tens of thousands written above it on the right and the hundreds on the left. If other smaller numbers are to be expressed, they are placed separately, as in Ptolemy, book 4, page 100: "All the days are 310000 and 1783, or together 311783" [Πάντ̀ς δ ἡμέρας ⟨ΛϞ⟩ ἡ ϛ↓τγ]. And on page 102: "These things, divided into the multitude of days collected in the given time, come to 224609 days" [ταῦτα ἐν ἐπιμεσὸν ἐλες εἰς τὸ πλῆρ ἡμ ἐν τῷ πεπλημμένῳ χρόνῳ συναχθέντα ἡμέρων ⟨ϗβ ϛχθ⟩]. Here you should also observe that the letters written above this figure are raised from units to tens and from tens to hundreds: in the last example the letter ϐ written above stands for 20, and ϰ for 200, whereas elsewhere the former signifies only 2 and the latter 20. So by the same reasoning, if centenary characters were placed before these thousands, they would express millions as well.

units.la: 4. Præterea, Græcos numeris quibuslibet designandis etiam sex tantùm literis olim usos fuisse constat, viz, ΙΠΔΗΧΜ, quarum valorem hìc videre est; Ι Μονὰς 1. Π Πέντε 5. Δ Δέκα 10. Η Ἑκατὸν 100. Χ Χίλια 1000. Μ Μυρία 10000. ut & eas omnes capitales esse literas eorum numerorum quos significant, exceptâ sc 1 5 ut π est prima litera ν̃ πίντε. Δ prima Δίκα, &c. Et quamvis H non videatur litera prima ν̃ ἑκατὸν, antiquitùs tamen fuit; olim enim aspiratio per H expressa Græcis etiam fuit, ut Ἑκαῖον scriberetur Ἡκαῖον. Et adhuc etiam Latinis aspirationi tantùm inservit. Omnes hæ literæ præter π ad numeros exprimendos repetuntur; ut I II,III, 1,2,3; Δ 10, ΔΔ 20, ΔΔΔΔ 40, HHH 300, xxxx 4000, MMMM 40000. Decadum autem, centuriarum, chiliadum, & myriadum quinarios per literas ΔHXM literæ π inclusas exprimunt; ut |Δ| vel |Δ| sit 50, |H| 500, |X| 5000, |M| 50000. In numeris autem per hosce etiam characteres exprimendis major minorem semper præcedit; ut ΔΔΔΔII 32, |M XXX H|ΔΔΔΔΔII 53542.
units.tr: 4. Moreover, it is established that the Greeks, to express numbers of any kind, once used only six letters: I, Π, Δ, H, X, M (ΙΠΔΗΧΜ). Their values are as follows: I, monas (unit), 1; Π, pente (five), 5; Δ, deka (ten), 10; H, hekaton (hundred), 100; X, chilia (thousand), 1000; M, myria (ten thousand), 10000. All of these are the initial letters of the numbers they signify, with two exceptions: the I stands for one, and Π, the initial of pente, stands for five. H is not obviously the initial of hekaton, but it was used in earlier times, since the Greeks also expressed the breathing by H, so that Hekaion was written as Hekaion. Even now the Latins use H only for the breathing. All these letters, except Π, are repeated to express numbers: I, II, III for 1, 2, 3; Δ for 10, ΔΔ for 20, ΔΔΔΔ for 40, HHH for 300, XXXX for 4000, MMMM for 40000. For the fives of tens, hundreds, thousands and ten thousands, they use the letters Δ, H, X, M with Π enclosed in them: |Δ| or Δ with the Π inside is 50, |H| is 500, |X| is 5000, |M| is 50000. In numbers written with these characters, the larger always precedes the smaller: ΔΔΔΔII is 42, and M XXX H ΔΔΔΔΔII is 53542.

units.la: 5. Hæc characteristica Græcorum numeros exprimendi ratio ab Herodiano περὶ ἀριθμῶν describitur, qui solus (ut opinor) ex antiquis de eâ meminit. At etiamnum extat in marmoribus Arundellianis, literis magnis sive uncialibus scriptis, sub quorum initio hæc habemus.
units.tr: 5. Herodian, in his work On Numbers, describes this method of the Greeks for expressing numbers by characters. He alone, as I think, of the ancients mentions it. It is still found, however, in the Arundel marbles, written in capital or uncial letters, at the beginning of which we have the following.

units.la: ΑΦΟΤΚΕΚΡΟΨΑΘΗΝΩΝΕΒΑΣΙΛΕΥ ΣΕΚΑΙΗΧΩΡΑΚΕΚΡΟΠΙΑΕΚΛΗΘΗ ΤΟΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝΚΑΛΟΥ ΜΕΝΗΑΚΤΙΚΗΑΠΟΑΚΤΑΙΟΥΤΟΥΑΥΤΟΧ ΘΟΝΟΣΕΤΗΧΗΗΗΔΠΠΙΙΙ.
units.tr: ΑΦΟΤΚΕΚΡΟΨΑΘΗΝΩΝΕΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣΕΚΑΙΗΧΩΡΑΚΕΚΡΟΠΙΑΕΚΛΗΘΗΤΟΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝΚΑΛΟΥΜΕΝΗΑΚΤΙΚΗΑΠΟΑΚΤΑΙΟΥΤΟΥΑΥΤΟΧΘΟΝΟΣΕΤΗΧΗΗΗΔΠΠΙΙΙ.

units.la: Id est.
units.tr: That is.

units.la: ᾿Αφ᾿ ὧ Κέκεψ᾿ Αθηνῶν ἐβασίλευσε, χῆ ἡ Χώρα Κεκροπία ἐκλήθη τὸ πρότερον καλυμμένη ᾿Αχτικὴ ἀπὸ ᾿Αχταίου ἕ ᾿Αυτοχθόνος ἔτη ΧΗΗΗΔΠΠΙΙ.
units.tr: From when Cecrops reigned over the Athenians, and the land was called Cecropia, formerly named Actica from Actaeus the Autochthon, years 1322. [Ἀφ᾽ ὧ Κέκεψ᾽ Ἀθηνῶν ἐβασίλευσε, χῆ ἡ Χώρα Κεκροπία ἐκλήθη τὸ πρότερον καλουμένη Ἀκτικὴ ἀπὸ Ἀκταίου τοῦ Αὐτοχθόνος ἔτη ΧΗΗΗΔΠΠΙΙ.]

units.la: Quem numerum ultimò descriptum Romani eodem ferè modo depingunt, sic MCCCXVIII ; unde nullus dubito quin hanc numerandi formam Romani à Græcis unà cum literis mutuati sunt. Iisdem etiam inscriptionibus marmoreis dicitur, ΑΦΟΤΟΜΗΡΟΣΟΠΟΙΗΤΗΣΕΦΑΝΗΕΤΗ ΗΗ ΗΔΔΔΔΙΙΙ.
units.tr: This number, written last, the Romans depict in almost the same way, thus: MCCCXVIII. Hence I have no doubt that the Romans borrowed this method of numbering from the Greeks along with the letters. The same marble inscriptions are said to read: From when Homer the poet flourished, years 643. [ΑΦΟΤΟΜΗΡΟΣΟΠΟΙΗΤΗΣΕΦΑΝΗΕΤΗΗΗΗΔΔΔΔΙΙΙ.]

units.la: Ex quo Homerus poeta floruit anni DCXXXXIII. Ubi vides ut H significans centum includitur π valenti quinque, ut valor totius figuræ sit ͅ. Et eodem modo litera Δ inclusa π valet. Et sic in reliquis. Hi antiquissimi haud dubiè fuerunt Arithmetici Græcorum characteres, & quibus solis usi sunt, usque dum literas magnas cum parvis hodiè usitatis commutabant.
units.tr: From when Homer the poet flourished, years 643. Here you see how H, signifying a hundred, is enclosed with Π, which is worth five, so that the value of the whole figure is 500. In the same way the letter Δ enclosed with Π has the value 50, and so on for the rest. These were without doubt the most ancient arithmetical characters of the Greeks, and the only ones they used until they changed their capital letters to the small letters in use today.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De Characteribus Syriacis.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. On the Syriac Characters.

units.la: I. Characteres Syriaci sunt omnes Alphabeti literæ, quarum valor ex hac tabella patet. 1 | 10 | 100 2 | 20 | 200 3 | 30 | 300 4 | 40 | 400 5 | 50 6 | 60 7 | 70 8 | 80 9 | 90
units.tr: I. The Syriac characters are all the letters of the alphabet, whose values are shown in this table. 1 | 10 | 100 2 | 20 | 200 3 | 30 | 300 4 | 40 | 400 5 | 50 6 | 60 7 | 70 8 | 80 9 | 90

units.la: 1. Hucusque procedunt characteres Syriaci, Hebraicis omninò similes, præterquam literarum figurâ; nam ܐ valet 12, ܫ 33, ܥ 56, &c. Quandoquidem autem per nudas Alphabeti literas tantùm ad 400 inclusivè perveniatur, hinc defectum illum vel puncto, vel lineolâ, aliâve figurâ supplere solent, ídque hoc modo: Ad centenarios designandos literis denariis punctulum superscribunt, ut prima litera denaria ܕ cum punctulo superscripto sic ܕ̇ valeat 100, ܩ 200, ܪ vel ܫ 300, ܬ vel ܬ 400, ܓ 500; & sic usque ad ܛ 900; ut ܝܘܗ est 455, ܡܠܟ 649, &c. Ad millenarios verò exprimendos literis monadicis virgulam dextrorsùm flexam subscribunt, ut ܐ sit 1000, ܐ 2000, ܐ 3000, ܐ 4000, ܐ 9000; qui characteres millenarii à reliquis aliquantulùm distant, ut ܐ 5383, ܐ 9424. Nonnunquam characteri millenario lineolam superducunt, ut & aliis numeris, millenario per suam tantùm à reliquis distantiam & indicato, ut ad calcem libri Jobi, ܐ ܒ ܓ ܕ ܗ ܘ ܙ. Absolvitur liber Jobi justi & insignis, in quo continentur versus 2553.
units.tr: 1. Up to this point the Syriac characters go forward, entirely like the Hebrew ones except in the shape of the letters. For example, aleph is 12, shin 33, ayin 56, and so on. Since the bare letters of the alphabet reach only as far as 400 inclusive, they usually supply the missing values with a dot, a small line, or some other mark, in this way. To denote hundreds, they place a small dot above the letter, so that the first tens letter, daleth, with a dot above it, is 100; qoph is 200; resh or shin is 300; taw is 400; gimel is 500; and so on up to tsade, which is 900. Thus yod-waw-he is 455, mem-lamed-kaph is 649, and so on. To express thousands, they place a line bent to the right beneath the units letters, so that aleph is 1000, beth 2000, gimel 3000, daleth 4000, and teth 9000. These thousand-signs differ somewhat from the others, so that, for example, aleph is 5383 and aleph is 9424. Sometimes they also draw a small line over the thousand-sign, as with other numbers, the thousand being indicated only by its distinction from the others; as at the end of the book of Job: aleph, beth, gimel, daleth, he, waw, zayin. The book of Job, the just and remarkable one, is finished, in which there are 2553 verses.

units.la: 2. Decades millium sive myriades ad indicandas literis lineolam transversam subscribunt; ut 2C0000. 100000. 9C000. 50000. 20C00. 10000.
units.tr: 2. For indicating tens of thousands, or myriads, they place a transverse line beneath the letters, as in 20000, 100000, 90000, 50000, 20000, 10000.

units.la: Eâdem quoque ratione ܐ millionem valet, ܒ duos milliones, ܓ tres milliones, & ܠ quatuor milliones, sive 4000000.
units.tr: By the same method, aleph denotes a million, beth two million, gimel three million, and lamed four million, that is, 4000000.

units.la: Aliquoties etiam hanc figuram literæ subducunt, quæ facit ut litera cui subjicitur tot decades millionū valeat quot per se unitates ; ut 𐎀 10000000, i. e. decem milliones ; ơ 50000000, ـه 200000000, ـل 4000000000. Si una virgula supra, altera infra literam collocetur, varia millia millionum significantur, ut ـه 20000000000, i.e. viginti millia millionum.
units.tr: Sometimes they also add a figure under a letter, which makes the letter to which it is subjoined stand for as many tens of millions as it stands for units by itself. Thus one letter with such a mark is 10000000, that is, ten millions; another is 50000000, another 200000000, and another 4000000000. If one stroke is placed above a letter and another below it, various thousands of millions are signified, as one letter with such marks is 20000000000, that is, twenty thousand millions.

units.la: 3. Quandò varii numeri his characteribus sunt describendi, majores perpetuò minoribus præmittuntur ; ut ھجي ـهـ 23624, ـسهـ 3236569,
units.tr: 3. When various numbers are to be written with these characters, the greater are always placed before the smaller; thus yod-heth-kaph (waw-he), that is 23624, and so on, the number 3236569.

units.la: CAP. IX. De Characteribus Arabicis.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. On the Arabic Characters.

units.la: I. Characteres Arabici sunt 28, quarum figuram & valorem laterculo subjecto exhibemus. ا 1 | ي 10 | ف 100 ب 2 | ك 20 | ر 200 ج 3 | ل 30 | ش 300 د 4 | م 40 | ت 400 ه 5 | ن 50 | ت 500 و 6 | س 60 | خ 600 ز 7 7 | ز | 70 | ... | 700 8 | ح | 80 | ... | 800 9 | ط | 90 | ... | 900 1000
units.tr: I. There are 28 Arabic characters, whose forms and values we display in the table below. alif 1 | yā 10 | qāf 100; bā 2 | kāf 20 | rā 200; jīm 3 | lām 30 | shīn 300; dāl 4 | mīm 40 | tā 400; hā 5 | nūn 50 | thā 500; wāw 6 | sīn 60 | khā 600; zāy 7 | ʿayn 70 | dhāl 700; hā 8 | fā 80 | ḍād 800; ṭā 9 | ṣād 90 | ẓā 900; ghayn 1000.

units.la: 1. Hosce characteres ab Arabibus & Persis usitatos ut intelligas, primò tenendum est Arabes in literis suis usui numerico applicandis, non sui vulgaris, sed Hebraici Alphabeti ordinem observare ; quod & ex ipsâ tabellâ patet. Secundò, cùm varia sit omnium propemodùm literarum Arabicarum figura, quatenùs in initio, medio, vel fine vocis collocentur ; majores autem numeros pluribus expressos literis tanquam unicam vocem scribunt, hinc nos in laterculo suprascripto singulas cujusque literæ figuras adnotavimus, ubicunque notabilis aliqua sit discrepantia. Igitur ر & ب sunt duæ tantùm figuræ ejusdem literæ, & ه & ه & ى tres figuræ ejusdem literæ, & quælibet è figuris ص & ش & ع & غ mille valet : & sic in reliquis. Quod præmonemus, nè quispiam literarum Arabicarum ignarus, ubi duæ vel plures figuræ simul occurrunt, eas omnes ad numerum suum indicandum conjungendas autumaret, ut in laterculo viz. collocantur. Tertiò, cum Alphabetum Arabicum literis constet 28, hoc est ter novem & unâ ; hinc primò in tres classes Hebraici ad instar novenarias distribuitur, quarum prima unitates designat, altera denarios, tertia millenarios, ultima verò litera غ, quæ seorsim collocatur, mille valet.
units.tr: 1. To understand these characters, as used by the Arabs and Persians, you must first hold that in applying their letters to numerical use the Arabs do not follow their common alphabetical order but that of the Hebrew alphabet; the table itself shows this. Second, since almost all Arabic letters vary in form according to whether they stand at the beginning, the middle or the end of a word, and since they write larger numbers expressed by several letters as a single word, I have noted in the table above each letter's separate forms wherever there is a noticeable difference. Thus ra and ba are only two forms of the same letter, and ha, ha and ya are three forms of the same letter, and any one of the forms of ṣād, shīn, ʿayn and ghayn is worth a thousand; and so with the rest. We give this warning so that anyone unfamiliar with Arabic letters does not suppose that, where two or more forms occur together, they are all to be joined to indicate their one number, as they are placed in the table. Third, since the Arabic alphabet consists of 28 letters, that is three nines plus one, following the Hebrew pattern it is first divided into three classes of nine, of which the first denotes units, the second tens, and the third hundreds; the last letter, ghayn, which is set apart, is worth a thousand.

units.la: 2.Porrò,
units.tr: 2. Moreover,

units.la: Lib.I. Chronologicæ. 223
units.tr: Lib. I. Chronologicae. 223

units.la: 2. Porrò, ratio hosce characteres componendi eadem est quaʒ in reliquis, viz. ut major præcedat minorem ; ut ۱۱ ۱4 ۲5 Abulpheda in Descriptione Mawaralnahræ, من كتاب الا الاطوال انها حيث
units.tr: 2. Further, the method of composing these characters is the same as in the others, namely that the greater precedes the lesser, as in the numerals 11, 14, 25 (in Arabic script) that Abulpheda gives in his Description of Mawaralnahra, from the book of longitudes, where they are written in the Arabic order (transliterated: "min kitab al-atwal inna hiya").

units.la: الطول فط له والعرض لح مه ; E libro longitudinum. Longitudo ejus, viz. Bazdæ, est 89, 35'. latitudo 38, 45'.
units.tr: (transliterated: "al-tul fa-t lahu wa-l-'ard la-h mah"). From the book of longitudes. Its longitude, namely that of Bazda, is 89° 35', and its latitude 38° 45'.

units.la: Sic ۱۰۲ قب ۱556 عمدو ۲58 طن ۹50 رمخ ۱667. Ad plures millenarios indicandos, numeri minores millenariæ figuræ ح præponuntur, ut یج 2000, حح 3000, ط 9000, لح 30000, ع 100000, حم 600000, عم 1000000, يمم 2000000, &c. Hisce verò majoribus minores numeri sic annectuntur, 462235996.
units.tr: Thus the numbers 102 (qb), 1556 (in the Arabic letter-notation), 58, 50 and 1667 are written. To indicate several thousands, smaller numerals are placed before the thousands-sign (transliterated "h"): yj 2000, hh 3000, t 9000, lh 30000, ʻ 100000, hm 600000, ʻm 1000000, ymm 2000000, etc. To these larger numbers smaller ones are joined thus: 462235996.

units.la: 2. Habent præterea Arabes & cifræ notam à literis diversam, viz. ṭ Astronomis & Geographis sæpius usitatam ; ut Nassir Eddinus Effusæus in tabulis Geographicis ait, civitatis Jag (sive Shash)longitudinem esse ṭ ط 109, 0'. longitudinem Canradorah ṭ مج 180, 0'. latitudinem ṭ, ṭ. c, 0'. Sic Ulug Beig de Epoch. c. 5. ait, Epocham Persicam priorem esse Melirææ diebus 163173, eos autem in sexagenas conversos esse ح ط مه ṭ 0'''. 45''. 19'. 33'. 3. Sed non omittendum est literas Arabicas numeris exprimendis usitatas contrario ordine in nonnullis MSS. collocari ; ut si exprimerent 532, literas suas non communi ordine ﻝﺐﺜﺃ sed contrario, viz. ﺃﺐﺜﻝ scribunt ; ut unitates nimirum ad dextram ponantur. Quod in Indicorum characterum imitationem factum videtur.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, the Arabs also have a sign for zero, different from the letters, namely "ṭ", which is very often used by astronomers and geographers. Thus Nassir Eddinus Effusaeus says in his geographical tables that the longitude of the city Jag (or Shash) is 109° 0', the longitude of Canradorah 180° 0', and its latitude 0'. So Ulug Beg, in De Epochis, chapter 5, says that the Persian epoch is 163173 days earlier than Melireae, and that these days, converted into sexagesimal parts, give 0° 45' 19" 33"'. 3. But it must not be omitted that in some manuscripts the Arabic letters used for expressing numbers are placed in the reverse order. So if they were to express 532, they do not write the letters in the usual order but in the opposite one, that is, with the units placed on the right; this seems to have been done in imitation of the Indian characters.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: De Characteribus Æthiopicis.
units.tr: On the Ethiopic Characters.

units.la: I. Characteres Æthiopici sunt undeviginti, qui sequuntur. ā | I | ı̄ | 10 β̄ | 2 | ῑ̄ | 20 γ̄ | 3 | ῡ̄ | 30 ō | 4 | ῡ̄ | 40 ε̄ | 5 | ȳ | 50 ζ̄ | 6 | ξ̄ | 60 ζ̄ | 7 | ο̄ | 70 η̄ | 8 | π̄ | 80 θ̄ | 9 | ϡ̄ | 90 P̄ | 100.
units.tr: I. The Ethiopic characters are nineteen, as follows: 1, 10, 2, 20, 3, 30, 4, 40, 5, 50, 6, 60, 7, 70, 8, 80, 9, 90, 100. Each value is shown by its symbol in the original table.

units.la: I. Hos numerales Æthiopum characteres inter literales recenseo, non quòd ipsæ sunt Æthiopum literæ, ab iis enim quamplurimùm figurâ discrepant, sed quòd ut primò patet intuitu, è Græcis literis efformantur, per eos autem Æthiopes numeros suos hoc modo describunt. Novem primi characteres unitates, reliqui denarios usque ad ultimum, qui centum valet. Cùm ipsi verò Æthiopes non sinistrorsùm ut reliqui orientales, sed dextrorsùm ut nos, legunt, scribúntque; hinc nostrûm ad instar majores characteres ad sinistram, minores ad dextram collocant; ut Id 11, IB 12, IF 23, IT 87, PYB 159. Plures autem centenarios ad exprimendos characteres minores centenario præponunt; ut BP 200, CP 300, EP 500, IP 1000, decies centum, sive mille; TP 2000, sive vigesies centum; UP 3000, sive trigesies centum; PP 10000, sive centies centum; BPP 20000, q.d. bis centies centum; IPP 100000: & sic usque ad millionem, qui sic notatur PPP quasi dicas centies centies centum.
units.tr: I. I list these Ethiopic numerals among the letters, not because they are the Ethiopic letters (they differ from them greatly in shape), but because, as is plain at first glance, they are formed from Greek letters, and the Ethiopians write their numbers with them in this way. The first nine characters are units, and the rest are tens up to the last, which is worth one hundred. Since the Ethiopians read and write from right to left, as we do, and not from left to right as the other Eastern peoples do, they place the larger characters on the left and the smaller on the right, as we do: for example, 11, 12, 23, 87, 159. To express hundreds they put the smaller character before the character for a hundred: 200, 300, 500, 1000 (ten times a hundred, or a thousand), 2000 (twenty times a hundred), 3000 (thirty times a hundred), 10000 (a hundred times a hundred), 20000 (that is, twice a hundred times a hundred), 100000; and so on up to a million, which is written thus, as if you were to say a hundred times a hundred times a hundred.

units.la: 2. Porrò notandum est Æthiopes characteribus suis numerum quemlibet compositum indicantibus literam Ꝺ significantem Et, sæpius interserere. Hoc satis constat è Claudii regis Æthiopiæ confessione fidei, à quâ dicit se suósque non declinare. ኣምተምሀርተ: ዝበዊ: 1 Ꝺ ጀ ሐዋርያት: ѲᲐѲᲠᲐ: ᲧᲐᲧᲐ: ᲨᲒᲩ: Ꝺ ꝰ ᲡᲐ ᲐᲠᲔᲦᲐ: Ꝺ ᲠᲖ Ꝺ Ꝺ ᲡᲥᲗ: ᲨᲓᲦᲠᲗ: ᲐᲓᲞᲐ: Ꝺ Ꝑ Ꝺ Ꝗ Ꝺ ᲖᲢᲗ: Ꝺ ᲒᲠ: Ꝑ ᲐᲚᲐᲖᲡ: A doctrinâ patrum nostrorum 12 Apostolorum, & Pauli fontis sapientiæ, 7 ? Apostolorum, & 318 rectorum fide, qui congregati sunt Niceæ, & 15c Constantinopoli, & 200 Ephesi. Verbatim autem numeri sic pronunciandi sunt, 10 & 2 Apostolorum, 70 & 2 Discipulorum, 310 & 8 Patrum Nicææ, 100 & 50 Constantinopoli, & 200 Ephesi congregatorum: Ubi vides quoties Ꝺ Et interseritur. Observes etiam vellem in ultimo numero 200, characteres B & P duobus punctis à se invicem secerni, qualia viz. inter distinctas voces perpetuò collocantur. Hæc confessio fidei scripta dicitur ΠΙΘΕΠΗΘΕΙ i.e. 1555 anno Christi; characteres autem verbatim sic sonant, In decimo & quinto centesimo in quinquagesimo & quinto anno. His (ut par est) animadversis, nihil (ut opinor) in Æthiopicis occurrat characteribus, quod difficile sit intellectu.
units.tr: 2. It should further be noted that the Ethiopians often insert the letter meaning "and" into numbers composed of several characters. This is sufficiently clear from the confession of faith of Claudius, king of Ethiopia, from which he says that he and his people do not depart. In that confession the numbers stand with "and" between them: "from the doctrine of our fathers, 12 [and] of the Apostles, and of Paul the fount of wisdom, 7 [and] of the Apostles, and 318 [and] of the orthodox who assembled at Nicaea, and 150 [and] at Constantinople, and 200 at Ephesus." Word for word, the numbers are to be read thus: 10 and 2 Apostles, 70 and 2 Disciples, 310 and 8 Fathers of Nicaea, 100 and 50 assembled at Constantinople, and 200 assembled at Ephesus. Here you see how often "and" is inserted. I would also have you observe that in the last number, 200, the characters B and P are separated from each other by two points, such as are always placed between distinct words. This confession of faith is said to have been written in the year of Christ 1555, written [ΠΙΘΕΠΗΘΕΙ]; the characters, word for word, read: "in the fifteenth and fifty-fifth year of the hundredth." Once these points have been noted, as they should be, I think nothing in the Ethiopic characters will be hard to understand.

units.la: Hactenùs de variis numerorum characteribus, iisque quidem omnibus quorum adhuc scientiam nos assequi potuimus, & forsitan quos scire necesse est. Nullus enim est Chronologus, nullus Astronomus, nullus Geographus, nullus Historicus, nec alius quicunque liber, linguâ Romana, Anglicana, Gallica, Hispanica, &c. Græca, Hebraica, Samaritana, Syriaca, Persica, Arabica, Turcica, vel Æthiopica conscriptus, cujus numeri aliquibus è characteribus jam explicatis non exprimuntur. Quod ad Armenios, Copticos, aliòsque ejusdem farinæ spectat characteres, isti non magni sunt momenti, ut qui nobis raro si ublibi occurrunt, vel si operæ pretium fuerit, ipsis cum linguis facillimè edidcantur.
units.tr: So far I have dealt with the various numeral characters, all those which we have been able to learn so far and perhaps those which it is necessary to know. For there is no chronologer, no astronomer, no geographer, no historian, nor any other book written in Latin, English, French, Spanish, and so on, or in Greek, Hebrew, Samaritan, Syriac, Persian, Arabic, Turkish, or Ethiopic, whose numbers cannot be expressed by some of the characters already explained. As for the Armenian, Coptic, and other characters of that kind, they are of no great importance, since they rarely occur to us anywhere, and, if it is worth the trouble, they can very easily be learned along with their languages.
