units.la: Arithmetices Chronologicæ Liber Secundus.
units.tr: Arithmetic of Chronology, Book Two.

units.la: CAP. I. De Additione.
units.tr: CHAP. I. Of Addition.

units.la: I. In priori libro de Characteristicâ Arithmeticæ parte actum est, sequitur Practica, quæ praxes sive operationes Arithmeticas tradit.
units.tr: I. In the previous book the characteristic part of arithmetic was dealt with. What follows is the Practice, which sets out the arithmetical procedures or operations.

units.la: II. Praxes Arithmeticæ sunt vel primæ, vel à primis ortæ.
units.tr: II. Arithmetical procedures are either primary, or derived from the primary ones.

units.la: III. Praxes primæ (quæ & elementa) sunt quatuor, Additio, Subtractio, Multiplicatio, & Divisio.
units.tr: III. The primary procedures (also called the elements) are four: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

units.la: IV. Additio est duorum pluriumve numerorum in unam summam (quasi unum, aggregatum & totum etiam vocatam) collectio.
units.tr: IV. Addition is the collecting of two or more numbers into one sum (also called the aggregate or total, as if it were a single whole).

units.la: V. In Additione duo consideranda sunt, Numerorum dispositio, & Collectio.
units.tr: V. In addition two things are to be considered: the arrangement of the numbers, and the collection.

units.la: VI. Dispositio est recta numerorum collocatio, ut omnes datorum unitates, decades, centuriæ, &c. sibi invicem respondeant.
units.tr: VI. Arrangement is the correct placing of the numbers, so that the units, tens, hundreds, and so on, of the given numbers correspond to one another.

units.la: VII. Collectio est quâ numeri sic dispositi rite colliguntur: In quâ hæ observantur regulæ.
units.tr: VII. Collection is the proper summing up of numbers so arranged. In it the following rules are observed.

units.la: 1. Incipit à dextrâ, & sinistrorsum gradatim procedit.
units.tr: 1. Begin on the right and proceed gradually to the left.

units.la: 2. Numerus è quavis serie collectus unû constans figurâ eidem seriei subjiciatur.
units.tr: 2. A number collected from any series, consisting of one figure, is placed under that same series.

units.la: 3. Si duabus verò constet figuris, earum prima tantum ad dextram ipsi seriei subjicitur, altera verò primæ figuræ in proximâ seriè collocanda adjiciatur.
units.tr: 3. If it consists of two figures, only the first of them is placed under the right-hand series, and the second is added to the first figure of the next series to be placed to the left.

units.la: Exemplum
units.tr: Example

units.la: IN numeris hic datis in unam summam colligendis sic procedo, à dextrâ viz. incipiens. Primæ seriei notæ 0, 4, 5 5235 524 670 6419
units.tr: Here, in adding together the numbers given, I proceed as follows, beginning from the right. The notes of the first series, 0, 4, 5 (5235, 524, 670, 6419 as set out in the columns)

units.la: faciunt 9, quam itaque figuram infra lineam eo nomine subductam colloco. Notæ secundi loci 7, 2, 3 faciunt 12, numerum duabus constantem figuris, quarum itaq; primam (sive 2) sub ista serie colloco, secundâ 1 proximæ reservatâ, ut primæ ejus figuræ (sive 6) addatur, & fiat 7: dico itaque 7, 5, & 2 faciunt 14, qui verò numerus cum duabus itidem constet figuris, primam (quæ est 4) suo ordini subscribo, alteram 1 ad proximum locum transfero, ubi unica tantùm occurrit figura, quæ est 5; at prædictâ figurâ 1 ei addità fit 6: ut totum aggregatum fiat 6429.
units.tr: make 9, which I therefore place below the line under that series. The notes of the second place, 7, 2, 3, make 12, a number of two figures; of these I place the first (2) under this series, and carry the second (1) to the next place, to be added to the first figure there (6), so that it becomes 7. So I say: 7, 5 and 2 make 14; of this number I write the first figure (4) under its own series, and carry the 1 to the next place, where only one figure occurs, namely 5; adding the carried 1 to it makes 6. So the whole aggregate becomes 6429.

units.la: 4 Si numeri dati sint diversæ denominationis sive speciei, initium fiat à minimis, quorum summa si minor sit quàm proxima species, tota subscribatur; sin major, videsis quoties proximam speciem continet, & tot unitates ad eam referantur, residuo solo infra lineam subscripto.
units.tr: 4. If the given numbers are of different denomination or kind, begin with the smallest. If their sum is less than the next kind, write the whole of it underneath; but if it is greater, see how many times it contains the next kind, refer that many units to it, and write underneath the line only the remainder.

units.la: 1. Ut in hoc exemplo. Prima species est scrupulorum d. | b. | ′ | ″ 365 | 5 | 49 | 16 38 | 20 | 36 | 25 404 | 2 | 25 | 41
units.tr: 1. As in this example. The first kind is of scruples: d. | h. | ′ | ″ 365 | 5 | 49 | 16 38 | 20 | 36 | 25 404 | 2 | 25 | 41

units.la: secundorum, quorum hic sunt 25 & 16, quæ faciunt 41; qui numerus ut minor quàm 60, (quot secunda in uno primo continentur) totus subscribitur. In proximâ specie 6 & 9 sunt 15; primam itaque figuram 5 subscribe, alteram 1 adjice ad 3, & dic 4 & 4 faciunt 8 decades primorum; at in unâ horâ (quæ proxima est species) 60 tantùm continentur prima. Ex 8 igitùr aufer 6, & residuum 2 ad sinistram ante subscriptæ 5 dispone, & quoniam 60 jam relinquuntur prima, hæc autem unam horam constituunt, unitatem adjicias ad horas, ut 20 fiant 21, quæ cum 5 faciunt 26; aufer 24 numerum horarum unius diei (quæ est ultima species) & reliquæ sunt 2 subscribendæ. Una ista dies ex horis collecta diebus addita facit ut summa quæsita sit d. 404. h. 2. 25'. 41".
units.tr: of seconds, of which here are 25 and 16, which make 41. Since this number is less than 60 (the number of seconds contained in one minute), it is written down whole. In the next kind, 6 and 9 make 15. So I write down 5 as the first figure, add the 1 to the 3, and say 4 and 4 make 8 tens of minutes. But in one hour (the next kind) only 60 minutes are contained. So from 8 I take away 6, and place the remainder 2 to the left of the 5 already written. Since 60 minutes now remain, which make one hour, I add a unit to the hours, so that 20 becomes 21; with 5 this makes 26. I take away 24, the number of hours in one day (the last kind), and the remaining 2 is to be written down. This one day, collected from the hours and added to the days, makes the sum sought: d. 404. h. 2. 25′. 41″.

units.la: Aliud exemplum in computo Judaico, in quo singulæ horæ colligunt helakim sive scrupula 1080. Summa hed. h. hel. 354 8 876 383 21 589 738 6 385
units.tr: Another example, from the Jewish reckoning, in which each hour makes 1080 helakim or scruples. Sum: hed. h. hel. 354 8 876 383 21 589 738 6 385

units.la: lakim hic datorum est 1465, aufer 1080, & residuum 385 subscribe. Hora ista ex helakim collecta cum aliis 21 & 8 suâ serie collatis, efficit ut horæ sint 30, è quibus aufer 24, & reliquas 6 sub lineâ colloca. Horas istas 24, hoc est, unam diem ad datos adjice, & totum aggregatum erit d. 738. h. 6. helak 385.
units.tr: The helakim of the given numbers come to 1465. Take away 1080 and write down the remainder, 385. This hour, collected from the helakim, together with the other 21 and 8 brought together in their series, makes the hours 30. From these take away 24 and place the remaining 6 under the line. Add those 24 hours, that is, one day, to the given days, and the whole aggregate will be d. 738. h. 6. helak 385.

units.la: 2. Judæi suis hunc calculum characteribus sic exprimeיום שעות חלקים שנד ח חחשו שפג כא תאפט תשלח ו שפה rent. Eodem etiam modo Additio per literales æquè ac figuratos numerorum characteres administrari potest.
units.tr: 2. The Jews would express this calculation with their own characters: יום שעות חלקים שנד ח חחשו שפג כא תאפט תשלח ו שפה. In the same way, addition can be carried out with letters as well as with figured characters of numbers.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: De Subtractione.
units.tr: On Subtraction.

units.la: I. Subtractio est quâ numerus minor à majori subtrahitur, ut differentia sive residuum habeatur.
units.tr: I. Subtraction is the operation by which a smaller number is taken away from a larger, so that the difference or remainder is obtained.

units.la: II. Ut hæc praxis rite instituatur, hæ observentur regulæ.
units.tr: II. For this procedure to be carried out correctly, the following rules are observed.

units.la: III. 1. Minor ita majori subscribatur, ut similes utriusque numeri notæ similibus respondeant.
units.tr: III. 1. The smaller number is written under the larger so that like figures correspond to like.

units.la: IV. 2. Primò auferatur prima inferioris numeri nota à primâ superioris, & residuum primo loco infra lineam subductam scribatur: sic etiam secunda inferior è secundâ superiori dematur, & ejus residuum secundo loco subscribatur; & sic deinceps.
units.tr: IV. 2. First, the first figure of the lower number is taken from the first figure of the upper, and the remainder is written in the first place below the line drawn. Likewise the second lower figure is taken from the second upper, and its remainder is written in the second place below; and so on in turn.

units.la: 1. UT in numeris hîc datis, cùm primò rité collocati sunt, viz. ut similes similibus, (hoc est) unitates unitatibus, decades decadibus, &c. respondeant; minorem è majori sic subtraho: 6 è 9 restat 3, quæ itaque figura directè subscribatur. 4 è 6 restat 2, & 2 è 5 restat 3. Totum itaque residuum sive differentia inter hos numeros est 323.
units.tr: 1. In the numbers given here, once they are properly placed, so that like corresponds to like (that is, units to units, tens to tens, etc.), I subtract the smaller from the larger as follows: 6 from 9 leaves 3, which figure is therefore written directly beneath. 4 from 6 leaves 2, and 2 from 5 leaves 3. The whole remainder, or difference, between these numbers is therefore 323.

units.la: V. 3. Si nota quæpiam inferior sit major superiore, è quâ subtrahenda est, ad superiorem mente adjicias decem, & ad notam proximè subtrahendam unitatem,
units.tr: V. 3. If any lower figure is greater than the upper from which it is to be subtracted, add ten mentally to the upper figure, and add a unit to the next figure to be subtracted.

units.la: 1. Ut
units.tr: 1. As

units.la: I. Ut detur numerus 365 demendus ex 628: 5 ex 8 restat 3 5 at 6 è 2 subtrahi nequit, ad 2 itaque mente adjicias 628 365 263
units.tr: I. Let the number 365 be taken away from 628. 5 from 8 leaves 3. 6 cannot be subtracted from 2, so mentally add ten to the 2, and say 6 from 12 leaves 6. 628 365 263

units.la: 10, & dic 6 è 12 restat 6. At quoniam unam decadem hic mutuò accepisti, ad proximam itaque notam subtrahendam (quæ est 3) adjicies unitatem; at 4 è 6 restat 2: numerus itaque residuus est 263. Eâdem etiam ratione numerus 30597 ex 40406 ablatus reliquum facit 9809.
units.tr: But because you have borrowed one ten here, you add a unit to the next figure to be subtracted (which is 3); then 4 from 6 leaves 2. The remaining number is therefore 263. By the same reasoning, 30597 taken from 40406 leaves 9809.

units.la: VI. 4. Si numeri dati sint diversæ speciei, minor maiori subscribatur, ita ut similia similibus respondeant. Si autem inferior cujusvis speciei numerus major sit quàm qui à superiore subtrahatur, tot unitates superiori adjicies quot ad unum proximæ speciei constituendum requiruntur, & primo inferiori numero proximæ speciei adjicies unitatem.
units.tr: VI. 4. If the given numbers are of different kinds, the smaller is written under the larger so that like corresponds to like. If, however, a lower number of any kind is greater than the one from which it is to be subtracted, you add to the upper figure as many units as are required to make one of the next kind, and you add one unit to the first lower number of the next kind.

units.la: 1. Ut in hoc exemplo. 5 è 5 restat 0. 4 è 3 subtrahi nequit, igitur ad 3 adjice 6, (quoniam 60 secunda unum primum faciunt, at 6 isto loco valet 60) ergò 4 è 9 restat 5; & quoniam 60 hic mutuò accepisti, hinc unitatem adde ad proximam figuram subtrahendam; at 7 è 6 demi nequit, sed 7 è 16 restat 9. Et unitate proximæ figuræ 3 aggregatâ, dic 4 è 2 subtrahi nequit, at 4 ex 6 & 2, sive 8, (quoniam 60 prima unam horam; quæ est proxima species, constituunt) restat 4. At quoniam hic mutuatus es horam in 60 prima d. h. ' " 340 13 26 35 210 15 36 45 129 21 49 50 prima reductam, hinc ad proximam speciem (quae est horarum) subtrahendam adjicies unitatem; at 16 è 13 subduci non potest, unam igitur diem (quae est ultima species) in horas 24 resolves, quas ad datas 13 addes, ut fiant 37; at 16 è 37 subductis reliquae sunt horae 21. Verum diem istam mutuò acceptam aggreges ad cifram proximò subducendam, ut fiat 1; at haec è o demi nequit, sed 1 è 10 restat 9: 2 è 4 restat 2, & 2 è 3 restat 1; ut numerus residuus idem sit qui subscribitur.
units.tr: 1. As in this example: 5 from 5 leaves 0. 4 cannot be subtracted from 3, so to the 3 add 6 (since 60 seconds make one minute, and 6 in that place is worth 60); then 4 from 9 leaves 5. And since you have borrowed 60 here, add one unit to the next figure to be subtracted. 7 cannot be taken from 6, but 7 from 16 leaves 9. With the unit added to the next figure, 3, you say 4 cannot be subtracted from 2; but 4 from 6 and 2, that is 8 (since 60 minutes make one hour, which is the next kind), leaves 4. And because you have borrowed an hour from the minutes, which have been reduced, you add one unit to the next kind to be subtracted (which is hours). 16 cannot be taken from 13, so you resolve one day (which is the last kind) into 24 hours, and add these to the given 13 to make 37. Then 16 from 37 leaves 21 hours. Moreover, you add this day borrowed to the cipher to be subtracted next, making 1; but this cannot be taken from 0, so 1 from 10 leaves 9; 2 from 4 leaves 2, and 2 from 3 leaves 1. Thus the remaining number is the same as the one written beneath.

units.la: 2. Aliud exemplum in computo Judaico, hic helakim 793 ex 589 subduci nequeunt, igitur ad 589 addantur tot d. h. hel. 383 21 589 29 12 793 354 8 876
units.tr: 2. Another example in Jewish computation: helakim 793 cannot be subtracted from 589, so to 589 add as many days, hours ... 383 21 589 29 12 793 354 8 876

units.la: helakim quot unam horam adaequant, hoc est 1080, ut summa sit 1669 helakim; è quibus aufer 793, & residua fient 876. Horâ hâc assumptâ unà cum reliquis 12 in proxima serie collocatis, ex 21 subtractis restant 8, & diebus 29 è 383, reliqui sunt 354.
units.tr: helakim as make one hour, that is 1080, so that the sum is 1669 helakim. From this take away 793, and the remainder will be 876. With this hour taken, together with the remaining 12 placed in the next series, 8 remains when 21 is subtracted, and 354 remains when 29 is taken from 383.

units.la: VII. 4. Ad examen subtractionis, numerus residuus addatur subtractio, si summa conveniat cum numero è quo subtractum est, probata fuit operatio, aliter erronea.
units.tr: VII. 4. For the check of subtraction, add the remainder to the subtrahend. If the sum agrees with the number from which the subtraction was made, the operation is proved; otherwise it is erroneous.

units.la: 1. Ut in exemplo superiùs allato, ad numerum subtra628 365 263 628
units.tr: 1. As in the example given above: 628 365 263 628

units.la: ctum 365 addo residuum 263, & numerus exindè exurgens idem est ac superior è quo subtractum est: Proba itaque fuit operatio.
units.tr: To the number 365 subtracted I add the remainder 263, and the number arising from this is the same as the upper number from which it was subtracted. The operation is therefore proved.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAP. III.

units.la: De Multiplicatione.
units.tr: On Multiplication.

units.la: I. Multiplicatio est ductus unius numeri in alterum, ut inveniatur tertius, in quo unus eorum toties continetur, quoties unitas in altero.
units.tr: I. Multiplication is the leading of one number into another, so that a third is found in which one of them is contained as many times as there are units in the other.

units.la: I. UT si multiplicetur 6 in 5, invenietur tertius 30, in quo 6 toties continetur quot sunt unitates in 5, vel 5 toties quot sunt unitates in 6. E numeris autem datis unus vocatur multiplicans sive multiplicator, alter multiplicatus, tertius autem inventus dicitur, & productus, factus, genitus, quæsitus; ut & summa, nam Multiplicatio nihil aliud est quàm multiplex Additio.
units.tr: I. For example, if 6 is multiplied by 5, a third number, 30, is found, in which 6 is contained as many times as there are units in 5, or 5 as many times as there are units in 6. Of the given numbers, one is called the multiplier or multiplicator, the other the multiplicand, and the third is called the found number, the product, the made, the generated, or the sought number; also the sum, for multiplication is nothing other than multiple addition.

units.la: II. Multiplicatio est vel simplex vel composita.
units.tr: II. Multiplication is either simple or compound.

units.la: III. Simplex est quâ una nota in unam multiplicatur.
units.tr: III. Simple multiplication is that in which one digit is multiplied by one digit.

units.la: IV. Hæc per subjectam tabulam citò peragatur.
units.tr: IV. This is quickly carried out by the table set out below.

units.la: Tabula Pythagorica.
units.tr: The Pythagorean Table.
[Table: the corners marked A, B, C and D; the digits 1 to 9 run along the upper side AB and the left side AC, and the squares between them are filled with the products.]

units.la: Hh
units.tr: Hh

units.la: Usus hujusce Tabulæ Pythagoricæ ab auctore dictæ, hic est; Datis duobus numeris, unum eorum quære in latere superiore AB, alterum in latere sinistro AC, & in communi utriusque concursu datur numerus ex uno eorum in alterum multiplicato productus: ut dentur 6 & 5; primò quære 6 in latere AB, deinde 5 in AC; numerus autem 30, in communi quadrangulo positus, & utrique datorum respondens est quæsitus ex 6 in 5 genitus.
units.tr: The use of this table, which the author calls Pythagorean, is as follows. Given two numbers, look for one of them on the upper side AB and the other on the left side AC; the number at the point where they meet is the product of one multiplied by the other. For example, given 6 and 5: first find 6 on side AB, then 5 on AC; the number 30, placed in the common square and answering to both given numbers, is the sought product of 6 times 5.

units.la: V. Multiplicatio composita est, numerorum, quorum ambo vel saltem unus ex pluribus conflet figuris.
units.tr: V. Compound multiplication is that of numbers of which both, or at least one, consist of several figures.

units.la: VI. Ad hanc perficiendam sequentes observentur regulæ.
units.tr: VI. The following rules are to be observed in carrying this out.

units.la: VII. 1.Si multiplicans unica sit figura, ea sub primâ multiplicandi notâ posita, in omnes istius figuras singillatim ducatur, numerus autem è quavis notâ multiplicatâ productus eidem subscribatur.
units.tr: VII. 1. If the multiplier is a single figure, place it under the first digit of the multiplicand and multiply it by each figure of that number separately, writing the number produced from each multiplied digit beneath it.

units.la: Ut in hoc exemplo quo multiplicans est 2, multiplicandus 124: primò duco 2 in 4, & productum 8 subscribo; 124 2 248
units.tr: As in this example, where the multiplier is 2 and the multiplicand 124: first I multiply 2 by 4, and write the product 8 underneath; 124 2 248

units.la: deinde 2 in 2 facit 4, proximo loco subscribendum; 2 in 1 gignit 2, quo etiam subscripto, totus productus est 248.
units.tr: Then 2 times 2 makes 4, to be written in the next place; 2 times 1 gives 2, which is also written down. The whole product is 248.

units.la: VIII. 2.Si productus unius figuræ duabus constet notis, prima tantum ad dextram ei subjiciatur, altera autem proximo producto addenda reservetur.
units.tr: VIII. 2. If the product of one figure consists of two digits, only the first digit, on the right, is set under it, and the other is kept back to be added to the next product.

units.la: Ex gr. Detur 6 ducendus in 467; 6 in 7 facit 42, cujus itaque producti prima ad dextram nota, quæ est 2, 467 6 2802
units.tr: E.g. Let 6 be multiplied by 467. 6 times 7 makes 42, of which the first digit on the right, which is 2, is to be written down: 467 6 2802

units.la: subscribatur: 6 in 6 facit 36, cui adde 4 alteram notam præcedentis producti, & fiet 40; subscribas igitur reserves 4 itidem proximo producto adjungendam; 6 in 4 producit 24, cui cum adjecisti notam reservatam 4, fiet 285 totus itaque productus est 2802.
units.tr: 6 times 6 makes 36; add 4, the carried digit of the previous product, and it becomes 40. Write down 0 and carry 4 to be added to the next product. 6 times 4 gives 24; when you have added the carried 4, it becomes 28. The whole product is therefore 2802.

units.la: IX. 3. Si tam multiplicans quàm multiplicatus ex pluribus constet figuris, singulæ multiplicantis figuræ in singulas multiplicandi ducantur, & prima numeri ex quâvis multiplicantis figurâ producti nota, sub eâdem figurâ collocetur, & omnes producti particulares in unam summam per Additionem redigantur.
units.tr: IX. 3. If both multiplier and multiplicand consist of several figures, each figure of the multiplier is multiplied into each figure of the multiplicand, the first digit of the number produced from each figure of the multiplier is placed under that same figure, and all the partial products are reduced to one sum by addition.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Detur 42 ducendus in 2436. Primò duco 2 in multiplicandum 2436, & productum subscribo: deinde 2436 42 4872 9744 102312
units.tr: 1. For example, let 42 be multiplied by 2436. First I multiply 2 by the multiplicand 2436 and write down the product; 2436 42 4872 9744 102312

units.la: duco etiam 4 in eundem numerum 2436, ejus autem productum 9744 ita subscribo, ut prima istius nota 4 suo multiplicanti directè subjiciatur, quam reliquæ etiam notæ productæ excipiunt, ut in exemplo videre est: ambos denique productos in unam summam per Additionem reduco, quæ est 102312. Eodem etiam modo procedendum est, si multiplicans ex tribus pluribúsve figuris constiterit. Hoc nimirùm diligenter observato, ut productus è quâvis figurâ multiplicantis eidem directè subscribatur.
units.tr: I also multiply 4 by the same number, 2436, and write its product, 9744, so that its first digit, 4, lies directly beneath its multiplier, and the remaining digits of the product follow it, as can be seen in the example. Finally I reduce both products into one sum by addition, which is 102312. The same procedure is to be followed if the multiplier consists of three or more figures. It must be carefully observed that the product of each figure of the multiplier is written directly beneath that figure.

units.la: X. 4. Si ad dextram utriusque vel unius è numeris datis una vel plures occurrant cifræ, notæ significativæ tantùm multiplicentur, producto autem annectantur omnes cifræ utriusque numeri.
units.tr: X. 4. If one or more ciphers stand at the right of either or both of the given numbers, only the significant digits are multiplied, and all the ciphers of both numbers are annexed to the product.

units.la: 1. Ut si detur 60 multiplicandus in 300, duc 6 in 3, & producto 18 adjice tres cifras, & summa 18000 erit productus quæsitus.
units.tr: 1. Thus if 60 is to be multiplied by 300, multiply 6 by 3 and add three ciphers to the product 18; the sum, 18000, is the sought product.

units.la: XI. 5. Si multiplicans unitate & unâ vel pluribus cifris constiterit, addantur tantùm cifræ ad multiplicandum, & habebis productum.
units.tr: XI. 5. If the multiplier consists of a unit and one or more ciphers, then only the ciphers are added to the multiplicand, and you have the product.

units.la: I. Ut si multiplicans sit 10, multiplicatus 62, ad 62 adde 0, summa 620 est numerus productus. Sit etiam 100 ducendus in 3560, ad 3560 adde duas cifras (quot sunt in 100) & habebis productum 356000.
units.tr: I. Thus if the multiplier is 10 and the multiplicand 62, add 0 to 62; the sum, 620, is the product. Likewise, if 100 is to be multiplied by 3560, add two ciphers (as many as there are in 100) to 3560, and you will have the product 356000.

units.la: XII. 6. Si multiplicandus ex numeris diversæ speciei constiterit, duc multiplicantem primò in minimam speciem, & quotcunque unitates istius speciei proximam speciem adæquant, per istum unitatum numerum productum tunc divides, cujus divisionis residuum sub dicta specie collocetur, quotus autem ad proximæ speciei productum referatur. Eâdem denique methodo per omnes species utendum est. I. Ut dentur dies 25, horæ 16, 45', 21", multiplicanda per 4: duc 4 primò in 24, & productum 96 divide per 60, (quoniam 60 secunda unum primum scrupulum, quæ proxima est species, constituunt) & quoto 1 reservato residuum 36 scribe sub 24; deinde duc 4 in 45, & producto 180 adde quotum reservatum, summa 181 per 60 itidem divisa (quoniam 60 prima unam horam, quæ proxima est species, adæquant) dat quotum 3 reservandum, in residuo unitatem subscribendam. Duc jam 4 in 16, & producto 64 adjice quotum reservatum 3, summâ 67 per 24 divisâ, (quoniam horæ 24 unam faciunt diem) quotus reservandus est 2, residuum subscribendum 19. Denique 4 in 25 gignit 100. Table: d. h. ' " / 25 16 45 24 / 4 / 102 19 1 36. ico, cui adde 2, viz. quotum relervatum,& summa diernm erit 102 ; totus autem numerus produͤtus d. 102. h. 19. 1'. 36''.
units.tr: XII. 6. If the multiplicand consists of numbers of different kinds, multiply the multiplier first by the smallest kind. Divide that product by the number of units of this kind which make up one unit of the next kind; write the remainder under this kind and carry the quotient to the product of the next kind. Proceed in the same way through all the kinds. For example, let days 25, hours 16, minutes 45 and seconds 21 be multiplied by 4. Multiply 4 first by 24 and divide the product, 96, by 60 (since 60 seconds make one minute, the next kind); reserve the quotient 1 and write the remainder 36 under the 24. Then multiply 4 by 45 and add the reserved quotient to the product, 180, making 181; divide this again by 60 (since 60 minutes make one hour, the next kind), which gives a quotient of 3 to be carried, and a remainder of 1 to be written under the minutes. Now multiply 4 by 16 and add the carried quotient 3 to the product, 64, making 67; divide by 24 (since 24 hours make one day), so the quotient 2 is carried and the remainder 19 is written down. Finally 4 times 25 gives 100; add the carried 2, the reserved quotient, and the sum for days is 102. The whole product is therefore 102 days, 19 hours, 1 minute, 36 seconds.

units.la: 2. Aliud exemplum, in anno Judaico, Arithmeticum cujus calculum proposuimus Iustit.Chron.l.i.c.14, ubi docuimus ad initium anni Judaici 5428 calculandum inter alia cyclos completos 285 ducendos esse in 2, 16, 595 ; i.e. in feriam 2, horas 16, helakim 595: qui quidem calculus sic procedit. Primō duc 285 in 595, & produͤctum 169575 d. h. hel. 2 16 595 285 3 13 15
units.tr: 2. Another example is the Jewish year, whose calculation we set out in our Institutiones Chronologicae, book 1, chapter 14, where we taught that to calculate the beginning of the Jewish year 5428 one must, among other things, multiply the complete cycles, 285, by 2 days, 16 hours, 595 helakim, that is, by the weekday 2, the hours 16, and the helakim 595. This calculation proceeds as follows. First multiply 285 by 595; the product is 169575, that is, 3 days, 13 hours, 15 helakim. [d. h. hel.: 2, 16, 595 times 285 gives 3, 13, 15]

units.la: divide per 1080, (quot helakim unam horam constituunt) & quoto 157 reservato residuum 15 subscribatur. Deinde duc 285 in 16,& produͤcto 4560 adde horas 157 in quoto prioris divisionis collectã, summam 4717 divide per 24, (quoniam horæ 24 unam diem, quæ proxima est species, constituunt) & quoto 196 reservato, residuum 13 subscribe. Denique duc 285 in 2,& produͤcto 570 adde quotum ultimō reservatum, sive 196, summa est 766. Verum non quot dies, sed quota feria quæritur ; dictã igitur summam 766 divide per 7, (qui numerus est dierum unius hebdomadis) quotus est 109. residuum 3 subscribendum. Ergo in diebus 766 continentur septimanæ 109, & dies prætereà 3, qui tertiam feriam septimanæ 110 denotant. Hanc operationem fusius prosecuti sumus, ut dictum calculum facilius quispiam deprehendat.
units.tr: Divide by 1080, the number of helakim in one hour; keep the quotient, 157, in reserve and write the remainder, 15, underneath. Then multiply 285 by 16 and add to the product, 4560, the 157 hours collected in the quotient of the previous division; divide the sum, 4717, by 24 (since 24 hours make one day, the next kind), keep the quotient, 196, in reserve, and write down the remainder, 13. Finally multiply 285 by 2 and add to the product, 570, the last reserved quotient, 196; the sum is 766. But it is not the number of days that is sought, but the weekday. So divide the sum, 766, by 7 (the number of days in one week); the quotient is 109 and the remainder 3 is written down. Thus in 766 days there are 109 weeks and, besides, 3 days, which denote the third weekday of the 110th week. We have pursued this operation at greater length so that anyone may more easily grasp the calculation.

units.la: VII. Ad examen multiplicationis, productum divide per multiplicantem, & si recte instituta fuit multiplicatio, quotus idem erit atque multiplicandus.
units.tr: VII. To check a multiplication, divide the product by the multiplier. If the multiplication was done correctly, the quotient will be the same as the multiplicand.

units.la: 1. Ex.gr. Numerus 42 in 2436 ductus producit 102312, quem productum si dividas per 42, quotus erit 2436, ipse videlicet multiplicandus.
units.tr: 1. E.g. The number 42 multiplied by 2436 gives 102312. If you divide this product by 42, the quotient will be 2436, namely the multiplicand itself.

units.la: 2. Ad probandam multiplicationem numerorum diversæ speciei, omnes species tam multiplicandi quàm producti in minimam reducendæ sunt, & deinde productus per multiplicantem dividendus.
units.tr: 2. To check a multiplication of numbers of different denominations, reduce all the denominations of both the multiplicand and the product to the smallest unit, and then divide the product by the multiplier.

units.la: CAP. IV. De Divisione.
units.tr: CHAP. IV. On Division.

units.la: I. Divisio est inventio numeri in quo toties continetur unitas, quoties divisor in dividendo.
units.tr: I. Division is the finding of a number in which the unit is contained as many times as the divisor is contained in the dividend.

units.la: II. In divisione igitur duo numeri proponuntur, & tertius quæritur.
units.tr: II. In division, then, two numbers are proposed, and a third is sought.

units.la: III. Numeri propositi sunt divisor & dividendus.
units.tr: III. The proposed numbers are the divisor and the dividend.

units.la: IV. Divisor est, de quo quæritur quoties continetur in dividendo.
units.tr: IV. The divisor is that number of which we ask how many times it is contained in the dividend.

units.la: V. Dividendus est, de quo quæritur quoties continet divisorem.
units.tr: V. The dividend is that number of which we ask how many times it contains the divisor.

units.la: VI. Numerus quæsitus dicitur quotus sive quotiens, ut qui ostendit quoties divisor in dividendo continetur.
units.tr: VI. The number sought is called the quotient, or quotient number, since it shows how many times the divisor is contained in the dividend.

units.la: I. UT si dentur duo numeri 2 & 8, & quæratur quoties 2 contineatur in 8, respondetur quater; Ergò 2 est divisor, 8 dividendus, 4 quotus. At si quæratur quoties 3 contineatur in 17, respondetur quinquies, & 2 superest: Hìc 3 est divisor, 17 dividendus, 5 quotus; at numerus 2 qui superest ad complementum dividendi 17 vocatur residuus, sive absolutè residuum.
units.tr: I. For example, if the two numbers 2 and 8 are given, and we ask how many times 2 is contained in 8, the answer is four times. So 2 is the divisor, 8 the dividend, and 4 the quotient. But if we ask how many times 3 is contained in 17, the answer is five times, with 2 left over. Here 3 is the divisor, 17 the dividend, and 5 the quotient; the number 2 that remains to make up the dividend 17 is called the residue, or simply the remainder.

units.la: VII. In divisione spectanda sunt numerorum collocatio & operatio. VIII, Col.
units.tr: VII. In division we must consider the arrangement of the numbers and the operation. VIII. Col.

units.la: VIII. Collocentur autem numeri hunc in modum. Primò ad sinistram collocetur divisor dimidiâ lunulâ comprehensus, ad cujus dextram scribatur dividendus quem sequatur alia dimidia lunula cornibus dextrorsum spectantibus, cui inscribatur quotus.
units.tr: VIII. The numbers are to be arranged in this way. First, the divisor is placed on the left, enclosed in a half-bracket; to its right the dividend is written, followed by another half-bracket, with its horns turned to the right, in which the quotient is written.

units.la: I. Ut sit divisor 4. dividendus 56: primò 4 ad sinistram dimidiæ lunulæ sinistrorsùm versæ inscribas, lunulæ verò 4) 56 (
units.tr: I. So let the divisor be 4 and the dividend 56: first write the 4 inside the half-bracket turned to the left, and on the back of that bracket describe the dividend 56,

units.la: dorso describatur dividendus 56,quem alia lunula excipiat dextrorsùm flexa, cui peractâ divisione quotus injiciatur.
units.tr: which another bracket, bent to the right, receives; into this, when the division is finished, the quotient is put.

units.la: IX. Operatio hisce regulis expediatur.
units.tr: IX. The operation is carried out by these rules.

units.la: X. 1.Si divisor unica sit figura, primò quaeras quoties ista in prima ad sinistram dividendi; velsi in eâ nec semel, quoties in duabus primis continetur, numerum quaesitioni isti respondentem inscribas dimidiæ lunulæ quoto destinatæ, per quem multiplices etiam divisorem productum autem figuræ vel figuris dividendi ex quibus extractus fuit quotus, subscriptum, ab eâdem vel eisdem detrahas, & ad residuum transferas proximam figuram dividendi. Numerus iste ex dicto residuo & figurâ translatâ collectus pro novo dividendo habeatur, de quo etiam quaeres quoties in eo continetur divisor, & eodem modo procedes ut antea, ex quotcunque figuris divisor constat: hoc tantùm observato, ut tam primæ quàm singulis figuris (ut eas transfers) punctulum subjicias, quo transferendas à translatis dignoscas.
units.tr: X. 1. If the divisor is a single figure, first ask how many times it is contained in the first figure of the dividend on the left; or, if it is not contained even once in that, how many times it is contained in the first two figures. Write the number that answers this question in the half-bracket set aside for the quotient, and multiply the divisor by it. Write the product under the figure or figures of the dividend from which the quotient was taken, subtract it from them, and carry the next figure of the dividend down to the remainder. The number made up of this remainder and the carried figure is taken as the new dividend, and again you ask how many times the divisor is contained in it, and proceed as before. This holds whatever the number of figures in the divisor, with this one observation: under the first figure, and under each of the others as you carry it down, place a little dot, so that you can tell the figures to be carried down from those already carried.

units.la: 1. Ex.gr. Sit 4 divisor, 56 dividendus. Quaere primò quoties divisor 4 contineatur in primâ dividendi figurâ, quæ est 5; quoniam autem semel in eâ continetur, punctulum ei subjice, & intra dimidiam lunulam quoto destinatam pinge 1 pro primâ figurâ quoti; per hanc multiplica divi4) 56 (14 4 16 16 00 divisorem 4,productum, qui etiam est 4,sub 5 collocatum, ex eâ subtrahe,& ad residuum 1 transfer proximā figuram dividendi 6, ut novum jam habeas dividendum 16,de quo quæres quoties in eo continetur divisor; at quoniam quater in eo continetur, hinc post 1 in quoto scribe 4, quem duc in divisorem, & productum 16 subscriptum subduc ex 16,& nihil supererit. Ergò divisor 4 continetur in dividendo 56 quater decies.
units.tr: 1. E.g. Let the divisor be 4 and the dividend 56. First ask how many times the divisor 4 is contained in the first figure of the dividend, which is 5. Since it is contained once in it, put a dot under the 5 and write 1 in the half-bracket set aside for the quotient, as the first figure of the quotient. Multiply the divisor 4 by this; the product is 4, which you place under the 5 and subtract from it. Carry down the next figure of the dividend, 6, to the remainder 1, so that you now have the new dividend 16. Ask how many times the divisor is contained in it: since it is contained four times, write 4 after the 1 in the quotient, multiply it by the divisor, and subtract the product 16, written underneath, from 16. Nothing is left over. So the divisor 4 is contained in the dividend 56 fourteen times.

units.la: 2. Aliud exemplum. Sit divisor 6,dividendus 348243. Hìc primò quaere quoties 6 continetur in primâ figurâ dividendi 3 ? nec semel : punctum ergò subjice secundæ figuræ 4. Quoties ergò continetur 6 in 34 ? quinquies : quoto 6) 348243 (58040 30 48 48 0024 24 003 igitur inscribe 5, at 5 in 6 facit 30, quo è 34 subducto restat 4, ad quem proximâ figurâ 8, puncto priùs subjecto, translatâ, quærequoties 6 continetur in 48? respondetur octies; at 8 in 6 producit 48, quo ex 48 subducto restat oo, sive nihil, ad quod transfer 2 proximam figuram dividendi; at 6 nec semel in 2 continetur, post 8 itaque in quoto pinge o, & ad dictam figuram 2 transfer proximam dividendi 4, ut fiat 24, in quo 6 continetur quater, quoto igitur adjice 4, & duc 4 in 6, & productum 24 subtrahe ex 24, & ad residuum oo transfer ultimam figuram dividendi 3, in quâ divisor 6 nec semel continetur, ergo quoto adde cifram. Igitur numero 348243 per 6 diviso quotus est 58040, & residuum 3. Adeò ut si ultima figura dividendi fuisset 6, quotus esset 58041, nunc autem est tantum 58040 1/2.
units.tr: 2. Another example. Let the divisor be 6 and the dividend 348243. Here first ask how many times 6 is contained in the first figure of the dividend, 3. Not even once; so put a dot under the second figure, 4. How many times, then, is 6 contained in 34? Five times. Write 5 in the quotient. Now 5 times 6 makes 30, which subtracted from 34 leaves 4. To this carry down the next figure, 8, which was marked with a dot earlier, and ask how many times 6 is contained in 48. The answer is eight times. Eight times 6 makes 48, which subtracted from 48 leaves 0, or nothing. To this 0 carry down the next figure of the dividend, 2. But 6 is not contained even once in 2; so after the 8 in the quotient write 0, and carry down to the figure 2 the next figure of the dividend, 4, to make 24. In 24, 6 is contained four times, so add 4 to the quotient; multiply 4 by 6, and subtract the product 24 from 24. Carry down to the remainder 0 the last figure of the dividend, 3. The divisor 6 is not contained even once in it, so add a zero to the quotient. Thus when 348243 is divided by 6 the quotient is 58040, and the remainder 3. So if the last figure of the dividend had been 6, the quotient would have been 58041; as it is, the quotient is only 58040 and a half.

units.la: 3. Tota hæc operatio hoc versiculo continetur:
units.tr: 3. The whole of this operation is contained in this verse:

units.la: Dic quot, multiplica, subduc, transferque secandum. i. e. Dic quoties divisor continetur in dividendo, deinde per numerum quæstioni isti respondentem & in quoto positum multiplica divisorem, productum subduc è figurâ vel figuris divisis, & ad residuum transfer secandi sive dividendi proximam figuram.
units.tr: Dic quot, multiplica, subduc, transferque secandum. That is: say how many times the divisor is contained in the dividend; then multiply the divisor by the number that answers the question and is placed in the quotient; subtract the product from the figure or figures divided; and carry down to the remainder the next figure of the dividend.

units.la: XI. 2. Si divisor ex duabus pluribusve figuris constiterit, videsis quoties omnes ista continentur in totidem primis ad sinistram dividendi, altera etiam assumpta, si totidem primæ minores sint divisore. Quotcunque autem figuras seliges primò dividendas, ultimæ earum punctum subjicies: deinde quæres quoties divisor totus in figuris dividendi usque ad puncto notatam inclusive continetur, numerum quæstioni respondentem in quoto describes, per quem etiam omnes divisoris notas multiplices, & productum ex dictis figuris subtrahas, residuo autem proximam figuram dividendi, puncto etiam ab aliis distinctam adjicies, & summâ pro novo dividendo habitâ procedes ut antea traditum est.
units.tr: XI. 2. If the divisor consists of two or more figures, see how many times all of them are contained in as many of the first figures of the dividend on the left, taking one more also if those first figures are smaller than the divisor. Whatever number of figures you select as the first to be divided, put a dot under the last of them. Then ask how many times the whole divisor is contained in the figures of the dividend up to and including the one marked with a dot. Write the number answering this question in the quotient, multiply all the figures of the divisor by it, and subtract the product from the said figures. To the remainder add the next figure of the dividend, likewise set off from the others by a dot, and take the sum as the new dividend, proceeding as has been taught above.

units.la: 1. Ex. gr. Sit divisor 42, dividendus 460: quandoquidem ambæ figuræ divisoris continentur in duabus pri42) 460 (10 42 40
units.tr: 1. E.g. Let the divisor be 42 and the dividend 460. Since both figures of the divisor are contained in the first two figures of the dividend,

units.la: mis dividendi, sub secundâ 6 punctum colloca: deinde quære quoties 42 continetur in 46? respondetur semel; post lunulam itaque quoto designatam scribe 1, quæ in divisorem ducta producit eundem, viz. 42, quo è 46 subtracto superest 4, cui transfer proximam dividendi notam 0, ut fiat 40; in quo numero cùm nec semel continetur 42, quoto adjice 0: Ergò 460 per 42 diviso quotus est 10, & residuum 40.
units.tr: put a dot under the second figure, 6. Then ask how many times 42 is contained in 46. The answer is once. So write 1 after the bracket marked for the quotient; multiplied by the divisor it gives the same, namely 42, which subtracted from 46 leaves 4. To this carry down the next figure of the dividend, 0, to make 40. Since 42 is not contained even once in 40, add 0 to the quotient. Thus when 460 is divided by 42 the quotient is 10, and the remainder 40.

units.la: 2. Priusquàm alterum proferam exemplum, lectorem hæc tria præmonitum vellem. 1.In quoto plusquam unicam figuram simùl scribere nunquam licebit. 2.Talis nota in quotiente perpetuò scribenda est, per quam divisor multiplicatus à suprapositis dividendi figuris subduci queat,& residuum vel nullum fit, vel divisore minus. 3.Si quid peracta divisione supererit,residuum istud supra divisorem lineâ interpositâ scribendum est ut fiat fractio.
units.tr: 2. Before I give another example, I want the reader to be warned of three things. First, only one figure may ever be written in the quotient at a time. Second, such a figure must always be written so that the divisor multiplied by it can be subtracted from the figures of the dividend above it, and the remainder is either nothing or less than the divisor. Third, if anything is left over when the division is finished, that remainder must be written above the divisor, with a line drawn between them, to make a fraction.

units.la: 3. Aliud exemplum. Annus quilibet Nabonasareus dies colligit præcisè 365: videamus quot anni, sive quoties dies 365) 2630410 (7206 2555 754 730 2410 2190 220 365 365 continentur in 2630410, praxis sic administratur. Divisor 365 in tribus primis dividendi figuris nec semel continetur; assumenda igitur etiam quarta, & quære quoties divisor 365 continetur in 2630, puncto priùs ultimæ figuræ o subscripto. Hoc ut invenias, hâc utaris methodo: Primò, vide quoties prima figura divisionis 3 continetur in duabus primis dividendi, quæ sunt 265; in iis autem continetur octies, nam 3 in 8 facit 24, & restat 2 ad complementum 26, hæc nota 2 cum proximâ dividendi 3 facit 23; videsis itaque num proxima figura divisoris 6 octies etiam continetur in 23, at toties non continetur, ergò proximè minor numerus pro quoto sumendus est, viz. 7; at 3 continetur in 26 septies, & superest 5, quæ cum proximâ figurâ dividendi 3 facit 53, in quo etiam 6 continetur septies, & restat 11, cui adde ultimam primæ hujus dividendi partis notam, quæ est 0, & fiet 110; in quo numero ultima figura divisoris 5 scpties etiam continetur. Cùm pro comperto igitur habeas 365 septies contineri in 2630, in quoto scribe 7, qui in 365 ductus gignit 2555, quo ex 2630 subducto residuum est 75, ad quod transferes proximam dividendi notam 4, ut proximus dividendus sit 754, in quo 365 continetur bis; quoto igitur adjice 2, at 2 in 365 ductus producit 730, quo ex 754 subtracto restat 24, cui adde proximam dividendi figuram 1, & fiet 241, in quo 365 nec semel continetur; quoto igitur adjice cifram, & ad 241 transfer ultimam figuram dividendi, quæ est 0, & ultimus exurget dividendus 2410, in quo divisor continetur sexies, quoto igitur adde 6; at 6 in 365 producit 2190, quo è 2410 dempto, residuum est 220, minus ut necesse est divisore In diebus igitur 2630410 continentur anni Nabonaʼarei 7206 , h. e. anni completi 7206, & dies præterea 220.
units.tr: 3. Another example. Each Nabonassarean year gathers exactly 365 days. Let us see how many years, or how many times 365, are contained in 2630410. The procedure is carried out as follows. The divisor 365 is not contained even once in the first three figures of the dividend, so take also the fourth, and ask how many times the divisor 365 is contained in 2630, with a dot placed under the last figure, 0. To find this, use this method. First, see how many times the first figure of the divisor, 3, is contained in the first two figures of the dividend, which are 26. It is contained in them eight times, for 3 times 8 makes 24, leaving 2 to make up 26. This remainder 2 together with the next figure of the dividend, 3, makes 23. Now see whether the next figure of the divisor, 6, is also contained eight times in 23. It is not, so the next smaller number, namely 7, must be taken for the quotient. But 3 is contained seven times in 26, leaving 5, which with the next figure of the dividend, 3, makes 53. In 53, 6 is also contained seven times, leaving 11, to which add the last figure of this part of the dividend, 0, and it becomes 110. In 110 the last figure of the divisor, 5, is also contained seven times. Since you have now found that 365 is contained seven times in 2630, write 7 in the quotient. Multiplied by 365 it gives 2555, which subtracted from 2630 leaves 75. To this carry down the next figure of the dividend, 4, so that the next dividend is 754, in which 365 is contained twice. Add 2 to the quotient; 2 times 365 gives 730, which subtracted from 754 leaves 24. To this add the next figure of the dividend, 1, making 241, in which 365 is not contained even once. So add a zero to the quotient and carry down to 241 the last figure of the dividend, 0. Then the last dividend appears, 2410, in which the divisor is contained six times. Add 6 to the quotient; 6 times 365 gives 2190, which subtracted from 2410 leaves 220, less than the divisor, as it must be. So in 2630410 days there are 7206 Nabonassarean years, that is, 7206 complete years, and 220 days over.

units.la: XII. Si divisor ex unitate, & cifrâ sive cifris tantùm constiterit, tot figuræ ex dividendo rejiciantur quot sunt cifræ in divisore, & perficietur divisio.
units.tr: XII. If the divisor consists of a unit followed by a cipher or ciphers only, cut off from the dividend as many figures as there are ciphers in the divisor, and the division is complete.

units.la: 1. Ut
units.tr: 1. For example

units.la: I. Ut sit 10 divisor 246 dividendus, è quo abjice 6, & quotus relinquetur 24, & abjectâ figurâ 6 pro residuo habeatur.
units.tr: I. Let the divisor be 10 and the dividend 246. Cut off the 6 from the dividend; the quotient will be 24, and the cut-off figure 6 is taken as the remainder.

units.la: XIII. 4. Si divisor unam vel plures ad dextram habeat cifras, tamistæ quàm totidem ad dextram dividendi figuræ abscindantur, & per reliquas institutur operatio, peractâ autem divisione abscissas dividendi figuras residuo apponas.
units.tr: XIII. 4. If the divisor has one or more ciphers at its right, cut off from the right of the dividend as many figures as there are ciphers in the divisor, and carry out the operation with the remaining figures. When the division is finished, attach the cut-off figures of the dividend to the remainder.

units.la: 1. Ut sit divisor 3200, dividendus 8 1660. Primò duas divisoris cifras à figuris significativis commate secernas, ut 32,00) 865,60 (27 64 225 224 160
units.tr: 1. For example, let the divisor be 3200 and the dividend 86560. First separate the two ciphers of the divisor from its significant figures with a comma, thus: 32,00) 865,60 (27 64 225 224 160

units.la: & duas ad dextram dividendi figuras, viz 60, deinde reliquas dividendi, quæ sunt 865, divide per reliquas divisoris 325 at 865 per 3 divisio quotus est 27, residuum 1, cui adde abscissas dividendi figuras, & fiet 160, ut totus quotus sit 27 160.
units.tr: and the two figures at the right of the dividend, namely 60. Then divide the remaining figures of the dividend, which are 865, by the remaining figures of the divisor, 32. 865 divided by 32 gives the quotient 27 with remainder 1, to which add the cut-off figures of the dividend, and it becomes 160. So the whole quotient is 27 160.

units.la: XIV. Si numeri dati sint ambo diversarum specierum, primò reducantur in minimam speciem, & deinde juxtà præcedentes regulas dividantur.
units.tr: XIV. If the given numbers are both of different kinds, first reduce them to the smallest kind, and then divide them according to the preceding rules.

units.la: 1. Ut detur annus Julianus colligens d 365. h.6. o'. o'', dividendus per mensem lunarem sive per d.29. h.12. 44'. 3''. Hic cùm scrupula etiam secunda colligantur, ambo numeri in istam speciem per regulas capite sequenti traditas reducantur. At in mense lunari scrupula secunda sunt 2551443, in anno Juliano 31557600, quibus per ista divisis quotus est 12, & residua sunt scrupula secunda quæ in reliquas species reducta faciunt d. 10. h. 21. 11′. 24′′′ In anno igitur Juliano duodecim menses lunares continentur, & præterea d. 10. h. 21. 11′. 24′′.
units.tr: 1. For example, let the Julian year of 365 d. 6 h. 0' 0'' be given, to be divided by the lunar month of 29 d. 12 h. 44' 3''. Since the seconds are also included here, both numbers are reduced to this kind by the rules given in the following chapter. In a lunar month there are 2551443 seconds, and in the Julian year 31557600. Dividing these, the quotient is 12, and the remaining seconds, reduced to the other kinds, make 10 d. 21 h. 11' 24'''. So in the Julian year twelve lunar months are contained, and besides, 10 d. 21 h. 11' 24''.

units.la: XV. Divisio probatur per Multiplicationem; nam si ducas quotum in divisorem, & producto adjicias residuum, summa erit ipse dividendus, si divisio recte peracta sit.
units.tr: Division is proved by multiplication. For if you multiply the quotient by the divisor and add the remainder to the product, the sum will be the dividend itself, provided the division has been correctly performed.

units.la: I. Ut in exemplo supra posito, numerus 460 per 42 divisus in quoto dedit 10, in residuo 40; duc ergo quotum 10 in divisorem 42, & producto 420 cum adjeceris residuum 40, summa erit ipse dividendus 460. Recte igitur divisum est.
units.tr: 1. For example, in the example given above, the number 460 divided by 42 gave 10 as the quotient and 40 as the remainder. Multiply the quotient 10 by the divisor 42, and when you add the remainder 40 to the product 420, the sum is the dividend itself, 460. Therefore the division was correctly done.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAP. V.

units.la: De Reductione.
units.tr: On Reduction.

units.la: I. Hactenus de operationibus primis, sequuntur à primis ortæ.
units.tr: Thus far of the primary operations; there follow those arising from the primary ones.

units.la: II. Operationes à primis ortæ sunt Reductio, & Regula Proportionum.
units.tr: The operations arising from the primary ones are reduction and the rule of proportions.

units.la: I. HAs operationes Arithmeticas à primis ortas propterea nuncupamus, quòd à primis inter se variè compositis oriuntur. Sunt autem & aliæ quam quæ hic recensentur à primis ortæ, quas ut chronologo non necessarias consultò prætermittimus.
units.tr: I. We call these arithmetical operations "arising from the primary ones" because they arise from the primary operations variously combined with one another. There are, however, other operations arising from the primary ones besides those listed here, which we deliberately pass over as not necessary for the chronologer.

units.la: III. Reductio est vel Descendens, vel Ascendens.
units.tr: Reduction is either descending or ascending.

units.la: IV. Reductio descendens est quâ numerus majoris denominationis in alium minoris denominationis (sed ejusdem quantitatis) reducitur.
units.tr: Descending reduction is that by which a number of a larger denomination is reduced to another of a smaller denomination, but of the same quantity.

units.la: 1. Ut si dies reducendi sint in horas, horæ in scrupula prima, prima in secunda, &c,
units.tr: 1. For example, when days are to be reduced into hours, hours into first minutes, first minutes into seconds, and so on.

units.la: V. Reductio descendens perficitur multiplicando numerum datum in talem numerum proximae minoris denominationis qui æqualis sit unitati in numero dato. Nam productus est numerus minoris denominationis quæsitus.
units.tr: Descending reduction is performed by multiplying the given number by that number of the next smaller denomination which equals one unit of the given number. For the product is the number of the smaller denomination sought.

units.la: Ut dentur dies 365 reducendi in horas ; horæ 24 æquales sunt uni diei: duc ergò 24 in 365, & productus 8760 est summa horarum quæsita, sive quæ in diebus 365 continentur. 60 prima æqualia sunt uni horæ: duc ergò 60 in 8760, & fiet 525600 summa scrupulorum primorum, quam si ducas itidem in 60, (quoniam 60 secunda æqualia sunt uni primo) productus 31536000 est numerus secundorum quæ in datis diebus 365 continentur.
units.tr: Let 365 days be given to be reduced into hours. Since 24 hours equal one day, multiply 24 by 365; the product, 8760, is the sum of hours sought, that is, the hours contained in 365 days. Since 60 first minutes equal one hour, multiply 60 by 8760; this gives 525600, the sum of first minutes. If you multiply this likewise by 60 (since 60 seconds equal one first minute), the product, 31536000, is the number of seconds contained in the given 365 days.

units.la: VI Stipse numerus datus sit diversarum specierum, post quamlibet multiplicationem similes species datas similibus adjicies.
units.tr: If the given number is of various species, after any multiplication you will add the given like species to like.

units.la: Ut Annus Tropicus est d 365. h. 5. 49'. si prima in eo contenta desideres, duc 365 in 24, horis 8760 productis adjice 5 datas, summam 8765 duc in 60, & producto 525900 adjunge scrupula 49 data, & summa scrupulorum quæsita exurget 525949.
units.tr: For example, the tropical year is d 365 h. 5 49'. If you want the first minutes contained in it, multiply 365 by 24; to the 8760 hours produced add the 5 given hours; multiply the sum, 8765, by 60, and to the product, 525900, add the 49 given scruples. The sum of scruples sought comes to 525949.

units.la: VII. Reductio Ascendens est, quâ numerus minoris denominationis ad alium majoris denominationis, sed ejusdem quantitatis reducitur.
units.tr: Ascending reduction is that by which a number of a smaller denomination is reduced to another of a larger denomination, but of the same quantity.

units.la: VIII. Hæc fit per divisionem. Nam si dividas numerum minoris denominationis datum per talem numerum ejusdem denominationis, qui unitatem proximè majoris æquat, quotus erit numerus majoris denominationis quæsitus.
units.tr: This is done by division. For if you divide the given number of the smaller denomination by that number of the same denomination which equals one unit of the next larger denomination, the quotient will be the number of the larger denomination sought.

units.la: 1. Ut dentur secunda 31536000 in prima, horas, & dies reducenda, primò divide secunda data per 60, (quoniam 60 secunda unum primum, quæ proximè major est denominatio, æquant) & quotus dabit 525600 prima in iis contenta, quæ si dividas itidem per 60, (quot prima in unâ horâ continentur) quotiens dabit horas 8760. At in uno die colliguntur horæ 24. Ergò divide 8760 per 24, quotus 365 erit numerus dierum qui in iis continentur, ubi videsut idem numerus sursùm & deorsùm reducatur.
units.tr: 1. For example, if the seconds 31536000 are to be reduced into first minutes, hours and days: first divide the given seconds by 60 (since 60 seconds make one first minute, the next larger denomination). The quotient gives 525600 first minutes contained in them. If you divide these likewise by 60 (the number of first minutes in one hour), the quotient gives 8760 hours. But 24 hours make up one day, so divide 8760 by 24. The quotient, 365, is the number of days contained in them. Here it is seen that the same number is reduced both upwards and downwards.

units.la: IX. Si quid post divisionem supererit, ejusdem erit denominationis atque dividendus.
units.tr: If anything remains after division, it will be of the same denomination as the dividend.

units.la: I. Ut dentur 525949 primæ in dies, horas, & scrupula reducenda. Hunc numerum si dividas per 60, quotus erit 8765, residuum 49; ergò præter completos dies ac horas, scrupula 49 ejusdem denominationis ac dividendus in iis continentur, viz. prima. Hunc quotum 8765 si dividas per 24, quotus erit 365, residuum 5; at quoniam divisor 24 est numerus horarum unius diei, & horæ per eum dividuntur, hinc quotus 365 dies, residuum 5, horas designat. Ergò in 525949 primis d 365 h.5. 49'. continentur.
units.tr: I. For example, let 525949 first minutes be reduced into days, hours and scruples. If you divide this number by 60, the quotient will be 8765 and the remainder 49. Therefore, besides the complete hours and days, 49 scruples of the same denomination as the dividend, namely first minutes, are contained in them. If you divide this quotient, 8765, by 24, the quotient will be 365 and the remainder 5. But since the divisor 24 is the number of hours in one day, and hours are divided by it, the quotient 365 denotes days and the remainder 5 denotes hours. Therefore 525949 first minutes contain d 365 h. 5 49'.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: De Regulâ Proportionum.
units.tr: On the Rule of Proportions.

units.la: I. Regula Proportionum est quâ datis tribus numeris quartus proportionalis invenitur.
units.tr: I. The Rule of Proportions is that by which, given three numbers, a fourth proportional is found.

units.la: II. HÆc regula tria sortita est nomina; nam à formâ vocatur Regula Proportionum, à materiâ Regula Trium, à præstantiâ verò Aurea nuncupatur.
units.tr: II. This rule has three names. From its form it is called the Rule of Proportions, from its matter the Rule of Three, and from its excellence it is called the Golden rule.

units.la: II. Regula Proportionum est vel Directa, vel Inversa.
units.tr: II. The Rule of Proportions is either Direct or Inverse.

units.la: III. Regula directa est quâ ut primus se habet ad tertium, itâ secundus ad quartum quæsitum.
units.tr: III. The direct rule is that by which, as the first is to the third, so the second is to the fourth, which is sought.

units.la: Ex.gr. Annis Julianis 4 æquinoctia retrocedunt scrupulis 44; quot igitur scrupulis retrocedunt annis 8? Hic tres (uti vides) dantur numeri, & quartus quæritur ad quem secundus eandem habeat proportionem, quam primus ad tertium, viz. ut 4 est ad 8, sic 44 ad numerum quæsitum. Ubi notes etiam, quòd ut primus numerus est homogeneus tertio, sic & secundus quæsito: nam primus & tertius de annis est, secundus autem & quæsitus de scrupulis. Et quod unus etiam è datis annexam habeat quæstionem.
units.tr: For example. By the Julian years, the equinoxes move back 44 scruples in 4 years. How many scruples do they move back in 8 years? Here (as you see) three numbers are given, and a fourth is sought, to which the second has the same proportion as the first has to the third: namely, as 4 is to 8, so is 44 to the number sought. Note also that, as the first number is homogeneous with the third, so the second is with the sought number: for the first and third are of years, while the second and the sought number are of scruples. And that one of the given numbers carries with it the question.

units.la: IV. In hac regulâ duo observentur, Datorum collocatio, & Quæsiti inventio.
units.tr: IV. In this rule two things are to be observed: the arrangement of the given numbers, and the finding of the sought number.

units.la: V. Tres dati numeri sic collocandi sunt, ut qui quæstionem movet tertio loco ponatur, alter de eâdem re primo, reliquus autem (qui & homogeneus est quarto incognito) medium locum occupet.
units.tr: V. The three given numbers are to be arranged so that the one which raises the question is placed in the third position, the other of the same kind as it in the first position, and the remaining one (which is homogeneous with the unknown fourth) occupies the middle position.

units.la: 1. Ut in exemplo proposito, numerus 8 (ut annexam habens quæstionem) tertio loco collocetur; numerus 4 ei homogeneus, ut annos etiam significans, primo loco consistat, tertius 44 (qui de scrupulis est æquè ac quæsitus) medium possideat: hunc in modum, anni. scrup. anni. 4 44 8
units.tr: 1. As in the proposed example, the number 8 (which carries the question) is placed in the third position; the number 4, homogeneous with it as also signifying years, stands in the first position; the third, 44 (which is of scruples just like the sought number), takes the middle: in this way: years, scruples, years: 4, 44, 8.

units.la: VI. Datis sic dispositis, ut quæsitus inveniatur, duc secundum in tertium, & productum divide per primum, & quotus erit quartus quæsitus.
units.tr: VI. With the data so arranged that the sought number is found, multiply the second by the third, and divide the product by the first, and the quotient will be the fourth, which is sought.

units.la: Ut in exemplo proposito, duc secundum 44 in tertium 8, sive (quod idem est) duc 8 in 44, & productum 352 divide per primum 4, & quotus erit 88. Totam autem operationem sic instituas, anni. scrup. anni. 4 44 8 8 4) 352 (88 scrupula quæsita. 32 32 32 co
units.tr: As in the proposed example, multiply the second, 44, by the third, 8, or (what is the same) multiply 8 by 44, and divide the product, 352, by the first, 4, and the quotient will be 88. Set out the whole operation thus: years, scruples, years: 4, 44, 8; 8 into 4) 352 (88 scruples sought; with remainders 32, 32, 32.

units.la: Ergò si annis 4 æquinoctia retroaguntur scrupulis 44 annus 8 retrocedunt scrupulis 88.
units.tr: Therefore, if the equinoxes move back 44 scruples in 4 years, then in 8 years they move back 88 scruples.

units.la: Aliud exemplum.Helakim sive scrupula Chaldaica 1080 æqualia sunt communibus 60 primis, quot ergò communibus æquivalent Chaldaica 793 ? Operatio administratur 1080 · 60 793 60 108,o) 4758,o (44 432 438 432 60 60 108,o) 360,o (3 324 360 60 108,o) 2160,o (20 216 00000
units.tr: Another example. The Helakim, or Chaldean scruples, 1080, are equal to 60 common minutes. How many common minutes, then, are equivalent to 793 Chaldean scruples? The operation is carried out as follows: 1080 : 60 = 793 : x. 60 × 793 = 47580, divided by 1080 gives 44, remainder 420... [the division as printed is: 1080 into 4758 gives 4, then 432, and so on; the quotient is 44, with remainder 60 in the next place; then 60 × 60 divided by 1080 gives 3, and 60 × 360 divided by 1080 gives 20].

units.la: per repetitam proportionum regulam, hunc in modum. Primò, duc 60 in 793, & producto diviso per primum K k 1080
units.tr: by the repeated rule of proportions, in this way. First, multiply 60 by 793, and divide the product by the first term, 1080.

units.la: 1080 quotus est 44′, residuum 60″ quod ut quantum valeat dignoscas, reduc unitatem speciei in quoto designatæ in speciem proximè minorem, at quotus scrupula prima 44 exhibet, unum igitur scrupulum primum in speciem proximè minorem, hoc est, in scrupula secunda resolve; at 60 secunda unum primum exæquant. Si itaque Helakim 1080 æqualia sunt 60 secundis, quot secundis æquivalent Helakim hæc residua 60? Duc ergo 60 in 60, & productum 3600 divide per 1080, & quotus dabit 3 secunda, & residuum erit 360, quod si ducas itidem in 60 (quoniam unum secundum 60 tertia continet) & productum 21600 dividas per 1080, in quoto habebis 20 tertia præcisè. In scrupulis itaque Chaldaicis 793 continentur communia 44′. 3″. 20‴. Quæ exactè conveniunt cum iis quæ tradita sunt Institit. Chronol. l. 1. c. 3. p. 9.
units.tr: The quotient is 44 minutes, with a remainder of 60 seconds. To know how much this is worth, reduce the unit of the kind designated in the quotient to the next smaller kind: the quotient gives 44 first minutes, so one first minute is resolved into the next smaller kind, that is, into seconds; and 60 seconds equal one first minute. If therefore 1080 Helakim are equal to 60 seconds, how many seconds are equivalent to these remaining 60 Helakim? Multiply 60 by 60, and divide the product, 3600, by 1080; the quotient gives 3 seconds, and the remainder is 360. If you multiply this likewise by 60 (since one second contains 60 thirds) and divide the product, 21600, by 1080, you will have precisely 20 thirds in the quotient. Therefore 793 Chaldean scruples contain 44′ 3″ 20‴ of common units. These agree exactly with what was set out in the Institut. Chronol., book 1, chapter 3, p. 9.

units.la: VII. Ad examen huius regulæ duc quartum sive inventum numerum in primum, nam si productus sit numerus æqua- lis producto ex secundo in tertium rite processit operatio.
units.tr: VII. To test this rule, multiply the fourth number, or the one found, by the first. If the product is equal to the product of the second and third, the operation has been carried out correctly.

units.la: 1. Ut in primo exemplo, duc quartum 88 in primum 4, & productus erit 352; at idem producetur ex secundo 44 in tertium 8 ducto. Ergo proba fuit operatio.
units.tr: 1. As in the first example, multiply the fourth, 88, by the first, 4, and the product will be 352; but the same product is obtained by multiplying the second, 44, by the third, 8. Therefore the operation has been proved.

units.la: VIII. Regula proportionum inversa est, quâ ut primus è datis numeris se habet ad tertium, sic quartus quæsitus ad secundum.
units.tr: VIII. The inverse rule of proportions is that by which, as the first of the given numbers is to the third, so the fourth, which is sought, is to the second.

units.la: 1. Ut si 25 operarii opus aliquod absolvant diebus 16, quot diebus operarii 46 idem opus absolvant? Hic dici non potest, ut 25 ad 46, ita 16 ad numerum quæsitum, ut in regulâ directâ, sed ordine inverso; ut 25 ad 46, itâ numerus quæsitus ad 16: nam 25 est minor quàm 46, & 16 major quàm numerus quæsitus, cùm operarii 46 paucioribus diebus idem opus absolvant quàm 25.
units.tr: 1. For example: if 25 workmen finish some task in 16 days, in how many days will 46 workmen finish the same task? Here it cannot be said, as in the direct rule, that as 25 is to 46, so 16 is to the number sought; but the order is reversed: as 25 is to 46, so the number sought is to 16. For 25 is less than 46, and 16 is greater than the number sought, since 46 workmen finish the same task in fewer days than 25 workmen.

units.la: IX. Ad numerum per hanc regulam inveniendum duc primum
units.tr: IX. To find the number by this rule, first multiply

units.la: mum datum in secundum, & produstum divide per ter tium, & quotus erit numerus quæsitus.
units.tr: the first given number by the second, and divide the product by the third; the quotient will be the number sought.

units.la: 1. Ut in exemplo proposito, tres dati (ut in regulâ directâ) sic disponantur, 25 16 46
units.tr: 1. As in the example proposed, the three given numbers (as in the direct rule) are arranged thus: 25, 16, 46.

units.la: duc igitur primum 25 in secundum 16, & productum 400 divide per tertium 46, & quotus erit 8 2/46, quo residuo juxta priorem regulam in minores species reducto, totus quotiens erit d.8. h.16. 41'. Adeo ut si operarii 25 diebus 16 opus aliquid absolvant, idem absolvent operarii 46 d. 8. h.16. 41'.
units.tr: Therefore multiply the first, 25, by the second, 16, and divide the product, 400, by the third, 46. The quotient is 8 2/46, and when this remainder is reduced to smaller units by the earlier rule, the whole quotient is d.8 h.16 41'. So if 25 workmen would finish some work in 16 days, the same work will be finished by 46 workmen in d.8 h.16 41'.

units.la: 2. Hæc autem regula inversa rarioris si ullius est usus in Chronologiâ, ut & utraque regula proportionum composita, quas itaque unà cum radicibus, aliisque operationibus Arithmeticis (ut quibus Chronologo non opus est) missas confulto facimus.
units.tr: 2. This inverse rule, however, has rare if any use in chronology, and the same is true of the compound rule of proportions. We have therefore deliberately omitted these, together with roots and other arithmetical operations, since the chronologer has no need of them.

units.la: EXERCITATIO ARITHMETICA
units.tr: ARITHMETICAL EXERCISE

units.la: De minimo numero, quo per duos trésve divisores datos divisó, data fiant resi- dua, inveniendo.
units.tr: On finding the smallest number which, divided by two or three given divisors, leaves given residues.

units.la: QUandoquidem novas facillimásque annum Periodi Dianysianæ ex datis Solis & Lunæ, necnon Julianæ è Solis, Lunæ, ac Indictionis cyclis inveniendi methodos Instit.Chronol. l. 2. c. 8. & 9 traditas, nos demonstratas ibidem exhibere fidem dederimus;eam hic, quamvis non Geometricâ subtilitate,quantâ tamen possumus perspicuitate pariter ac brevitate exsolvere molimur: ídque in duobus hisce Problematibus, partim è Constructione, partim ex Euclidis Elementis, & partim denique è Sequentibus(ut itâ dicam) axiomatis demonstrandis. Cùm enim nova res hic agatur, quam nec Euclidis (ut opinor) Elementa sunt demonstrando, nos quatuor hæc tanquàm axiomata præmittere coacti sumus, ut è quibus inter alia problematum subsequentium demonstratio necessariò dependet.
units.tr: Since I have promised to demonstrate here the new and very easy methods of finding the year of the Dionysian period from the given cycles of the Sun and Moon, and of the Julian period from the cycles of the Sun, Moon and Indiction, which were set out in the Institutiones Chronologicae, book 2, chapters 8 and 9, I now undertake to work these out, not with geometrical subtlety but with as much clarity and brevity as I can. I shall do this in these two problems, partly from construction, partly from Euclid's Elements, and partly from the following axioms, as I may call them, which must first be demonstrated. For since a new matter is treated here, which (in my opinion) cannot be demonstrated from Euclid's Elements, I have been obliged to set down these four propositions as axioms, on which, among other things, the demonstration of the following problems necessarily depends.

units.la: AXIOMATA.
units.tr: AXIOMS.

units.la: I. Unitas numerum quemcunque multiplicans eundem producit,
units.tr: I. A unit multiplying any number produces that same number.

units.la: II. Si B per A diviso restet C, & si B dividatur per multi-plum A, etiam numero residuo per A diviso super-erit C.
units.tr: II. If B divided by A leaves C, and if B is divided by a multiple of A, then the residue, divided by A, will also leave C.

units.la: Ut 18 per 4 diviso restat 2; ergò si dividas 18 per 12, multiplicem divisoris 4, etiam residuo 6 per 4 diviso, idem fiet residuum 2.
units.tr: For example, 18 divided by 4 leaves 2; therefore if you divide 18 by 12, a multiple of the divisor 4, the residue 6 divided by 4 gives the same residue, 2.

units.la: III. Si minor aliquis numerus A majoris B partem aliquam vel partes metiatur, sed reliquam dividens residuum fe-cerit C, idem residuum facit & si totum dividat.
units.tr: III. If a smaller number A measures some part or parts of a larger number B, but dividing the remaining part yields the residue C, the same residue results if the whole is divided.

units.la: Ut in numero 18, 4 partem ejus 12 metitur; sed reliquam 6 dividens residuum facit 2; ergò & toto numero 18 per 4 diviso restat 2. Numeri 28 ex 9, 12, & 7 compositi, duas partes, viz. 9 & 12, metitur 3; at reliquâ parte 7 per 3 divisâ restat 1; idem ergò residuum 1 fiet, etsi 28 per 3 dividatur.
units.tr: For example, in the number 18, 4 measures the part 12 of it; but dividing the remaining 6 gives the residue 2; therefore when the whole number 18 is divided by 4, 2 also remains. The number 28, made up of 9, 12 and 7, is measured by 3 in two of its parts, namely 9 and 12; but when the remaining part 7 is divided by 3, 1 remains; therefore the same residue, 1, results even if 28 is divided by 3.

units.la: IV. Si C sit minimus numerus quem A & B metiuntur, unicus tantùm datur numerus minor (vel non major) quàm C, qui per A & B divisus, residua faciat G & H
units.tr: IV. If C is the least number which A and B both measure, there is only one number less than (or not greater than) C which, divided by A and B, gives the residues G and H.

units.la: Ut 6 minimus est, quem 2 & 3 metiuntur; ergò unicus tantùm est numerus minor quàm 6, putà 5, qui per 2 divisus relinquit 1, per 3 relinquit 2. Sic & nullus præter 4 per 2 relinquit 0, per 3 relinquit 1. Sic 532 (Periodus Dionysiana) minimus est, quem 28 & 19 metiuntur: Ergò unicus tantùm datur numerus, isque 326 minor quàm 532, qui per 28 divisus relinquit 18, per 19 residuum facit 3. Hinc est, quòd per totum hujus Periodi contextum idem cycli Solis & Lunæ nunquam recurrant. Valet hæc regula in tribus (vel pluribus) etiam numeris: ut in Periodo Julianâ ex 28, 19, & 15, in se ductis genitâ, cùm enim solidus eorum 7980 minimus sit quem hi tres 28, 19, & 15 metiuntur, unicus tantùm datur numerus minor quàm 7980, nempe 5646, qui per 28, 19, & 15 divisus, residua faciat 18, 3, & 6: & sic in reliquis.
units.tr: For example, 6 is the least number which 2 and 3 measure; therefore there is only one number less than 6, namely 5, which divided by 2 leaves 1 and divided by 3 leaves 2. Likewise, apart from 4 alone, no number leaves 0 when divided by 2 and 1 when divided by 3. So 532 (the Dionysian period) is the least number which 28 and 19 measure; therefore there is only one number less than 532, namely 326, which divided by 28 leaves 18 and divided by 19 leaves the residue 3. Hence it is that through the whole course of this period the cycles of the Sun and Moon never recur together. This rule holds also for three (or more) numbers, as in the Julian period, produced by multiplying 28, 19 and 15 together; for since their product 7980 is the least number which these three, 28, 19 and 15, measure, there is only one number less than 7980, namely 5646, which divided by 28, 19 and 15 leaves the residues 18, 3 and 6; and so on for the rest.
