units.la: Invenire numerum P minimum, quo per datos quoscunque A, B, inter se primos diviso, residua sunt data K, L. A | K | C 4 | 2 | 8 B | L | D 7 | 5 | 21 F | M | P 28 | 82 | 26
units.tr: To find the least number P which, when divided by any given numbers A and B (which are prime to each other), leaves the given remainders K and L. (Example: A = 4, K = 2, C = 8; B = 7, L = 5, D = 21; F = 28, M = 82, P = 26.)

units.la: Primò inveniatur D minimus multiplex numeri B talis, quo per A diviso superstit unitas, & inveniatur etiam C minimus numeri A multiplex talis, quo per B diviso restat unitas. Deinde multiplices residua tua data, K quidem (residuum ex A) in D multiplum B, & L (residuum ex B) in C multiplicem A; denique summam horum productorum ex K in D & L in C, divides per F ex A in B factum, & residuus fiet P, quo per A diviso supererit K, & per B diviso residuum erit L. Dico P esse numerum quaesitum.
units.tr: First, let D be the least multiple of B such that, when it is divided by A, a unit remains. Let C also be the least multiple of A such that, when it is divided by B, a unit remains. Next, multiply the remainder K (the remainder from A) by D, a multiple of B, and the remainder L (the remainder from B) by C, a multiple of A. Then divide the sum of these products, K times D plus L times C, by F, the product of A and B. The remainder will be P, which, when divided by A, leaves K, and when divided by B, leaves L. I say that P is the number sought.

units.la: Dem. Quod primò P per A diviso restat K, sic ostendo. D multiplex (a) numeri B per A divisus residuam facit (b) unitatem; Ergò unitate ex D demptâ residuus fit multiplex A: Ergò K in D ductus multiplicat multiplum A, & istam praeterea unitatem quae ex D per A diviso supererit. At multiplo A per A diviso (c) nihil superest; ergo K in D ducto, & per A diviso, iste tantùm numerus restat quem K in unitatem ductus gignit: at K in unitatem (d) facit K, ergò K in D ductus, & per A divisus residuum facit K.
units.tr: Proof. That P, when divided by A, leaves K, I show as follows. D, a multiple of B, leaves a unit when divided by A (a: construction; b: construction). So if the unit is taken away from D, what remains is a multiple of A. Therefore K times D gives a multiple of A, plus that extra unit which is left over from D when divided by A. But nothing remains when a multiple of A is divided by A (c: Euclid I.7, def. 5, roughly, by rule of thumb). So when K times D is divided by A, only the number that K times the unit produces remains. But K times the unit makes K (d: Axiom 1). Therefore K times D, divided by A, leaves K.

units.la: (a) Construct. (b) Construct. (c) Euclid. I.7. def.5. juxta clavum. (d) Ax.1.
units.tr: (a) Construction. (b) Construction. (c) Euclid I.7, def. 5, roughly, by rule of thumb. (d) Axiom 1.

units.la: Porrò A metitur (e) sui multiplum C ; at C metitur (f) L in C, ergò & (g) A metitur L in C. Ergò in M composito ex K in D & L in C, A unam istius partem (quæ est L in C) metitur, & alteram K in D dividens residuum facit K : Ergo & (h) toto composito M per A diviso restat K. Deni- que fi dividas M per F ex A in B genitum, eum divides per multiplicem A, ut (i) quem A metitur per B. Numerus itaque residuus P per A solùm divisus (k) idem refidu- um faciet quod ipse M ; at M ergo & P per A diviso. re- stat K.
units.tr: Furthermore, A measures its own multiple C; and C measures L times C; therefore A also measures L times C (e: Eucl. VII def. 5; f: ibid. ax. 7; g: ibid. ax. 11). So in M, which is composed of K times D and L times C, A measures one part of it (namely L times C), and when the other part, K times D, is divided by A, it leaves K. Therefore the whole composite M, when divided by A, also leaves K (h: Axiom 3). Next, if you divide M by F, the product of A and B, and then divide that quotient by the multiple of A that A measures by B (i: Eucl. VII ax. 7). Hence the remainder P, divided only by A, leaves the same remainder as M itself (k: Axiom 2; l: construction). But M, when divided by A, leaves K; therefore P, when divided by A, also leaves K.

units.la: Secundò, quòd P per B diviso restat L, eodem modo probatur. Nam ut D per A, sic C per B diviso (l) restat unitas : Ergo eâdem ratione quâ K in D per A restat K, etiam L in C per B diviso restat L. At (m) B metitur D, & D metitur (n) K in D, ergo & B metitur (o) K in D. Ergo in M ex L in C, & K in D composito, B unam istius partem, viz. K in D metitur ; at altera quæ est L in C per B divisâ restat L; ergo & (p) toto M per B diviso restat L. Et fi dividas M per F ex A in B factum, eum dividis per (q) multiplicem B : Ergo residuus P per B divisus (r) idem re- fiduum faciet quod totus M, at M, ergo & P per B diviso restat L.
units.tr: Second, that P, when divided by B, leaves L is proved in the same way. For as D, when divided by A, leaves a unit, so C, when divided by B, leaves a unit (m: construction). Therefore, by the same reasoning by which K times D leaves K when divided by A, L times C also leaves L when divided by B. But B measures D (m: construction), and D measures K times D (n: Eucl. VII ax. 7); therefore B also measures K times D (o: ibid. ax. 11). So in M, composed of L times C and K times D, B measures one part of it, namely K times D; and the other part, L times C, leaves L when divided by B. Therefore the whole M, when divided by B, leaves L (p: Axiom 3). And if you divide M by F, the product of A and B, then divide by the multiple of B (q: Eucl. VII ax. 7). Hence P, when divided by B, leaves the same remainder as the whole M does (r: Axiom 2). But M leaves L; therefore P, when divided by B, also leaves L.

units.la: Tertiò, quòd P minimus fit numerus qui per A, B divi- sus, hæc data faciat residua, sic probatur : F genitus ex A, B (s) minimus est quem A, B metiuntur. Ergo (t) unicus tantùm datur numerus minor quàm F, qui per A & B divisus residua faciat K & L. At P ut residuus minor est quàm F divisor ; Ergo minimus est, qui per datos divisores residua data faciat.
units.tr: Third, that P is the least number which, when divided by A and B, gives these data as remainders, is proved as follows. F, the product of A and B, is the least number that A and B measure (s: Eucl. VII prop. 36). Therefore there is only one number less than F which, when divided by A and B, leaves K and L (t: Axiom 4). But P, being a remainder, is less than the divisor F. Therefore P is the least number which, when divided by the given divisors, leaves the given remainders.

units.tr: Corollary.

units.la: Hinc patet quarè si cyclus Solis currens ducatur in 57,& cyclusLunæ in 476 productorū summa per 532 ex 28 in 19 factum divisa residuum faciet annum Periodi Dionysianæ datis cyclis præditum. Nam cycli 28 & 19 sunt inter se primi, & 57 est primus multiplex 19, quo per 28, & 476 minimus multiplex 28, quo per 19 diviso residua fit unitas. Quæ unitas utrobique relicta efficit, ut si cyclus Solis currens (putà 18) ducatur in 57,& cyclus Lunæ (putà 3) ducatur in 476, productorum summa 2454 per 532 divisa residuum faciet minimum quo per 28 diviso restat 18, & per 19 diviso restat 3, qui igitur annus est Periodi Dionysianæ in quem solùm dati cycli concurrunt.
units.tr: Hence it is evident why: if the current cycle of the Sun is multiplied by 57 and the cycle of the Moon by 476, and the sum of the products is divided by 532 (the product of 28 and 19), the remainder gives the year of the Dionysian Period that has the given cycles. For the cycles 28 and 19 are mutually prime; 57 is the least multiple of 19 which, divided by 28, leaves a remainder of 1; and 476 is the least multiple of 28 which, divided by 19, leaves a remainder of 1. Since this unit is left over in each case, if the current cycle of the Sun (say 18) is multiplied by 57, and the cycle of the Moon (say 3) by 476, the sum of the products, 2454, divided by 532, leaves a remainder which is the least number that, divided by 28, leaves 18 and, divided by 19, leaves 3. This, therefore, is the year of the Dionysian Period in which only the given cycles concur.

units.la: PROBLEMA II.
units.tr: PROBLEM II.

units.la: Invenire numerum O minimum, quo diviso per datos M, B, A inter se omnimodò primos, residua sint data K,L,Z. M | B | A 9 | 7 | 4 K | L | Z 2 | 5 | 3 F | N | Q 28 | 36 | 189 R | X | O 103 | 252 | 47
units.tr: To find the smallest number O which, when divided by the given M, B, A (wholly prime to one another), leaves the given residues K, L, Z. M | B | A 9 | 7 | 4 K | L | Z 2 | 5 | 3 F | N | Q 28 | 36 | 189 R | X | O 103 | 252 | 47

units.la: Primò inveniatur F minimus multiplex A in B talis quo per M diviso superfit unitas; deinde inveniatur N primus sive minimus multiplex A in M talis, ut eo per B diviso restet unitas: denique inveniatur & ♉ minimus multiplex B in M talis, ut eo per A diviso restet etiam unitas: his inventis, K residuum datum ex M ducatur in F, L residuum ex B ducatur in N, & Z residuum ex A multiplicetur in ♉. Summa trium horum Productorum, quæ est R, dividatur per X solidum MBA, & residuus fiet O, quem dico quæsitum esse, sive minimum quod per MBA diviso residuu sunt data KLZ.
units.tr: First let F be found, the least multiple of A in B, such that when divided by M it leaves a unity. Then let N be found, the first or least multiple of A in M, such that when divided by B it leaves a unity. Finally let ♉ be found, the least multiple of B in M, such that when divided by A it also leaves a unity. These being found, let the residue K given from M be multiplied by F, the residue L from B be multiplied by N, and the residue Z from A be multiplied by ♉. Let the sum of these three products, which is R, be divided by X, the solid MBA, and the remainder will be O. I say that this O is the thing sought, that is, the smallest number which, when divided by MBA, leaves the given KLZ.

units.la: Dem. Quòd primò O per M diviso restat K, sic ostendo: F (a) multiplex A in B, (qui in exemplo hic allato est simplex tantum productus) per M divisus residuam facit (b) unitatem, quâ itaque ex F subductâ, residuus fit multiplex M. Ergo K in F ductus multiplicat multiplum M, & istam præterea unitatem. At multiplo M per M diviso (c) nihil restat. Ergo K in F per M diviso, residuus fit tantùm productus ex K in unitatem. At (d) K in unitatem facit K: Ergo K in F per M diviso restat K. Præterea (e) M metitur N, ut productum ex A in M; at N metitur (f) L in N; ergò & (g) M metitur L in N: At M metitur etiam ♉, ut (h) multiplum B in M; at ♉ metitur (i) Z in ♉: Ergò & (k) M metitur Z in ♉. Ergo in R summâ productorum horum ex K in F, L in N, & Z in ♉; M duas istius partes, sive L in N & Z in ♉, metitur: at reliqua, quæ est K in F per M divisâ restat K. Ergò & tota summa R ex tribus istis Productis composita per M divisa residuum facit K. Et si dividatur R per X solidum MBA, dividetur tantùm per (m) multiplum M; Ergò numerus residuus O (n) idem quod R per M divisus residuum faciet. At R, ergò & O, per M diviso restat K; quod erat demonstrandum.
units.tr: Proof. That O, when divided by M, leaves K, I show as follows. F (a), a multiple of A in B (which in the example here given is merely a simple product), when divided by M, leaves a remainder (b) of unity. Subtracting that unity from F, what remains is a multiple of M. Therefore K multiplied by F gives a multiple of M plus that unity multiplied by K. But when a multiple of M is divided by M, nothing remains (c). Therefore K times F, when divided by M, leaves only the product of K and unity. But (d) K times unity is K. Therefore K times F, when divided by M, leaves K. Furthermore, (e) M measures N, being the product of A and M; and N measures (f) L times N; therefore (g) M also measures L times N. Again, M measures ♉ too, being (h) a multiple of B in M; and ♉ measures (i) Z times ♉; therefore (k) M also measures Z times ♉. Therefore in R, the sum of these products, K times F, L times N, and Z times ♉, M measures two of its parts, namely L times N and Z times ♉, while the remaining part, K times F, leaves K when divided by M. Therefore the whole sum R, made up of these three products, when divided by M, leaves K. And if R is divided by X, the solid MBA, it is divided only by (m) a multiple of M; therefore the remainder O (n) will leave the same remainder on division by M as R does. But R, and therefore O, leaves K when divided by M; which was to be demonstrated.

units.tr: Book II.

units.la: Secundò, quòd idem numerus O per B divisus residuum facit L, & per A relinquit Z eodem modo probetur. Nam ut F ex A in B facto per M, sic N ex A in M per B, & Q ex B in M per A diviso (o) restat unitas; quo fit ut L in N per B diviso restet L, & Z in Q per A diviso superfit Z. Adeò ut in R summâ productorum ex K in F, L in N, & Z in Q; sic ut M duas istius partes, viz. L in N, & Z in Q, metitur; sed reliquam K in F dividens residuum facit K: sic B duas partes sui multiplices, viz. K in F & Z in Q, metitur; at L in N per B diviso restat L, & A duas etiam metitur, viz, K in F & L in N; at tertiam, quæ est Z in Q, dividens residuum facit Z. Et cùm tota summa R dividitur per MBA, per cujusque multiplum dividitur. Ergò O residuus per B & A divisus eadem faciet residua quæ R. At R, ergò & O per B divisus relinquit L, & per A residuum facit Z, quod etiam erat demonstrandum.
units.tr: Secondly, the same number O, divided by B, leaves L as its remainder, and divided by A it leaves Z; this is proved in the same way. For just as F, the product of A and B, divided by M, gives N as the product of A and M divided by B, and Q as the product of B and M divided by A, leaves unity; so L times N, divided by B, leaves L, and Z times Q, divided by A, leaves Z. Hence in R, the sum of the products K times F, L times N, and Z times Q, M measures two of its parts, namely L times N and Z times Q, but when the remaining part, K times F, is divided by M, the remainder is K. So B measures two of its multiples, namely K times F and Z times Q, but L times N, divided by B, leaves L, and A measures two as well, namely K times F and L times N, while the third part, Z times Q, divided by A, leaves Z. And since the whole sum R is divided by MBA, it is divided by each of its multiples. Therefore O, divided by B and A, will give the same remainders as R. But R, and therefore O divided by B, leaves L, and divided by A leaves Z, which was also to be demonstrated.

units.la: Quod autem hic minimus sit numerus qui per datos divisores residua data faciat, sic probo. X solidus MBA, (p) minimus est quem MBA metiuntur. Ergo (q) unicus est tantum numerus minor quàm X, qui per MBA divisus residua faciat KLZ. At O ut residuus ex divisore X minor est quàm X, ergo minimus.
units.tr: That this is the smallest number which gives the given remainders when divided by the given divisors, I prove as follows. X, the solid MBA, is the least number which M, B and A measure. Therefore there is only one number less than X which, divided by M, B and A, leaves the remainders K, L and Z. But O, as a residue from the divisor X, is less than X; therefore it is the least.

units.la: Corollarium.
units.tr: Corollary.

units.la: Hinc constat quare si cyclus Solis currens ducatur in 4845, Lunæ in 4200, & Indictio in 6916, productorum summa per 7980 divisa residuum faciet annum Periodi Julianæ in quem dati cycli concurrunt. Nam cyclus Solis 28, Lunæ 19, & Indictio 15, sunt numeri inter se omnimodò primi, tales nimirùm ut nec quosvis eorum duos communis aliqua mensura præter unitatem metiatur. At 4845 est multiplex numeri ex 19 in 15 producti, (nam 19 in 15 facit 285, quo in 17 ducto fit 4845) & quidem minimus, quo
units.tr: Hence it is clear why, if the current cycle of the Sun is taken as 4845, that of the Moon as 4200, and the Indiction as 6916, the sum of the products divided by 7980 leaves a remainder which gives the year of the Julian Period in which the given cycles coincide. For the cycle of the Sun, 28, the cycle of the Moon, 19, and the Indiction, 15, are numbers that are wholly prime to one another, that is, no common measure of any two of them measures anything except unity. But 4845 is a multiple of the product of 19 and 15 (for 19 times 15 makes 285, and 285 times 17 makes 4845), and indeed the least such multiple, which when divided by 28 leaves a remainder of unity. 4200 is the least multiple of 28 times 15, divided by 19, and 6916 is the least multiple of 28 times 19, divided by 15, each leaving unity.

units.la: (o) Construct. (p) Eucl. l. 7. prop. 38. (q) Ax. 4. quo per 28 diviso reliqua fit unitas, & 4200 est minimus multiplex 28 in 15 quo per 19,& 6916 minimus multiplex 28 in 19, quo per 15 diviso restat unitas. Ex qua unitate sic ubique relicta, sequitur ut si cycli currentes ducantur in hosce numeros, quisque viz in suum suprascriptum, summa productorum per 7980 solidum 28, 19, & 15 divisa residuum faciet numerum quo per 28, 19, & 15 diviso residui fiunt cycli currentes dati, qui proinde est ipse annus Periodi Julianæ quæsitus, ut in quem dati cycli conveniunt.
units.tr: (o) Construct. (p) Eucl. l. 7. prop. 38. (q) Ax. 4. From this unity, left over in this way everywhere, it follows that if the current cycles are multiplied by these numbers, each by its own number written above, the sum of the products divided by 7980, the solid of 28, 19 and 15, leaves a remainder. When that remainder is divided by 28, 19 and 15, the result is the current cycles given. This remainder is therefore the very year of the Julian Period that we sought, namely the year in which the given cycles coincide.
